units.goal: Get up and down the tree without ever being unclipped.

lessons.title: Stay clipped in from ground to ground
lessons.hook: You're halfway up the tree, reaching to hang the next stick, and your boot slips off the step. What happens in the next second depends on one thing, which is whether anything connects you to that tree. This lesson is about making sure the answer is always yes, from the first step off the ground to the last step back onto it.

sections.heading: Wear a harness, every sit
sections.text: This is the one rule every source agrees on. Six different hunters and outfits teach it, which makes it the strongest safety agreement we have. Every year hunters die, break legs, or end up paralyzed after falling from tree stands, and nearly all of those falls could have been stopped by a harness. Harnesses are cheap and sold everywhere, so there's no excuse to go without one. Next Step Outdoors points out that plenty of hunters with portable stands still climb with no harness at all. Don't be one of them, and never free-climb, which means climbing with nothing holding you to the tree.

sections.heading: Climb on a lineman's rope
sections.text: A lineman's rope, or lineman's belt, is a rope that loops around the trunk and clips to your harness at the waist, the way a utility worker climbs a pole. Put it around the tree before your first step, and slide it up as you climb so it stays above your waist. Then you can lean your weight back into it and have both hands free to hang sticks and the stand. If a stick kicks out or you slip, the rope catches you. Use one at least as long as your stick ropes so it fits any tree your sticks do, and carry a second rope so you can clip in above a limb before you unclip below it.

sections.heading: Switch ropes before you step
sections.text: The top of the climb is the tricky part, because that's where you trade one rope for another, and it's the moment you'd otherwise have nothing holding you. So attach your tether, the strap you'll hunt on, around the tree at about head or eye height before you step from the sticks onto the platform. Only then take off the lineman's rope. For that one step you're connected twice, and there's never a moment when nothing holds you. Coming down, do it in reverse and clip into the lower rope before you unhook the tether. Four sources teach this, and even the Hunting Public host admits he almost forgot the second tether himself.

sections.heading: Hunt with the tether high and tight
sections.text: Once the stand is locked in, hunt on the tree tether, cinched tight around the trunk and clipped to the back strap of your harness, not on the lineman's rope at your waist. The Kentucky Afield host puts it at head height, and Bow Only Outdoors puts it at eye level or higher. The reason is where a fall ends. With the tether high and tight, Bow Only Outdoors says you only drop a couple of feet and can climb straight back into the stand. With it low, you can end up hanging too far below the stand to get back in. A high tether also stays clear of your bow arm, so you can draw in any direction.

sections.heading: A lifeline takes the switch away
sections.text: A lifeline is a strong rope tied at the base of the tree and again at your hunting height. You clip into it on the ground, slide the clip up as you climb, and hunt without ever changing straps. Jeff Sturgis of Whitetail Habitat Solutions started putting them up when his boys began hunting, and he wishes he'd protected himself sooner. He puts one on every stand, including the ones his kids and hunting partners use.

lessons.tryThis: Before the season, in daylight and only a few feet off the ground, say the order out loud as you go. Lineman's rope on before the first step, tether on before the platform, lineman's rope off last. Then come down in reverse. Do it until the order feels automatic.
lessons.headsUp: Sources differ a little on lifelines. Jeff Sturgis puts one on every stand, while North American Whitetail says to consider one. Both agree that staying connected the whole way is the goal, and a lifeline is one clean way to get there.

check.q: You reach the top of your sticks. What do you attach before you step onto the platform?
check.a: Your tree tether, at about head or eye height. Take the lineman's rope off only after that.

check.q: Why hang the tether high and tight instead of low?
check.a: If you fall you only drop a couple of feet and can climb back in. A low tether can leave you hanging below the stand.

lessons.title: Hanging a stand you can trust
lessons.hook: Picture stepping onto a stand in the dark and feeling it slide an inch down the trunk. Nobody forgets that feeling. The good news is that a stand that holds solid comes from a few simple habits, and you can learn every one of them in your yard before the season.

sections.heading: Learn it low, at home
sections.text: Whatever you buy, practice setting it up and climbing into it low to the ground in your yard. Next Step Outdoors and the Hunting Public crew both teach this. You don't need to be 15 or 20 feet up to learn how your gear works. The Hunting Public host says his first time in a saddle was nerve-wracking and he didn't know what he was doing, and hang-on stands were the same when he started as a teenager. Once your system is down, either one gets very efficient, so don't let your first real climb be a hunt.

sections.heading: Check the straps, then lock them tight
sections.text: Straps and cables are what hold you up, and worn or rusted parts fail. The Kentucky Afield host tests the seat and checks every strap and cable before the season and before each climb. If a cable shows rust, buy a replacement, and know that many parts now carry an expiration date. Once the stand is on the tree, the Hunting Public crew adds a trick for any stand with cinch straps. Fold the platform up to take the weight off the straps, pull them tighter, then fold it back down. That cams it tight so it won't slip when you step on. Each of these tips comes from one source.

sections.heading: Step down onto the platform
sections.text: Where the stand sits compared with your sticks matters more than people think. Jeff Sturgis hangs the stand about 90 degrees around the trunk from the side his ladder or sticks go up, and says anywhere from about 70 to 120 degrees is fine. He runs the top of the sticks 1 to 2 feet above the platform, so you climb up and step down onto it without stretching. Never hang the stand on the opposite side of the tree and higher than the sticks, because then you have to stretch a leg around the trunk and push up to reach it. Next Step Outdoors adds a few habits of its own. The bottom stick goes at about knee height, every strap stays level so it bites the tree, and you set the platform while standing on the second-to-last step.

sections.heading: Pull your gear up after you're clipped in
sections.text: Don't climb with a heavy pack or your weapon. Tie a pull rope to the stand and raise them once you're strapped in, with a gun unloaded and a bow's arrow in the quiver. Your hands and balance stay free, and nothing snags on the sticks. The Kentucky Afield host ties the rope on the side away from the sticks, up high where he can reach it without leaning out. He ties the bow on with a simple knot to the cam, string clear, because he's had a clip fail and drop a bow to the ground. Once the bow is up, drop the rope away from your feet so it can't tangle you or the bow.

sections.heading: Stand flat on a hang-on
sections.text: A saddle platform is built to be pushed from the side, and its grooves grip your boot, so you can push off the edges to swing around the tree for a shot. A hang-on platform is not. If you push hard on one side it can kick out from under you, so stand flat on it. This comes from the Hunting Public crew alone.

lessons.tryThis: Hang your stand on a tree in the yard at knee height. Check every strap, cinch it using the fold-up trick, and step on and off it ten times with your harness and tether on. Then practice raising an empty bow case with the pull rope.
lessons.headsUp: Saddle hunters set things up differently. Jeff Sturgis wants the sticks 1 to 2 feet above a hang-on platform so you step down onto it. Next Step Outdoors, hunting from a saddle, sets the platform 10 to 18 inches above the top stick and steps up onto it. These are different systems, so follow the one that matches your gear.

check.q: Where should the top of your sticks be compared with a hang-on platform?
check.a: About 1 to 2 feet above it, with the stand roughly 90 degrees around the trunk, so you step down onto it.

check.q: Why tie the bow to the pull rope with a knot instead of the rope's clip?
check.a: Clips can fail. One host had a bow come loose and fall to the ground.

lessons.title: Climbers, and getting home safe
lessons.hook: A climbing stand lets you walk into the woods and go up almost any straight tree you like. That freedom comes with its own risks, and they start before you ever leave the ground. The same goes for the walk home in big country, where the danger isn't falling but getting lost.

sections.heading: Choose a healthy tree with tight bark
sections.text: The Kentucky Afield host picks a climbing tree that is alive and healthy, with full leaves, no dead branches, and bark that is firmly attached. It has to be small enough for your straps to go around it, but not so small that it's unsafe. Skip shaggy-bark hickory, sycamore, and any tree whose bark peels off in sheets. His reason is simple. A climber may only bite about an eighth of an inch into the tree, and if that bark slides off, you go with it.

sections.heading: Step in at the bottom
sections.text: Set the climber at the base of the tree where you can step into it right off the ground. On a slope, the uphill side makes that easier. Stepping in is the only moment you aren't tethered, so do it as close to the ground as you can. Keep the top and bottom sections connected to each other the whole climb. If they aren't and the bottom slips off your feet, it falls all the way to the ground and leaves you hanging from the top half.

sections.heading: Tether before you start up
sections.text: With a climber, the tether goes on before you climb, not at the top. The Kentucky Afield host runs a strap around the trunk, clips it with a screw-lock carabiner, and screws the gate shut, because a carabiner that pops open is the same as no tether. Leave the strap loose enough to slide up with you. Set your feet, press down to lock the platform, then lock the seat as you go, and keep moving the strap up as you climb.

sections.heading: Carry a compass in big woods
sections.text: In big timber with lots of elevation change, Jeff Sturgis carries a compass around his neck and doesn't rely only on his phone or GPS, because those die or lose battery. Learn to read a topo map, the kind that shows the hills and ridges. Match a point or ridge you can see to the map, take a heading, and walk it. That gives you a way out that doesn't depend on a battery. This is Sturgis's advice alone.

sections.heading: Leave the drone at home
sections.text: Don't use a drone to scout or hunt deer on public land. Derek Dixon, who studies deer with thermal drones on private land in southern Missouri, says it's illegal in his home state and banned on most public land, and you're likely to get caught and be in real trouble. Check your own state's laws first, because many ban it for hunting and some require a permit to fly any drone on public land. Dixon's research is about deer, not the law, so treat this as a reason to look up your rules rather than the final word on them.

lessons.tryThis: Walk your hunting woods and look at the bark on every tree you'd consider for a climber. Push on it with your thumb. If it flakes or peels, cross that tree off, and practice stepping into your climber at the base of a good one.

check.q: Why is a shaggy-bark hickory a bad tree for a climbing stand?
check.a: A climber may only bite about an eighth of an inch into the tree. If the bark peels off, you go with it.

check.q: Why keep the top and bottom of a climber connected while you climb?
check.a: If the bottom slips off your feet, it would fall to the ground and leave you hanging from the top section.

units.goal: What to bring, what to leave, and how to pick a stand or saddle.

lessons.title: Bring less, bring the right things
lessons.hook: Most new hunters walk in carrying far too much. The pack gets heavy, zippers rattle, something falls out of the tree, and the one thing you actually needed is buried at the bottom. The fix isn't a better pack. It's knowing what's worth bringing and leaving the rest in the truck.

sections.heading: Go in light
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis of Whitetail Habitat Solutions has hunted for about 41 years, and he says he brings less every year. For a stand he can walk or bike to, he skips the big backpack. A hand-warmer muff or small pouch holds the essentials, which for him are gloves and a face mask, a grunt tube, his phone, a rangefinder, binoculars, a spare release, a small flashlight, and maybe a meal bar, with spare batteries in his pockets. His reasoning is that everything you carry is a chance for noise, something to drop, one more thing to forget, and more time setting up. Less gear also takes away the temptation to use products at the wrong time and place. Keep in mind this is his early-season setup on his own ground with short walks, so a long walk-in changes the list.

sections.heading: Drink at the truck
sections.text: Instead of carrying water on a hot evening sit of 4 to 5 hours, Sturgis drinks plenty before he walks in. He's sat 5 to 6 hours in 100 degree heat in Kentucky this way. Less to carry means less noise. An all-day sit is different, because you need calories to stay alert, so bring a small bottle of water and high-calorie food like meal bars or a sandwich. Both tips come from Sturgis alone.

sections.heading: Use the dimmest light you can
sections.text: You'll need a light to get in and out in the dark, and both sources in this lesson agree white light spooks deer. Sturgis carries a small rechargeable flashlight with a very dim low mode, sometimes called a moonbeam setting, because a light that low barely spooks anything. He doesn't trust a red or green lens to hide it. Colorblind or not, he says, deer still see the light itself, the same way a red lens over the sun wouldn't stop it from burning your eyes. So treat any colored light as fully visible.

sections.heading: Two bow details that save a hunt
sections.text: Sturgis keeps a spare release clipped in his pouch, so if he drops his out of the tree or it stops working, the sit isn't over. The other detail is draw weight, which is how hard the bow is to pull back. A ground bowhunter who was a guest on Southern Outdoorsmen says not to overdo it. Pick a weight you can hold at full draw for about two minutes, because you may have to wait while a deer clears a tree. He says 50 to 55 pounds is enough for an arrow to pass through a deer at 30 to 40 yards, and that holding steady matters more than raw weight. Each of these comes from one hunter.

lessons.tryThis: Empty your hunting pack onto the floor. Put back only what fits in a small pouch or your pockets, using Sturgis's list as a guide, and add a spare release if you shoot a bow. See how much stays behind.
lessons.headsUp: Downwind Hunting, a listicle rather than a hunter speaking from experience, recommends a red or green filter on your headlamp. It says white light floods the rods in a deer's eye and can be seen far off, while red or green is far less visible and keeps your own night vision. Sturgis, who hunts, says deer still see colored light. Both agree white light is the problem, so a dim light is the safer bet.

check.q: Why does Jeff Sturgis skip the big backpack for a close stand?
check.a: Everything you carry is a chance for noise, something to drop or forget, and more setup time.

check.q: How do you pick a draw weight?
check.a: Pick one you can hold at full draw for about two minutes. Holding steady matters more than raw weight.

lessons.title: Dress so deer can't pick you out
lessons.hook: A deer glances up at your tree and something doesn't look right. Maybe it was the flash of a bare hand, or the swish of a jacket sleeve as you reached for your bow. Your clothes can hide you or give you away, and the difference comes down to a few choices you make before you leave the truck.

sections.heading: Cover your skin
sections.text: Deer pick out light, bare skin easily. When you bowhunt, wear gloves and a face mask or headnet, or use face paint, even in the early season, and put them on once you're settled. Jeff Sturgis wants his white hands covered, and a natural beard helps too. A ground bowhunter who was a guest on Southern Outdoorsmen carries a light leafy suit in his pack during early bow season and puts it on over plain camo once he's set up, so briars don't shred it on the walk in. With a rifle or muzzleloader you can skip the headnet, since deer are usually 100 yards or more away, but still wear gloves because your hands move when you raise the gun.

sections.heading: Quiet clothes and a harness that doesn't catch
sections.text: With a bow you have to move to draw, so wear clothing that won't rustle when you do. Yamaha Whitetail Diaries also says to check your harness and stand for anything that can clang against the stand. The Kentucky Afield host adds that you can wear a light jacket or shirt over the harness vest so the vest doesn't catch the bowstring on the draw. That also lets you layer more than fits under the vest. Just make sure the spot where the tether clips on stays easy to reach. Each of these tips comes from a single source.

sections.heading: Rubber knee boots
sections.text: Downwind Hunting recommends rubber knee boots over leather hunting boots. It says rubber doesn't soak up odor from your truck, house, or gas station, hoses clean, and leaves almost no ground scent, and that the boots cost about 30 to 40 dollars. That source is a listicle, not a hunter's own experience, so on its own it wouldn't carry much weight. The advice holds up because hunters say the same thing elsewhere. Diamond Archery wears rubber boots, and Jeff Sturgis wears clean knee-high boots with his pants tucked in.

sections.heading: When it's bitter cold, dress for it
sections.text: Sturgis's view is that when it's cold, there's no substitute for being warm. If you're warm you enjoy the hunt and stay on stand, and if you're not, you spend the whole sit shivering. For extreme cold he layers windproof outer layers, heavy merino base layers, a face mask, a knit cap, a hand-warmer muff, and battery-heated socks and a vest. He says to buy good warm clothes once, because they last decades. He mentions his sponsors' brands, but the lesson is the layering, and he gives no temperature where this kicks in.

lessons.tryThis: Put on your full hunting outfit with your harness, then draw your bow slowly in front of a mirror. Listen for rustling, watch whether the string touches the vest, and check that you can still reach the tether clip.

check.q: With a rifle, can you skip the gloves?
check.a: No. You can skip the headnet because deer are usually far off, but your hands still move to raise the gun.

check.q: Why wear a light jacket over your harness vest when bowhunting?
check.a: It keeps the vest from catching the bowstring on the draw. Keep the tether clip easy to reach.

lessons.title: Your first minutes in the tree
lessons.hook: You finally get to the top, strapped in and breathing hard, and there's a pile of gear on a rope below you. It's tempting to sit down and catch your breath. The trouble is that deer don't wait for you to get comfortable, so the first few minutes up there need a plan.

sections.heading: Get the bow ready first
sections.text: Bow Only Outdoors hangs the bow hanger before anything else, usually on his left side or on a limb right in front if there is one. He pulls the bow up and nocks an arrow before he finishes settling in. Then the pack goes on a hook out of the way of his draw, with his grunt call and rattling antlers within reach. His reason is that a deer can walk by while you're still setting up, so you want to be able to shoot as early as possible. This routine comes from him alone.

sections.heading: Hang it, don't hold it
sections.text: North American Whitetail screws a gear hook or bow hanger into the tree slightly above your head, and hangs the bow or gun there while you wait instead of holding it on your lap. It stays within reach and off your lap until a deer shows up. Downwind Hunting adds a scent reason, that body heat warms a stock or riser on your lap and raising a warm weapon sends scent toward the deer. That scent claim comes only from one unverified listicle, so treat it as a maybe.

sections.heading: Keep the pack small and low
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis doesn't hang a big backpack in the tree at all, because a big pack up there can look like another person. His answer is the small pouch or hand-warmer muff from the last lesson. If you do bring a pack, a saddle product demo from Deer and Deer Hunting shows one way to handle it. Once you're at height and done with the lineman's rope, cinch it around the tree and use it as a hanger to hold the pack low on either side, out of your shot. That comes from a product video, so it's one idea rather than a proven rule.

sections.heading: Know exactly how high you are
sections.text: Samko Trad Bow, who hunts with a traditional bow, uses a pull-up rope of known length to read his height. His is 21 feet from the carabiner to the loop. He also knows his stick setup reaches a maximum of 17 feet, so he can look at a tree from the ground and judge whether its cover is reachable. He marks his reach on the trunk and counts up from it to estimate heights. That way you pick trees and heights on purpose instead of guessing. This is one hunter's method.

lessons.tryThis: On your next sit, time yourself from the moment you're clipped in to the moment an arrow is nocked and the bow is on the hanger. Then try to cut that time on the next sit by doing the bow first.
lessons.headsUp: Hunters split on packs in the tree. Jeff Sturgis says a big pack can look like another person, while North American Whitetail hangs the backpack on a hook above your head, and Bow Only Outdoors and the saddle demo also hang a pack in the tree, out of the draw. Everyone hangs the bow or gun. A small pack or pouch sidesteps the argument.

check.q: You just reached your stand. What's the first thing you set up?
check.a: The bow hanger, then the bow with an arrow nocked, because a deer can show up while you're still settling in.

check.q: Why does Jeff Sturgis avoid hanging a big backpack in the tree?
check.a: A big pack up there can look like another person to a deer.

lessons.title: Saddle or hang-on stand
lessons.hook: Sooner or later every new hunter asks which to buy, a tree saddle or a hang-on stand. In a saddle your weight hangs from the tree and you stand on a small platform or steps, while a hang-on stand gives you a seat and a bigger platform. The honest answer is that both work, and the better one depends on how and where you hunt.

sections.heading: Why saddles suit hunters who move
sections.text: Three sources agree here, Mark Kenyon of MeatEater, the Hunting Public crew, and Next Step Outdoors. A saddle with light sticks and a small platform, or none at all, fits public land, hunters who move often, and anyone who wants a quiet walk in and a quiet climb. You carry a harness either way, so a saddle only adds a small platform that fits in a pack. There's no big metal stand to catch branches or bang against things, it's fast to hang and pull down, and one kit hunts almost any tree. The Hunting Public now hunt from a saddle about 90 percent of the time, and once spotted a buck from the tree, climbed down, and killed him on the ground. Next Step Outdoors lists the costs, which are a learning curve, more ropes and parts, and a high upfront price, though used gear helps.

sections.heading: All-day comfort
sections.text: For long sits, like Kenyon's 11 to 12 hour rut sits at a funnel or pinch point, he and the Hunting Public find a lightweight hang-on with a seat more comfortable. Sitting is natural, the platform is bigger, and you can hang your pack and eat. Take the saddle for a half-day strike. Neither is truly comfortable for 12 hours, so keep changing position and don't let the pressure sit in one place. If a saddle hurts, Next Step Outdoors says to adjust the tether and bridge until it fits your body before giving up on it.

sections.heading: Cold weather favors a hang-on
sections.text: Relentless Sportsman, who hunts Wisconsin in December and January, uses a hang-on in the cold. Bulky clothes and boots are hard to manage on a saddle's small platform 20 to 25 feet up in the wind. Sitting with your back to the tree is warmer and makes it much easier to stay still, while a saddle's discomfort makes you shift, and that movement can get you seen. He suggests a test. Sit still for 5 minutes, then stand still for 5 minutes, and notice the difference.

sections.heading: Pick one and get good with it
sections.text: Kenyon and Relentless Sportsman both say to pick the setup you trust and get very good with it instead of switching because of TV or marketing. Practice at home before the season by hanging your saddle or stand there, the way one MeatEater host tethers to a beam on his back patio. Shoot the odd angles you'll get in the tree, and rehearse the whole setup until you can do it quietly in the dark. Otherwise opening morning means clanking around, sweating, while the sun comes up.

lessons.tryThis: Write down how you'll hunt this season. Will you move a lot or sit the same spots, sit half days or all day, and hunt in bitter cold? Let those answers pick your setup, then practice it at home.
lessons.headsUp: Comfort is where people disagree. The Hunting Public and Kenyon find a hang-on more comfortable all day, and Relentless Sportsman prefers one in the cold. Next Step Outdoors does several all-day saddle sits every season and says his older father hunts from a saddle in heavy cold-weather layers. Fit seems to decide it, and nobody gives a temperature.

check.q: You hunt public land and like to move to where you're seeing deer. Saddle or hang-on?
check.a: A saddle. It's light, quiet, quick to hang and pull down, and one kit fits almost any tree.

check.q: Why does Relentless Sportsman prefer a hang-on in bitter cold?
check.a: Bulky clothes are hard to manage in a saddle, and sitting against the tree is warmer and easier to stay still.

units.goal: Practice, pick a spot, and only take shots you'll make.

lessons.title: Which deer, and how close
lessons.hook: A doe is feeding at 35 yards, and your heart is going so hard you can feel it in your ears. You've practiced at that distance in the yard. Should you shoot? Before you ever draw, the best hunters have already decided which deer they'll take and how close it has to be, and that decision is what this lesson is about.

sections.heading: Your first deer doesn't need antlers
sections.text: Informed Outdoors and Bowhunters United both tell new bowhunters not to hold out for a big buck. Set your goal on any legal deer you'd be happy with and excited about, a doe included, unless the landowner you hunt with has rules of their own. Hunting shows and social media make beginners wait for giants, and expectations that high get frustrating enough that people quit. Early success is what gets you hooked. One Bowhunters United host says being picky early was a mistake, and he was trying to shoot a doe the year he got his first buck. Get pickier after you've taken a few.

sections.heading: Close shots with a bow
sections.text: Three sources agree that bow shots should be close, and they pick setups where deer walk right by rather than ones where they see lots of deer far off. The Hunting Public crew want deer inside 20 yards, ideally 15 or less, and won't take 25 yards or more on a big buck. Across their archery kills the average shot was 16 yards. Mike Rex keeps every archery shot, crossbow included, to 30 yards or less, even across a wide-open field. Bowhunters United wait for a clean shot inside about 25 to 30 yards and say not to force one. Getting a deer that close is the hard part of bowhunting, and one of their hosts, who started at 11, took two years to kill his first bow deer.

sections.heading: Why distance matters so much
sections.text: Rex explains it with speed. Even a crossbow bolt going over 400 feet per second is about three times slower than the sound of the shot, which travels about 1,200 feet per second, so a deer can react before the arrow gets there. At 30 yards even a perfect shot can miss or wound, because you can't predict how far a deer will move, drop, or wheel. The Hunting Public say that inside 10 to 12 yards deer don't have time to react at all. They also note that a private-land hunter in a box blind over a food plot may need to practice 30 to 50 yard shots, because that's where feeding deer will be.

sections.heading: Let the bad angles walk
sections.text: Samko Trad Bow, who hunts with a traditional bow and caps his range at 20 yards, only releases when he's sure the arrow will go through both lungs. He passes on deer walking straight away and deer right under or nearly under his tree, because the steeper the angle down, the smaller the window to hit both lungs. A steep arrow tends to catch one lung and miss the other. A one-lung deer will very likely die, he says, but it can take two or three days and you probably won't find it. The one year he hunted from 24 feet up, he one-lunged four of the six deer he shot. He has let hundreds of deer walk, including some of the biggest he's seen.

lessons.tryThis: Before the season, write down your own rules. Which deer will you shoot, what is your longest bow shot, and which angles will you pass on? Keep the card in your pouch and read it when you sit down.
lessons.headsUp: The right max range depends on your weapon and setup. The Hunting Public say 20 yards, Rex says 30, and Bowhunters United say 25 to 30. Samko thinks no traditional bow hunter should shoot at 25 to 30 yards, though compound and crossbow shooters may go farther, and he's skeptical of 40 to 50.

check.q: Why is a 30 yard bow shot riskier than a 12 yard one, even if you aim perfectly?
check.a: The deer hears the shot before the arrow arrives and can move, drop, or wheel. Inside 10 to 12 yards it has no time to react.

check.q: A deer is standing almost straight under your tree. Should you shoot?
check.a: No. A steep angle tends to hit only one lung. Wait for a better angle.

lessons.title: Where to aim
lessons.hook: You've probably heard to aim behind the shoulder, halfway up. It sounds simple, but deer move when they hear the shot, and the vitals by the shoulder sit lower than you'd guess. The hunters here all steer away from that high middle hold, though they don't aim at exactly the same spot.

sections.heading: Deer drop at the shot
sections.text: The Hunting Public crew say most deer react to the sound of the shot by dropping their body to load their legs. Past 20 to 25 yards they can drop 6 to 10 inches or more. That turns a center hold into a miss or a high hit that doesn't kill. So they aim lower and farther forward than behind the shoulder, halfway up. Go straight up the front leg about a third of the way up the body, which puts you on the top of the heart. That hold goes through both lungs, the top of the heart, and major vessels, and it still hits the heart if the deer doesn't drop.

sections.heading: How they adjust for distance
sections.text: Inside about 17 to 18 yards, the Hunting Public aim dead on at that spot. Beyond 20 yards they aim low heart, and on an alert deer, like one that came in to rattling, they expect it to duck. Their example is a South Dakota buck at 23 yards. The hunter held his 20 yard pin just above the bottom of the body, the buck ducked into it, and the arrow hit just under halfway up, through the top of the heart. The buck ran 70 yards. A center hold would have hit the top of his back. This method comes from the Hunting Public alone.

sections.heading: Don't aim tight on the shoulder
sections.text: Jamie McKay aims a little farther back. He picks the center of the area from just behind the shoulder back to the last rib, because there's plenty of vital area there. The vitals near the shoulder sit low and taper down, and he says focusing on the shoulder has been a bad mistake for him. Like the Hunting Public, he's steering you away from a high hold in the middle of the body.

sections.heading: Aim for the lungs, not the small targets
sections.text: Samko Trad Bow aims for both lungs and nothing smaller. No frontal shots, and don't aim for the heart, spine, neck, or femoral artery, because he says nobody is good enough to hit small targets on purpose and live animals move unpredictably. He's extra careful on does and young bucks, which are wiry and react faster at the shot than mature bucks.

sections.heading: With a rifle, find a rest
sections.text: A ground hunter who was a guest on Southern Outdoorsmen takes a rest for a rifle shot any time he can get one. On the ground he stands up behind his tree and uses its side as the rest rather than shooting offhand, meaning standing with nothing to lean on. It steadies longer shots of 100 to 150 yards so you don't miss. This comes from one hunter.

lessons.tryThis: Look at a photo of a broadside deer and trace a line straight up the front leg. Find the spot a third of the way up, then the center of the area behind the shoulder to the last rib. Notice that neither one is halfway up the body.
lessons.headsUp: The aiming advice here doesn't fully agree. The Hunting Public aim low and forward at the top of the heart, Jamie McKay aims farther back behind the shoulder, and Samko Trad Bow says never to aim for the heart at all, though he shoots a traditional bow at 20 yards or less. What all three agree on is avoiding a high hold in the middle of the body.

check.q: Why can a center hold go high on a deer at 25 yards?
check.a: Deer drop their body at the sound of the shot, sometimes 6 to 10 inches or more past 20 to 25 yards.

check.q: You're on the ground with a rifle and a deer at 120 yards. What do you do before shooting?
check.a: Get a rest. Stand behind your tree and use its side to steady the gun.

lessons.title: Practice that carries into the woods
lessons.hook: Shooting a bullseye in the backyard feels great. Then a real deer walks in, you draw, it takes one step behind a branch, and your arms start to shake. Good practice gets you ready for that moment, not just for the target.

sections.heading: Practice most, and set a standard
sections.text: Yamaha Whitetail Diaries and the Hunting Public crew both call practice before the season the single most important thing in bowhunting. The Hunting Public give you a standard to meet. Hit a paper plate, about 6 to 8 inches across, every time at 15 to 20 yards, including from an elevated stand. If you can't, don't go, and don't take long shots. The host missed many deer as a kid until he practiced all summer under his uncle's rule, then made a perfect 20 yard shot on his first bow buck. Shooting a target is one skill, though, and being a good hunter in the stand is more to learn.

sections.heading: Fix your form and judge distance by eye
sections.text: Informed Outdoors suggests blind bale shooting before the season. You stand close to a bale target and shoot with your eyes closed, which lets you fix your form and bad habits like target panic. They also practice judging distance by eye instead of ranging every shot, because deer often give you a small window with no time for a rangefinder. New bowhunters tend to lean on the rangefinder too much. This comes from one source.

sections.heading: Shoot a 3D deer and hold at full draw
sections.text: Informed Outdoors also practices on a 3D target shaped like a deer, from different distances and angles. It has no bright dot, so you learn where to aim on a real body. They practice holding at full draw for 5 or 10 seconds or longer before shooting. In the field a deer often steps or turns after you draw, and letting down is too much movement, so you have to hold until it gives you a clear shot again. Tired muscles make an accurate shot much harder unless you've practiced it, and even experienced hunters sometimes draw too early out of excitement.

sections.heading: Practice from your knees if you hunt the ground
sections.text: If you bowhunt from the ground, the Southern Outdoorsmen guest says to practice from a seat and from your knees behind a tree, not only standing. Kneeling puts more of you on the ground, so your body sways far less at full draw than when you stand sideways to the target. This is one hunter's tip.

sections.heading: Practice in your real setup
sections.text: Shooting from the yard is not the same as shooting from your stand or saddle. Mark Kenyon of MeatEater and Relentless Sportsman both say to practice with the setup you'll actually hunt from. Hang it at home, shoot the odd angles you'll get in the tree, and rehearse the whole setup until you can do it quietly in the dark. Confidence in your system, they say, is the difference maker.

lessons.tryThis: Tape a paper plate to your target and shoot it at 15 and 20 yards. Draw and hold for a slow count of ten before each shot. If you can't hit the plate every time, keep practicing before you hunt.

check.q: What standard should you hit before bowhunting, according to the Hunting Public?
check.a: Hit a 6 to 8 inch paper plate every time at 15 to 20 yards, including from an elevated stand.

check.q: Why practice holding at full draw for 10 seconds?
check.a: Deer often step or turn after you draw, and letting down is too much movement, so you need to be able to hold steady.

lessons.title: When the deer shows up
lessons.hook: This is the moment you've been waiting all season for. A deer is coming, and everything you've practiced has to happen while your heart is pounding. The best help for a pounding heart is a plan you made before the deer ever showed up.

sections.heading: Run the script before it happens
sections.text: Every sit, the Hunting Public crew play the whole shot in their heads before any deer shows up. They picture which way deer will come, where they'll draw, which is when the deer is behind a big tree at 30 to 40 yards, and where they'll stop it broadside at about 20 yards, with a grunt if needed. With a bow you're guessing every time, and you only have to be right once. That rehearsal is what lets you act when a buck finally reads the script.

sections.heading: Know your yardages before you need them
sections.text: Downwind Hunting suggests that as soon as you sit down, you range three objects in your shooting lanes, like a stump, a limb, or a rock, and memorize the yardages. When a deer shows up you know the distance without the movement of raising a rangefinder. That source is a listicle, but Mike Rex does the same thing, stepping off or ranging his shooting spots like scrapes and trails ahead of time. He also learns where his seat and gear can clank.

sections.heading: Draw when the deer can't see you
sections.text: The drawing motion is what gets you caught. The Southern Outdoorsmen guest and Mark Kenyon both keep the tree or cover between them and the deer, and draw only when its head is down or behind a tree or log. Then hold until it steps into the open. Once you're drawn and still, you won't get busted, as long as your draw weight is one you can hold. In a saddle, rotate slowly around the trunk to keep the tree between you and the deer as it passes.

sections.heading: Look at the chest, not the antlers
sections.text: Mike Rex says no amount of target practice prepares you for the adrenaline. A friend of his stared at a giant buck's rack and shot it in the antlers. Rex himself rushed to stand for the biggest typical he ever saw, clipped his boot on the seat, shook for 30 seconds, and cleanly missed at 21 yards he'd already stepped off. So pick a spot on the chest, and get into position slowly and quietly.

sections.heading: Freeze, and hide your eyes
sections.text: Yamaha Whitetail Diaries has spent years filming other hunters and has seen small movements pop deer heads up more than quiet sounds. A deep, muffled cough often doesn't alert a group, but shifting in your seat does. If a close deer stares right at you, Jamie McKay closes his eyes and very slowly leans his head behind the tree until it looks away. He did that with a doe, and the buck following her still came in to become his first big bow buck. Each tip comes from one hunter.

lessons.tryThis: On your next sit, range three objects as soon as you settle in. Then pick the tree you'll draw behind and the spot you'll stop a deer, and walk through the shot in your head once before anything shows up.

check.q: A deer is walking toward you in the open. When do you draw?
check.a: When its head is down or behind a tree or log, so it can't see the motion. Then hold until it steps out.

check.q: A doe is staring right at you from close range. What do you do?
check.a: Stay still, close your eyes, and very slowly lean your head behind the tree until she looks away.

units.goal: When to wait, when to track, and how to get your deer out.

lessons.title: Wait or go now
lessons.hook: The arrow is gone, the deer crashed off into the brush, and the woods are quiet again. Every part of you wants to climb down and start looking. What you do in the next few hours decides whether you find that deer, and the right answer depends on what you saw at the shot.

sections.heading: If you're not sure of the hit, back out
sections.text: A marginal hit is one you're unsure of, like a hit through only one lung, a shoulder-blade hit with shallow penetration, or a steep shot from above that passed low through one lung. For any of those, back out and give the deer a long time before you track it. Derek Dixon, who studies deer with thermal drones and has used them to find hit deer, has seen single-lung deer live more than 20 hours. He says going in after about 5 hours often bumps a live deer. One single-lung deer he shot was killed by a rifle hunter three weeks later, and a shoulder-blade, one-lung buck from podcast host Beau Martonik is still alive years later.

sections.heading: Why pushing a hit deer loses it
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis of Whitetail Habitat Solutions says a marginally hit deer left alone usually goes 200 to 300 yards to the nearest thick bedding cover and dies there. Push it, and it keeps going. Dixon says a pushed deer runs a couple hundred yards more, and Sturgis has seen them go half to three quarters of a mile in big open woods. Those deer are often never found, even with dogs. So when the trail runs out, search the first thick cover or bedding area about 200 to 300 yards from the shot. Rain makes all of this harder, because Sturgis says it often washes out the blood in the first 60 to 70 yards, but he still says not to rush in to beat it.

sections.heading: A gut-shot deer may still be alive
sections.text: The usual wait on a gut shot is 6 to 8 hours, and it's easy to assume the deer is dead by then. Dixon found a crossbow gut-shot buck with his drone about 10 hours after the shot, still alive and bedded 600 yards away. Later it got up and walked 200 yards to a creek to drink. Coyotes found it and tested it with bluff charges, and it died in the creek overnight. That's one buck, so it isn't a rule, but it's a good reason to expect a gut-shot deer may be alive in thick cover hundreds of yards away and to check nearby water.

sections.heading: If you saw it go down, go that night
sections.text: Waiting is for hits you're unsure of. If you saw the deer go down, or stagger nearly out of sight, Jamie McKay says to go back that same night with help rather than leave it until morning. He'd heard of a deer left overnight that got chewed up by scavengers. He backed out first, left his bow and stand at the tree, and came back with people. When the blood ran out, the five of them spread out to circle the gap he thought the buck was heading for, and they found it near there. This is one hunter's story, and it doesn't clash with the wait-longer advice because it covers a different kind of hit.

lessons.tryThis: Right after your next shot, before you move, say out loud what you saw. Did the deer go down, was the hit clean through both lungs, or are you unsure? Decide from that whether you're waiting or calling for help tonight, and note the time.
lessons.headsUp: Nobody here gives a set number of hours to wait on a marginal hit. Sturgis gave no wait time, and Dixon's point is only that about 5 hours is often too soon for a one-lung deer. The usual 6 to 8 hours on a gut shot was too soon for the buck Dixon found. When in doubt, wait longer.

check.q: You think you hit only one lung. Do you start tracking after an hour?
check.a: No. Back out and wait a long time. Single-lung deer can live more than 20 hours, and pushing one can lose it.

check.q: You watched your deer fall at the edge of sight just after dark. What do you do?
check.a: Back out, get help, and go back that night, because scavengers can find a deer left until morning.

lessons.title: Finding the trail and getting your deer out
lessons.hook: Your deer is down somewhere out there, and now there are two more jobs. You have to find it, and then you have to get it back to the truck. Both are a lot easier if you think about them before you ever take the shot.

sections.heading: No blood yet doesn't mean a miss
sections.text: A ground hunter who was a guest on Southern Outdoorsmen explains why a shot from the ground can leave little blood at first. From a tree, the exit hole is low, so blood comes out quickly. On a level shot, the chest has to fill up to the exit hole before blood leaves, so the start of the trail is sparse. Once it reaches the holes, he says, blood is everywhere. It can take up to 100 yards before blood starts. So after a level shot, watch exactly where the deer runs and set a compass bearing, meaning a direction on the compass, to the last spot you saw it by turning the dial to point there. Then follow that bearing even if you find nothing at first. This comes from one hunter.

sections.heading: Plan the drag before you sit
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis knows how he'll get a deer out before he ever climbs a tree. One of his steep bottoms has 250 to 300 feet of climb in about 250 yards, and dragging a deer up that is brutal, so he plans a vehicle ride out instead. On his long walk-in hunts in Pennsylvania, about an hour and a half of walking in, he brings a frame pack and plans to bone the deer out, which means taking the meat off the bones, and carry it out on his back. Those far-back hunts need the gear to carry the meat.

sections.heading: Float it before you gut it
sections.text: If there's a creek between you and the truck, Jamie McKay has a tip from moving two deer that way. Don't field dress a deer you plan to float out. An ungutted deer floats like a cork and can even help pull a gutted one through deeper water. His gutted deer had to be dragged through the shallows. That's one hunter's experience, so take it as a handy idea rather than a rule.

sections.heading: A habit, not a rule
sections.text: Sturgis leaves his knife home on his local sits, because he never guts a deer until family and friends come back with him to get it. He says that's his personal choice, partly superstition, and not something you need to copy. What's worth copying is the planning underneath it. He knows before the shot who is coming to help and how the deer is getting out.

lessons.tryThis: Open a map of the spot you'll hunt next and trace how you'd get a deer from your stand to the truck. Note any steep climbs or creeks, and decide whether you'd drag, float, get a ride, or pack it out.

check.q: You shot a deer from the ground on a level shot and find no blood for 50 yards. Is it a miss?
check.a: Not necessarily. On a level shot the chest has to fill before blood leaves, which can take up to 100 yards. Follow your compass bearing.

check.q: You'll move a deer down a creek. Should you field dress it first?
check.a: No. An ungutted deer floats like a cork, and a gutted one has to be dragged through the shallows.

units.goal: A deer's nose wins; play the wind first, products second.

lessons.title: The wind beats everything
lessons.hook: You've been in the stand for two hours. A doe finally steps out, walks about twenty yards, stops, and throws her nose in the air. One loud snort and she's gone, along with every deer within earshot. She didn't see you and she didn't hear you. She smelled you. This lesson is about making sure that doesn't happen.

sections.heading: Your nose problem is a wind problem
sections.text: A deer trusts its nose more than its eyes or ears, and you can't hide from it. That's why the wind decides more about your hunt than anything you buy. Informed Outdoors says they blew countless sits early on because they trusted the marketing on scent-control products. The folks at WHTL put it simply: the best a product can do is make a deer think you're a bit farther away than you are. A mature doe will still circle downwind and pick you off. So think of sprays, special detergents, and carbon suits as a small bonus on top of a good wind, never a reason to sit a bad one.

sections.heading: Put the wind in your face
sections.text: The basic setup is easy to remember. Figure out where you expect deer to come from, then sit so the wind blows from there toward you. Your scent drifts away behind you, into ground the deer aren't using. Deer won't always cooperate, because they'll sometimes come from wherever they please. Pick a spot where the most likely paths stay upwind of you, and you've done the most important thing right.

sections.heading: Every stand has its winds
sections.text: Here's the habit that separates good hunters from lucky ones. For every stand, know the one or two wind directions it's actually safe on, and only sit it on those days. Jon Sturgis, who manages and hunts land in Wisconsin, lists them for each stand. In hilly ground he works out where the wind will really carry his scent, because the hills, not the forecast, decide that. If your best stand needs a west wind and today is east, stay out and wait. Informed Outdoors points out that hunters who force a stand on the wrong wind slowly ruin it: the sign dries up, and they blame the "October lull" for a problem they caused.

sections.heading: Trust the air, not the app
sections.text: The forecast is where you start, not where you finish. It might say west when the air at your tree is actually drifting northeast, and hills can make it swirl. The Hunting Public crew carries milkweed fluff on every hunt for this reason. Pull a few fibers, let them go, and watch where they float. Unlike powder, which drops a couple of feet and disappears, milkweed rides the small drafts all the way down the hill. Letting some go about every ten minutes during a sit shows you where a deer walking in would hit your scent, so you can plan the shot before he gets there.

lessons.tryThis: Before your next sit, write down the one or two winds your stand works on. On the way in, check the real wind at the tree with milkweed or a light thread. If it doesn't match, go to a different spot.
lessons.headsUp: Not everyone is strict about this. Jamie McKay, who hunts steep mountain country, says to go check the real air before scratching a spot on the forecast, and that in the peak rut he'll hunt a great spot on a marginal wind because bucks chasing does pay less attention. That's an exception for experienced hunters, not a starting rule.

check.q: The wind is wrong for your best stand, but you just bought a new scent spray. Do you sit it?
check.a: No. Spray won't save a bad wind. Sit a stand that works on today's wind and save your best one.

check.q: The forecast says a west wind. What do you do when you get to the tree?
check.a: Check the real air with milkweed or thread. The wind at your spot can be very different from the forecast.

lessons.title: Thermals: the wind you can't see
lessons.hook: It's a dead-calm morning and you figure the wind doesn't matter today. It does. Even when the leaves aren't moving, the air is sliding up or down the hills around you, and it's carrying your scent the whole time. Hunters call these slow currents thermals, and once you understand them, a lot of "the wind swirled" moments start to make sense.

sections.heading: Morning: air sinks, then rises
sections.text: At first light the ground is cold, so the air sitting on it is cold and heavy. It drains downhill into the low spots. Then the sun comes up and warms the ground, and the air flips almost completely around and starts rising. Mike Rex, who has killed dozens of record-book bucks in the southeast Ohio hills, plans his mornings around that switch. Before the flip, your scent is sliding downhill. After it, your scent is lifting uphill.

sections.heading: Why low ground is safer in the morning
sections.text: Once the air is rising, it lifts your scent up and out of low ground. That's why Jeff Sturgis calls bottoms and low spots more forgiving on a morning sit than an evening one. He's even had deer about 30 yards below him, technically downwind, without them smelling him, because the rising air carried his scent up and over them like a ramp. The catch is timing. Walk into a bottom an hour before daylight and your scent just pools there before the lift starts. Sturgis likes to be settled only about ten minutes before first light.

sections.heading: Evening: the drain at the end of the day
sections.text: All afternoon, warm air keeps rising. Sometime around early afternoon the temperature levels off, and in the last 45 minutes to an hour of light, the air cools and starts sinking downhill again. Your scent goes with it. That matters, because it's the exact time deer start moving. Derek Dixon, who studies bucks with thermal drones, found bedded bucks consistently stood up within 5 to 15 minutes of that evening switch.

sections.heading: Plan evening sits for two winds
sections.text: Put those together and you get Sturgis's rule for evening sits in hill country: your stand has to work on two winds. It needs to handle the forecast wind for most of the afternoon, and the downhill drain for the last hour. A stand that works fine all afternoon can fail in the last hour, right when the air starts sliding downhill toward the deer. If it only works on one of the two, pick another stand for that evening.

lessons.tryThis: On your next evening sit in hilly ground, drop some milkweed every so often and watch what happens in the last hour of light. You'll likely see it start drifting downhill. That's the drain, and now you know what it looks like.
lessons.headsUp: Hunters disagree about valleys. Sturgis finds bottoms forgiving on a morning sit. Mike Rex, in steeper country, avoids valley stands entirely because the air swirls there with no good direction, and hunts higher where the wind is steadier. It probably depends on how steep your ground is. If a low spot keeps getting you busted, move up.

check.q: Is a stand in a low bottom better for a morning sit or an evening sit?
check.a: Morning. After sunrise, rising air lifts your scent out of the bottom. In the evening your scent sinks into it.

check.q: Why is the last hour of daylight tricky for scent?
check.a: The air cools and starts sliding downhill, right when deer are getting up and moving.

lessons.title: Scent: leave no trace
lessons.hook: Even if you play the wind perfectly, you still leave scent behind. It's on the trail you walked in on, the grass you brushed past, and the clothes you wore to the gas station. You can't beat a deer's nose, but you can cut down how much of yourself you bring into the woods and how much you leave there.

sections.heading: It starts at home
sections.text: Switch to unscented soap, shampoo, deodorant, and laundry detergent. Skin holds onto fragrance longer than you'd think. Eddie McRae, a Georgia bowhunter with 40 years in the woods, noticed he could still smell a scented hand soap on his hands the morning after a shower. If you can smell it, a deer can smell it from a long way off. McRae goes further than most and avoids scented products all year, not just during the season.

sections.heading: Keep your hunting clothes clean of everyday life
sections.text: Your house smells like cooking, your truck smells like your truck, and a gas pump can put fuel on your hands and sleeves. Keep hunting clothes, underwear included, away from all of that. McRae hangs his outside and gets dressed there. Diamond Archery keeps theirs sealed in a bag and never wears them on the drive. Either way, the goal is to put them on when you arrive, not when you leave home.

sections.heading: Don't leave a trail
sections.text: Every step in regular boots, and every stem of grass your pants brush, leaves scent that stays there after you're gone. Jeff Sturgis calls it a spider web. His example: two hunters sitting five different stands on 40 acres over one weekend can cover the whole property with it, and a mature buck that walks into that web simply leaves. Rubber boots hold your scent in, so wear them anywhere deer live, including when you check cameras. Try not to brush the vegetation along your route.

sections.heading: Tuck your pants in
sections.text: This one surprises people. Every step pumps warm, damp air out of the top of your boot. With your pants tucked into your boots, that air goes up. With your pants pulled over the boots, it gets pushed straight down onto the ground you're walking on. Sturgis tucks them in and wears clean knee-high boots, especially in the warm early season.

sections.heading: Two cheap extras
sections.text: A few tricks only show up in one source, so treat them as tips rather than rules. Wash your hunting clothes in about half a cup of baking soda instead of detergent, which leaves no scent or brighteners behind. Before you walk in, rub your boot soles with dirt from the property you're hunting so they smell like they belong there.

lessons.tryThis: Before your next hunt, swap one thing at home for an unscented version and store your hunting clothes in a sealed tub. On the walk in, notice how often your legs brush the grass, and see if there's a cleaner route.
lessons.headsUp: Hunters disagree about how far scent control can go. Jeff Sturgis says you truly can't fool a deer's nose, and a deer that seems not to wind you was really getting your scent carried another way. Eddie McRae says that after 6 to 8 years of living scent-free, deer that circle straight downwind of him no longer wind him. Both of them still play the wind first.

check.q: You did everything right with scent. Can you sit with the wind blowing toward where deer will come from?
check.a: No. Scent control lowers the odds of getting winded. It doesn't stop a deer's nose.

check.q: Why wear rubber boots even when you're just checking a trail camera?
check.a: Regular boots leave a scent trail deer run into. Rubber boots hold your scent in.

units.goal: Bed, food, and the path between them.

lessons.title: Beds, food, and the path between
lessons.hook: You walk into a new piece of woods and there's sign everywhere. Tracks in the mud, a rub on a sapling, a trail worn down to bare dirt. It's easy to spend a whole day chasing each clue on its own. Every one of them makes more sense once you know two things, where the deer sleep and where they eat.

sections.heading: Two places matter most
sections.text: When you scout, your main job is to find where deer bed and where they feed. Everything else, the rubs, the scrapes, the tracks, even the way bucks travel in the rut, gets read in relation to those two places. Next Step Outdoors explains why. Deer are most active at dawn and dusk. They spend daylight in or near security cover, get up around dusk to feed through the night, and head back to bed in the morning. That trip between bed and food is where a bowhunter catches them, and even the routes bucks cruise in the rut are built around where the does bed.

sections.heading: Start at the food
sections.text: On a new property, scout on a map first, then walk it. In farm country, Next Step Outdoors starts at the crop field, an orchard, or even crops on the neighboring private land, and scouts from the food back toward the bedding. The food is the easiest piece to find, and the trails lead from it to the beds. It's harder where food is scattered, like a couple of oak flats or natural browse, because the sign is spread thin and the travel direction is less clear. In that case, walk until you find a concentration of sign, then work forward and backward from it to find both ends. This method comes from one source hunting Ohio public land with farm fields on it, so treat it as a solid way to start rather than the only way.

sections.heading: What the beaten trails tell you
sections.text: The trails that are pounded down to dirt are usually doe-family routes between bed and feed. Doe groups walk the same line every day, so those trails get worn in. That makes them useful even if not every deer beds in the same place, because they point you toward the food the deer prefer and the general direction they travel. Don't expect a buck's trail to look like that. Next Step Outdoors says buck trails are less obvious, so the dirt highway tells you about the does first.

sections.heading: If you only get one stand
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis of Whitetail Habitat Solutions puts it simply. Hang it between bedding and food, and water if there is any, close to both but in neither. Deer pass that spot in the morning and in the evening, so it's the rare stand you can hunt any time, all season. A stand right on the food mostly works in the evening, and one in the bedding mostly works in the morning. Look for a pinch that squeezes the movement, like a ditch, the edge of thick cover, a bench, or a swamp edge, with a hidden way in and out that doesn't cross the bedding or the food. He also likes a water hole back in a wooded funnel about 100 yards off a food plot. A mature buck won't walk into a small open plot in the middle of the day, but he will visit water back in cover. This one comes from Sturgis alone.

lessons.tryThis: Pull up an aerial map of a place you can hunt. Mark the most obvious food, then trace the likely path back into the thickest cover nearby. Walk that line once, find the most beaten trail, and note which way it runs.
lessons.headsUp: Guessing where deer bed isn't always easy. Mike Rex warns that bedding is hard to pin down in hill country, so he works out from the food instead of trying to set up between two places he can only guess at. If you can't find the beds, start from what you can find.

check.q: You find a trail pounded down to bare dirt. What does it most likely tell you?
check.a: It's probably a doe-family route between bed and food, so it points you to the food and the travel direction. Buck trails are usually less obvious.

check.q: Why is a stand between bedding and food better than one right on the food?
check.a: Deer pass it both morning and evening, so you can hunt it any time. A stand on the food mostly works only in the evening.

lessons.title: Who beds where, and how bucks move
lessons.hook: You found the food and the doe trails, and you set up right where they meet the cover. Does show up every evening. The buck from your trail camera never does. That usually isn't bad luck. Deer sort themselves out in the cover, and older bucks live by different rules.

sections.heading: Deer bed in layers
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis describes bedding as layers moving back from the food. Does and fawns bed closest, young bucks come next, and the mature buck beds farthest back in the cover, apart from the others. On his managed private ground that's roughly the first 50 to 100 yards for does and fawns, the next 100 to 150 for young bucks, and about 250 to 300 yards back for a mature buck. On public land he expects that buck much farther out, around 600 yards to half a mile. The reason is that mature bucks don't want to bed with does, fawns, or younger bucks, while does put up with traffic near the food. To find him, walk back from the food, past the doe bedding, to the next change in the habitat. You should find fewer deer the deeper you go.

sections.heading: What the drones saw
sections.text: Derek Dixon, who studies deer with thermal drones, backs up the layering with what he's filmed. Around a big food plot ringed by plain mature timber, does bedded within 50 yards of it and bucks only passed through. So a big plot with no mixed cover around it holds does but no resident mature buck, and it's best hunted from the pre-rut through the late season, when bucks cruise through checking the does. The distances shift with the season too. In the late season Sturgis finds does within 100 yards and bucks 200 to 400 yards out, because in the cold deer won't travel half a mile every day to eat. Treat all these numbers as rough guides, since Sturgis's shorter ones come from managed Midwest ground where cutting squeezes the layers together.

sections.heading: Night photos don't mean a night buck
sections.text: A Mississippi State GPS-collar study led by Bronson Strickland measured how bucks actually spend their time. Bucks were never more than about half bedded at any moment, day or night, and outside the rut they were bedded only about 38 percent of daylight, often in up to three short naps at midday with slow snacking in between. A buck bedded a couple thousand yards away can walk all afternoon and still reach your food after dark. So if he only shows on camera at night, he's probably up in daylight somewhere else, and you should move toward his cover instead of sitting the food longer. Mark Kenyon of MeatEater, who hunts Minnesota, sees the same thing from the stand. Bucks stay just inside thick cover, follow its edge between bed and food, and almost never cross open timber you can see through. Here the data and the hunters agree.

sections.heading: Know what kind of deer you're hunting
sections.text: Eddie McRae sorts deer into four kinds before he picks tactics. Wild deer have no tolerance for people, suburban deer are used to people, pets, and cars, managed deer are fed with plots, feeders, and troughs and get used to people, and public-land deer are their own case. Busy public land with trails, camping, and ranges acts more like suburban or managed deer, while restricted public land with one or two access roads acts wild. That type alone changes how far deer travel and what will blow them out. His example is a managed-property county-record buck that came to a feeder within about 45 minutes of the farm hand refilling it.

sections.heading: The focus changes with the season
sections.text: Yamaha Whitetail Diaries keeps it short. Early in bow season, focus on food, water, and bedding. In the rut, hunt trails, food, and water, and expect a buck chasing a doe to show up almost anywhere. It's only one source, but it fits everything above, because deer follow different patterns early than they do later in the season.

lessons.tryThis: On a map, pick a food source and measure 100, 300, and 600 yards back into the nearest cover. Mark where the habitat changes along that line. Those changes are where to start looking for a buck bedded apart from the does.

check.q: Does keep showing up at your food plot, but the mature buck never does. Where do you look for him?
check.a: Farther back in the cover, past the doe bedding, at the next change in habitat. Mature bucks bed apart from does and younger bucks.

check.q: Your camera only gets a certain buck after dark. Is he nocturnal?
check.a: Probably not. The GPS data shows bucks are up in daylight too, just somewhere else. Move toward his cover instead of sitting the food longer.

units.goal: The rut, temperature, rain, and picking your days.

lessons.title: The rut beats the weather
lessons.hook: You've saved up your vacation days, and the week you picked looks warm. Do you still go? It's one of the biggest calls you'll make each season. The good news is that on this one, the hunters and the research have something solid to tell you.

sections.heading: Plan your big block around the rut
sections.text: The rut is the breeding season, when bucks are out looking for does. Jeff Danker of Realtree says the biggest thing in the rut is time in the woods, so get out as much as you can, even if you only get 45 minutes after work. Off at 5, in the stand by 5:15, dark at 6 is still a hunt as long as the wind is right. Bucks cover the most ground then, and any sit can produce a buck you've never seen. David Blanton, also of Realtree, goes in the rut even when it's warm, because a buck that just left a bred doe can be on his feet looking for the next one at any time.

sections.heading: What the GPS collars show
sections.text: A Mississippi State GPS-collar study led by Bronson Strickland measured it. Outside the rut, bucks covered about 1,500 to 2,000 yards a day, and in the rut more than 4,000. They were bedded about 35 to 38 percent of daylight outside the rut and only about 21 percent in it. Weather, by comparison, changed movement by a few yards an hour up to about 50. Strickland says the rut supersedes everything, and movement steps up from pre-rut to early rut to peak, then tapers off. One caution is that this data comes from Mississippi and the Southeast, where the rut peaks around December, so go by your own local rut dates.

sections.heading: Warm is the weather that really hurts
sections.text: Outside the rut, everyone agrees that warm days are bad. Blanton says nothing keeps a mature buck in bed until after dark more than warmer than normal temperatures, in any month and any region. His example is late October in Illinois with a normal high of 71 and a forecast of 83, and he'd think about moving the trip. Jeff Sturgis of Whitetail Habitat Solutions sees mature bucks barely move in a hot late-October stretch and move a lot, mostly in the morning, when it turns cool. The MSU data matches. Movement rose as the temperature went from about 30 up to 50 F and dropped toward 80 F, and a day 10 F or more warmer than yesterday meant more time bedded. That band is for the Deep South, so compare to what's normal where you hunt.

sections.heading: Don't climb down at 8
sections.text: The MSU collars found buck travel is fastest about two hours after sunrise. Around first light bucks are still feeding on slow, twisting paths, and then they head in long straight lines to their first bed. Derek Dixon, who studies bucks with thermal drones, often sees them pass between 8 and 9:30 in the morning, and hunter Beau Martonik has never killed one at first light. In the rut, Jeff Danker of Realtree stays until 11, takes a lunch break, and is back in by 1:30, and he counts leaving at 9:30 among his own biggest mistakes. Two research sources and a hunter agree, so stay put, especially on a route between food and bedding.

lessons.tryThis: Look up when the rut usually peaks where you hunt and block off your best days around it. Then, on your next morning sit, set a rule for yourself that you won't climb down before 10.
lessons.headsUp: In the rut the sources split. Sturgis picks his days by the weather and would hunt the cooler day instead, even in the peak rut. Blanton says go in the rut even when it's warm, and the MSU numbers back him, because the rut's effect on movement is far bigger than any weather effect they measured. Outside the rut, everyone agrees warm days hurt.

check.q: It's the peak rut where you hunt, and it's warmer than normal. Do you go?
check.a: Most of the evidence says go. The rut raises buck movement far more than any measured weather effect, though Sturgis would pick a cooler day if he could.

check.q: It's 8 AM on a morning sit and nothing has moved. Why stay?
check.a: Buck travel peaks about two hours after sunrise, and many bucks pass between 8 and 9:30.

lessons.title: Cold snaps, rain, and storms
lessons.hook: A cold front shows up in the forecast and every hunting group chat you're in lights up. Some of that excitement is earned and some of it isn't. This lesson sorts out which weather changes the data backs up and which ones are mostly hunter belief.

sections.heading: Weather is a tiebreaker
sections.text: The MSU collar study needed a very large sample and heavy math to see any weather signal at all. Put another way, if your odds on a sit are 10 percent, cold weather might make them 11, not 90. Whitetail Properties, summarizing collar research, says studies of wind, temperature, rain, snow, and barometric pressure (air pressure) haven't found the changes hunters expect from any single one. Within the same stage of the rut, days under a cold air mass did show slightly more daylight buck movement. So don't count on a front or a barometer reading by itself to put deer on their feet, and don't skip a good day because the barometer looks wrong.

sections.heading: A big temperature drop is the exception
sections.text: One signal does hold up. In the MSU data, day-to-day swings within 10 F either way changed bedding time by about nothing, but past a drop of about 10 to 15 F, bucks spent less time bedded the next day. Hunters land in the same place. Sturgis looks for a 15 to 20 degree drop, even while pressure is still low, especially if the wind has laid down from 25 or 30 mph to 8 or 12. Eddie McRae in Georgia treats the high dropping 11 to 15 degrees, like 60 to 49, as a major event, because it only has to get a buck up half an hour earlier to put him in daylight. He killed his buck on his third sit like that. He also says a swing that size matters much less up north or out west, where deer are used to big changes.

sections.heading: Light rain is a good day
sections.text: Blanton says deer seem to like moving in a light drizzle and bed down in a hard, steady rain. Sturgis explains why. In a light drizzle all their senses work, since damp air helps their nose, the trees aren't thrashing, and it's quiet enough to hear, and deer move when they have their senses. In the rut, he says a little light rain won't keep any buck in bed. Whitetail Properties points to a Penn State researcher who found rain was the one weather factor that raised deer movement, especially for bucks, and wet woods let you walk in quieter. That research gave no numbers and didn't separate light rain from heavy, but hunters and research agree rain alone isn't a reason to stay home.

sections.heading: Sit out the worst of it
sections.text: Heavy rain, heavy snow, thunder and lightning, hail, and very heavy wind are different. Sturgis says most deer stay in their bedding through extremes like that, conserving energy, stressed, and surrounded by noisy woods. Heavy rain also washes away a blood trail fast if you do shoot one. He'd rather watch it from somewhere dry and be ready to go the moment it breaks, and he uses those days for stand work. He says never say never, and he gave no exact cutoff for extreme, so this is one experienced hunter's judgment.

lessons.tryThis: For the next two weeks, check each day's forecast high against the day before. Circle any day that drops 15 F or more, and any day with light drizzle, and plan to be in the stand on those.
lessons.headsUp: Two disagreements here. Sturgis says very heavy wind keeps deer bedded, but the MSU data found wind level alone barely changed movement, even above 20 mph. And a Downwind Hunting listicle, an unverified compiled article, says a 10 F drop makes movement spike sharply, while the MSU data counts a 10 F change as no change and needs about 15.

check.q: Tomorrow's high is 5 degrees cooler than today's. Is that a big deal?
check.a: No. The MSU data treats a change within about 10 F as no change. Look for a drop of about 15 F or more.

check.q: Light drizzle is forecast for your Saturday sit. Go or stay home?
check.a: Go. Hunters and research agree light rain isn't a reason to stay home. Skip thunderstorms and heavy, steady rain.

lessons.title: Picking your days
lessons.hook: Most of us can't hunt every day. There's work, there's family, and there's a short stack of days off. Choosing which days to spend, and which stand to sit on each one, is a skill of its own, and it's one you can start practicing a week before you ever walk in.

sections.heading: Save your best stands for your best days
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis hunts his best stands only on the best weather days and stays out of them the rest of the time. He says he tags out most years because he isn't burning out his stands on bad days. If today is windy and hot and tomorrow is forecast calm to moderate with a drop of 10 F or more, he waits and moves his time off to match. Whitetail Evolution, hunting Michigan's early season, does the same thing. On warm days or the wrong wind they stay out and wait for a cold front after a warm stretch, with a 15 to 20 degree drop, the rain moving out, and the wind slowing. That afternoon they push a bit deeper to a staging food source, a spot deer snack at on their way to the main field.

sections.heading: Bank time on the bluebird days
sections.text: Whitetail Evolution's example of a day to skip is 75 F on October 15 in Michigan. They spend warm bluebird days like that with family, or trade work time with the boss, so they're free when a big cold front shows up in next week's forecast. The goodwill you bank on those days pays off when the important days arrive. One great weekday morning and evening beats a warm five-day weekend.

sections.heading: Plan from the forecast
sections.text: Sturgis picks his hunt days from the daily forecast 8 to 10 days out. Then, within 72 hours, he uses the hourly forecast to decide which stand he'll sit each morning and evening based on its wind. He trusts the wind direction most, because it comes from big weather patterns and holds 7 to 10 days out within about half a day. Rain and snow amounts are much less reliable. That's Sturgis's claim alone, and nobody here has checked it against forecast data, so treat it as a working habit.

sections.heading: Read the day before you pick the spot
sections.text: The Hunting Public crew, who hunt big woods, start each day with a few questions. Are the leaves wet? Did it just rain? Is it windy or calm, hot or cold? Is a cold front coming through? Each answer changes where deer bed, how they move, and how close you can get to them. Deer hunting is very situational, so the same spot can be right one day and wrong the next.

sections.heading: Rest counts too
sections.text: A guest on Southern Outdoorsmen makes a point that's easy to skip. Get a good night's sleep and eat well before a hunt, even if it costs you some hunting time. When you're tired, your mind isn't fully in the game and you won't stay alert. It's one hunter's advice, but it's cheap to follow.

lessons.tryThis: Eight to ten days before your next open weekend, pick the one or two days that look coolest. Three days out, check the hourly wind and write down which stand you'll sit each morning and evening.
lessons.headsUp: The research pushes back on this approach. The MSU study puts weather at about a 10 to 11 percent change in odds, and in the rut Blanton and the data say go regardless.
