A reasonable blend is to let weather pick the days for your best stands and let the calendar decide how many days you hunt. What the data can't measure is that a stand sat only a few times stays fresh, which may be much of why picking days works for these hunters.

check.q: Your best stand needs a cold day, and next week's forecast shows a big front on Thursday. What do you do now?
check.a: Stay out of that stand on the warm days and try to move time off to Thursday. Within 72 hours, use the hourly wind to pick your stand.

check.q: Which part of a forecast 8 to 10 days out does Sturgis trust most?
check.a: The wind direction. Rain and snow amounts are much less reliable.

units.goal: Deer that never know you were there.

lessons.title: Getting to the tree unseen
lessons.hook: You can find the perfect tree and still ruin it before you sit down. A light swinging across a field, a stick clanking on your pack, a path that cuts right through where deer are feeding in the dark. Deer that see or hear you coming learn where you'll be, and the best hunters treat the walk in as part of the hunt.

sections.heading: Pick the tree and the route while you're standing there
sections.text: When you find a spot you want to hunt, choose the exact tree, or the spot on the ground, and the way you'll walk to it right then. Mark both on your mapping app. Next Step Outdoors learned this the hard way. For years he'd tell himself he'd figure it out later and then not get back until the season. Knowing every bed, rub, and scrape does you no good if you don't know where you'll ambush a deer and how you'll get in without spooking him or the other deer that would bump him. While you're there, clear dead branches and brush from the base of the tree so you can climb it quietly in the dark.

sections.heading: Keep cover between you and the deer
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis of Whitetail Habitat Solutions ranks not spooking deer above any habitat or food plot work on his land. He tunnels his way in behind tall cover, like a mowed trail through switchgrass about 5 feet tall, a hedgerow, or willows, instead of crossing the food. He walks in with the wind in his face or blowing off to the side, away from the deer. A guest on Southern Outdoorsmen uses a creek with 10 to 12 foot banks the same way, walking up the creek bed past deer already feeding in the dark and climbing out at the tree. They've killed two bucks at that tree that they would have spooked coming in any other way.

sections.heading: Keep your light low
sections.text: Deer see light from hundreds of yards away. Sturgis once had deer blowing and running 700 to 800 yards off while he walked a fence row with a small flashlight back in the 1980s, with the wind in his face. On a Wisconsin gun opener he watched someone's headlamp push deer off a hillside 500 to 600 yards away. So use your light's lowest setting, around 1 to 2 lumens, pointed straight down at your feet, or cover the lens with your thumb so only a sliver reaches the ground. Be strictest in the open near fields and food plots, where deer are before daylight. It helps to let your eyes adjust after the truck, clear your trails ahead of time, and follow the opening in the treetops. All of this comes from Sturgis alone.

sections.heading: Pack so nothing sticks out or clanks
sections.text: Next Step Outdoors packs everything inside the outline of his shoulders and hips. Climbing sticks go vertical, the platform lies flat on his back, and nothing is wider than his body or taller than his shoulders. If your body fits through a gap in the brush, your gear will too. He wears his saddle and knee pads from the truck. Relentless Sportsman adds that a hang-on stand should be soundproofed and packed so the stand and sticks can't clank together or bang on brush. Balance the load on both shoulders with a waist strap, because a 10 to 20 pound stand is hardly noticed when it's balanced, and even light gear is miserable when the sticks all hang off one side.

lessons.tryThis: Load up your stand gear in the yard and walk through the tightest gap you can find. Anything that snags or clanks gets repacked. Then check what your light's lowest setting actually is.

check.q: You're walking along a field edge before daylight. How should you use your light?
check.a: Barely. Use the lowest setting pointed at your feet, or cover the lens with your thumb. Deer can see a light from hundreds of yards.

check.q: When should you decide on the exact tree and your route to it?
check.a: Right when you find the spot, while you're standing there. Mark both on your map and clear the base of the tree.

lessons.title: Quiet at the tree, clean on the way out
lessons.hook: You made it to the tree without a sound. Now comes the part most new hunters rush, hanging the stand and climbing, and later, the part almost everyone forgets to plan, leaving. Deer can catch you at either end of the sit, and some of them will be watching.

sections.heading: Know how long setup takes
sections.text: Build setup time into when you leave for the tree, and practice in the yard before the season. The Hunting Public crew, who are experienced mobile hunters, need about 5 to 10 minutes on an easy, straight tree, 10 to 15 on a tree with branches to work around, and about 30 with camera gear. Bow Only Outdoors figures about 15 minutes on a normal tree, 30 to 45 on an odd or limby one, and 45 to 60 with cameras. Coming down takes about 5. As a beginner you'll likely be slower, so leave early.

sections.heading: Up the tree in one trip
sections.text: Next Step Outdoors climbs in one quiet trip. He hangs the first stick from the ground, carries the rest on a carabiner at his hip and the platform on the back of his saddle, and ties his bow to a hoist rope before anything else, laying it so it pulls straight up. Every loose strap gets buckled or wrapped so nothing flaps. Going up and down to fetch each stick is louder, takes much longer, and gets you sweaty before the hunt. Bow Only Outdoors adds one small habit. On cool, still mornings, cover the ratchet strap with your gloved hand while you tighten it, because sound carries far in the cold. He admits he's killed a buck on a frosty morning after ratcheting in, so it's a precaution, not a rule.

sections.heading: Plan the exit like the entry
sections.text: Four hunters here agree that leaving unseen matters as much as getting in. Mike Rex assumes a mature buck is watching, and several times his camera caught the target buck watching him and his son leave before they reached the truck. Leaving an evening stand, Sturgis looks first, then walks out along an edge behind screening or through the middle of an ag field. If he has to bump deer, he'd rather bump them off a big crop field, which they forget, than off a small food plot, which they learn to avoid. Whitetail Evolution, sitting near a food source deer stop at on the way to a bigger field, waits after dark for the deer to move on, then slips down. Otherwise you can end up with 15 to 20 deer around you and no clean way out.

sections.heading: Don't bail early
sections.text: Eddie McRae climbed down 20 minutes before dark on a hot, muggy evening so he wouldn't get pinned in the tree. A doe and a small buck at 40 yards caught him, blew, and spooked everything in the cutover. His camera showed his target buck watching him climb down, and that buck never came back to the spot. Deer may be filtering toward you where you can't see them, so don't bail out just because nothing is in sight.

sections.heading: Agree on a plan with your partner
sections.text: Jamie McKay hunts gun season with partners set up 200 to 300 yards apart. They agree beforehand that if one of them shoots, the shooter stays in the tree and doesn't go after the deer until the other has finished the morning sit. Climbing down and walking around would spoil the other hunter's morning. It's one hunter's rule, and he says to use judgment on a marginal hit or in warm weather.

lessons.tryThis: Time yourself hanging your stand and sticks in the yard, start to finish, and leave yourself extra time for doing it in the dark. Before your next evening sit, decide exactly how you'll walk out if deer are in front of you at dark.
lessons.headsUp: Hunters differ on how much one mistake costs. McRae's buck never came back after catching him once, and Sturgis says deer bumped off a small plot learn to avoid it. Mike Rex says deer don't abandon a place after one spook, since coyotes bump them a dozen times a day, and what they react to is a lot of sudden human presence. McRae's spot was being hunted over and over, which may be the difference. Rex still says to leave unseen.

check.q: Nothing's in sight 20 minutes before dark and you're hot and tired. Do you climb down?
check.a: No. Deer may be moving toward you unseen, and getting caught climbing down can ruin the spot.

check.q: If you have to bump deer on the way out, where is it least harmful?
check.a: Off a big crop field, which deer forget. Deer bumped off a small food plot you hunt learn to avoid it.

units.goal: Where to sit for mornings, evenings, and the wind you have.

lessons.title: Evening stands: back off the food
lessons.hook: You watched a buck step out at the corner of a bean field all summer, so opening week you hang a stand right on that corner. Does and young bucks pour out every evening, but the big one never shows, and you decide he only moves at night. He's probably moving, just a little way back in the cover.

sections.heading: Get off the field edge
sections.text: Mature bucks travel the same general way as the other deer, but they stop just inside the thick where they feel safe and are often the last deer out, sometimes after dark. So skip the open edge, the summer corner, and the does' trail, and back into the cover. Mark Kenyon of MeatEater, who filmed this in Minnesota farm country, backs in 30 to 100 yards and says it holds in the rut and out of it. Eddie McRae cut a room-sized opening about 40 yards inside the thick, hunted it from a ground blind with two lanes of 12 to 15 yards, and watched his buck mill around in there for 9 minutes before he stepped into a lane.

sections.heading: What the drone footage shows
sections.text: This one has measured data behind it. Derek Dixon, who films bucks with thermal drones, found a mature buck's evening daylight movement looks like "a toddler scribbling" around a staging area of under about 200 acres, with about three favored evening spots. One buck even bedded again 5 yards off a food plot corner with 45 to 50 minutes of light left. Catch a buck once at a spot in the evening, Dixon says, and he's probably there often.

sections.heading: Hunt on the way to the food
sections.text: Four hunters agree here, including Jeff Sturgis of Whitetail Habitat Solutions, Mike Rex, and Grant Woods. Skip the big destination food, like a bean field, a big plot, or bait. Deer hit a small "appetizer" in cover first, in daylight, and reach the big field by dark, where an old doe eventually picks you off. So hunt a small plot, a fruit tree, a white oak dropping acorns, a water hole, or the "spokes," the logical paths leading in. Rex says old bucks wait for the crowd to thin, which is why your food photos of them come at midnight.

sections.heading: How close to the bed
sections.text: Bronson Strickland's MSU GPS-collar study measured the evening movement peak at about an hour after sunset, when you're already walking out. Sturgis and Jamie McKay take that to mean you should set up close to where the buck gets out of bed, since a buck that only walks 50 yards can reach you in daylight. Sturgis hunts the staging flat with rubs and scrapes 50 to 100 yards off the bedding, off to its side. McKay sits tight to the edge of the thick on a trail coming out. Whitetail Evolution, hunting Michigan's early season, leans the other way and shades the stand toward the food end so they don't bump the buck. Everyone agrees on one thing, which is that you never walk into the bedding in the afternoon.

sections.heading: Inside corners
sections.text: Where a field's tree line bends in toward the timber, deer walking the edge cut across the corner, so it funnels them. Transition lines, where hardwoods meet a thicket or pines, work the same way. McKay's first sit at one had 13 to 15 does and two bucks chasing a doe. Sturgis likes small hidden plots of a quarter to half an acre on the way to the main food, because deer pass through them in daylight without sitting there till dark.

lessons.tryThis: Pull up the field you hunt most on a map. Mark the open corner you've been sitting, then mark two spots 30 to 100 yards back in the thick cover along the trails leading in. Hang your next evening setup at one of those.
lessons.headsUp: How close to get to the bedding is a real split. The MSU collar data, Sturgis, and McKay say get near it because the evening peak is after dark. Whitetail Evolution, one source, says stay toward the food end in the early season so you don't bump the buck. The measured part is only the timing of the peak, and the rest is each hunter's reasoning.

check.q: Does and small bucks show up on the field edge every evening but the big buck never does. What's the most likely reason?
check.a: He's staging back in the cover and coming out last or after dark. Move 30 to 100 yards back into the thick.

check.q: Why sit a small food spot on the way instead of the big field?
check.a: Deer hit it earlier in daylight, and you avoid getting picked off by a field full of deer or bumping them on the way out.

lessons.title: Morning stands and a safe downwind side
lessons.hook: A morning sit is a different puzzle from an evening one. In the evening you're waiting for deer to leave their beds. In the morning they're coming back from a night of feeding, and you have to be in their way without them smelling where you walked in.

sections.heading: Mornings happen back in the cover
sections.text: Deer leave cover for food in the evening and come back to it in the morning, so Jeff Sturgis sets his morning stands back in the cover or brush and his afternoon stands toward food. Across about 30 stand locations in Minnesota and Wisconsin, 70 to 80 percent of his crew's bucks come from those morning brush stands. The shot windows are tight, about 40 yards, so a bow works there even in gun season. Sneak in slowly in the dark. Only Sturgis teaches this, but he has a lot of stands behind it.

sections.heading: Sit the back side of the bedding
sections.text: Sturgis also likes to come in from the side and set up on the back side of a mature buck's bedding, at a habitat change where nothing beds. That can be a steep ravine or drop-off, open mature hardwoods, or an open field. Your scent blows into the ravine or off the hill where no deer are, and once the air starts rising in the morning it lifts away. You're waiting right where the buck ends his morning. This is Sturgis's idea alone.

sections.heading: Put your scent where deer won't walk
sections.text: Pick a stand so the ground downwind of you is ground deer won't use, like a creek, a point, a steep hillside, a wet swamp, open water, or very thick brush. Sturgis calls stand location the first step of scent control and says that set up this way, you could smell like a pig and still shoot a deer. It matters most on all-day sits and whenever you call, because The Hunting Public crew has watched a called buck circle straight downwind to check out the sound. With a barrier behind you, he can't. Don't sit in the middle of where deer feed, like an oak flat raining acorns.

sections.heading: Where trails come together
sections.text: Jamie McKay looks for spots where several trails pinch together, like a creek crossing, the head of a draw, or a clear lane through a blowdown, because deer come from several directions instead of down one trail. His tip is to walk a trail until others join it. A listicle from Downwind Hunting adds that deer follow benches, the flat shelves on a hillside, like sidewalks, so places where benches meet are natural intersections.

sections.heading: Stay on the outside edge
sections.text: When you find the movement, set up on its outside edge and don't push another 30 yards past it. If a deer ends up behind you after you've crossed its trail, the hunt is blown. If you need deer closer, Sturgis pulls them in with a mock scrape about 25 yards in front of you, a water hole, or a dropped tree on private land. Downwind Hunting says brush piles from your lane cuttings can squeeze a corridor 15 to 20 yards narrower, but that number comes only from a listicle.

lessons.tryThis: For one morning stand you already have, stand at the tree and look downwind. Name what's there. If it's a trail or a feeding area, find a spot nearby where the downwind side is a creek, a drop-off, or thick brush instead.
lessons.headsUp: Not everyone loves mornings. McKay says he rarely catches big bucks going back to bed and prefers evenings at the bedding edge, while Sturgis's crew gets most of their bucks on morning stands. Sturgis's morning stands sit in the cover near the bedding, never in it.

check.q: Why does Sturgis put morning stands back in the cover?
check.a: Deer come back from food to cover in the morning, so you wait where they're heading.

check.q: You plan to call from a stand. What should be downwind of you?
check.a: Ground a deer won't use, like water or a steep drop, so a called buck can't circle downwind and smell you.

lessons.title: Choosing the tree
lessons.hook: You found the spot. Now there are five trees that could work, and one of them is fat, straight, and easy to climb. It's tempting. But the tree decides whether a deer walks past a shape it can't read or looks up and sees a person.

sections.heading: Cover behind you beats cover in front
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis and North American Whitetail both want lots of cover behind you and to the sides, like limbs, cedars, other trees, or the slope of a ridge. A deer that looks up sees trunk and branches instead of a human outline, and your lanes in front stay open. That's why a smaller tree in front of the cover often beats a big one buried in it. Sturgis once picked an 8 to 10 inch red cedar over bigger trees and big white oaks because it sat in front of the cover and needed far fewer limbs cut.

sections.heading: Don't sit against the sky
sections.text: Near a ridge top, set up far enough down the slope that you have hill behind you, even if the best sign is on top. A deer looking uphill will pick out a hunter against the sky. This comes from one guest on Southern Outdoorsmen, so treat it as a tip.

sections.heading: The right tree, not the easy one
sections.text: Next Step Outdoors makes the point that a climbing stand needs a perfectly straight tree with no branches, and that forces you into the wrong spot. Pick the tree that's right for the deer. A saddle or a light hang-on with sticks can go where a climber can't. The two sources split on saddles, though. Relentless Sportsman, who hunts pressured public land, says a branchy tree like a pine is for a hang-on, where the limbs hide you and hold gear, and a saddle needs a clean trunk so you can move around it.

sections.heading: In a saddle, the trunk is your cover
sections.text: In a saddle, put the trunk between you and where you expect deer, then draw and shoot around it, ideally to your strong side. Next Step Outdoors says a deer coming head-on can't see you unless the tree is tiny, so you can hunt trees with almost no cover. The trouble is deer from the side or behind. Relentless Sportsman says turning around the tree for them usually gets you picked off, even by does and fawns.

sections.heading: Walk it like a deer
sections.text: The Hunting Public crew doesn't just drop a pin when they find a tree. They walk the deer trail and look back at it the way a deer would. Can he see you? Where can you draw, maybe when he passes behind a small cedar? Which branches are in the way? They note how high the best cover is (a fork at 18 feet means 4 sticks), whether it suits a saddle or a stand, which wind it's for, and the route out.

lessons.tryThis: At your next spot, pick two candidate trees. Walk the trail past both and look at each from the deer's side. Choose the one with more cover behind you, even if it's the harder climb.
lessons.headsUp: Saddles and branchy trees are disputed. Next Step Outdoors says a saddle works on crooked and branchy trees a climber can't use. Relentless Sportsman says branches kill a saddle's ability to move around the tree, and a hang-on fits more trees. Both agree the climber is the most limited.

check.q: A big straight oak sits in the middle of thick cover, and a smaller tree sits in front of it. Which is usually better?
check.a: Often the smaller tree in front, because the cover behind you breaks your outline and your lanes stay open.

check.q: Why set up below a ridge top instead of on it?
check.a: A deer looking uphill can pick you out against the sky.

lessons.title: Height, angle, and your shot
lessons.hook: It's easy to figure higher is better. Then a buck walks in at six yards, and from way up the tree there's no shot at all because the angle is straight down. Height is a tradeoff, and so is which way your stand faces.

sections.heading: You don't need to be very high
sections.text: Two bowhunters agree here. Samko Trad Bow sits 14 to 18 feet on about 70 percent of hunts, with 15 to 16 as his sweet spot, and often only 10 to 12. Bow Only Outdoors typically sits 14 to 18 and adds a rope aider to reach 20 to 22 feet only when a spot needs it. Their reason is the angle. From 20 feet, Samko says, you lose the 5 to 8 yard shots and can only shoot from about 12 yards out, yet his average shot is about 9 yards. He also says height gives no real wind benefit until 25 to 30 feet and steep angles cause one-lung hits. Bow Only Outdoors shot their biggest buck from about 8 feet. Their rule is to climb to the cover, meaning only as high as the tree's cover needs.

sections.heading: The case for 20 feet
sections.text: A Downwind Hunting listicle says to hang at 20 to 22 feet instead of the usual 12 to 15. It cites Texas A&M research that scent disperses better from higher up, and says height cuts the chance a deer picks out your outline and makes little accuracy difference at 15 to 30 yards. That study is cited, not shown, and it's the only source on this side.

sections.heading: Face the shot before you hang
sections.text: Before you hang a stand or saddle, decide where your most likely shot will be, like where deer step into a field or the first opening on the trail. Then face the setup so that spot is in front of you or on your strong side. Next Step Outdoors puts it at roughly 7 to 11 o'clock for a right-handed shooter, with deer passing on your left, and the opposite for a lefty. Your bow is already pointed there, so you lift it off the hanger, draw, and shoot with little movement. Weak-side shots can be made, but they're harder.

sections.heading: Sit level and shoot seated
sections.text: Bow Only Outdoors sets a hang-on level or tilted just slightly back toward the tree, never forward or to the side, so you sit against the trunk instead of leaning out. Pick the bracket height for your lanes and any limbs you can hold. Then plan to take your expected shots sitting down. Jeff Sturgis says a standing human outline in a tree is probably the scariest thing a deer can see, so shooting seated cuts your movement. In a saddle, Next Step Outdoors hangs the bow on the side it comes off easiest and keeps the pack small on the belt so neither side is blocked.

lessons.tryThis: Before you hang your next stand, stand at the tree and point to where you expect the shot. Turn the setup so that spot is in front of you or on your strong side, and hang it only as high as the cover needs. Then practice that shot sitting down.
lessons.headsUp: Stand height is disputed, but the sides aren't equal. Two independent bowhunters, Samko and Bow Only Outdoors, say 14 to 18 feet is plenty. The only source for 20 to 22 feet is a single unverified listicle citing a study it doesn't show.

check.q: You're right-handed. Which side should the trail pass on?
check.a: Your left, roughly 7 to 11 o'clock, so the shot is on your strong side.

check.q: What do you lose by climbing to 20 feet with a bow?
check.a: The very close shots, because the angle gets too steep, and steep angles can cause one-lung hits.

lessons.title: Lanes and stand work
lessons.hook: Hanging a stand means cutting, stepping, and touching things in the exact spot you want deer to feel safe. Do it at the wrong time or cut too much, and you can wreck the spot before you ever hunt it. Here's how to do the work quietly.

sections.heading: Keep lanes small
sections.text: North American Whitetail says to trim just enough to get an arrow through where you expect a deer to stop. Jeff Sturgis clears about three small shooting holes instead of wide lanes and puts a mock scrape in the middle one, so you see the buck in one hole and shoot him in the next. Leave the low brush standing behind and around the stand, and pile your cuttings there. You walk in behind a wall of brush, and deer are unlikely to push through it. Keep in mind the woods open up as leaves fall, so a lane that's snug in September is wide open by December.

sections.heading: Trim from up in the stand
sections.text: A lane that looks clear from the ground often has a branch across it up where your arrow actually travels, 15 to 20 feet off the ground. So trim while sitting in the stand at hunting height. This tip comes from a single Downwind Hunting listicle.

sections.heading: Do the work early
sections.text: The same listicle says to hang stands and cut lanes in July, not the week before season. Every cut, step, and bolt leaves scent, noise, and change that take weeks to fade, and three months ahead the spot smells like the woods again by October. It also says to use a fine-tooth pruning saw instead of loppers, because lopper cuts stay green and sappy and bleed scent for days.

sections.heading: Or do it in the rain
sections.text: Sturgis's answer for work during the season is to hang, move, and maintain stands during moderate or hard rain with lots of wind. Your scent doesn't linger and the commotion hides you, so it's a non-event unless you spook deer right at the spot. Skip thunder and lightning, still wear your harness, and scout for fresh sign while you're there. Avoid doing it on a hot, sweaty day unless you won't hunt there for a week.

sections.heading: Early season leaves help and hurt
sections.text: A guest on Southern Outdoorsmen points out that early season leaves let you tuck into a hardwood and get away with much more than later on. The catch is that the leaves on the ground are old and damp, so deer walk in almost silently, and a big buck got to 25 yards before he noticed. So keep your eyes up and watch constantly, because you won't always hear them coming. He also warns that early season wind is finicky and swirls, in flat land, hills, and mountains alike. That's one source's experience, so treat it as a tip.

lessons.tryThis: Before your next stand job, check the forecast for a day of steady rain and wind, and plan the work for then. When you cut, count your lanes and stop at three small holes.
lessons.headsUp: The summer-work rule, the saw tip, and the trim-from-the-stand tip all come from one unverified listicle. Sturgis's rain-and-wind method is a hunter's own practice and works during the season too, so if you missed summer, wait for weather instead.

check.q: Why keep shooting lanes smaller than seems necessary in September?
check.a: The woods open up as leaves fall, so a snug lane now is wide open later.

check.q: It's mid October and you need to move a stand. When should you do it?
check.a: During moderate or hard rain with wind, not thunderstorms, so your scent and noise don't linger.

units.goal: Find deer first, then read what they left.

lessons.title: Find the deer first
lessons.hook: It's easy to fall in love with a spot on the map, hang a stand, and wait. Weeks later you've seen nothing, and you still don't know whether a good buck even lives there. Experienced hunters flip the order. They find the deer first, and only then worry about the tree.

sections.heading: No deer, no hunt
sections.text: Lee Ellis of Seek One puts it bluntly. A great setup does nothing if no deer walks by it, and if you're not around a big deer you're not going to kill one. His crew's motto is to leave no stone unturned because the search never stops, and he says staying mobile is a big part of why they succeed. So on new ground, make sure deer, and a good buck, actually live there before you fuss over the setup. If a spot has no good deer, move on to the next one and keep going until you find one.

sections.heading: Match the method to the country
sections.text: Where you can see a long way, like open country in South Dakota, glass. Watching deer from a distance shows you where they are and where they cross. Mark Kenyon of MeatEater says that seeing where the young deer go and where the buck hangs back teaches you a travel pattern you can then spot anywhere. A trail camera can help connect the dots, but watching is how you really see it. The Hunting Public crew, who travel to unfamiliar states on short public-land trips, drive the roads and read soft-dirt ditches for tracks, then go in where they see a bunch. In thick country they walk for fresh droppings, stirred-up leaves, fresh tracks, and the odd fresh rub. On scouting days they'll even spook deer on purpose to see how they were bedded and what they were eating, but never in a spot they plan to hunt that week.

sections.heading: Map it first, then walk it
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis scouts by air first and by foot second. At home he uses aerial photos and topo maps to find benches, saddles, and points, and even in unbroken forest the shaded sides of the hills show where the ridges run. Then he walks the spots he picked and checks them off one at a time on a laminated map card, or a phone screenshot he colors in. With a list, you can check one important place in an hour instead of wandering into other hunters' sign. Derek Dixon, who studies bucks with thermal drones, explains why the walking matters. A bowl that looks steep on the map can hold a small bench that deer hammer, and of ten promising spots on a map, he finds maybe two are worth hunting.

sections.heading: Speed-scout, then find the pattern
sections.text: On a short trip, the Hunting Public crew speed-scouts with a buddy. One person gets dropped off, walks about half a mile in, spends about 30 minutes, and walks back out, while the other drives half a mile up the road and does the same. They regroup, compare notes, and repeat that 10 to 15 times a day, aiming for 5 or 6 backup spots. They did this in thick, flat Michigan country with a steady wind and say mountains are a different story. Be honest about remote spots, too, because 3 miles on a map can be a 3-hour walk in the dark. Once you find deer, work out what the spot is, like the kind of thicket they bed in, which acorns just fell, or the elevation, and look for the same thing in three or four other places. In the Georgia mountains the crew found deer hammering red oak acorns on one bench band in the drainages, and matching it kept them walking into fresh sign.

lessons.tryThis: Pick three spots on a map of a place you hunt and mark them on a screenshot. Walk each one this month, spend about half an hour there, and color it in only after you've seen fresh sign with your own eyes.

check.q: You've found a great-looking stand site, but there's no sign a good buck lives nearby. What now?
check.a: Move on and keep looking. A setup is worthless if no good deer walks by it.

check.q: Why walk a spot you found on a map before trusting it?
check.a: Maps miss how deer actually use the land. Of ten spots that look good on a map, maybe two are worth hunting.

lessons.title: Reading rubs and scrapes
lessons.hook: The first time you find a torn-up sapling or a pawed-out patch of dirt, it feels like you've found the buck's front door. Sometimes you have. More often you've found one moment in his day. Learning which sign matters, and which is just noise, will save you a lot of empty sits.

sections.heading: Most sign is random
sections.text: Derek Dixon watched with thermal drones as a mature buck made about half a dozen small, random scrapes along one morning route, and he saw bucks rub trees 20 or more times in a day, in daylight. Whitetail Evolution adds that pre-rut and rut bucks leave lots of random sign, a subordinate buck that got pushed off may tear up a spot out of frustration, and a fresh rub only proves a buck was there once. So don't build a hunt around new, random sign. Mark it on your map and check next year. Sign that shows up in the same spot year after year earns a stand.

sections.heading: Signposts at landmarks
sections.text: Some scrapes and rubs sit at landmarks, like terrain features, habitat edges, certain flats that get scraped every season, tall lone trees left in big clearcuts, young beech trees that hold their leaves late, or a lone cedar in the hardwoods. Dixon watched bucks reach a signpost scrape or habitat edge and then change direction, as if they'd just figured out where they were. Beau Martonik finds scrapes and sheds under tall hemlocks left standing in big Pennsylvania cuts, which he compares to a lighthouse for a boat at night. Mike Rex, who hunts southeast Ohio, thinks something about the wind currents and those trees makes the same places right for deer year after year, and where cedars are scarce, every passing buck rubs a lone one.

sections.heading: What a rub can and can't tell you
sections.text: Rex says a rub on a bigger tree usually means an older buck, though not necessarily a big rack, because he rarely sees spikes and yearlings hit big trees. An area torn up with lots of rubs and scrapes means bucks of similar age are overlapping and competing, which is encouraging. He doesn't trust track size, since he's killed big deer with small feet, and he says actually seeing a deer beats all sign. Whitetail Evolution checks which side of the trees the rubs face on a trail between food and bedding. Rubs facing the food hint at a morning trail back to bed, and rubs facing the bedding hint at an afternoon trail to food. He calls it far from an exact science, so treat it as a hint.

sections.heading: The quiet sign matters more
sections.text: Jamie McKay's top advice is to hunt deer, hunt the sign, hunt the droppings, and hunt the trails. He means the everyday stuff, like buds and tender tips bitten off (hunters call that browse), faint tracks, droppings, and faint trails. Several of his best bucks came from spots where you'd be lucky to find a rub or scrape, and he's sat over heavy rubs and scrapes and seen nothing. When he took a younger hunter scouting, the young hunter didn't see the subtle sign until McKay pointed it out, so expect it to take practice.

sections.heading: Old sign hides
sections.text: McKay also warns about scouting after the season or in spring and summer. Once beech trees finally drop their leaves, they bury most scrapes, which he estimated at 95 percent in one hot area, and old rubs fade. Someone who didn't know the spot would walk right past it. So don't write off an area for lack of scrapes and rubs. Look for the faint remains, and trust what you saw there in the fall.

lessons.tryThis: On your next walk, drop a pin with the date on every rub and scrape you find. Next year, go back and see which ones showed up again. The repeat spots are the ones worth a stand.

check.q: You find one fresh rub on a trail you've never seen used. Do you hang a stand?
check.a: Not yet. Mark it and see if it shows up again. A single fresh rub only proves a buck was there once.

check.q: What does a rub on a big tree usually tell you?
check.a: That an older buck probably made it, though not necessarily one with a big rack.

lessons.title: Finding beds
lessons.hook: Food is easy to find, but deer spend most of the daylight lying down. If you understand why a deer picks one spot to bed, you can find beds on ground you've never walked, and you can guess where bucks will travel once the rut starts.

sections.heading: Beds sit on the edge
sections.text: When Derek Dixon looks for bedding, on a map or on the ground, he starts with habitat edges and variety, like a wood edge against an old clearcut. Then he looks for food and water close by, then terrain features such as saddles. His drone work showed bucks don't always bed on the textbook point, and mixed cover is the strongest clue. No food or water means few deer. On the ground, don't assume deer bed in the middle of the thick stuff. Look on the edge of the cover, where a deer can see danger coming from a distance, has the wind at its back, and can escape straight back through the thick.

sections.heading: Learn why a bed gets used
sections.text: The Hunting Public crew says learning how and why deer pick beds is what turned their big buck hunting around. The best beds they find have permanent water and several food sources within 40 to 50 yards, in places people rarely go. Their example was a willow patch only 10 by 15 yards at the bottom of a hole next to water, with two big beds on the end looking across the water to the far hillside. Once you know why a bed is there, you can predict similar spots across the landscape.

sections.heading: Beds in a marsh
sections.text: Next Step Outdoors says deer won't bed in open marsh grass. They want shade and cover at their back, a view of where danger would come from, and plenty of ways out. So look for structure, like trees or woody shrubs out in the grass, or any high spot, since trees and shrubs only grow out there on ground dry enough to bed on. Confirm it with beds holding hair, matted grass, droppings, and grass tips nipped off around the bed.

sections.heading: Slow down and read the bed
sections.text: When you find a promising spot, Next Step Outdoors spends real time in it, about 10 minutes in an area about 40 by 50 yards, looking at individual beds, rubs, tracks, and sheds before deciding what it is. A bed with a rub right beside it may be a buck bed. Lots of small tracks and several small beds on a high spot near food point to a doe family group. In one spot they found old hair under the leaves with small rubs nearby. That suggested a buck bedded there earlier in the season and left once pressure picked up or the grass got knocked down, so it may have been a spare bed rather than his main one.

sections.heading: Mark the does, and use the snow
sections.text: All year, the Hunting Public crew marks every spot where they keep finding does bedded, even if they can't tell it's the same deer. In the rut, bucks play connect-the-dots between doe bedding areas, so those marks become your rut spots. Snow helps too. After a fresh winter snow, Mike Rex walks and looks for beds. In his southeast Ohio hills the one consistent pattern was beds on south-facing slopes, where it's warmer and the snow melts first. Beyond that he found no rhyme or reason, which is why he shifted to hunting food and the trails into it.

lessons.tryThis: The next time you jump a deer or find a bed, stop and spend ten minutes there. Note which way the bed faces, where the wind would come from, what food and water sit within about 50 yards, and how the deer would escape. Mark it on your map as a doe bed or a possible buck bed.
lessons.headsUp: Jeff Sturgis disagrees with Rex about late-season beds. He says south-slope bedding is mostly a myth and that deer bed on whichever slope is sheltered from the wind. Neither view comes from research, so check both against your own snow scouting.

check.q: Where in a patch of thick cover should you expect to find beds?
check.a: On the edge, where a deer can see danger coming, has the wind at its back, and can escape into the thick stuff.

check.q: Why mark doe bedding areas if you're hunting bucks?
check.a: In the rut, bucks travel between doe bedding areas, so those marks become your rut spots.

lessons.title: Reading food and feed trees
lessons.hook: In early fall, one oak dropping the right acorns can hold every deer in the area, and a week later they're gone somewhere else. That's frustrating until you learn to read what's under the trees and to find the next food before the deer switch to it.

sections.heading: Fresh beats a lot
sections.text: Judge sign by how fresh it is, not by how much there is. A rub bleeding sap from this morning beats a woods full of old droppings and rubs. The Hunting Public crew explains the trap. After deer feed in one spot for two weeks sign is everywhere, but they may already be gone. In Missouri, white oaks drop from late August or early September, and by late September, when everyone hunts that sign, the deer have moved on. If a spot that's always been hot has no fresh sign this year, scout on the way out and find where the deer went. Jamie McKay's usual creek bottom had no sign one year, and moving up into thick browse got him into bucks. Patterns can come back, though. One Southern Outdoorsmen host's camera spot had bucks one year, nothing the next, and then bucks doing exactly what they'd done two summers earlier, so keep cameras on known spots across years.

sections.heading: Read the ground under the tree
sections.text: Hunt the oak deer are feeding on, not the one with the most acorns. The Southern Outdoorsmen hosts and one of their guests read the same sign, which is leaves mulched up and turned over with individual hoof prints (not turkey scratching), plus acorn caps and busted pieces. Ground covered in whole acorns is not a good sign, because if they're still lying there, deer aren't eating them. Squirrels cutting in a tree tell you it's dropping. Don't rely on droppings, since one guest has killed many deer at torn-up white oaks with hardly any droppings under them. Rain helps you age the sign by laying the leaves back down, so if you check a tree an hour or two after a rain and the leaves are freshly torn up with wet undersides, deer were just there.

sections.heading: Move when the good oaks drop
sections.text: Check feed sign every time you walk out. One guest watched sign under one or two big chestnut oaks get heavier every trip, but the deer only shifted once all the white oaks were dropping. Feed sign there got heavy within a couple of days, and bucks came in on his first or second sit. So when a whole group of preferred oaks starts dropping hard, move to them right away. Don't write off chestnut oaks either. Many chestnut oak ridges are covered in acorns that just rot, so hunters decide deer don't eat them, when often deer are feeding on only a couple of trees.

sections.heading: Look up in summer, walk more in fall
sections.text: The Hunting Public crew checks the acorn crop in summer with binoculars. Pick an isolated limb with only sky behind it, sit under the tree, and brace the binoculars on a trekking pole. By late summer you can see the acorns. Don't trust someone else's mast report, since one mountain can be loaded while one 15 miles away is nearly bare. And if you think feed trees don't work where you hunt, a Southern Outdoorsmen guest says you probably aren't walking enough. You won't find a hot tree in every 5-acre patch, and it's harder in a heavy mast year, when deer have 100 trees to choose from instead of 10.

sections.heading: Scout three weeks ahead
sections.text: Grant Woods of GrowingDeer.tv says not to count on the early-season food pattern lasting. Watch for it to fade, with soybeans turning yellow, native plants hardening off and going to seed, and acorns starting to drop. When acorns start falling, patterns change fast and deer seem to vanish. Their needs are changing too, from high-protein summer food for antlers and milk toward carbs that build fat for the rut and winter, when a buck can lose up to 30 percent of his body weight. So scout ahead to know what deer will be eating in about three weeks, and move your stands when they switch.

lessons.tryThis: Walk to three oaks near where you hunt this week. Under each one, look for mulched leaves with hoof prints, caps, and busted pieces, compared with whole acorns lying untouched. Go back after the next rain and see which tree is freshly torn up.

check.q: One oak has the ground covered in whole acorns. Another is torn up with caps and pieces. Which do you hunt?
check.a: The torn-up one. Whole acorns lying on the ground mean deer aren't eating them.

check.q: A spot that was hot last year has no fresh sign. What do you do?
check.a: Don't sit and wait. Scout on the way out, find where the deer moved, and go there.

lessons.title: When and how to scout
lessons.hook: Scouting at the wrong time can cost you the very deer you're trying to learn about, because every trip into the woods leaves scent and pushes deer. The trick is to do your heavy scouting when it can't hurt your season, and to learn a little from every walk once the season starts.

sections.heading: Scout more than you hunt
sections.text: A Southern Outdoorsmen guest who spent his first five years relearning the mountains, mostly walking with a stand on his back, says to spend two to three times as much time scouting as hunting, especially when you're starting out, and to ask why each trail is where it is. Jeff Sturgis uses warm days that way. When movement is poor, like the warm days before a front in the pre-rut, he scouts, checks cameras, or takes an easy evening sit, and stays out of his best morning spots until the cold arrives. There's research behind the idea. A Mississippi State GPS-collar study found bucks bed more and move less when the next day is 10 degrees or more warmer, and suggests using that day to scout or hang cameras. No source says what counts as warm in general, though.

sections.heading: Late winter is the time to dig in
sections.text: Do your invasive scouting in late winter, before green-up. Next Step Outdoors says February to April, and the Hunting Public says February and March. The woods are open and last season's sign is still readable, and once everything is green, thorny, and full of poison ivy, it's very hard. Next Step picks up sheds on those walks, which shows which bucks made it through the season. The Hunting Public crew backtracks from sign they noted during the season, like a line of scrapes along an access path, then picks the tree for each wind and works out how to get in at 3 AM. In the fall they make quick checks about every two weeks, and when the sign turns fresh and the forecast wind matches the tree, they hunt it that weekend.

sections.heading: After gun season and after snow
sections.text: In a heavily hunted state, the Hunting Public crew scouts right after gun season closes. Places full of deer then are where the pressure pushed them, the spots nobody went, so they target those holes the next gun season, especially thick, nasty cover with close shots. He'd rather be there with open sights and shoot one at 13 steps than look for a long scope shot like most gun hunters. Fresh snow is another gift. The Downwind Hunting list says to walk the whole property after about 2 inches of new snow and photograph every trail, noting heavy traffic versus single tracks, since the snow records roughly the last 12 hours of what deer actually did. That one comes only from a listicle, so treat it as an idea to try.

sections.heading: Scout on every walk in and out
sections.text: During the season, Sturgis scouts every time he walks to and from a stand, especially in wind and rain, since bad weather lets you look without leaving a footprint. He looks for rubs, fresh scrapes, tracks, and beaten-down trails that are just starting to form, and he lightly checks field edges near the stands he trusts least. Deer patterns change through the fall, which he calls the annual whitetail shift, and trails used heavily by late October often weren't being used in mid-September.

sections.heading: The observation sit
sections.text: Whitetail Evolution spends warm, wrong-wind, or poor-weather early-season days on observation sits instead of burning a good stand. Sit an edge stand you can reach without pushing into the property, like one off a road, by the barn, or on the property line, that looks into a destination food plot. Watch which trails deer use in and out and where your target buck comes from. Bring your bow, because sometimes the buck walks by. His example was a ladder stand in a bur oak dropping acorns, 5 yards from his pole barn. If nothing happens, you've lost nothing.

lessons.tryThis: Look at the forecast for the next warm, low-movement day. Plan it as a scouting day or an observation sit from an edge you can reach without walking through the property, and save your best morning stand for when the cold comes.

check.q: When is the best time for heavy, in-the-woods scouting?
check.a: Late winter and early spring, before green-up, when it can't hurt your season and last year's sign is still readable.

check.q: It's a warm, wrong-wind day early in the season. What's a good use of it?
check.a: Scout, check cameras, or take an observation sit from an edge stand looking into food, and stay out of your best spots.

units.goal: What photos really tell you (and what they don't).

lessons.title: Where to hang a camera
lessons.hook: Your first trail camera usually ends up strapped to a tree at chest height, pointed at the first trail you found. It takes pictures, so it feels like it's working. But where and how you hang it decides whether it shows you the buck or teaches him to avoid the spot.

sections.heading: Cameras show direction and timing
sections.text: Grant Woods uses cameras to learn which way deer move through an area and at what time. If lots of deer pass a camera but aren't feeding there, they're headed somewhere to eat. So back out along the direction they're traveling and scout until you find that food, because that's where you can set up. Only Woods teaches this in our sources, but it's a simple way to turn a pile of photos into a plan.

sections.heading: Up high, hidden, and dim
sections.text: Deer stare at glowing red infrared bulbs, and Jeff Sturgis of Whitetail Habitat Solutions says mature bucks learn to avoid a camera from 100 yards. He mounts cameras 6 to 7 feet up, angled down, on low glow and the shortest flash range he needs, about 15 to 20 feet at a mock scrape. A Kentucky outfitter's buck stared at a bright camera and backed off, and after it was dimmed the same buck worked the scrape without noticing. Mike Rex agrees that up high or concealed beats eye level. In a new area, Rex starts on travel corridors, pinch points, and food or the trails leading to it, and when a camera is working he adds a second one rather than moving it.

sections.heading: Hang it where trails cross
sections.text: Jamie McKay moved one camera about 300 yards, from a single trail on a bluff top to a spot where several trails intersect. It went from one big buck to two, a big 10 and an 8, on the same camera. It's one hunter's example, but it lines up with starting cameras at pinch points.

sections.heading: A camera on a scrape
sections.text: Sturgis and Next Step Outdoors both run cameras on scrapes. Sturgis's setup is about 6 feet high, angled down, off to the side about 15 feet, with the scrape in the left or right third of the frame so it also covers the trail. Many cameras trigger on the center of the frame, so a branch swinging there gives you false triggers. Then read the timing. A buck hitting it close to daylight is bedded nearby, every day means a bed close by, and about once a week means he's just checking for does. Expect far fewer pictures than at food.

sections.heading: But not on a hot natural scrape
sections.text: Mike Rex has learned that walking in to hang a camera near a natural scrape that's getting hit all the time shuts it down faster than anything, probably from your scent and the intrusion. Scrapes are mostly hit at night anyway. He watches from a distance or puts the camera on the trails leading to it.

lessons.tryThis: Take one camera you already have out and move it up to about 6 or 7 feet, angled down, at a spot where two or more trails cross. Turn the flash to the shortest range you need.
lessons.headsUp: The scrape advice looks like a contradiction, but the details differ. Sturgis's cameras are mostly on mock scrapes he set weeks before season, while Rex is warning about walking into a live natural scrape during the season. Sturgis and Rex also differ on flash. Sturgis says a quick white flash bothers deer less than bulbs that stay lit, and Rex says some deer bolt at a flash.

check.q: Lots of deer pass your camera but none feed there. What does that tell you?
check.a: They're heading to food somewhere. Follow their direction of travel and scout for it.

check.q: Why put the scrape off to one side of the frame instead of in the center?
check.a: Many cameras trigger on the center, so something moving there causes false triggers, and the side placement also covers the trail.

lessons.title: What a photo really tells you
lessons.hook: You pull a card and there he is, the buck you've been hoping for, at 2:14 in the morning. It's easy to read too much or too little into that one frame. The hunters here don't agree on what it means, so it helps to know what each side sees.

sections.heading: One photo means more visits than you saw
sections.text: Derek Dixon, who films bucks with thermal drones, would guess a buck on camera once is there 6 to 10 times a week, counting night. Beau Martonik figures one daylight photo a week means 3 or 4 daylight visits, and he's sat great rut days with bucks cruising and none walking in front of a camera 20 yards away. So treat one photo as a sign the buck uses that area a lot. Hunt it with patience, protect your access, consider a couple of stand options, and don't wait for a cell camera to show him before you go.

sections.heading: Don't hunt the exact camera tree
sections.text: Jamie McKay sees it from the other side. A photo tells you where the buck was yesterday, not where he is today, and hanging a stand right on the camera spot is what his hosts call "lottery hunting." McKay had one 8-point on camera, hunted that spot twice with no luck, then killed him back at his doe group. So he uses cameras to learn what's in the area and hunts the doe groups, trails, and sign nearby.

sections.heading: Night-only doesn't mean nocturnal
sections.text: This one has data behind it. Dixon went back and filmed bucks that showed up only at night on October cameras, and he found them moving around all day, just not where the cameras were. So when a buck only appears in the dark, don't write him off. Look for where he spends daylight, like deep timber where he's feeding on acorns.

sections.heading: Count day photos against night photos
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis wants fewer nighttime pictures than daylight ones on his ground, or at worst an even split. If most photos come at night, the place is being hunted too hard or deer only use it as a night food source, and you need to change how you hunt and get in. He says mature bucks do 90 to 95 percent of their moving after dark, over about 3 square miles, and an older buck learns which property isn't safe in daylight and stops coming. One buck missing from his cameras for 2 years was shot by a neighbor half a mile away who had pictures of him all along.

sections.heading: Compare years
sections.text: Whitetail Evolution compares their camera photos from year to year to see whether their bucks follow the usual pattern from collared-buck studies. That pattern is bedded most of the day, moving at night, and heading back to bed right before sunup. Their bucks mostly match, and that tells them when not to push in.

lessons.tryThis: Sort last season's buck photos into day and night piles for each camera. If one spot is almost all night, change how you get in there before you hunt it again.
lessons.headsUp: Dixon and McKay disagree about what to do with a photo. Dixon, whose view is backed by drone filming, says hunt that area patiently with a couple of stands. McKay says don't sit the camera spot and hunt the doe groups nearby instead. Both agree the buck lives in the general area. Also note Sturgis's night figures are his experience, not a measured study in these notes.

check.q: Your buck only shows up on camera at night. What should you assume?
check.a: Not that he's nocturnal. He's probably up in daylight somewhere else, so look for where.

check.q: Most photos on your property are at night. What does Sturgis say that means?
check.a: The ground is being hunted too hard or used only as night food, so change how you hunt and access it.

lessons.title: When a buck disappears
lessons.hook: For three weeks a buck shows up on the same camera, then nothing. It's natural to assume a neighbor shot him or a car got him. More often he's just somewhere else, and knowing why he left tells you where to look.

sections.heading: Missing is not the same as dead
sections.text: This part is measured. Bronson Strickland's MSU GPS-collar study found a buck's daily range stayed remarkably steady at about 200 acres every week from September to February. Outside the rut he used the same 200 acres day after day, overlapping "like rose petals." In the rut it was a different 200 acres each day. Strickland expected rut ranges to jump to 600 acres, and they didn't. So a buck missing for a few days in the rut has most likely shifted his daily area. Over longer stretches, Mike Rex says a buck may get pushed out by a bully buck and show back up a year or two later. That's hunter experience, and it has happened to Rex many times.

sections.heading: When a scrape goes cold
sections.text: The flip side comes from Jeff Sturgis. Mature bucks make far more rubs and scrapes than young ones, and on his land, scrapes that went cold often did so right after they shot the buck that lived there. So if a mock scrape that used to get hit hard stays quiet for a year or two, consider that the buck may be gone before you blame the setup. He says consider it, not assume it.

sections.heading: The August lap
sections.text: Lee Ellis of Seek One has his cameras on his fall spots by early August. Summer ranges are small, and in August bucks seem to make a one-time "reconnaissance lap" of their fall range, checking the does, other bucks, and whether the woods got logged. A buck you haven't seen all summer passes once and vanishes until he moves in during October or November. That single photo tells you he's around. Ellis puts it around the third week of August, and Beau Martonik sees it more in the first or second week.

sections.heading: Velvet shed changes everything
sections.text: When bucks shed velvet, rising testosterone makes them testy. Bachelor groups break up, and food sources change at the same time. Grant Woods says a patterned buck that vanishes then has shifted within his home range, so scout for his new core, meaning his current food, water, cover, and security, and put out several cameras running around the clock. Jamie McKay says bucks often move three or four miles after velvet, so he doesn't count on summer bucks. He uses summer to learn the ground and only counts a buck once he's on camera in hard antler.

lessons.tryThis: Write down the date each of your bucks last showed on camera. When one goes missing, check whether it's the rut or velvet shed before you decide what happened, and give him time.
lessons.headsUp: Woods and McKay disagree about velvet shed. Woods says the buck moved within his home range and you should go find him. McKay says he may be three or four miles gone and you shouldn't count on him. Both agree the summer pattern breaks at velvet shed.

check.q: A regular buck disappears from your cameras for four days in the rut. What's most likely?
check.a: He shifted to a different daily area, since in the rut bucks use a different 200 acres each day.

check.q: A mock scrape that was hot for years goes quiet for two seasons. What should you consider first?
check.a: That the buck using it may be gone, before you blame the setup.

lessons.title: Running cameras without ruining the spot
lessons.hook: Checking cameras is fun, and that's the problem. Every trip to pull a card is a walk through the woods you want deer to feel safe in. The best camera hunters check less, time their visits, and let the cameras sit.

sections.heading: Check less often
sections.text: Don't make special trips to check cameras during the season. A Downwind Hunting listicle says to check SD-card cameras no more than about once every 14 days, citing Auburn research that weekly or more frequent checks changed how mature bucks used an area. That study is second-hand and not verified. Jeff Sturgis makes the same point from experience. He's watched clients drive around pulling every card the Friday night they arrive, and it hurts not just that hunt but the next week or two. Use cellular cameras, or swap cards only when you're already hunting that stand, in bad weather, or when you drive in after dark to get a deer.

sections.heading: Use the storm
sections.text: Sturgis uses hard rain and wind to change cards and batteries or add a camera, even in spots he normally can't reach during the season. In nasty weather deer are pinned down and can't see, hear, or smell well, so you slip in and out without them knowing. Skip real thunder and lightning.

sections.heading: Leave cameras where they are
sections.text: Lee Ellis doesn't pull a camera just because a promising spot shows nothing in summer or after 10 days. Bucks shift ranges when the season starts, and a buck may use a spot for just two weeks in November to breed the does there. Ellis and Beau Martonik both figure they've moved a camera a week before the buck showed. So leave them through the season, and only pull one that covered about 4 months with nothing. Long-running cameras also show you windows, like a late-season group of deer moving in, that lead you to the food they're on.

sections.heading: Let the ground take pictures too
sections.text: A track trap makes the dirt tell you what came through. Jamie McKay clears the leaves on both sides of a log across a trail, because deer hit the ground harder stepping over it, and rakes patches of trail bare. On a Southern Outdoorsmen episode, the advice is to rake a line across a ridge point deer travel, or blow the leaves off. Check it next trip for what passed and how big the tracks are. In a dry year it won't work, since hard ground doesn't hold tracks, and one listener had a bachelor group walk within 10 yards and leave none. Then that episode says to check soft creek crossings and put out cameras, moving each one after about 10 days with nothing.

lessons.tryThis: Pick a check schedule before the season and write it down, no more often than every two weeks per camera. Then watch the forecast for a day of hard rain and wind and save your card pulls for it.
lessons.headsUp: Ellis says never move a camera after 10 empty days, and the Southern Outdoorsmen episode says to move one after about 10 days with nothing. The situations differ. That advice was for searching fast for a buck in a dry late summer before the season, while Ellis is running cameras on known fall spots.

check.q: When is a good time to pull a card from a camera in a spot you usually stay out of?
check.a: During hard rain and wind, without thunder and lightning, when deer can't sense you well.

check.q: A new camera spot has shown nothing for 10 days in early fall. Pull it?
check.a: No. Bucks shift when the season starts. Leave it, and only pull it after about 4 months with nothing.

units.goal: Hunt the food deer are on right now.

lessons.title: Hunt the food that's hot right now
lessons.hook: Last fall the big oak on the ridge was covered in deer, so this year you go straight back to it. The ground underneath is bare and so are your trail cameras. Deer didn't forget the spot. The food moved, and they moved with it.

sections.heading: Every food has a window
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis of Whitetail Habitat Solutions says any one food, whether clover, beans, corn, or brassicas, draws deer for about 6 to 8 weeks of the season at most. In his upper Midwest country that means green beans in September, beans gone once they're harvested in October, standing corn not eaten until around November, and clover fading by early December. When a food source has a hole in its season, deer go elsewhere, so a buck only holds where some food lasts all season with no gaps. If deer hit a neighbor's field instead of yours, he looks at pressure, location, and cover before blaming the seed.

sections.heading: Start at the food and work back
sections.text: Food sets where everything else beds, so Sturgis starts every search for a buck at the current food source. On public land the "food of the moment" keeps changing. It might be a clearcut, oaks dropping acorns, an old homesite with apple trees, or a swamp edge where hardwoods turn to conifers. In Michigan's Upper Peninsula it can even be a cluster of bait sites at the end of dead-end roads for about two weeks after the gun opener.

sections.heading: Hunt the oaks dropping this year
sections.text: Three hunters agree here. Grant Woods and Jamie McKay use binoculars in late summer and early season to see which trees are loaded, and they don't sit under an oak just because it dropped the last two years. Woods says white oak acorns taste better, so deer go to them first, and a tree with no acorns this year probably has no deer this year. Red oaks don't make a crop every year, but McKay once found a red oak stand so thick with acorns "you could rake it up with a five gallon bucket," and three hunters killed good bucks there. A guest on Southern Outdoorsmen who hunts South Carolina and Georgia tells his guests a hot white oak in its window gives about a 90 percent chance at a shot, though not always at a buck.

sections.heading: Don't save a short window
sections.text: The Hunting Public crew says that if you find fresh sign and fresh rubs at the tail end of the white oak drop in the early season, hunt it now with an aggressive setup, even on an 80 degree evening. In big woods deer stay on white oak acorns for a very short time. The buck might be bedded 60 yards away and get up to feed about 30 minutes before dark, and you won't be hunting him there in two weeks anyway, so blowing him out costs little.

sections.heading: When the acorns fail
sections.text: In a bust acorn year, stop looking for the one dropping oak. On a Southern Outdoorsmen episode about an Alabama bust year, a hunter walked miles, found a few oaks with a little sign, and never saw a deer on them, while logged national forest had far more sign and deer. McKay found privet thickets with more droppings than a food plot. So hunt green browse where sunlight reaches the ground, like logged cuts, forest edges, and thickets of honeysuckle or greenbrier, and look for buds bitten off. Browse sign is subtle and takes more woodsmanship than spotting acorns.

lessons.tryThis: This week, glass the oaks on your property or hunting area and write down which ones are actually dropping and what kind they are. Then start your next scouting trip from the best one and work back toward bedding.
lessons.headsUp: Sources disagree on which oaks drop first. Sturgis, with northern examples, puts white oaks in early September and red oaks in October and November. The South Carolina and Georgia guest says red oaks start first and white oaks peak around late October. Both are regional. The Southern Outdoorsmen hosts note swamp chestnut oaks drop around Halloween in some places but mid September in South Georgia, so go by what's dropping where you hunt.

check.q: An oak was loaded with deer the last two falls. Should you hang a stand there this year?
check.a: Only if it's dropping acorns this year. Check with binoculars first.

check.q: Acorns are a bust this year. Where do deer go?
check.a: To whatever food is easy, often green browse in logged cuts, edges, and thickets where sunlight hits the ground.

lessons.title: Heat, drought, and water
lessons.hook: It's the first week of the season, it's hot, and it hasn't rained in weeks. Deer have been lying in dry cover all day, and when they get up, many of them will hit water before they reach the food.

sections.heading: In the heat, hunt the juiciest food
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis hunts the food with the most moisture when it's hot and dry. Fruit like apples, crabapples, pears, plums, and persimmons carries far more moisture than acorns, and deer that have sat dry all day crave it. Look for it just outside the bedding or on the way to the evening food. Lush green food, like brassicas, clover, or late beans, pulls deer too, because it's the opposite of the dry cover they bed in. On public land, find green spots where sunlight reaches the ground, like a wet swamp edge with clover.

sections.heading: Sit water on the way to food
sections.text: In heat or a long dry spell, Sturgis sits water that lies between the bedding and the evening food. Deer bedded high and dry hit it first thing when they get up. They won't drop 300 feet and walk 700 yards to a creek and back, but they'll drink on the way, and they keep doing it all season. On one warm opener he saw a 2 year old 8-point, a doe and fawn, and another doe at a single water hole. The drier it gets, the more they use it, and his tanks dropped 6 to 7 inches out of 20 to 24 after 18 days without rain. A drought also sets a pattern. The morning after the first real rain, with puddles everywhere, deer still came to his water holes, so keep hunting them for a while after rain returns.

sections.heading: Water matters in the rut too
sections.text: Water isn't just an early season trick. Sturgis hunts water holes in the pre-rut and rut, late October and November, even when it's cold, because bucks cruising and checking does cover more ground and work up a thirst. Whitetail Evolution, filming during a severe Midwest drought, says the best spot combines water with a perennial scrape on the downwind side of doe bedding or along the trail from bedding to food. In a drought, the whole herd leans on water more, so it matters even more.

sections.heading: One water source in dry mountains
sections.text: In mountain country, the Southern Outdoorsmen hosts recalled a seminar by Dylan Harper on North Georgia terrain. Look on the map for an area with very few spring heads or water sources, then find the one source in it and hunt around it. Where water is scarce, deer, bears, and everything else get pulled to that one spot. This is a secondhand summary of one talk, so treat it as a tip.

lessons.tryThis: On your next hot, dry scouting trip, look for water between a bedding area and the evening food. Check a creek edge, a pond, or a low wet spot, and see if the ground around it is covered in tracks.
lessons.headsUp: Almost everything here comes from Jeff Sturgis, and neither he nor anyone else gives a number for how hot counts as "hot" or how long a dry spell has to last. Treat these as patterns to watch for, not exact triggers.

check.q: It's hot and dry. Why sit water between bedding and food instead of a creek down in the bottom?
check.a: Deer drink on the way to food, but they won't make a long trip down to a creek and back.

check.q: It finally rains after a drought. Should you give up on the water hole?
check.a: Not right away. Deer kept coming to Sturgis's water holes after the first rain because the drought set the pattern.

lessons.title: Building a water hole
lessons.hook: A water hole is something you can build yourself, and in the right spot a buck may visit it in daylight far more often than he reaches the food. Jeff Sturgis builds and hunts them, and all of this lesson comes from him. Done right, one can be hunted within a few weeks. Done wrong, it scares deer off for months.

sections.heading: Put it on the route
sections.text: Place the water hole on the travel route between bedding and food, somewhere secure in the woods where deer already cruise and where you can picture a big buck stopping in the middle of the day. Don't put it in the bedding, in the food plot, or somewhere you'd have to pull deer 100 yards to reach. In the right spot a mature buck may drink every other day in daylight, while he might reach the food in daylight once a week or less. Sturgis's target buck was showing up within 3 to 9 minutes of shooting light. More deer using it means more scent, trails, rubs, and scrapes, which makes them even more comfortable there.

sections.heading: Make it look like it belongs
sections.text: Bury the tank so no edge sticks out, and never set it on top of the ground. When Sturgis's tanks were only half buried, does stomped, stared, and ran, and a whole herd split and left. Use a black tank instead of white or light blue. Rake the area smooth and seed it before a rain, so a green carpet grows instead of a bare dirt pad, and clear dead brush out of view. A bare pad and bright colors look like something that doesn't belong and can keep deer wary for months.

sections.heading: Give it about three weeks
sections.text: Sturgis put one in on August 30 to hunt the September 19 opener, and his target buck was using it by day 11. Young bucks come right in within a day or two. Does and fawns hesitate and then get used to it quickly, and older bucks are slower but come. He's also had success putting one in during late September or early October to hunt it in the rut.

sections.heading: Don't let it go dry
sections.text: Every trip to fill a water hole spooks deer, so size it to last. A 100 gallon tank lasts only about a month in a drought with moderate use. A smaller surface loses less, since an 8 foot wide tank evaporates over 3 gallons a day and a 4 by 6 foot one about 1.5. If it dries up, deer stop coming within about 2 weeks and take 2 to 3 weeks to come back after you refill it, because they've moved to a new pattern. Some seasons Sturgis never filled his, and in others he filled them three times, depending on drought and runoff.

lessons.tryThis: On a map of your hunting ground, draw the line deer travel from bedding to food. Mark one spot on it that's in the woods, away from both ends, where you could slip in from the side. That's where a water hole would go.
lessons.headsUp: Every detail here is from one hunter on his own managed land, so it's well tested by him but not checked by anyone else in our sources. His numbers on evaporation and tank life depend on drought and runoff, so watch your own water level the first season.

check.q: Why not put the water hole right in the food plot?
check.a: A buck may reach the food in daylight only rarely, but he'll hit water on the route in daylight much more often.

check.q: Your water hole dried up for two weeks. What happens after you refill it?
check.a: Deer may take 2 to 3 weeks to come back, because they've shifted to a new pattern.

lessons.title: Late season food
lessons.hook: By December the crops are cut, the acorns are gone, and the woods feel empty. The deer are still there, but they've tightened up around the little food that's left. Find that food with good cover beside it, and afternoons can be some of the best hunting of the year.

sections.heading: Cover right next to food
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis looks for two things side by side in the cold late season. The first is high stem-count cover, meaning thick briars, young hardwood regrowth, brush, or blowdowns, where deer bed and browse in daylight. The second is a good afternoon food source right next to it, like standing corn, a clearcut, brassicas, or late beans. Deer won't be in the brush unless good food is close. Great food with no thick cover nearby only gets visited at midnight, after deer sneak across open ground they know is pressured. On public land, he says you can hunt a big clearcut almost like a cornfield.

sections.heading: Browse carries them through winter
sections.text: For December and January, Sturgis favors stands near young hardwood regrowth and browse, because that's what deer lean on once the crops and acorns are gone. Deer need that daytime browse as much as they need cover, which is why the two work best side by side. This timing is for the northern half of the country. Farther south, or where land is burned on purpose, green growth lasts into October and November and browse is everywhere early.

sections.heading: Hunt afternoons, skip mornings
sections.text: In the late season Sturgis hunts the afternoon food source and stays out in the mornings. The food is the bottom of the funnel, so deer from several bedding areas come to it before dark. In the mornings they aren't moving much in daylight, so a morning hunt only pressures and pushes them. The one exception he makes is the second rut. Otherwise, put a premium on those afternoon sits and protect them. He's shot many good bucks this way in the Wisconsin late muzzleloader season.

sections.heading: The big one isn't with the group
sections.text: In farm country, bucks group back up in bachelor groups on cut cornfields, the best food left. Lee Ellis of Seek One saw 10 to 12 bucks together on cut corn, but the giant he later killed was never with them. So when you glass a late-season bachelor group, expect the oldest buck to be off by himself rather than with the group. This comes from Ellis alone, so treat it as one hunter's tip.

lessons.tryThis: Find one late-season food source near you, like standing corn or a clearcut, and check whether thick cover sits right against it. If it does, plan an afternoon sit there and stay out of it in the mornings.
lessons.headsUp: Nearly all of this lesson comes from Sturgis, who hunts the upper Midwest. It fits his country well, but the timing of browse and green food shifts a lot as you go south.

check.q: It's late December. Morning or afternoon sit at the food?
check.a: Afternoon. Deer come to the food before dark, and a morning hunt only pushes them.

check.q: You glass ten bucks together on a cut cornfield in December. Is the biggest one likely among them?
check.a: Maybe not. Lee Ellis's giant was never with the group, so look for an older buck off on his own.

units.goal: Fronts, pressure, wind, rain, heat, and cold: what the data says.

lessons.title: Cold fronts: what hunters say and what the data shows
lessons.hook: The forecast shows a cold front rolling through on Thursday, and every hunter you know is talking about taking Friday off. Is that front really worth a vacation day? Experienced hunters and researchers with GPS collars answer that a little differently, and knowing both answers makes you a better planner.

sections.heading: The hunters' recipe
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis of Whitetail Habitat Solutions, who hunts the Wisconsin and Minnesota hills, says to hunt the first sit after a cold front passes and to put your best stand on it. He reads it off a 7-day forecast graph. The temperature line drops, the pressure line climbs to meet it, and the wind speed falls. He says most of his top 25 mature bucks were shot when those three lined up. Clay Hayes, who hunts North Idaho, adds heavy rain easing off, and calls it the perfect storm when it all happens around daybreak. His reasoning is that nasty weather keeps deer hunkered in thick bedding and makes them miss feedings, so they're hungry when it breaks.
