Whitetail Evolution, hunting Michigan, says the same holds in the early season and the pre-rut, and since every trip in leaves a trace, these are the days to spend your trips on.

sections.heading: What the GPS collars measured
sections.text: A Mississippi State GPS-collar study led by Bronson Strickland did find a front effect, but a small one. Days under a cold air mass had slightly more daylight buck movement. If your odds on a sit are 10 percent, cold weather might make them 11, not 90, and it took a very large sample and heavy math to see even that. The morning after a warm-to-cold switch had about 25 yards per hour more movement than the day the front hit, mostly about an hour after sunrise. Over a three-hour sit that's about 75 more yards of buck walking, which could decide whether he steps out. Strickland doesn't think it's big enough to change your plans on its own. Whitetail Properties, summarizing collar research across the whitetail range, says no single factor has produced the jump hunters expect, though some combination might matter.

sections.heading: The day before the front
sections.text: In the MSU data, the day before a cold front had the most morning movement of the three days around it, and the weakest afternoon. Strickland calls his explanation a guess and the effect small, but if you get one sit that day, the data favors the morning. Sturgis likes a slightly different setup in hot early-season weather. When it's already about 10 degrees cooler than yesterday (his example is 86 dropping to the low 70s), cloudy with some wind, and the rain won't start until after dark, he'll sit the evening before a rain on a stand he doesn't use often. It's his least favorite of his rain options, because rain that starts too soon can wash out a blood trail.

sections.heading: Settled weather and the rut
sections.text: Sturgis treats stable weather as a low-value day. Two or three days after a front, once temperatures settle into a new normal, he says movement drops off again, and he has built his hunting around post-front days since the early 90s. The research never measured that directly. It does show something that outweighs all of it, though. In the MSU data, bucks covered about 1,500 to 2,000 yards a day outside the rut and 4,000 or more in it, while weather effects ran from a few to about 50 yards per hour. Strickland says the rut supersedes everything, so once it's on, go regardless of the forecast.

lessons.tryThis: Open a 7-day forecast graph and find the next day where the temperature drops, the pressure climbs, and the wind falls. Pencil in your best stand for that sit, and keep hunting the other days too.
lessons.headsUp: Sturgis, Whitetail Evolution, and Hayes treat the post-front sit as the one you can't miss. The MSU data and Whitetail Properties say the edge is real but small, roughly 10 percent odds becoming 11. Part of the hunters' success may come from saving their freshest, best stands for those days. Use a front to choose between days, not to write every other day off.

check.q: In the MSU collar data, how much did cold-front weather raise a 10 percent sit?
check.a: To about 11 percent. The effect is real but small.

check.q: You get one sit on the day before a cold front. Morning or evening?
check.a: Morning. The MSU data found the afternoon before a front was the weakest of the three days.

lessons.title: Barometers, moons, and feeding clocks
lessons.hook: Plenty of hunters check the barometer before they check the wind. Some swear by a rising needle, some by a falling one, and a lot of people plan their vacation around the moon. This lesson looks at what those beliefs rest on and what the research actually found.

sections.heading: Pressure alone doesn't move deer
sections.text: When the Mississippi State team isolated each weather variable, temperature drove the relationship and the others mostly rode along with it. Pressure varies very little, and Strickland couldn't point to a pressure result at all. Their meteorologist colleagues made the key point. Pressure, humidity, and temperature move together as a front, so judge the front, not one number. Whitetail Properties' research summary agrees that the barometer alone doesn't move deer, and even Sturgis says pressure-only models miss about half the great days. The one small exception was very dry air. Humidity under about 20 percent cut movement by up to about 30 yards per hour, which Strickland says isn't enough to call a day good or bad.

sections.heading: Two barometer rules that point opposite ways
sections.text: David Blanton of Realtree says a morning with a rising barometer hunts better than one with it falling. That's what he's always seen, and he thinks humid air holds deer down, especially in the East and Midwest. The MSU data found the opposite on humidity, since very dry air trimmed movement slightly. The Downwind Hunting list goes the other way on pressure. It says that on a falling barometer or a new moon you should skip the predawn walk, head in around 8 AM, and sit from 10 to 2. It cites a University of Georgia collar study that put 60 percent of mature bucks' big daytime moves in that window. That study wasn't checked, and this is a single unverified listicle, so treat it as a claim rather than a finding.

sections.heading: The moon
sections.text: Blanton also watches when the moon rises and sets, not just its phase. The closer moonrise or moonset falls to dawn or dusk, the better he's seen deer move, and he's had deer pile into a food plot an hour before dark under a rising full moon. He expects pushback on this, and the research gives it. Whitetail Properties says GPS-collar studies with millions of locations show very little difference between moon phases, at most a slightly earlier evening and a slightly longer morning feed. The old saying that the day after a full moon is poor isn't supported either. Plan around the time of year and the wind instead. As Whitetail Properties puts it, if believing in the moon keeps you on stand longer, keep believing, because the confidence is what helps.

sections.heading: Deer eat on a loose clock
sections.text: Clay Hayes expects whitetails to feed in bouts roughly every 5 hours. They get up, eat fast, then lie back down to chew their cud. Deer are ruminants, so they gulp food with little chewing to limit their time exposed, then process it later somewhere safe. He's clear that it isn't clockwork, and it's the main reason he gives for storm breaks moving deer, since a storm makes them miss a bout. He also says the moon can shift the cycle, but the Whitetail Properties summary doesn't support that part. Only Hayes teaches the five-hour cycle, so take it as a useful picture, not a rule.

lessons.tryThis: Before your next hunt, skip the barometer reading and look at the whole forecast instead. Is a front passing, with the temperature falling and the wind easing? That's what the pressure number was only hinting at.
lessons.headsUp: Hunters here disagree with each other and with the data about pressure. Blanton likes a rising barometer, the Downwind Hunting list likes a falling one, Whitetail Evolution believes high pressure itself moves deer, and Sturgis uses climbing pressure as part of his front recipe. The MSU data found no usable effect from pressure by itself. Use pressure only as a sign that a front is passing.

check.q: The barometer is climbing fast this morning. Should that alone make you rate the day higher?
check.a: No. The MSU data found no usable pressure effect. Look at the whole front, especially temperature.

check.q: Should you plan your hunting days around the full moon?
check.a: No. Collar studies with millions of locations show very little difference between moon phases.

lessons.title: Temperature: the change that counts
lessons.hook: It was warm yesterday, and this morning your truck's thermometer reads a lot colder. A day like that feels different, and for once the hunters' gut feeling and the research line up pretty well. The trick is knowing how big a change it takes, and when in the day it matters.

sections.heading: Ten degrees isn't enough
sections.text: The Downwind Hunting list says movement spikes when the temperature drops 10 or more degrees from the day before, and suggests reading a cheap thermometer at the same time each morning. The MSU collar data is stricter. For day-to-day swings anywhere within about 10 degrees either way, the change in time bucks spent bedded was flat at zero. Past about a 10 to 15 degree drop, bucks bedded less the next day. Sturgis looks for 15 to 20, and Eddie McRae in Georgia counts a 12-degree drop in the forecast high as a major event, while noting it matters less up north or out West. So treat 10 degrees as weak and about 15 as the real trigger.

sections.heading: The evening sweet spot
sections.text: This was the MSU study's most consistent weather finding. In the last two hours of daylight, temperatures between 32 and 55 F had the highest movement rate in essentially every two-week stage from pre-rut to post-rut. Strickland trusts it because it repeats. The edge was often modest and biggest in the late rut. It's also a fixed band measured on Mississippi deer, so northern deer likely have a different one.

sections.heading: Cold mornings help, a little
sections.text: Across the whole season, bucks with a 20 to 32 degree dawn moved about 360 yards per hour and were bedded about 25 percent of the time, versus about 240 yards and 30 percent in the warmest dawns of 70 to 85. That sounds big, but once the rut stage was accounted for, the morning pattern got inconsistent. Cold mornings were best in the pre-rut and peak rut, yet warmer mornings had more movement in the early rut, and some gaps were only about 5 yards per hour, inside the collar error. Morning movement was high almost regardless of temperature, which makes mornings the steadier bet when the weather is off.

sections.heading: Frosty pre-rut mornings
sections.text: Sturgis saves his morning sits for the first cold, frosty mornings of late October and November, especially just after a front. In the last ten days of October he watches for a forecast low of about 35, or the first 27 to 31 degree mornings. Fewer than 20 percent of his sits are mornings, yet mornings account for about 60 to 70 percent of his oldest bucks over decades. The timing is regional, so use your local pre-rut. The data mostly backs him, as a small edge.

sections.heading: The South's rare early front
sections.text: Jamie McKay, who hunts public land in North Alabama, doesn't expect to see a good public-land buck until November, but he killed one on October 6 when an unusual cold front came through. One Southern Outdoorsmen host's best encounter came October 7 in Tennessee, on a morning of about 35 degrees after a front. He walked through an oak ridge to the edge of a bedding thicket, saw 14 deer, and then a big buck walked in to 25 yards at 8:30. Both say a front that cold that early doesn't always come.

lessons.tryThis: For the next two weeks, write down each day's average temperature. When one day comes in about 15 degrees colder than the one before, make that a day you hunt.
lessons.headsUp: Two disagreements here. The listicle's 10-degree trigger is weaker than what the MSU data measured, which needs about 15. And on early-season cold-front mornings, Whitetail Evolution bumped his target buck about an hour before light on exactly that kind of morning in Michigan, and he and Sturgis say to stay out of bedding on early mornings on private farm ground. The Southern hunters were in big public woods, which likely explains the difference.

check.q: It was 62 yesterday and 54 today. Is that a big enough drop to count?
check.a: Not by the MSU data. Swings within about 10 degrees showed no change. Look for about 15.

check.q: The last two hours of light will be around 45 degrees. Good or bad for an evening sit?
check.a: Good. The 32 to 55 degree band had the most evening movement in nearly every stage.

lessons.title: Wind speed: the drop, not the level
lessons.hook: The wind has been howling for two days, and the forecast finally shows it laying down tomorrow, though it'll still be breezy. Should you go? This is one of the places where a veteran hunter and the collar data agree, and the reason is worth knowing.

sections.heading: Hunt the day the wind drops
sections.text: Sturgis hunts the day the wind speed drops compared with what it has been. After a day or two of 40 to 50 mph, a fall to 20 is huge to him, and so are 20 down to 8 or 10 and 50 down to 30. The MSU data put the line at a daily average about 7 or 8 mph lower than the day before, and past that bucks bedded less. A rise in wind, or a small change, didn't matter. Sturgis's 15-point came on October 26, 2007, right after a cold front as the wind dropped, while the buck was chasing does on the quiet side below a windy ridge. Strickland called the wind response more subtle than the temperature one, but hunter and data agree on the direction.

sections.heading: A windy day isn't a wasted day
sections.text: The level of the wind is a different story. In the MSU data, buck movement was essentially flat across wind speeds, with a slight bump near no wind and a slight increase above 20 mph, at most 10 to 12 yards per hour either way. The hosts of the MSU video point out that many hunters see fewer deer on windy days partly because they sit less in cold wind. So don't skip a hunt just because it's windy. Decide on comfort and safety instead, and pick a box blind or ground blind over a climbing stand swaying in the gusts.

sections.heading: Blanton's regional view
sections.text: David Blanton sees it differently. He says sustained winds of 15 to 20 mph really cut movement in the East and Southeast, while on the Plains and out West it matters much less because deer there are used to it. He's watched deer feed in alfalfa in Montana in 50 mph winds. The trouble is that the MSU study was done in Mississippi, in the Southeast, and found wind level made almost no difference. The Plains and West part hasn't been tested.

sections.heading: Direction and a buck's nose
sections.text: Blanton also expects less movement on an east wind, going by the old line "wind out of the east, fish bite least." That's years of his own experience, and no research here tested wind direction. Mike Rex, who hunts the southeast Ohio hills, did something closer to a test. He charted more than 100 camera events of one target buck coming down a cut against historical wind data. With the wind in the buck's face, he came through about 2.5 hours earlier than with it at his back, when he couldn't smell what was below. All but two events were after dark, but the lesson holds. Hunt a buck's route on days the wind lets him smell ahead. It's one buck in one place, so treat it as a strong clue.

lessons.tryThis: Check the forecast for tomorrow's average wind speed against today's. If it's 7 or 8 mph lower or more, that's a day to hunt, even if it's still breezy.
lessons.headsUp: Hunters and data split on steady wind. Blanton says 15 to 20 mph cuts movement in the East, Sturgis says very heavy wind keeps deer bedded, and Illinois harvest data favored calmer days. The MSU collars found wind level changed movement by 10 to 12 yards per hour at most. Part of the gap may be hunters sitting less, and seeing and hearing less, when it blows.

check.q: Yesterday averaged 25 mph and today is forecast at 17. Good day?
check.a: Yes. That's about an 8 mph drop, right at the line the MSU data found mattered.

check.q: It's been a steady 20 mph for three days. Should you stay home?
check.a: No. Wind level barely changed buck movement in the data. Just pick a safe, steady stand.

lessons.title: Where deer go when it blows
lessons.hook: Stand on a ridge top on a windy day and the trees roar. Walk a hundred feet down the back side and you can hear yourself think again. Deer notice that difference too, and it tells you where to sit and how to sneak in.

sections.heading: Deer go to the quiet side
sections.text: Sturgis says deer do move more when it's windy, but they move to get out of the wind, which crowds a lot of them onto the quiet side. So skip your favorite exposed ridge-top oak and hunt low ground, the lee side of a ridge, a bowl or draw, or the downwind side of conifers, a swamp, thick brush, or tall grass. With the wind roaring 200 feet above him, he's had it nearly still 60 yards below, and that's where the deer went. His record day of over 40 deer was deer walking from a windy hollow, over a saddle, and into the lee draw. This comes from Sturgis alone, across two videos.

sections.heading: How far down to go
sections.text: In hills with 300 to 400 feet of relief, Sturgis gets 50 to 100 feet or more below the ridge top on the lee side. Once you're about 100 feet down, the wind mostly passes overhead. You'll hear the treetops roaring while hardly a leaf moves around you. Deer can still be up top, but the calm pocket is where they shelter and move.

sections.heading: Tall grass on a windy day
sections.text: Where there's tall grass like switchgrass, big bluestem, or CRP on field edges or near bedding, Sturgis expects deer, including does hiding fawns, to bed in it when it's windy. The grass keeps them out of the wind, breaks up the sun, and hides them. Hunt the downwind edge of that grass on a windy day.

sections.heading: Late-season beds and the wind
sections.text: In late-season cold, with daytime highs of 5 to 10 degrees and strong south winds, Sturgis looks for deer bedded on north-facing slopes out of the wind and feeding on south-facing ones. Getting out of the wind saves them more energy than sun does, he says, so the slope flips with the wind direction. He finds lots of sheds on south slopes because deer feed there overnight, not because they bed there.

sections.heading: Let the weather cover you
sections.text: Loud weather is also your chance to get close. The Hunting Public crew saves their most sensitive spots, like the middle of a bedding area, for a wet, windy day, and goes in during the dark. Wet leaves are quiet and everything is moving, and they've walked within a few yards of deer that way. On a calm, crunchy day your steps carry for hundreds of yards, so slow down and walk like a squirrel. Sturgis uses the wind to slip past bedding up high on a windy evening, then drops about 200 feet into a quiet bowl below to sit.

lessons.tryThis: On the next windy day, walk a ridge and notice how far down the lee side you have to go before the air goes quiet. Mark that spot on your map as a windy-day stand.
lessons.headsUp: Derek Dixon, who studies bucks with thermal drones, often found bucks bedded on the windward side facing into the wind, even at 5 degrees with sleet, especially where that side had the thick cover and the lee side was open timber. Where both sides have similar cover, Sturgis's rule may hold. Where only the windward side is thick, expect bucks there.

check.q: It's gusty and your favorite stand is a ridge-top oak. Do you sit it?
check.a: No. Deer move to the quiet side. Get 50 to 100 feet or more below the top on the lee side.

check.q: When should you sneak into your most sensitive spot?
check.a: On a wet, windy day, in the dark, when wet leaves are quiet and the woods are moving.

lessons.title: Timing the storm break
lessons.hook: It's rained since dawn, and the radar shows the back edge of the storm crossing your county late in the afternoon. You could stay on the couch, or you could be in the tree when it clears. Most of the hunters here would pick the tree. They just don't all agree on exactly when to get there.

sections.heading: Be there when it clears
sections.text: Sturgis watches the radar and hourly forecast for when a storm clears, and he wants to be sitting when it does. Sturgis's favorite is rain all day that clears about an hour before dark, or rain all night that breaks by morning, especially after a windy day ahead of the front. His reasoning is that deer held down by a storm burned energy and missed feedings, so when it breaks they put the feed bag on. He also thinks rain takes away their hearing, so they wait it out. Jamie McKay heads for the woods as soon as the rain stops. He once waited out a rainy morning and saw deer crossing the road as soon as it quit, and on another rainy morning a buck tucked under a bluff was shot moving right after. The same idea applies to snow, hail, thunderstorms, and heavy wind.

sections.heading: Get in before it breaks
sections.text: Clay Hayes says to be in your stand before the weather breaks, not walking in after it has. Deer get up and move quickly once it clears, so if you're already there you're less likely to bump them. If the clear-up is close, Sturgis walks in during the rain in rain gear, because the rain washes his trail away. That works on the way out too. Normally the scent you leave walking to and from a stand lingers 3 to 4 hours, but not after a rain, so when rain is due right after your hunt you can afford to be a little bolder, like swapping a camera card.

sections.heading: Or wait for the drips to stop
sections.text: Sturgis also teaches a more patient version. He counts it as a real break when the rain has stopped completely, with no drips falling through the trees, and the wind has dropped a lot, like 50 to 30 or 30 to 10 mph. For snow, it's when a heavy, windy snow turns light and calm. He watches the forecast for a dry hole of 4 or 5 hours or more and goes once it has been dry for at least an hour, because dripping trees keep the woods noisy. The longer it rained before the break, the better. A long dry hole also gives you time to track a deer before the rain returns. He shot a giant buck in a 4 to 5 hour calm break between thunderstorms.

lessons.tryThis: The next time an all-day rain is forecast, pull up the hourly forecast and find when it's due to clear. Plan to be sitting at that time, with rain gear if you have to walk in wet.
lessons.headsUp: The mentors split on timing. Sturgis's hit-the-break approach, McKay, Whitetail Evolution, and Hayes want you in the stand as the rain stops, which covers your approach. Sturgis's hole-in-the-rain approach waits until it's been dry an hour so the woods go quiet. The research doesn't settle it, because no collar study here measured the moment rain ends. Whitetail Properties cites Penn State finding bucks move a little more during rain, which cuts against the idea that rain makes them sit tight.

check.q: Why do deer often move right after a storm breaks?
check.a: They were held down, burned energy, and missed feedings, so they get up hungry.

check.q: Why can you be a bit bolder on the way out when rain is due right after your hunt?
check.a: Rain washes your trail. Normally your scent lingers 3 to 4 hours.

lessons.title: Where to sit after the storm
lessons.hook: The storm is over and the deer are hungry. That much the hunters agree on. The next question is where they'll go to eat, and the answer depends on the time of day, the time of year, and how hard the storm hit.

sections.heading: Food close to the bed
sections.text: Clay Hayes waits at an isolated food source close to the bedding area when a storm is about to break, because hungry deer that sat out the storm come off their beds and head straight to nearby food. Sturgis says the same and adds that it works even late morning or midday. Deer that were pinned down want to eat right away, but they won't walk out into an open field at 2 in the afternoon. So sit food tucked inside cover near bedding, like an acorn flat, a small plot, a cut or regrowth area, or a hidden apple tree. Sturgis shot at a mature buck that came out near his bedding at about 11 AM after he snuck in on a rainstorm.

sections.heading: Scrapes after a pre-rut storm
sections.text: In the pre-rut, Whitetail Evolution hunts scrapes right after a storm. If it's raining, even lightly, and he can see when it will stop, he's near a scrape that gets used year after year about 15 minutes before the rain ends. Right after even a small storm, bucks often get up and freshen their scrapes, maybe because the rain washed the scent away. Mike Rex hunts scrapes from late September in southern Ohio through the pre-rut, especially after a storm blows the leaves down onto them. Once the rut kicks in he stops hunting scrapes and switches to simply being out there, because scrape use trails off quickly. He also notes most scrape visits happen at night, and the South runs much later.

sections.heading: Late-season storms put deer on food
sections.text: In the late season, hunt the food during and right after a big storm or front that drops the temperature, like a hard snow or an ice storm. Sturgis says a big system makes deer miss feedings, and the cold makes them burn energy, so afterward they have to eat, and that puts them on food in daylight. Cold is relative to where you live. Sixty degrees can be cold in Florida while in northern North Dakota it takes 20 below. Mike Rex's target buck was almost entirely nocturnal all season, until January 29, when a snow emergency put ice over the snow. His stomach won, he came to food in daylight, and Rex's 16-year-old son killed him.

lessons.tryThis: Find one food source on your ground that sits inside cover close to bedding, like an acorn flat or a small plot. Make it your plan for the next storm break, even if it breaks at midday.
lessons.headsUp: Neither Sturgis nor Rex gave a temperature that makes a late-season storm count, only that it's relative to your region. The MSU finding that a 15 degree drop reduces bedding points the same way, though it was measured in Mississippi across the whole season. On timing at scrapes, Whitetail Evolution wants you there before the rain ends, while Sturgis elsewhere waits for the drips to stop.

check.q: A storm breaks at 1 PM. Do you wait for the evening field?
check.a: No. Sit food inside cover near bedding right away. Deer won't cross open fields at midday.

check.q: In the pre-rut, when does Whitetail Evolution want to be at a scrape during a rain?
check.a: About 15 minutes before the rain ends.

lessons.title: Hunting heat and hard cold
lessons.hook: Not every forecast hands you a front to chase. Some weeks it's just hot, and some weeks it's so cold the truck barely starts. Neither one is a reason to stay home, but each changes when and where you should sit.

sections.heading: In a warm spell, take the morning
sections.text: If you only get one sit during a warm spell, take the morning and skip the evening. In the MSU data, evening movement tracked temperature much more closely than morning movement did, so heat hurts evenings more while mornings stay fairly steady. When the forecast is hot, that makes the morning the safer sit. This is the video hosts' reading of the MSU graphs, which Strickland agreed with, rather than a separate measured result. It fits what Southern hunters say about hot early-season afternoons being dead while mornings run cool.

sections.heading: Find the shade
sections.text: The Hunting Public crew doesn't stay home when the early season runs hot, like 15 degrees above average in Missouri. The deer are still there, just using the ground differently. Look for them in the coolest shade, like a north-facing ridge under cliffs or boulders, or down in the sand of a dry creek bed, rather than on a sunny cedar ridge. Those beds can feel 10 degrees cooler than the ground around them. On public land there's a bonus, because on hot days almost nobody else is out. Only this one crew teaches it, but it's a good reason to keep hunting through a heat wave.

sections.heading: Bitter cold pulls bucks out early
sections.text: One of the hosts of the MSU-study video hunted late-season Iowa two years in a row. At 7 below zero, big bucks were feeding on a big food source two and a half hours before dark. The next year it was in the upper 30s to low 40s, and he saw many more does, but the bucks mostly came in the last 45 minutes of light. That's one hunter's two trips, not a collar result, so treat it as a story that points a direction.

sections.heading: Extreme cold means midday
sections.text: Sturgis has a similar rule. When it's far below the normal high for the date, he hunts late morning through midday, roughly 10 to 2 or 9 to 3, on browse like greenbrier, regrowing hardwoods, clearcuts, or blowdowns. Daybreak is the coldest part of the day, so deer save energy then and move once it warms up, say from 10 or 15 below at dawn to 10 above by midday. His examples are relative. In West Virginia in December the normal high is the low 40s, so 12 degrees is extreme, while in Wisconsin the normal is 28 to 31 and highs of 1 to 7 are frigid. He sees this especially on public land flats.

lessons.tryThis: Look up the normal high for your area this week. The next time the forecast high falls far below it, plan a late-morning to midday sit on browse or on food, instead of a dawn sit.
lessons.headsUp: These cold-weather rules each come from a single source, the Iowa story from one video host and the midday rule from Sturgis. They agree that extreme cold moves deer earlier than usual, but neither has been measured with collars.

check.q: It's a warm spell and you only get one sit. Morning or evening?
check.a: Morning. Heat hurts evening movement more, while mornings stay fairly steady.

check.q: It's far colder than normal for the date. When does Sturgis hunt?
check.a: Late morning through midday, roughly 10 to 2, on browse, once it warms up a little.

units.goal: Protect your spots all season.

lessons.title: Let the ground rest
lessons.hook: It's summer, and you've got stands to hang, lanes to trim, and cameras to put out. All of that work has to happen, and all of it tells the deer someone is around. This lesson is about when to do the loud work, and how to keep from spending what it bought you in the first weekend of the season.

sections.heading: Get the loud work done early
sections.text: Anything intrusive, like habitat jobs, hanging stands, trimming lanes, scouting, putting out cameras, or building a water hole, should be finished well ahead of the season. Then you stay out. Three hunters teach this. Whitetail Evolution, who bowhunts private land he manages in Michigan, finishes about a month before the opener. Mike Rex gets it done early in summer and stays out for the last 2 to 4 weeks before the season. Jeff Sturgis, of Whitetail Habitat Solutions, prepares the part of the property his target buck uses first, so he can get out of it early, and once his water hole and stand are in, he leaves that area completely alone. He won't even mow trails nearby. If you want to keep tabs on the spot, use cellular or solar trail cameras so you don't have to walk in to check them.

sections.heading: Why staying out pays
sections.text: Rex has noticed that mature bucks seen in fields all summer go sporadic 2 to 4 weeks before the season, and he doesn't think it's only acorns. From a buck's point of view, a predator that wasn't around all summer suddenly shows up, only in daylight, pruning and scouting and squirrel hunting. Old bucks have been through it before, and Rex says deer know days later that you were there. Leave the ground alone and the opposite happens, because deer use keeps building by the day. Sturgis had bucks sparring on his water-hole dirt pad within two weeks. Whitetail Evolution says the rest gives deer a false sense of security, and that's what makes their movement predictable once the season opens.

sections.heading: Don't spend it in two days
sections.text: All that rest can be undone fast. Whitetail Evolution warns against pushing into your best stands in the first two days just because you're excited. Hunt the early season, he says, but stay out of the thickest cover and the stands you're saving for the rut, and don't sit a rut stand in early October. Summer photos of velvet bucks and the few early kills on social media make that hard. You only see those few, though, not the hundreds of hunters who pushed too far, bumped their target buck, and never saw him again. Pushing deep educates deer with hunting pressure and lowers your odds in the pre-rut and rut, when your chances are higher. He puts it this way. The season is a marathon, not a sprint, so be patient when the information says wait and aggressive when it says go.

sections.heading: Set up a new spot in one trip
sections.text: Sometimes you find a new spot in thick cover and have to set it up. Eddie McRae does it all in one trip in the middle of the day. He went in at about 10 AM, outside prime movement, walked the spot for about an hour, cleared it, hung cameras, and left for good, then watched it on cell cameras. He brought everything he could need so he wouldn't have to come back, including a chainsaw, a weed eater with a brush blade, a limb saw, snips, and camo netting for a ground blind. His reasoning is that repeated trips are what do the damage. He credits the idea to Bobby Worthington, from a Parker McDonald interview. Only McRae teaches this here, so treat it as one good hunter's method rather than a rule.

lessons.tryThis: Find the date of your opener and count back a month. Put every stand-hanging, trimming, and camera job on the calendar before that date. Then pick the one or two stands you won't sit until the rut, and write them down so the excitement of opening weekend doesn't talk you into them.

check.q: It's early October and your best rut stand has a perfect wind. Do you sit it?
check.a: No. Hunt the early season from other stands and save the rut stand, because pressure now lowers your odds in the pre-rut and rut.

check.q: You need to clear a new spot in thick cover and hang cameras. How do you do it?
check.a: In one trip, in the middle of the day outside prime movement. Do it all at once, get out, and watch it on cell cameras.

lessons.title: Protect the food
lessons.hook: A food plot or crop field is where deer gather, so it's where you're most tempted to hunt. It's also the easiest place to ruin, and when it goes, it takes more than one stand with it. Almost all of this lesson comes from Jeff Sturgis of Whitetail Habitat Solutions, who hunts Wisconsin farm country.

sections.heading: Why food matters more than beds
sections.text: Sturgis ranks protecting food above everything else, and his reason is how deer respond. Pressure a bedding area and a mature buck will often just slide over to the next one. Pressure a food source and you lose every bedding area around it, because deer start coming only after dark and eventually stop coming. He puts the damage at about 250 yards in every direction, roughly 30 acres, and says one bad hunt can ruin a food source for two or three weeks, if the deer come back at all. He estimates about 95% of food plots are over-pressured. That's why, in his view, a neighbor with 30 to 40 acres who stays out can out-hunt someone with 400 acres who doesn't.

sections.heading: Hunt the feeding field carefully, if at all
sections.text: Don't drive an ATV through the property, don't access sloppily, and don't put blinds right on top of food plots. The field where deer gather to feed until dark is the one to be most careful with. Don't bowhunt it or put a blind on it unless you can get in and out without being seen and leave your stand without spooking deer off it. If you hunt it at all, Sturgis says, do it from a distance with a gun. Blow deer off that field and mature bucks recognize the pressure and come only after dark. The same test applies to any late-season food source or midday spot, so if you can't get in and out clean, don't go.

sections.heading: Hunt food from the outside
sections.text: Sturgis likes food sources he can reach from the outside of the property, like food about 100 yards off a road. Deer aren't living by the road. They're living behind the food, so you slip in and out without them knowing. Never walk through or past a food source, or into the middle of the property, to reach a stand, because that's where the deer live. He estimates that driving half a mile into an interior field ruins about 300 of 500 acres, and on 40 acres, hunting a 5-acre plot in the middle ruins the whole thing. A Downwind Hunting listicle makes a related point. It calls the walk from truck to tree the biggest scent bomb most hunters set off, and says to pick a route that never crosses a deer trail, using creek beds, drainage ditches, and old logging roads on public land.

sections.heading: Cross food only when it's empty
sections.text: Sometimes the only way in is across food. Sturgis does it only when he can count on no deer being there. In his area, alfalfa draws few deer once it frosts out in the fall, so he can cross a cut alfalfa field to his stand expecting nothing on it. Food preference is local, so check what deer ignore where you hunt. He also uses the clock. For a morning sit near a food plot, he walks in before daylight by a hidden route, sits late watching water for cruising bucks, and leaves around 11 AM to 1 PM. Deer aren't expected on the plot then, so he can walk out right across it without spooking anything.

lessons.tryThis: Pull up a map of where you hunt and circle every food source deer are using. For each stand, trace your walk in and out. If a line crosses or skirts one of those food sources, find another route or another stand before you hunt it.
lessons.headsUp: Two things here aren't settled. The Downwind Hunting listicle says to park at least 400 yards from your stand, while Sturgis hunts food about 100 yards off a road on purpose. They agree the walk must not cross where deer live or travel, and the 400-yard number comes from a single unverified source. Sturgis's warning that one bad hunt can ruin a food source also runs against Mike Rex, who says one spook doesn't ruin a spot, which you'll meet in a later lesson.

check.q: Why does pressuring a food source hurt more than pressuring a bedding area?
check.a: A pressured buck just slides to another bed, but pressure on food spoils every bedding area around it and can turn it into a night-only field.

check.q: When does Sturgis walk across food on purpose?
check.a: Only when he can count on no deer being there, like frosted-out alfalfa, or when leaving a morning sit around 11 AM to 1 PM.

lessons.title: Build a better route
lessons.hook: You've picked the tree, and now you have to get to it. A good access route is something you design, not something you stumble onto. With a little work before the season, you can walk in quietly, unseen, and without leaving scent where deer will find it. Most of this comes from Jon Sturgis, with one idea from Eddie McRae.

sections.heading: Come in from below and behind
sections.text: In hill country, Sturgis comes in from below and from the downhill back side, using the ridge to hide his approach. He never walks up and over the ridge top to reach a stand on the far side, because crossing the top exposes you to any deer up there and to the food beyond. His example is a 3 to 4 minute uphill walk from a clean, mowed access road to a stand on the end of a point, about 150 yards from a food plot over the ridge. From there his scent blows off the side of the ridge and out over the valley. A Downwind Hunting listicle adds a thermal reason for morning stands. Cool air drains downhill early, so walking in through creek bottoms, ravines, and low drainages keeps your scent away from the ridges and benches where deer bed. Whichever way you come, Sturgis also approaches and climbs from the side away from where he'll be watching and shooting, so he never crosses his own shooting lanes.

sections.heading: Mow it wide and bend it
sections.text: Where your trail runs through tall grass or brush, Sturgis mows it about 6 feet wide in July or August. Nothing brushes your legs and boots, so it's quiet and you leave no scent on the weeds. He also bends the trail at an angle so no one can look straight down it to your stand. On public land you can't mow, but you can pick routes that do the same job, like open hardwoods or a sandy creek edge.

sections.heading: End the trail at the tree
sections.text: Make your access trail dead-end at the stand, inside a wall of brush. If the trail keeps going past your tree, deer will follow it and smell where you climbed and touched. A doe may come back after that, but Sturgis says a mature buck that smells it may stay away for two or three weeks. In the same spirit, don't give deer a reason to hang around your path. Sturgis won't put a mock scrape near his walk-in route, or on something deer already come to, like an apple tree. His post-daybreak entry trail passes an apple tree, and he doesn't want to run into a deer there at 8 AM, half an hour after daylight, on his way in.

sections.heading: Two routes for a thick-cover set
sections.text: Eddie McRae gives a thick-cover set two separate routes. One is a clipped, silent hunting path that brings him in the back door of his blind unseen. The other, an old logging road, is only for camera and battery maintenance. That way maintenance trips never foul the path he hunts from, and he can slip in absolutely quiet. Only McRae teaches this one, but it fits everything else in this lesson.

lessons.tryThis: Walk the route to one of your stands and look at it the way a deer would. Check whether you top a ridge, brush through weeds, cross your own shooting lane, or leave a trail that keeps going past the tree. Fix one of those before the season.
lessons.headsUp: The Downwind Hunting thermal reason only holds in the morning. Once the sun warms the slope, the air flips uphill, and it's a single unverified listicle besides. Sturgis's rule about staying below the crest is about being seen and heard, so he applies it to points and ridge sides at any time of day.

check.q: Your stand is on a point, and the easy walk goes over the ridge top. What do you do?
check.a: Come in from below and from the back side, using the ridge to hide you. Crossing the top exposes you to deer up there and on the food beyond.

check.q: Why should an access trail dead-end at your stand?
check.a: If it keeps going, deer follow it past your tree and smell where you climbed, and a mature buck may stay away for weeks.

lessons.title: Morning or evening, and how to get in
lessons.hook: The alarm goes off long before daylight, and you're wondering whether to be in the tree an hour early or right as it gets light. That choice can matter as much as the stand itself. This lesson is about timing your entry and deciding which sits deserve the most protection.

sections.heading: Three ways into a morning stand
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis picks one of three entries for every morning stand. Early, about an hour before light, is only for a stand where your scent, once you're up, blows into a spot deer never use. Just in time, right at daylight, is for a stand where your scent could reach deer before light. Post-daybreak is for stands where you have to cross open fields, so you wait and watch until the deer leave the field and then walk in. The logic behind all three is that every minute on stand before light is a minute your scent can spook deer before the hunt starts. None of the three is worse than the others. Let current sign and your cameras pick the stand, then use the entry that stand needs.

sections.heading: Bottoms get the just-in-time entry
sections.text: You met this one in the basics, and it's the clearest case for arriving just in time. Before daylight the thermals haven't started lifting, so your scent pools and saturates a bottom. Sturgis walks in to be settled about 10 minutes before daylight, not an hour, which cuts the time your scent has to soak in.

sections.heading: Hunt mornings in places you know
sections.text: A guest on Southern Outdoorsmen adds a rule for morning hunts at feed trees. Go to an area you've already scouted or hunted, not a brand-new spot. You can't read a new area well in the dark, and blundering around bumps deer that are already feeding. If you check trees on the way in, keep it to that known patch and climb the one that's being hit. That's how he found the tree for his big South Carolina buck, because he knew that little patch and it was one of the first places he checked.

sections.heading: In the pre-rut, mornings come first
sections.text: Sturgis makes mornings the priority in the pre-rut, because that's when bucks are moving more in the morning. That changes how you use evening stands. Don't hunt an evening stand if getting in or out of it could spoil a high-quality morning stand, since a blown morning spot costs you the best sits.

sections.heading: The case for a 1 PM entry
sections.text: Bronson Strickland, from the Mississippi State GPS-collar study, looks at it from the other side. If you want the least chance of bumping deer on the way in, he favors afternoon sits with an early entry, around 1 PM. By then a good share of bucks are bedded or moving slowly, while a morning walk-in happens during their main movement bout. Be clear about what this is, though. It's Strickland's opinion drawn from the collar data, not a result the study measured.

lessons.tryThis: For each stand you plan to hunt in the morning, write down which of the three entries it needs, early, just in time, or post-daybreak. If you can't find a morning entry that stays clean, make it an afternoon stand instead.
lessons.headsUp: Sturgis and Strickland pull in different directions. Sturgis says pre-rut mornings are the priority, and Strickland favors afternoons so you don't walk in during the morning movement. They fit together if you ask one question about each stand. In the pre-rut, with a clean morning entry, go with Sturgis. Where a morning walk-in would cross moving deer, the afternoon is safer.

check.q: Your morning stand means crossing an open field where deer feed at night. When do you go in?
check.a: Post-daybreak. Watch until the deer leave the field, then walk in.

check.q: It's the pre-rut, and an evening stand's exit passes near your best morning stand. Do you hunt the evening stand?
check.a: No. In the pre-rut, protect the morning stand, because a blown morning spot costs you the best sits.

lessons.title: Getting close without getting caught
lessons.hook: Some of the best hunts happen close to where a buck beds, and the walk in is where they usually fall apart. A snapped stick, a clanking platform, or a straight line toward his bed can end it before you're in the tree. The tips here come from hunters who have made close setups work. Each one comes from a single source, so treat them as tools to try rather than rules.

sections.heading: Every step is the hunt
sections.text: On his East Meets West podcast, host Beau Martonik told Lee Ellis how he filled his Pennsylvania tag an hour and a half into opening day. He was hunting big woods with a hang-and-hunt setup, on a spot where he believed a buck bedded close by. He treated every step as part of the hunt. He didn't snap sticks, kept cover between himself and the bedding, kept looking ahead, and took his platform and sticks apart and set them up dead silent. He credits that focus on one deer, plus the incoming weather, for the confidence and care that made it work, and he has killed on the opener this way twice. He didn't say which weather made him confident, so don't read too much into that part.

sections.heading: Angle past, don't walk at him
sections.text: Jamie McKay has a simple rule for walking near a spot where a buck may be bedded. Don't walk straight toward it. Angle past it instead. In his experience a buck usually stays put and watches you go by, even when you circle around him, and only gets up and runs once you're coming directly at him. So a route that slides past a likely bed can be fine, while one that points right at it is asking for trouble.

sections.heading: Arrive cool and quiet
sections.text: Eddie McRae uses an e-bike to get to his spots. In his words it's scent-free and quiet, and he never breaks a sweat getting there. The bike isn't the point. Any quiet way in that keeps you from sweating does the same job.

sections.heading: Let the drop-off work for you
sections.text: Mike Rex turns the noise of arriving into an advantage. Have a partner walk or drive you to the stand and then leave, and be ready to shoot the moment you're settled. A deer that heard or saw the commotion often relaxes, or even comes to check it out, once it sees someone leave. His youngest son killed a buck before Rex's truck had even left the field, and the hosts he was talking with told the same kind of story from their own hunts. Only Rex teaches this here, but it's cheap to try whenever you have a ride.

lessons.tryThis: Next time you hunt with a partner, have them walk or drive you in and then leave while you get ready fast. Have your weapon in hand right away, and pay close attention in the minutes right after they go.

check.q: You're walking near a thicket where a buck might be bedded. How do you walk?
check.a: Angle past it. A buck usually watches you go by and only runs once you come straight at him.

check.q: Why have a partner drop you off and then leave?
check.a: Deer that noticed the commotion often relax or come check it out once they see someone leave, so be ready to shoot right away.

lessons.title: Keeping spots alive all season
lessons.hook: By mid-season you've sat some stands a few times, and a couple of them have gone quiet. It's tempting to blame the weather or the deer. The answer is usually in how you've been getting in, how often you've been there, and how much of yourself you've left behind.

sections.heading: The walk matters as much as the stand
sections.text: Informed Outdoors says planning your walk to and from the stand to be as scent-free and quiet as possible matters as much as, or more than, your setup in the stand. That's most true for permanent stands, like a ladder stand that's always in the same tree. If getting to it always blows your scent into known bedding or bumps deer, you'll have nowhere near the success of a stand that keeps your scent away. So when a stand's route or wind keeps doing that, stop using it.

sections.heading: Rotate stands and routes
sections.text: If you have more than one stand, Jeff Sturgis rotates them. He comes in one way and leaves another, and he hunts different sides and heights of the property in the morning than in the afternoon. Spreading out keeps the hunting pressure on any one spot low. That doesn't mean jumping all over the map. You can keep hunting the same general area without sitting the same tree every time.

sections.heading: Carry it in, carry it out
sections.text: Bow Only Outdoors often hunts with a portable hang-on stand he carries in and out every time. He can go in blind to a general area, or to a tree he picked on the map, get up quietly, hunt, and leave without leaving a stand or much scent behind. That keeps pressure and ground scent low in the area, and he says he's killed some of his biggest bucks this way. Only he teaches it here, so take it as one hunter's method, not a rule.

sections.heading: One bump isn't the end
sections.text: Don't give up on a spot because you spooked a deer there once. Mike Rex's reasoning is that coyotes bump deer a dozen times a day, and if deer never came back to places they'd been spooked, they'd have nowhere to go. What deer do notice and react to, he says, is a lot of sudden human presence. So the thing to worry about isn't one jumped deer. It's spending a lot of time in an area you haven't been in all year.

lessons.tryThis: List your stands and how you get to each one. Mark any whose route or wind keeps pushing scent into bedding, and retire or move it. For the rest, plan a way out that's different from the way in.
lessons.headsUp: Not everyone is this relaxed about bumping deer. Jeff Sturgis says one bad hunt can ruin a food source for two or three weeks, if the deer come back at all. Eddie McRae's target buck never came back to a spot after catching him climbing down once. The difference is the situation. Sturgis's and McRae's cases are deer seeing a person at a food source or at a stand being hunted repeatedly, while Rex is talking about a single bump.

check.q: You jumped a deer on the way to your stand last week. Is the spot ruined?
check.a: Not from one bump, according to Rex, since coyotes bump deer all the time. Worry more about a lot of sudden human presence.

check.q: Your ladder stand's only route blows scent into a bedding area. What do you do?
check.a: Stop using it. A stand whose route keeps putting scent into bedding won't produce like one that keeps your scent away.

lessons.title: Baking soda and the field routine
lessons.hook: You've got the basics down, with unscented soap, sealed clothes, and rubber boots. Some hunters go a step further before every sit and treat their body, their breath, and their gear. Most of this lesson comes from WHTL, who picked it up from old-time hunters, and nearly all of it runs on one cheap ingredient.

sections.heading: The baking soda pat-down
sections.text: WHTL uses baking soda as his field scent treatment. After your hunting clothes are washed and dried, put them on and mist yourself well with plain water from a spray bottle. Then pat yourself all over with a sock full of baking soda and rub it in until you look like a snowflake. His sock holds two boxes of baking soda in a breathable merino or cotton sock, tied off, with a second sock pulled over it. At about a dollar fifty a box, it's cheap.

sections.heading: Or mix a spray
sections.text: If you'd rather spray, dissolve 1 tablespoon of baking soda in a quart of water by bringing it to a boil, let it cool, and spray it on your body, hair, and clothes. Don't add more, because more than about a tablespoon per quart clogs the sprayer. His reasoning is that baking soda, or sodium bicarbonate, neutralizes odor and is the active ingredient in many scent-control soaps and field sprays, just at a lower dose. He says the homemade version is far stronger and cheaper and beats store spray by a wide margin. Notice what he claims it does, though. It makes deer think you're farther away than you are, not that you aren't there.

sections.heading: Breath, boots, and the tote
sections.text: WHTL uses the same trick in a few more places. On a morning sit he swishes baking-soda water in his mouth and spits it out, because morning breath is a real no-no. He also puts baking soda anywhere odor builds up, like the footbeds of his boots and the corner of the tote where he keeps his hunting clothes. It's the same reason people keep an open box in the fridge, and it keeps killing odor between hunts.

sections.heading: Spray your gear too
sections.text: Your clothes aren't the only thing that goes up the tree. Diamond Archery points out that your backpack, safety harness, hat, and rubber boots pick up odor too, so when you get to the field, spray a scent-eliminating field spray over everything you carry. That tip comes from an archery company's product video. Jeff Sturgis also sprays to cut the trail he walks in on, but he never counts on it.

sections.heading: Freezing your clothes
sections.text: A Downwind Hunting listicle suggests sealing your outer layers in a plastic trash bag after each hunt and keeping the bag in the freezer until the next sit. It says freezing kills the bacteria that cause human odor. That's the only source for it, and it's an unverified listicle, so treat it as an idea to try rather than something proven.

lessons.tryThis: Mix a batch of spray at 1 tablespoon to a quart, boiled and cooled, and drop some baking soda into the corner of your clothes tote. On your next sit, spray your pack and harness along with your clothes.
lessons.headsUp: Every tip in this lesson has just one source. The baking soda routine is one hunter's practice, the gear spray comes from a product video, and the freezer tip comes from an unverified listicle. None of it has been measured, and none of it replaces playing the wind.

check.q: Why not put three tablespoons of baking soda in your quart spray bottle?
check.a: More than about a tablespoon per quart clogs the sprayer.

check.q: What does WHTL say baking soda actually does for you in the field?
check.a: It neutralizes odor and makes deer think you're farther away than you are. It doesn't hide you from their nose.

lessons.title: Your body, your food, your cover scent
lessons.hook: Sweat on the walk in, a snack that smells, a rope hanging down the tree. Small things like these put odor into the air around your stand while you sit. This lesson covers a handful of habits, from getting in shape to choosing a cover scent, and it's honest about how well each one is backed up.

sections.heading: Get in shape so you sweat less
sections.text: A guest on Southern Outdoorsmen gets ready for the season by rucking, which means walking with a weighted backpack on a regular basis. Even a mile a day helps. It matches what hunting actually is, carrying a pack and a stand in. When your body is used to it, you sweat much less on the walk in. He says many hunters wrongly think heavy sweating is just how they're built.

sections.heading: Pack bland food
sections.text: Strong-smelling food puts odor into the air around your stand for the rest of the sit. A Downwind Hunting listicle suggests plain crackers, plain granola, and water instead of coffee, and says to skip peanut butter, jerky, and citrus. It's a single unverified source, but it's an easy change to make.

sections.heading: Trimming your hair, maybe
sections.text: The same listicle says to trim the hair on your forearms and the back of your neck before the season, and to cover as much skin as you can with scent-free fabric. It claims body hair traps scent and releases it slowly, and says outfitters in Kansas and Iowa recommend it. This is an unusual claim from a single unverified source, with no evidence given, so file it as something to think about rather than a rule.

sections.heading: Don't leave the rope hanging
sections.text: Bow Only Outdoors adds a detail that's easy to miss. After you haul up your stand, don't leave the rope dangling to the ground. A deer walking past the tree can smell a rope hanging low, so tie it up short and then pack it away.

sections.heading: If you use a cover scent, make it local
sections.text: Eddie McRae, who hunts Georgia, uses a cover scent, but only from a plant that already grows everywhere in his woods. He boils dog fennel, which is common there, into a spray and stores his next hunt's clothes in a bag packed with it. Before that he boiled mulch with pine limbs. A smell deer live with all day and night draws no attention. A strong foreign smell like vanilla makes deer curious at best, the way you'd look around if you smelled a skunk or smoke. He passes on a story, secondhand from another podcast, of a property used for more than 10 years where deer learned to bolt at a vanilla spray because they linked it to people or being shot at.

lessons.tryThis: Start walking a mile a day with the pack you'll hunt with. On your next sit, pack only plain food and water, and once you're up, tie your haul rope up short before you settle in.
lessons.headsUp: Jeff Sturgis sees cover scent differently from McRae. He says if you need a cover scent because deer will be downwind of you, the stand location is the mistake. They do agree on one thing, which is that strong foreign smells like vanilla are a bad idea.

check.q: Why use a local plant like dog fennel or pine as a cover scent instead of a vanilla spray?
check.a: Deer live with local plant smells all the time, so they draw no attention. A strong foreign smell makes deer curious and can teach them to bolt.

check.q: How can getting in shape help your scent control?
check.a: A body used to carrying a pack sweats much less on the walk in.

units.goal: Thermals, bottoms, ridges, and swirling wind.

lessons.title: A stand for every wind
lessons.hook: You've got one great stand, and it's all you think about. Then the season goes by, the wind only blows right for it a handful of times, and you either stay home or sit it anyway. Hunters who stay on deer all season fix that before opening day, by always having somewhere safe to go no matter which way the air is moving.

sections.heading: Plan for every direction, not just the usual one
sections.text: In the basics lesson you learned to sit a stand only on the winds it's safe for. The other half of that rule is having enough stands that some spot is always safe. Jeff Sturgis, who has spent decades laying out stands on hunting properties, says the predominant wind only blows about 35 percent of the time, and the other directions split the rest about equally. So he plans about 4 or 5 stands for each wind direction, for mornings and afternoons, which works out to 25 to 30 stands on a 500-acre property. The Downwind Hunting list makes the same point on a smaller scale. Hang two stands on opposite sides of one funnel or trail, one for a north wind and one for a south wind, and sit only the one the wind allows. That version comes from an unverified listicle, so treat it as a handy idea rather than tested advice.

sections.heading: Weight your stands toward the settled winds
sections.text: Sturgis hunts the Upper Midwest, and there the wind in settled weather sits south to southwest for about 35 percent of the season. That's why he sets most of his stands for south, southeast, and southwest winds and saves his northwest-wind stands for fronts. A northwest wind means temperatures are dropping, and cold doesn't keep deepening for weeks. It drops, then moderates, so the harsh northwest wind usually lasts a day or two before swinging back to the south side by the second or third day. He reads the wind as a weather clue too. A hard south wind means it's warming up, and winds turning east usually mean rain is coming. The prevailing wind differs by region, so learn yours before copying his layout.

sections.heading: The next wind shows up early
sections.text: Look at the hourly forecast for the hours after your sit, not only during it. Sturgis says a wind shift doesn't flip all at once, because the new direction creeps in hours early. If the wind is supposed to swing to northwest overnight ahead of a cold front, expect puffs from the northwest every 5 to 10 minutes during your evening sit. He thinks much of what hunters in flat country call a swirling wind is really a forecast shift arriving early. So on those evenings, pick a stand that's safe on both the wind you have and the one that's coming.

sections.heading: Climbing higher won't save a bad wind
sections.text: It's tempting to think that sitting higher lifts your scent over a deer's head. Samko Trad Bow says there's no scent benefit at 20 feet over 12 in most situations, and until you get up around 25 to 30 feet the wind is a problem any way you cut it. His advice is to choose your height for shot angle and cover, then play the wind exactly as you would at 12 feet. That's his opinion from experience, and nobody here measured it.

lessons.tryThis: Sketch the ground you hunt and write the safe winds next to each stand. Then circle any wind direction that has no stand at all. That empty direction is where your next stand should go, and the time to hang it is before the season starts.
lessons.headsUp: Stand height is a real disagreement. Samko Trad Bow sees no scent benefit at 20 feet over 12. The Downwind Hunting listicle says 20 to 22 feet disperses scent better, citing Texas A&M research it doesn't actually show. Samko also mentions one well-known hunter who sits 30 feet up and claims he never watches the wind. None of this is measured, so don't let a tall stand talk you into a bad wind.

check.q: The wind is forecast to swing northwest overnight. What does that mean for your evening sit?
check.a: Expect puffs from the northwest every 5 to 10 minutes before dark, so pick a stand that's safe on both winds.

check.q: Why plan stands for winds other than the prevailing one?
check.a: The prevailing wind only blows about 35 percent of the time. Without other stands, you'd have nowhere safe to sit most days.

lessons.title: Do bucks walk the wind?
lessons.hook: You've probably heard that a mature buck always travels with his nose into the wind so he can smell what's ahead. It's one of the most repeated ideas in deer hunting. This lesson looks at what hunters believe about that, what thermal drone footage actually shows, and why the answer changes where you sit.

sections.heading: The common belief
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis holds the traditional view. He says the older a buck gets, the more he uses the wind on his way into a food source. That's an advantage for the buck, but Sturgis points out that it also makes his route predictable, so you can set up to catch that approach without being in his nose. He didn't say exactly where to sit relative to it, so take this as a principle rather than a recipe.

sections.heading: What the drones saw
sections.text: Derek Dixon films bucks with thermal drones, and his footage tells a different story. Along a single route through hill country he watched bucks walk with the wind in their face, on their side, and at their tail, because they can't walk straight lines in the hills. Where the buck wants to be matters more than which way the wind blows. So pick travel stands by terrain and sign first, since the land shapes his route far more than the wind does, and then play your own wind at the stand. Dixon is careful about the limits. He filmed moderately pressured private hill country, heavily pressured public land might be different, and he says he doesn't have enough data to rule out a wind effect.

sections.heading: Bucks get up when the air changes
sections.text: Where Dixon's data is strongest is timing. The most consistent pattern in his whole season of drone footage was that bedded deer, especially mature bucks, stood up within 5 to 15 minutes of the evening thermal switch, the downhill drain you met in the basics lesson. The catch is that standing up isn't leaving. They may still browse, groom, and linger in the bedding area for 30 minutes or more before heading to staging, so a buck getting up doesn't mean he walks past you ten minutes later. Be settled on stand before the switch. Dixon saw no such link in the morning, when bucks are already traveling before the thermals change.

sections.heading: A midday wind shift can move a bedded buck
sections.text: The same thing can happen in the middle of the day. Dixon watched a bedded buck in the rain stand up at 12:31, right as the wind finished swinging from south to west, a shift his weather app had called for 12:30. The buck then circled to a new spot. Beau Martonik had a similar hunt during Ohio's January muzzleloader season. He waited out a rainy morning, moved toward a bedding finger when he felt a forecast 1 PM shift arrive, and had a buck walk to 15 yards within minutes, headed over a saddle to bed on another point. So when the hourly forecast shows a big midday shift, be set up before it near a bedding point, a finger, or the saddle between bedding areas. Dixon thinks the buck is heading toward where he wants to be that evening, not just fixing the wind at his bed.

lessons.tryThis: The next time the hourly forecast shows a big wind shift during daylight, write down the time. Plan to be settled near a bedding area, on a stand that's safe on both winds, well before it arrives, and watch whether deer start moving when it does.
lessons.headsUp: Sturgis and Dixon disagree about the wind and a buck's route. Sturgis, like most hunters, believes older bucks use the wind on the way to food. Dixon's drone footage shows hill-country bucks walking one terrain route with the wind on any side. A measured observation counts for more than a belief, but Dixon admits he can't rule out a wind effect, and flat farm country may be different. Mike Rex's camera data adds a wrinkle, since he found a buck came down his route about 2.5 hours earlier on a headwind. That's about the timing of the trip, not the route, so it doesn't settle the argument. Set by terrain first, then check your own wind.

check.q: A buck stands up in his bed right at the evening thermal switch. Should you expect him at your stand in ten minutes?
check.a: Not necessarily. Bucks often browse, groom, and linger in the bedding area for 30 minutes or more before heading to staging.

check.q: What should decide where you hang a travel stand, the wind or the terrain?
check.a: The terrain and sign. Drone footage shows the land shapes a buck's route more than the wind does. Then make sure your own wind works at the stand.

lessons.title: Hills: where your scent goes
lessons.hook: In flat country you can mostly trust the wind you feel. Hills change that. The same breeze bends over ridges and curls into benches, and the thermals from the basics lesson push your scent up or down the slope depending on the hour. The good news is that once you know which way the air will slide, you can put your scent where the deer aren't.

sections.heading: Morning: get above them
sections.text: Rising morning air carries your scent uphill, so the simple fix is to sit above the deer. Jeff Sturgis sits on the higher ground above the sign on a narrow bench or ridge flat, and on a wide flat he sits at the back edge where the slope starts to climb. Another option he uses is a low point beside a hollow that runs uphill, because the rising air follows the hollow and takes your scent up and away from deer below. A Southern Outdoorsmen guest who hunts the southern Appalachians likes being slightly above deer in any situation, for another reason. You see them before they see you, which he calls being in a tree stand without being in a tree stand.

sections.heading: Watch for the curl at a bench
sections.text: Sturgis warns about one morning trap on a slope. A wind forecast to come from the ridge top behind you often curls back into your face when you're on a bench below it. The forecast wind rides over the top, and the lifting thermal pulls air back up the slope toward you. The more the wind hits the ridge at an angle, the more it rises at an angle on the other side. So the wind the app promised at your back may actually be coming up the hill at you, and you'll only know by checking it at the tree.

sections.heading: Evening: sit above ground deer won't use
sections.text: In the evening the air sinks, and as it gets dark your scent filters down and soaks the low ground. That's fine only if deer won't be down there. Sturgis tucks up the side of a ravine in open hardwoods, out of the brush, watching ground he doesn't expect deer to come up through. The Hunting Public crew does a version of this where bucks hook a ridge in the last hour to check scrapes. They sit on the ground at the top of a ditch where they feel the air coming off the ridge and pulling down into it, so their scent goes down the ditch away from the deer. Up in a tree the wind can swirl too much, so they trade some visibility for not getting smelled. They also point out that hill spots have time windows. Some only work the first hour of the morning before the wind starts swirling, and others only work the last hour of the day.

sections.heading: On a point, a little wind beats none
sections.text: On a ridge point in the evening, Sturgis prefers a light, defined wind of 3 or 4 mph over dead calm. With a little wind he knows which side of the ridge his scent will slide down as dark comes on. In calm air the sinking thermals can pull it down either side, which is why he finds calm evenings pretty tough. That's about your scent, not deer movement. Illinois harvest data found calmer days had more deer movement, so both can be true. A calm evening may move deer and still make your scent harder to control.

sections.heading: Hot sign in a swirl means back out
sections.text: Sometimes you find a pile of fresh sign, like acorns and droppings everywhere, a hot scrape, or a rub line, down in a hollow where the wind swirls. Grant Woods of GrowingDeer.tv says not to set up on top of it. Deer spend so much time there because the thermals and swirling air protect them from every direction, and if you hunt in the swirl you'll blow the area out quickly and they'll start using that food only at night. Back out to the transition or travel corridor leading into it, where the wind is steadier and you can get in and out without alerting deer. He says this holds all season, not just early.

lessons.tryThis: On your next scouting trip in hill country, carry milkweed. Let some go on a bench in the morning and again at the top of a ditch in the evening, watch which way it drifts each time, and write down which hour each spot actually works.

check.q: It's a morning hunt in the hills. Do you sit above or below the sign?
check.a: Above it. Rising morning air carries your scent uphill, away from deer coming in below.

check.q: You find a hot scrape and acorns everywhere down in a swirly hollow. Where do you set up?
check.a: Back out to the transition or travel corridor leading into it, where the wind is steadier and you won't blow the spot out.

lessons.title: Bottoms, valleys, and mountains
lessons.hook: Ask three experienced hill hunters about creek bottoms and you'll get three answers. One avoids them, one hunts them only on certain winds, and one sits them on purpose because everyone else stays out. They all agree the air in low ground behaves differently than on a ridge. This lesson walks through each view so you can test them on your own ground.

sections.heading: Evening bottoms need a steady wind
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis only sits a bottom in the evening when a strong, steady wind is funneling up the valley away from where deer travel. In his example the valley ran about 500 to 600 yards before hitting a bank, and a steady wind zipped through it like a tunnel. If the forecast shows the wind calming, he skips it, because once the wind dies your scent drains downhill and spills into the area you're watching. He didn't give a wind speed for strong and steady, so you'll have to judge that on your own ground.

sections.heading: Watch winds that come straight over the ridge
sections.text: Sturgis also watches which way the wind crosses the ridge. Wind that tops the ridge head on tumbles down and swirls around the low ground, so he avoids a bottom stand then. Wind crossing the ridge from the sides is fine, because it pulls back uphill. At one of his stands the band of directions that swirled was about 90 to 120 degrees wide, and he still had almost 180 degrees of safe morning winds. So a bottom isn't simply bad. Like any stand, it has winds that work and winds that don't.

sections.heading: Or hunt high and skip the valleys
sections.text: Mike Rex, who hunts the steep hills of southeast Ohio, goes the other way. He hunts as high as he can, up on the ridges, where the forecast wind is the wind you actually get. In the valleys, he says, a west wind hitting a north-south ridge turns like a tornado, and there's no good wind direction at all. You can prove it with a campfire by counting how often you move because the smoke follows you. On a ridge, a west wind is a west wind. He also warns that in big country you don't know which direction a buck will come from, unlike a small woodlot in farm country.

sections.heading: Sit downstream of a creek crossing
sections.text: Jamie McKay, who hunts creek bottoms in the north Alabama hills, has a way to make low ground work. At a creek crossing he climbs right next to the creek on the downstream side of the trail. In a bottom the thermals follow the water, so the air sliding along the creek carries his scent away from the crossing. He's had it fail in a very light, swirling breeze, but it works often enough that he keeps hunting bottoms other hunters avoid.

sections.heading: In the mountains, go check
sections.text: McKay hunts mountain public land too, and there he won't scratch a good spot just because the forecast wind looks wrong for it. Mountain wind twists with the ridges and often has nothing to do with the forecast. Another hunter described it changing four directions on his walk up and ending 180 degrees from the forecast. So McKay goes and checks the actual air at the spot, and he says nine times out of ten it's fine where he's sitting. He agrees that ridge tops hold the steadiest air, and he accepts getting winded sometimes.

lessons.tryThis: Pick one low spot you've been avoiding. On a scouting walk, check the air there with milkweed on two or three different winds, and note which ones carry it cleanly down the drainage and which ones swirl. Now you know that bottom's safe winds instead of guessing.
lessons.headsUp: These views don't line up, and no research here has tested any of them. Rex says avoid valleys in steep hills, Sturgis says bottoms have safe wind windows, and McKay hunts bottoms by using the down-creek air. McKay also pushes back on the rule from the basics lesson. Sturgis and Informed Outdoors say never sit a stand on a wind it isn't safe for, while McKay says mountain forecasts are too unreliable to scratch a spot on. The difference is probably how steep and predictable your country is. In flatter ground the forecast rule works well, and in mountains you should go check the real air.

check.q: The forecast shows the wind dying at sunset. Is it a good evening to sit a creek bottom?
check.a: No. When the wind calms in a bottom, your scent drains downhill into the area you're watching.

check.q: Where do you sit at a creek crossing in a bottom?
check.a: Right next to the creek on the downstream side of the trail, so the air following the water carries your scent away.

units.goal: Beat the crowd: where others don't go, and where they push deer.

lessons.title: Scout for people first
lessons.hook: You pull into the parking area on opening morning and there are already four trucks. On public land, other hunters are part of the landscape, and the deer know it better than you do. Before you work out where the deer are, work out where the people are, because on public ground those two answers are tied together.

sections.heading: Scout for people as hard as you scout for deer
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis of Whitetail Habitat Solutions avoids any spot that shows signs of hunters. That means trash, tree stands, old blinds, footprints, beaten-down trails, ribbons, tacks, and even old axe notches in trees. In summer he scrapes a bare patch of soil 2 to 3 feet across on a trail, a sand trap, and comes back later to count how many different boot prints crossed it. What he's after is a remote spot with a history of buck sign, rubs and scrapes in the same places year after year, and no people. Bucks keep using those places because the lay of the land funnels them there. The Hunting Public crew adds one check. When you find lots of deer sign, ask whether it was made in daylight or only at night, because night-only sign won't give you a daylight shot.

sections.heading: Read what other hunters left behind
sections.text: Next Step Outdoors marks every sign of another hunter as he scouts, from trash and trail markers to reflective tacks, trimmed shooting lanes, stands, and trail cameras. On one property he found a stand 20 yards away and another 100 yards away in the first chunk of cover off the fields, so he didn't spend more time there. The most obvious cover nearest the access gets the stands and the pressure, so move farther into less obvious spots. Finding someone's stand isn't a dead end, though.
