The owner may rarely hunt it, so a weekday sit can still work.

sections.heading: Talk to people in the parking lot
sections.text: The Hunting Public crew expects other hunters and stays courteous. They talk to people in the parking lot and ask where they're heading, so nobody walks 3 miles in to find a camera or a hunter already set up. If someone beat you to a spot, it's first come, first served, and you go to plan B, C, or D. One of them once gave up a thicket to a hunter who'd waited three years to hunt it, went to plan D, and killed a buck on one of his best gun hunts.

sections.heading: Don't leave a trail to your spot
sections.text: Once you've found a good spot, hide that you were ever there. Sturgis leaves the main trail everyone uses early, avoids flattening ferns or trampling vegetation, and steps around sandy or muddy patches that hold a print. He never leaves flagging, tacks, or glow sticks to mark the way. Anything that shows your path lets another hunter follow it straight to the place you worked hard to find, whether it's 20 minutes in or over an hour.

lessons.tryThis: On your next scouting trip, carry a notebook or use your map app to mark every sign of people you see, not just deer sign. At the end, look at where the people sign stops. That's where your real scouting starts.

check.q: You find two stands in the first patch of cover off the parking area. What now?
check.a: Move farther from the access into less obvious spots. If you still like the area, a weekday sit can work, since the owner may rarely hunt that stand.

check.q: Why skip flagging tape and reflective tacks on public land?
check.a: They show other hunters your route straight to your spot.

lessons.title: Close or deep, find the ground others skip
lessons.hook: Every public-land hunter hears the same advice, which is to walk farther than everyone else. It works for some very good hunters. Other very good hunters kill their best bucks a short walk from the road. Both camps are chasing the same thing, the ground nobody else is hunting, and this lesson shows how each one finds it.

sections.heading: The case for going deep
sections.text: Jamie McKay, who hunts North Alabama public land, often walks 2 to 3 miles or more, and most of his public-land bucks came from deep spots. He uses a GPS tracker on a mapping app like onX to see where he's already been and goes to look at the gaps. Sturgis uses a back door into the middle of a big block of several hundred acres or more, where the access points are about a mile away in most directions. He gets in there in the morning and waits, because hunters coming in from every access point push deer toward the middle. That's how he shoots most of his public-land bucks.

sections.heading: The case for the spots people walk past
sections.text: Mike Rex, who interviewed the people who killed Ohio's highest-scoring bucks for a magazine story, puts it this way. Everybody goes way to the back to get away from the crowd, so that's where the crowd is, and old bucks survive by doing uncharacteristic things. The Hunting Public crew hunted mostly within half a mile of the road in Michigan, and a small thicket beside a timber line, which everyone walked past on their way two miles into a river bottom, produced encounter after encounter with big deer. Lee Ellis of Seek One finds his on private permission ground in tiny corners, like a bit of hardwoods by a river on someone's lot, backed up to the big cover a buck lives in. On a short trip, count the real hours too. The Hunting Public's example is 3 miles on the map that turned into 4.5 on foot and 3 hours in the dark, so keep five or six options ready.

sections.heading: Enter where others don't
sections.text: Sturgis also picks the way in that other hunters won't. Most people walk in from the parking lot, so he looks on the map for stretches of road between the official parking areas and cuts in from there. Even 5 to 10 minutes off the road can be excellent if it's a mile and a half or two from any parking. Another option is the hard way in. He says a 20-minute walk across a couple of beaver dams and a marsh in knee boots eliminates 90 to 95 percent of hunters, because most people won't get wet or walk far. A long, flat walk of around 45 minutes can do the same. This comes from one Sturgis video.

sections.heading: Look for places that can't be hunted
sections.text: Lee Ellis turns the question around. Instead of asking where you can hunt, ask where people can't, like a suburban no-hunting zone, a big block whose owner won't give permission, or ground that's hard to get into. Then get permission as close to it as you can. Every big deer he's hunted had a refuge where it could get old. Sturgis sees the same thing after gun season, when his clients find sign everywhere in February, the first time nobody has been on the property for more than two weeks. The Southern Outdoorsmen hosts apply the same idea to a small private place. If the neighbors shoot whatever walks by, make your place the safest spot around, with the best food, the best cover, and very little pressure, though deer won't stay on 100 acres all day.

lessons.tryThis: Open your mapping app on a public area you know. Mark every official parking spot, then look for the stretches of road between them and any water or marsh between the road and good cover. Check your old GPS tracks for pockets you've never walked into.
lessons.headsUp: McKay and Sturgis say most of their public-land bucks come from deep spots 1 to 3 or more miles from access. The Hunting Public, Rex, and Ellis say the crowd goes deep and the overlooked close spots hold the old bucks. Even the Hunting Public host admits he's the four-hours-to-my-dream-spot type and it has worked for him. Find out where the crowd actually goes on your ground, and on a short trip weigh the walking time.

check.q: You have a four-day trip and your dream spot is a three-hour walk in the dark. What should you weigh?
check.a: The real walking time against your short trip, and whether other hunters are already back there. Keep five or six options, including close spots others walk past.

check.q: What's one way to reach good ground that most hunters won't?
check.a: Cut in from the road between parking areas, or take a route that means crossing water, a marsh, or beaver dams.

lessons.title: A public-land game plan
lessons.hook: You've found a chunk of ground the crowd skips. Now you need a plan for what to do once you're there, and that plan changes with how big the area is, how long your trip is, and what time of year it is. Here's how a few experienced public-land hunters lay it out.

sections.heading: Shrink a huge area down to a few spots
sections.text: Sturgis can take a 10,000-acre public area down to a few hundred acres. First he crosses off the parts near access points and people trails, along with the obvious hardwoods people wander into from their cars. Then he circles the places where several edges come together, like a hillside meeting a swamp, mature timber meeting a clearcut, a natural waterway, uplands turning to hardwoods, or islands in a marsh. In steep country he looks at benches, saddles, and points. Public land tends to be big blocks of one kind of habitat, so deer movement bunches up where habitats meet, and marshes and steep ground make their routes more predictable.

sections.heading: Use both ends of the day
sections.text: Sturgis plans a public-land day as a layout. He gets remote, sits behind the bedding in the morning, then moves around and sets up mobile near the food for the afternoon. The same bedding layers you learned about earlier apply everywhere, and hunting pressure just pushes them farther out from the food. Hunting both ends of the day gets the most out of each trip.

sections.heading: On a short trip, sprint
sections.text: On a short hunt, like a five-day gun opener trip, Sturgis hunts like it's a sprint, not a marathon. Find the freshest sign of the moment, get right in on top of it, hunt it hard, and leave. Don't worry much about spooking something, because you aren't managing that ground for the whole season. Rain and poor weather make getting in close even easier. On land you hunt all season, he says the opposite, and you manage it like a marathon.

sections.heading: Hunt the push on crowded gun days
sections.text: Jamie McKay hunts Alabama public areas where gun hunts run a few permit days and draw a crowd. On those days he sets up on the escape routes the crowd will push deer into, such as a point leading up off a creek system, a gap off a bluff, or ground below where people walk in. If you know which way the crowd is coming from, you can bowhunt the push. It has worked well for him, though he's the only source here.

sections.heading: Velvet bucks in August
sections.text: Early bucks still in velvet, the soft covering on growing antlers, leave little fresh sign and travel in bachelor groups, so they live in pockets. One of the Southern Outdoorsmen hosts, hunting West Tennessee public land, points out that a spot can look great and still have no bachelor group anywhere near it, and his own ground looked excellent for October and November. He hunts habitat edges, and where private bean fields border the public, he cuts deer off in the woods on their way to the beans. He also picks spots where he can see deer, so he can move on them and reposition. Seeing deer is the fastest way to find them.

lessons.tryThis: Take one public area near you and do Sturgis's cut on a map. Cross off everything near parking and trails, then circle three places where two or more habitats meet. Pick one for a morning sit and one near food for the afternoon.

check.q: You have a five-day public-land gun trip. How careful should you be about spooking deer?
check.a: Not very. Treat it like a sprint. Find the freshest sign, get right on it, hunt it hard, and leave.

check.q: Where does Sturgis look for deer movement inside a huge block of public land?
check.a: Where several habitat edges come together, like a hillside meeting a swamp or timber meeting a clearcut, and on benches, saddles, and points in steep country.

units.goal: Call less, call soft, and know when to stop.

lessons.title: Call less, call soft
lessons.hook: Most new hunters buy a grunt call before their first season, and most of them use it too much. Nothing's moving, so you give it a blow, and then another fifteen minutes later. A call can bring a buck in. It can also tell every deer within earshot exactly where you're sitting.

sections.heading: Less is almost always more
sections.text: Mark Kenyon of MeatEater has called deer for 30 years, and his rule is that less is almost always more. Give a buck just what he needs to hear, then stop. Don't use every call at once, and if nothing comes, don't keep calling every 15 minutes. Jeff Sturgis of Whitetail Habitat Solutions explains the cost. The more you call, the more a deer figures out you aren't a deer, and a shy old buck will often circle downwind, smell you, and leave without you ever knowing he was there. Sturgis once watched deer run from a neighbor who had rattled, snort-wheezed, grunted, and bleated, and they were still nervous passing his stand 200 yards away. If the does and young bucks around you are on edge and looking back over their shoulders, assume any mature buck nearby is gone.

sections.heading: Start at a deer's volume
sections.text: Real deer are much quieter than most hunters think. The Deer Society says a fawn bleat is so quiet you can barely hear it at 5 yards, so use the least air you can. Kenyon opens on a buck that's out of range with the lowest-risk call, a light contact grunt, and watches for any sign he heard it, like a pause, a stop, or an ear turned your way. Only if the buck clearly didn't hear it does he go louder. Once the buck notices, stop and watch. Blasting a call is like shouting at a stranger while staring at them, and if a deer looks at your call and then fades off, you were probably too loud. With a buck already close, around 70 yards in Kenyon's example, don't open with rattling antlers.

sections.heading: Call at deer you can see or hear
sections.text: Blind calling means calling into the woods with no deer in sight. Kenyon and Sturgis both say don't. Call only at a buck whose location you know, one you can see or bucks you can hear sparring and grunting nearby. Kenyon says nine times out of ten or more, blind calling just makes noise and spooks deer, and on public land in early November a grunt call or antlers can do real damage. Sturgis adds that knowing where the buck is lowers the chance he gets downwind of you. On pressured public ground, or where mature bucks are scarce, carry a rattle bag but use it very sparingly.

sections.heading: If you do call blind, pick your moment
sections.text: Kenyon makes very few exceptions. If he blind calls, he does it when conditions give deer a reason to get up, like a weather change, clouds rolling in, rain stopping, or the light changing around 5 PM. He doesn't do it at 10 AM after two slow hours on an all-day sit, because the midday lull is when you most want something to happen and when you're least likely to call one in. One other source, a Downwind Hunting listicle, which is a compiled and unverified article, blind calls a single short contact grunt every 30 to 40 minutes with no deer in sight. It says Iowa and Illinois outfitters have switched to this. That's the only source for it.

lessons.tryThis: On your next sit, leave every call but a grunt tube at home. Only use it on a buck you can see, start with one soft grunt, and then watch his head and ears before doing anything else.
lessons.headsUp: Kenyon and Sturgis say not to blind call, and Sturgis specifically warns against calling every 20 to 30 minutes hoping something hears it. The Downwind Hunting listicle blind calls one grunt every 30 to 40 minutes. The hunters' view carries more weight here, and every source agrees that constant calling from one spot is a mistake.

check.q: You grunt softly and a buck at 100 yards pauses and turns an ear your way. What next?
check.a: Stop and watch what he does. He heard you, so there's no reason to call louder or again yet.

check.q: It's 10 AM, two slow hours into an all-day sit. Is this a good time for a blind grunt?
check.a: No. The midday lull is when you're least likely to call one in. If you blind call at all, do it when the weather or light changes.

lessons.title: Using the grunt call
lessons.hook: A buck walks by at 60 yards, headed somewhere else. He's not coming closer on his own. This is the moment the grunt call was made for, and it's also the moment most hunters overdo it. What you do in the next few seconds, and what you don't do, decides how it ends.

sections.heading: Carry a grunt every sit
sections.text: Sturgis carries a grunt call on every sit, all season, somewhere he can grab it without moving much. He keeps his in a hand-warmer tube on his waist belt. He uses it on a buck he can see that's passing out of bow range, going the wrong way, or that walked under him without giving a shot. A couple of soft grunts can stop or turn him. It's very low impact, so you have nothing to lose on a buck that's leaving, and a searching buck will often turn around. A grunt only carries about 50 to 80 yards in quiet conditions, so don't grunt at deer you can't see.

sections.heading: Early season, keep it soft
sections.text: In the early season Sturgis carries one call, a simple buck grunt, and uses a soft grunt or two or three on a buck he can see at about 50 to 60 yards. A buck won't come 150 yards out of his way for it. Early bucks are social and sorting out who's boss, so a low contact grunt sparks their curiosity. Kenyon uses it when bachelor groups are breaking up and bucks are hanging around nearby without coming your way. It works best when you're tucked in timber where they can't see where the sound came from. Sturgis hunts heavily pressured states, where deer get educated to calling fast, and says it may be different in places like Kansas, Iowa, or Texas.

sections.heading: Once he responds, put it away
sections.text: Three sources agree on this. Once a buck stops, snaps his head your way, or starts toward you, put the call away and slowly get ready for the shot. He already knows exactly where the sound came from, so more calling only draws his eyes to your spot. Sturgis grunted in a rut buck of 170-plus inches that came partway, called again while it stood deciding, and watched it walk off. Kenyon warns that if a buck hears an odd deer-like sound and 20 seconds later smells a person, he learns to connect the two. Save calls for deer about to skirt you out of range or walking away. The Hunting Public crew rattled at a buck they barely glimpsed walking away, and he came back within 15 minutes.

sections.heading: Read the first five seconds
sections.text: Kenyon watches the buck closely the moment the first call reaches him, because in about 5 seconds he'll usually tell you whether he's callable. If his head snaps up and he gets nervous and jittery, stop. If he looks calm and curious, or stops to rake a branch, rub, or scrape, Kenyon keeps working him. Hunters tend to panic and push a buck that already said no.

sections.heading: He may circle back
sections.text: Derek Dixon, who studies bucks with thermal drones, has seen traveling bucks ignore a grunt and keep walking, then circle back 15 to 30 minutes later and check it out for about 5 minutes before returning to their route. A buck on his morning route with his nose down often ignores the call at first. It's a single research source, but it's a good reason to stay ready after a buck walks on.

lessons.tryThis: Put your grunt call somewhere you can reach it without lifting your arm much. On the next buck that passes out of range, give him two soft grunts, then stay still and count five seconds while you read his reaction.
lessons.headsUp: Sturgis and Kenyon split on a buck that hangs up. Sturgis says once a buck has looked your way, don't call again even if he stops or works a scrape, because he knows where the sound came from. Kenyon says a buck that stays calm or stops to rake, rub, or scrape is still callable, so keep working him. They all agree to stop the moment he's actually coming. Kenyon and Sturgis also differ on early rattling, since Kenyon uses a little sparring tickle on early bachelor bucks and Sturgis says it rarely brings deer in before the pre-rut.

check.q: A buck at 60 yards hears your grunt and stares your way. Should you call again?
check.a: No. Put the call away and get ready. He knows where the sound came from, and more calling raises his suspicion.

check.q: A buck ignores your grunt and keeps walking. Are you done?
check.a: Not yet. Dixon's drone work shows some bucks circle back 15 to 30 minutes later, so stay ready.

lessons.title: Bleats and rattling
lessons.hook: Grunts are the everyday call. Bleats and rattling antlers are the other two tools you'll see in every hunting store, and they sit at opposite ends of the risk scale. A bleat almost never hurts you. Rattling can bring a buck running or empty the woods, and where you do it matters more than how.

sections.heading: The bleat is low risk
sections.text: A doe bleat, fawn bleat, or bleat can rarely gets a response, but it almost never spooks deer, even with does and fawns around. Sturgis would rather use a call that works sometimes and rarely spooks than an aggressive call that spooks deer a lot of the time. He uses it on a cruising or searching buck in the peak rut and post-rut, when a buck looking for a doe may come to it. He called a nice buck straight in with a bleat in 2002 and has killed a rut buck with a bleat can. Leave the fawn bleat home early in the season if you're after bucks. Fawns bleat all the time then, so a buck won't go out of his way, and it may only draw a doe looking for a lost fawn. Sturgis is mixed on carrying one at all, and in one video he says as a minimalist he usually leaves it home.

sections.heading: Rattle like sparring, not a brawl
sections.text: Real sparring is back-and-forth tickling, not two rams butting heads. Kenyon and Sturgis both rattle with a light tickling sequence, then hang up the antlers and pick up a grunt call. A mature buck often got old by avoiding fights, so loud, aggressive rattling tends to send him away. Kenyon saves loud, crashing fights for top-tier ground with lots of mature bucks, like an Iowa or Kansas tag, because on average ground a big fight mostly spooks deer. Sturgis's trick is to tie the antlers to his bow rope, lower them to the base of the tree away from the metal stand, and scuff them in the dirt and leaves so the sound comes from the ground, where real bucks would be.

sections.heading: Only rattle with the downwind side blocked
sections.text: Sturgis says almost every buck circles downwind of a call or antlers before he comes in. If he can get downwind, he smells you. So rattle only from a stand whose downwind side is blocked by something deer won't cross in daylight, like a cliff or bluff, a swamp, an open creek, a pond, an open pasture, open hardwoods, a field edge, or houses and a road. Thick brush downwind gives him cover to do it. In Michigan's Upper Peninsula, Sturgis heard one come from upwind, loop all the way downwind, blow, and run without ever being seen. He also rattles only where few hunters are around, because where hunter numbers are high, even young bucks learn that rattling means a hunter. He never rattles in Minnesota or Wisconsin. This is Sturgis's rule alone, and he treats rattling as a rut tactic.

lessons.tryThis: Look at your stand spots on a map and find the downwind side of each one. Mark any stand where a field, water, a bluff, or open timber blocks that side. Those are the only places to try rattling.
lessons.headsUp: Not everyone rattles softly. The Hunting Public crew rattled hard and loud on public land in the rut and brought a cruising buck to 5 yards. That buck was too far away for grunts, and the leaves were too crunchy to sneak closer. Kenyon and Sturgis would still keep it subtle on most ground.

check.q: You want to rattle, and there's thick brush on the downwind side of your stand. Good spot?
check.a: No. A buck will circle downwind through that brush and smell you. Rattle where something deer won't cross in daylight blocks the downwind side.

check.q: Why is a bleat called a low-risk call?
check.a: Deer rarely come to it, but it almost never spooks them either.

lessons.title: Making calls sound real
lessons.hook: Two hunters can blow the same grunt tube and get opposite results. The difference is usually in their breathing and their hands, not in the call. Everything in this lesson comes from one source, The Deer Society, so treat it as a good way to practice rather than settled fact.

sections.heading: Breathe, don't blow
sections.text: Close your upper lip over the top half of the mouthpiece and rest the bottom on your lower lip. Then breathe into it from your diaphragm, the muscle under your lungs, without puffing your cheeks. It takes very little air to make the reed vibrate, and controlling that air with your breathing instead of your mouth is the first step to sounding real. To get louder, add air pressure and open up the chamber your hands make. The buck setting gets loud with less air than the doe, and too much pressure while you're choking the call locks the reed up.

sections.heading: Quieter than you think
sections.text: The Deer Society watched a doe hear her fawn's near-silent bleat and come out of the timber. A real fawn bleat is so quiet you can barely hear it at 5 yards. That's the volume you're aiming for when you start, and it's why over-calling with volume is such a common mistake. Practice the fawn, doe, and buck volumes before the season so you know what quiet sounds like on your call.

sections.heading: Shape the grunt with your hands
sections.text: An open call doesn't sound like a buck in the timber. Hold the call between your thumb and forefinger and choke it with your other fingers, then cup your other hand tight, like it's holding water, to make a deep chamber. Vary the choke, the chamber, and the air pressure. Don't assume you need the deepest old-buck grunt to call in a big buck. Every buck has his own voice, and a deep, guttural grunt often turns out to be a little forkhorn, a young buck with small forked antlers.

sections.heading: Inflection carries the message
sections.text: On doe and fawn calls, use tone and inflection on purpose, rising or falling, soft or loud. The same call inflected differently means different things, the way how you say something to a person changes how they take it. Tone creates emotion, and that's what the deer responds to, so match the emotion you want to send and watch the deer's reaction. The Deer Society doesn't say in this video which inflection means what, so for now the deer's reaction is your guide.

lessons.tryThis: Spend ten minutes with your grunt call at home. Practice breathing from your diaphragm, then try the call open and choked with a cupped hand, and listen to how different it sounds. Finish with the softest fawn bleat you can make.

check.q: Your grunt call squeaks and locks up when you choke it. What's likely wrong?
check.a: Too much air pressure. Breathe from your diaphragm and use less air.

check.q: Does a deeper grunt bring in bigger bucks?
check.a: Not necessarily. Every buck has his own voice, and a deep grunt often comes from a little forkhorn.

units.goal: How old bucks live, bed, and travel differently.

lessons.title: Where an old buck really lives
lessons.hook: You've got a big buck on camera, and you start hunting him everywhere on the farm. A week later you've sat six stands, pushed scent across the whole place, and never seen him in daylight. The problem usually isn't your stands. It's that you're hunting his whole range when he spends his daylight hours in a much smaller piece of it.

sections.heading: His daylight world is small
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis of Whitetail Habitat Solutions puts a mature buck's home range at about three square miles, but most of that is night travel. Outside the rut he says a buck usually moves only 200 to 300 yards in daylight, from where he beds to where he feeds, and he puts it at about 300 yards for about 90% of the season. Even in the rut, when a buck may cover 5 miles at night, Sturgis sees him stay in the same 10 to 15 acres of cover by day. If he crossed every fence line and walked past every hunter in daylight, he'd be dead. So find his bed-to-food pair and set up on it, even on a small parcel. Sturgis hunted the same bucks year after year on a Wisconsin piece with only about 30 acres of cover.

sections.heading: Finding the core in pressured country
sections.text: Eddie McRae hunts small Georgia farms with pressured neighbors, and his mature bucks lived in cores of about 10 to 11 acres. One lived 430 yards from a spot McRae watched on camera for months and never walked by it once. To find a core like that, look for the 10 to 20% of the property that's nearly impossible to walk through. McRae means young regrowth about 8 to 10 years old with a very high stem count that still has grasses, weeds, briars, blackberry, privet, and green brier, ideally with a creek. With nine cameras out, his mature bucks never showed up at a second camera site, while two-year-olds turned up everywhere. He sets up right on the edge of that thick stuff or inside it.

sections.heading: Night photos mean he lives somewhere else
sections.text: Sturgis followed one buck, Junior, whose core was 30 to 40 acres. Junior showed up outside it less than 10% of the time, a little more from late October into early November, and he was back home by mid-November. Another buck showed up 11 times in six weeks, almost all at night. He lived on the next property, where the neighbor saw him in daylight nearly every day and shot him. So when a buck only appears 2 to 4 hours after dark, Sturgis treats him as a buck that doesn't live on your ground, and he hunts the buck whose core he's actually in.

sections.heading: Sign that fools you, and clues that don't
sections.text: Jamie McKay, who hunts the Deep South, says rubs and scrapes along creek bottoms are easy to find but mostly made after dark. If the bottom has no food, he moves up into thicker cover with more browse. A shed is a better clue. McKay found a buck's shed and a big bed on a bluff top above a thicket and killed that buck the next season within sight of the spot. He's honest that it's worked once and he's still trying to repeat it. Sturgis adds one more habit, which is to hunt a buck on the same winds he's already shown up on in your camera photos, so you aren't asking him to do anything new. That only works if you log the wind with each photo.

lessons.tryThis: Pull up your camera history for the buck you're after and split his photos into daylight and night. Mark the camera sites where he shows up in daylight, then look on the map for the thickest cover nearest those sites. That's your first guess at his core.
lessons.headsUp: The measured research is less tidy than the hunters' numbers. The Mississippi State GPS-collar study found bucks bedded only about 38% of daylight outside the rut, and a buck bedded a couple thousand yards away could move all afternoon and still reach your food after dark. So daylight movement may be longer than 200 to 300 yards, just hidden inside cover. Sturgis openly distrusts home-range research. Both still point you at his cover rather than the open food.

check.q: A buck shows up on your camera several times, always a few hours after dark. What does Sturgis make of that?
check.a: He probably lives on someone else's ground. Hunt the buck whose daylight core you're in.

check.q: What kind of cover did McRae look for to find a core on pressured farms?
check.a: The nearly impassable 10 to 20% of the property, young thick regrowth about 8 to 10 years old, ideally with a creek.

lessons.title: Where mature bucks bed
lessons.hook: You've heard the rules. Old bucks bed in the top third of the hill, on the leeward side, in the thickest brush. Hunters who watch bucks closely, and one researcher who flies thermal drones over them, keep finding bucks where those rules say they shouldn't be.

sections.heading: Not always the top third
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis doesn't assume mature bucks bed high. He looks for benches, and for the flat on a point just before it drops off steeply, placed out beyond where the does bed. What decides it is how bedding layers out from the food, not elevation. If food sits right next to the high ground, bucks won't bed there. He even warns that putting a food plot in a low flat would erase the mature-buck bedding that was there.

sections.heading: Thermal hubs
sections.text: Derek Dixon studies bucks with thermal drones, so this comes from watching real deer. He looks for thermal hubs, which are spots where several ridges and drainages funnel into one bowl, and he often finds a buck on a point about 50 yards above the hub. On one hub he could find a mature buck, not always the same one, bedded on the same point nearly every time he flew, day or night and in any wind or weather. Even a small hub with a couple of ridges counts, especially with a mouth leading out to food and water, saddles nearby, and mixed habitat. Beau Martonik found two good bucks bedded on tiny points in a small bowl halfway up a hill that he'd never have picked from a map. Keep in mind this is one hub plus one example, with no numbers on how often it holds.

sections.heading: Not always the lee side
sections.text: The textbook says bucks bed on the side of the ridge sheltered from the wind. Dixon's flights often found them on the windward side facing into it, even at 5°F with sleet. Expect them on the side they came from, like the side facing the food they just left, and on whichever side has thick cover such as mountain laurel. Martonik finds deer on the covered windward side when the lee side is open timber, especially in pressured places.

sections.heading: Thick brush or a view
sections.text: Mike Rex, who hunts the wooded hills of southeast Ohio, says bucks there have changed. With lots of coyotes and bobcats working the thick stuff by nose all year, mature bucks now bed on fairly open wooded ridges with a small patch of cover to break them up, like a treetop, a fallen tree, or a snag. They still browse in thick cover, but they bed where they can see, hear, and smell danger coming. In the late 70s and early 80s, he says, the same deer bedded in thick grouse cover. In farm country with CRP grass, they still bed in the CRP because it's the only cover.

sections.heading: Hunt the route, not the bed
sections.text: Don't build your hunt around sitting his bed. Dixon watched bucks arrive, stand at a rub or scrape for 10 to 15 minutes, then lie down and stay within about a 50-yard circle. Very few people can get into position inside a circle that small, so the travel in and out is where he's huntable. McKay, in the Deep South's big woods, cites GPS studies showing bucks use a different bed every day. One well-used bed he watched on camera was used by an 8-point, a spike, and several does, and sitting a bed waiting for the buck to return never worked for him. The hosts point out that Midwest farm country, with few bedding spots, is different, so bedding setups work better there.

lessons.tryThis: On a topo map, find one spot where three or more ridges and drainages come together into a bowl. Mark the points about 50 yards above it, and note which side of each ridge has the thickest cover. Plan to hunt the trails leading into that area, not the points themselves.
lessons.headsUp: Two disagreements here. Sturgis says late-season deer bed on the slope sheltered from the day's wind, while Dixon's drones often found bucks on the windward side. Where both sides have similar cover, Sturgis's rule may hold, and where only the windward side is thick, expect bucks there. Eddie McRae tells you to set up in nearly impassable regrowth, while Rex finds bucks on open ridges. Let the cover type and how many predators you have decide.

check.q: Why does Dixon say to hunt a buck's route instead of his bed?
check.a: Once bedded he stays inside about a 50-yard circle, and very few hunters can get into position that close.

check.q: In Rex's coyote-heavy hills, where do mature bucks bed now?
check.a: On fairly open wooded ridges with a small patch of cover, where they can see, hear, and smell danger coming.

lessons.title: Funnels an old buck has to use
lessons.hook: Every hunter loves a pinch point on the map, the narrow spot where the woods squeeze deer into a gap. Some of those spots do exactly what you hope. Others produce plenty of young bucks while the oldest one quietly walks around them. Knowing which is which is the whole trick.

sections.heading: Walls with gaps
sections.text: In hill and mountain country, start by marking every place deer physically can't travel, like cliffs, bluffs, rock walls, and slopes too steep to use. Do it with mapping software, then check it on foot. What's left are the gaps. Derek Dixon calls them invisible funnels, often 30 to 150 yards wide, and every buck he tracked with his thermal drone walked through them because there was no other way across. Jamie McKay hunts the gap or ledge where deer get up and down a bluff, and his had a scrape right at the top. Mike Rex looks for a cut in a long high wall where the doe trails funnel through. Stack a gap with a saddle and mixed habitat and your odds climb.

sections.heading: Be ready to wait
sections.text: Bucks use those gaps on purpose. On a warm November afternoon, Rex watched a 140-class buck walk to the cut in a wall about three quarters of a mile long, bed right there, fall asleep, and wait about 2 hours until a doe came up the bank. That's why sitting at the top of a drainage in one of these gaps is a strong rut setup, as long as you're ready to sit all afternoon. On gun-season days, sit at the bottom of a bluff gap instead, so deer pushed off the top by other hunters come down to you.

sections.heading: The perfect pinch may not be his
sections.text: Rex warns that a perfect pinch a buck can go around tends to produce 3- to 5-year-olds, while the oldest bucks may stop 60 to 80 yards short and loop through a ravine or drainage. An 8.5-year-old buck he called Teflon Don refused his pinch twice. Once the buck spotted him and backed out, and once he circled around on a perfect crosswind. Then on November 16 he walked right under Rex 20 minutes later, trailing a doe. Rex says Dixon's drone work found some old bucks never use a 30-yard ridge pinch. So in the rut, stay put, because a doe can still pull him through. This is Rex's story alone, and he cites Dixon secondhand.

sections.heading: Saddles and low dips
sections.text: Rex also likes saddles, the low spot between two high points, especially in the rut. It's the easiest way over, and in a big-hardwood national forest in late season he watched deer use saddles to cross from one area to another. Trails tend to run along the ridges, so a buck going up and over crosses more and more doe trails. Mark Kenyon of MeatEater adds a rule for open ground. Where a mature buck has to cross a field between two blocks of thick cover, find the lowest dip that's also the narrowest gap, and nine times out of ten that's where he crosses. Kenyon says even 6 to 10 feet of relief is enough to keep a buck out of sight. Each of these comes from one hunter.

sections.heading: Small clearcuts get walked around
sections.text: Dixon's drones showed that around smaller clearcuts, up to about 25 to 30 acres, ringed by mature timber, deer walk the outside edge instead of crossing. Even does that bed just inside the cut back out to the wood edge and follow it. With timber all around, nothing forces them through, so hunt the edges. Very large cuts may be different, and Beau Martonik notes that cuts ringed with other hunters' stands can change the pattern.

lessons.tryThis: On your hunting map, shade every cliff, bluff, and slope too steep to walk. Look at the gaps left between the shaded areas, then walk the two most promising ones and look for trails, rubs, or a scrape at the top.
lessons.headsUp: Dixon's research says every buck he tracked used the truly impassable gaps. Rex says the oldest bucks may refuse a pinch they can loop around, like a 30-yard ridge pinch. These fit together if you sort funnels into two kinds. Gaps in cliffs and walls are forced and reliable. Pinches a buck can go around may mostly give you younger bucks.

check.q: What's the difference between a forced gap and an optional pinch?
check.a: A forced gap is the only way through a cliff or wall, so every buck uses it. An optional pinch can be looped around, and the oldest bucks may do that.

check.q: A mature buck has to cross a field between two thick covers. Where does Kenyon expect him to cross?
check.a: At the lowest dip that's also the narrowest gap between the covers.

lessons.title: Setting up on his route
lessons.hook: You've found the funnel and the beaten-down trail running through it, and it's tempting to hang your stand right on top of that trail. The does and young bucks will walk it all day. The buck you actually want probably won't, and the hunters in this lesson explain where he goes instead.

sections.heading: Off the main trail
sections.text: Derek Dixon's thermal drones showed mature bucks walking through the same funnel, 30 to 300 yards wide, over and over, but rarely on the same trail within 3 yards from one day to the next. A buck crosses and scent-checks the main trail, then takes his own route around it, maybe 50 yards in front of your camera or behind it. Mike Rex's camera history says the same thing, since his oldest deer rarely use the trails everything else uses, so he covers the secondary trails near the big worn ones. Downwind Hunting, an unverified online list, says a buck parallels the worn trail 10 to 30 yards downwind and suggests a stand 20 yards downwind in the cover. Dixon describes the offset as in front or behind, not specifically downwind, so trust the general idea more than that exact number.

sections.heading: Two stands at a pinch, set for a crosswind
sections.text: Rex's best pinch was an inside field corner with a steep ravine just beyond it, leaving a 70-yard strip of woods everything had to use. They killed a lot of good bucks there. He hung two stands about 70 yards apart, one for each opposite wind, 30 to 35 feet up in trees with lots of cover. He picks the stand that puts a crosswind across the buck's approach, a little in the buck's favor and a little in yours. A buck with the wind at his back stops short, tests the air, and scans, and one did exactly that and spotted Rex even at 30 to 35 feet. That height is far above what Samko Trad Bow and Bow Only Outdoors recommend.

sections.heading: Pinches work with a rifle too
sections.text: Rifle season doesn't mean you need long shots. Jeff Sturgis says a pinch-point stand in close cover still works, and many of his gun-season bucks came at about 25 yards in farm-country woodlots. He sometimes even carries his bow in gun season for those setups. Pinches put deer close no matter what you're carrying.

sections.heading: Just over the ridge crest
sections.text: On long ridges in open hardwoods, Jamie McKay looks for the trail running parallel to the crest about 15 to 20 yards off the top, where it's a little thicker just over the break. Deer hug that thicker ground. He's the only one here who teaches it, so treat it as a good tip for that kind of country.

sections.heading: Don't be afraid of thick stuff
sections.text: McKay used to hunt only hardwoods. Now he'd rather hunt a pine thicket, because pine thickets, grown-up cutovers, and privet thickets full of browse hold deer that feel comfortable moving through them. You don't need to see 50 to 60 yards. He climbs where he can see down one or two old skidder trails. He watched hunters walk through thick cover to reach a creek bottom and see nothing, while he backed off, sat in the thick stuff, and saw deer all morning.

lessons.tryThis: At the next funnel you scout, find the main trail, then walk 30 to 50 yards off each side of it looking for fainter trails, rubs, or tracks. If you find one, hang your camera there instead of on the main trail and see what shows up.
lessons.headsUp: Stand height is a real split. Rex hunts pinches from 30 to 35 feet, and even so a buck with the wind at his back picked him out, while other sources recommend much lower stands. The downwind offset is also shaky. Dixon's research shows bucks swinging off the main trail, but the exact 20 yards downwind comes from a single unverified list.

check.q: Why hang a camera or stand off to the side of the most worn trail?
check.a: Mature bucks move through the same funnel but rarely on the main trail. They cross it, scent-check it, and take their own route nearby.

check.q: At Rex's two-stand pinch, which stand does he sit?
check.a: The one that gives a crosswind to the buck's approach, so neither the buck nor Rex has the wind at his back.

lessons.title: Know the buck, then adjust
lessons.hook: Two bucks can live on the same farm and act nothing alike. One might come to a rattle, and the other ignores every call. The hunters who kill old bucks pay attention to which kind they're after, and they're willing to move when the deer tell them their plan was wrong.

sections.heading: Spot the bully in summer
sections.text: Derek Dixon watches bachelor groups in late summer for the bully, the buck that walks up and gets bedded bucks on their feet or strikes at them. The aggressive bucks he filmed one summer turned out to be the solitary bucks that hated other deer once the season came. Calmer bucks, even the biggest on the property, tended to keep their buddies. Dixon says there are few hard rules with mature bucks, so knowing which kind you're after helps you guess what he'll do.

sections.heading: The biggest bucks rarely come to a call
sections.text: Lee Ellis of Seek One has never had a giant come running to a call, while young bucks come to rattling again and again. He thinks some bucks get old partly because they're wired to be less vulnerable. He watched a dominant buck simply flare his antlers at a bully and the bully backed off, so that buck rarely needs to fight. His late-season giant stayed alone while 10 to 12 other bucks grouped up. An aggressive bully may come to rattling, but a calm dominant buck won't. Ellis is the only one teaching this directly, though Jeff Sturgis also says rattling tends to bring younger bucks.

sections.heading: Watch him get up
sections.text: Some bucks can't be caught on the way in. The Hunting Public crew hunted one that bedded in a low hole out of the wind, well before daylight. They set up on the next ridge, looking down into the bedding, waited for him to stand up and browse around mid-morning, and then moved in for the shot. It's one hunt from their past, but it's a good play for a bed you can see into from above.

sections.heading: Move to where he actually walks
sections.text: Five different sources agree on this one. Set up where deer actually move, not where you planned. In a new area, watch from a distance first. When a buck uses a spot you're not covering, move onto it. Next Step Outdoors moves that same afternoon, Jamie McKay the next morning, and the Hunting Public crew after deer pass a spot 2 or 3 times. McKay's buck came the same exact way at 10 AM the morning after he watched it cruise by. Lee Ellis pulls his stand if the trail is about 100 yards away, and once climbed three test trees before one worked. Blowdowns shifted one Hunting Public trail 20 yards, turning a 40-yard shot into an 8-yard shot at a big buck. Mark Kenyon points out that ladders and box blinds tempt you to stay put, so a saddle or light hang-on helps you actually move.

sections.heading: Keep a stand for every kind of day
sections.text: Before the season, the Hunting Public crew builds a list of setups for hot days, cold fronts, dead-calm days, and low-impact mornings close to the road. Nine times out of ten, they say, you won't have the right conditions for your great spot in the middle of a bedding area, and hunters with only a couple of days force it anyway and blow it out. Sturgis's answer for a bad-weather day is to sit a stand you have less faith in, off to the side and easy to get in and out of. You still have a chance at a buck, and you save your best stand for a good day.

lessons.tryThis: Make a short list with four headings, hot day, cold front, calm day, and easy morning. Under each one, write the stand you'd sit. If a heading is empty, that's what to scout for next.
lessons.headsUp: The sources agree you should move to where deer are, but not on how fast. Next Step Outdoors moves the same afternoon, while the Hunting Public crew waits for 2 or 3 passes and then refines a new spot over 5 to 15 sits, testing the wind at the ground, 10 feet, and 20 feet. A quick move suits a buck you just watched, and a slower one suits a spot you'll hunt many times.

check.q: According to Ellis, what kind of mature buck might come to rattling?
check.a: An aggressive bully buck. A calm dominant buck usually won't.

check.q: The weather is bad but it's your only day off. What does Sturgis sit?
check.a: A low-risk stand off to the side that's easy to get in and out of, saving his best stand for good conditions.

lessons.title: When you bump him
lessons.hook: You're walking in, a branch snaps under your boot, and a big buck crashes off through the timber. Your stomach drops, and you start to think he's gone for the year. The hunters and the drone research in this lesson say he probably isn't, though they disagree on how soon to go after him.

sections.heading: What the research shows about a bump
sections.text: Derek Dixon bumped bucks on purpose with his drone, and his results matched GPS-collar studies. A bumped buck runs 200 to 300 yards, stays on edge for 30 minutes to an hour, and is back within about 8 to 12 hours. Once or twice doesn't seem to change anything, but walking the same bedding 7 to 10 times in 5 or 6 days will. Dixon even saw one mature buck regularly bed right off the edge of a cabin where people came and went. So on big ground, like public land or a big lease, don't be afraid to walk bedding areas while scouting. Go into the wind so deer hear or see you rather than smell you, and note where they bedded, where they ran, and the feeding sign coming out.

sections.heading: Small places are different
sections.text: The Hunting Public crew adds two things. A deer you bump on October 1 probably won't be in that spot on October 30 anyway, because his food and interests change, so you're gathering information on the 1st to kill one on the 15th. On a small property, though, they say don't. Bumping deer off their own small clover plot kept them off it for about a week. Being careful matters most when you're after one specific deer on a small place.

sections.heading: Go after him soon
sections.text: If a buck saw or heard you but didn't smell you, the Hunting Public crew doesn't give up. Watch where he goes, calm down, and think about the next cover he's headed for. A spooked buck usually runs to that cover and settles within an hour or two, and now you know where he lives. They've called a rut buck straight back in right after it spooked with a doe, shot a Georgia buck a couple of hours after bumping it hard, and killed a big-woods buck the next morning about 300 yards from where it was bumped after it ran 400 to 500 yards.

sections.heading: Hunt next door, not the same spot
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis spooked his buck Junior off a water hole around October 25, a spot the buck had used weekly for years. Junior only walked off 80 yards and stayed on the food until dark, but he never came back to that water hole in the six weeks before a hunter named Jeff killed him. He kept coming out of the same core, and Jeff shot him on a food source in that core where he hadn't been seen in over a month. So quit the exact spot, but keep hunting right next to it.

sections.heading: Or give him two weeks
sections.text: Eddie McRae had a buck watch him climb down from his stand on a Georgia property, and it never came back to that spot. He waited about two weeks, then went looking in the thickest, nastiest cover nearby instead of assuming the buck had left. He set a camera 430 yards away in the thick corner of the property and had the buck on it that same night. To check on a buck like this he uses a camera, a mock scrape, a mineral block, and a little scattered feed, where feed and mineral are legal.

lessons.tryThis: The next time you bump a deer while scouting, stop and watch where it goes. Mark the spot it was bedded and the direction it ran on your map, then look at the map for the nearest block of cover in that direction.
lessons.headsUp: They disagree on timing. The Hunting Public crew goes after a bumped buck the same day or within a few days, and Dixon's data shows bucks back within 8 to 12 hours. McRae waits about two weeks. Everyone agrees the buck stays close. The difference may be the situation, since McRae's buck saw him at his stand on a smaller private place, while the others were bumped by sight or sound on bigger ground.

check.q: According to Dixon's drone and collar data, how long before a bumped buck is usually back?
check.a: About 8 to 12 hours, after running 200 to 300 yards.

check.q: Sturgis spooked Junior off a water hole. Where was he killed?
check.a: On a food source in the same core area, not at the water hole he'd been spooked from.

units.goal: Does, doe trails, scrapes, and when to sit all day.

lessons.title: Timing the rut where you hunt
lessons.hook: Every fall, somebody prints a rut forecast with a date circled in red, and half the hunters you know plan their vacation around it. The hunters in this lesson trust something else, which is what happened on their own ground last year and the year before. The rut you care about is the one on your property.

sections.heading: It comes back on the same dates
sections.text: Whitetail Evolution, who hunt mid-Michigan, say the pre-rut and rut start on about the same dates on a property every year, because the timing is set by shrinking daylight, not by moon phase or temperature. On their ground the pre-rut starts around October 20 to 24, a little sooner farther north and a little later farther south. Weather, moon, and hunting pressure only change how much of that movement happens in daylight. Lee Ellis of Seek One sees the same with individual bucks, which show back up in a spot nearly to the day, around October 1 in his example, whether the fall is hot or cold. So use past years to set your window, then use conditions to pick days inside it. The research in Kairos finds moon and pressure weak day-pickers, so lean mostly on temperature changes and the wind dropping.

sections.heading: Let the fawns tell you
sections.text: Eddie McRae, who hunts Georgia farms, writes down the dates he sees brand-new fawns, the tiny tracks and spotted fawns still wobbly on their legs, and counts back to learn when his does were really bred. He's seen a newborn around April 1 to 9, meaning a September breeding, and newborn twins in the last week of August into early September, meaning February or March. He also sees more chasing, fighting, and breeding from September to mid-October than around the published early-November peak. It's a cheap way to check the calendar against your own deer.

sections.heading: The second rut
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis of Whitetail Habitat Solutions calls the second rut the most missed opportunity in deer hunting. It comes about 30 days after your local peak, when maybe 15 to 20% of the does are bred. Deer concentrate around unpressured pockets of cover and food, and hardly anyone else is in the woods. It's the one late-season time he hunts mornings too. If you have about 9 days, he splits them, 4 or 5 around the peak rut (early November in southwest Wisconsin, about November 2 to 7 by another of his videos, timed with a cold front if one comes) and 4 or 5 during the second rut.

sections.heading: The biggest bucks die late
sections.text: Mike Rex is secretary-treasurer of Ohio's Buckeye Big Buck club, so he's read every score sheet. Most record-book bucks there, the 130 to 150 inch 3- and 4-year-olds doing most of the breeding, die around the end of October and the first of November. The Boone and Crockett class bucks, 4 to 7 years old, are mostly killed the first week of the season or at the tail end of the rut, the second half of November in Ohio, when most bowhunters have slowed down. His theory is that they make fewer rut-crazed mistakes and feel safer once hunter numbers drop. That part is his own guess, not something the score sheets prove.

lessons.tryThis: Start a simple rut log for your property. Each fall, write down the first day you see chasing, the first fresh scrapes, and when your best bucks show up and disappear on camera. After two seasons you'll have your own dates.
lessons.headsUp: McRae goes further than the others and believes southern deer have no defined rut at all, breeding anywhere from September to March. That's his own view, and a state biologist told him the early fawn was a fluke. The dates in this lesson are all local, so Michigan, Wisconsin, Ohio, and Georgia numbers won't match your ground exactly.

check.q: According to Whitetail Evolution, what sets the timing of the rut?
check.a: Shrinking daylight, which is why it comes on about the same dates each year. Weather and moon only change how much happens in daylight.

check.q: About how long after the peak does Sturgis expect the second rut?
check.a: About 30 days, when roughly 15 to 20% of the does are bred.

lessons.title: Where to spend your days
lessons.hook: Most hunters only get so many days off, and the fight is always over where to spend them. Some say save everything for the rut. Others say the rut is when bucks are hardest to pin down. Both camps have good reasons, and the right answer depends on your ground and your goal.

sections.heading: Save your doe area for rut week
sections.text: Jamie McKay hunts public land in North Alabama. Once he finds a good doe area for the rut, he doesn't overhunt it early. He pops in to check it, looking at whether acorns are dropping and does are using it, then backs out and stays out until the week the rut hits there. Then he hunts it hard. He doesn't shoot does there before the rut, because the does come in at the same time every year and that's where his rut action will be. If you're bowhunting, narrow it down further, to the exact trail the does walk.

sections.heading: On a small parcel, wait for the rut
sections.text: A guest on the Southern Outdoorsmen podcast makes the case for a small private parcel, around 100 acres. There may be no shooter buck bedding on your place in October, and you can't roam after him like you could on public land. So he shoots his does early in bow season and saves his buck hunting for the pre-rut and rut, when bucks come off the neighbors' ground looking for doe groups. For a working hunter with limited days, he calls the rut the great equalizer.

sections.heading: After one buck, hunt around the rut
sections.text: The Mississippi State GPS-collar study measured something useful here. Outside the rut, bucks behave very consistently day to day and reuse the same daily area, so a pattern holds. In the rut they wander. That's measured data. The advice to hunt afternoons over his feeding pattern comes from the target-buck hunters the study's hosts interviewed and from Mike Rex. Rex says the Boone and Crockett class Ohio bucks are mostly killed the first week of the season, when bucks are still on their summer feeding pattern and food is much easier to figure out than bedding.

sections.heading: Late October scrapes
sections.text: The Hunting Public crew, hunting on Missouri timing, moves to scrapes toward the end of October, on the edges of thick cover and doe bedding, with setups for different winds. Bucks are running scrape lines closer to the does then, and a scrape puts a buck on a spot within bow range. He also comes in preoccupied, so you can draw, even though he may be lying just 70 yards away. If you find a hot scrape on the edge of bedding, you know you didn't spook anything, and the wind is right, hunt it right away. If scrapes are your strength, they'd take vacation at the end of October instead of the rut.

lessons.tryThis: Look at the bucks on your cameras right now. If one lives on your ground in daylight, plan afternoon sits for him early. If none does, mark your best doe areas and plan your vacation around your local rut dates.
lessons.headsUp: These sources pull in different directions. McKay says don't shoot does in your rut doe area before the rut, while the Southern Outdoorsmen hosts shoot their does early. The MSU data and Rex say the weeks before and after the rut are the time to target one buck, while the hosts save their buck hunting for the rut. Both can be right. Target a buck early if he lives on your ground, and wait for the rut if he doesn't.

check.q: Why is a specific buck easier to pattern outside the rut, according to the MSU data?
check.a: Outside the rut bucks are very consistent day to day and reuse the same area. In the rut they wander.

check.q: What does McKay do with a good rut doe area in October?
check.a: Checks it briefly, backs out, stays out until rut week, and doesn't shoot does there before then.

lessons.title: Find the does, find the bucks
lessons.hook: You've got a ridge full of does and not a single buck on it yet, and you're tempted to write it off. Jamie McKay says "find the does, find the bucks" took him a long time to learn. In the rut the bucks come to the does, and the question is where exactly they'll walk when they do.

sections.heading: Plan around the doe groups
sections.text: McKay's biggest bucks often came from where the does hung out, not from where he got the buck's picture. So don't give up on a doe ridge because no buck has shown up yet. The timing just wasn't right. Derek Dixon, who tracks bucks with thermal drones, found that in the peak rut some mature bucks bed just downwind of a group of bedded does, sometimes with two or three other bucks nearby, and scent-check them for the 4 to 6 hours they're bedded midday. That's some bucks, not all, since Dixon also finds loners that bed away from all deer and even run off deer that come near.

sections.heading: Setting up downwind of doe bedding
sections.text: Whitetail Evolution and Next Step Outdoors both set up on the downwind side of where the does are, to catch bucks scent-checking them. On pre-rut mornings, slip in while deer are still out on the food and set up just downwind of the trail along the inside edge of the thick doe bedding. On pre-rut evenings, back away from the big field and sit downwind of a smaller staging food source or the trail leading to it. In the rut, mark doe bedding, work out which way bucks would scent-check it on the likely winds, and plan to intercept that.

sections.heading: Where bucks cross the doe trails
sections.text: Dixon's drones show a different pattern on ridge systems in the morning. Does tend to walk straight up the draws, and bucks travel across them, running parallel to fields, ridges, and drainages. Find the spots where lots of doe trails come together, like an X where five trails meet, and connect those X's along the terrain. A traveling mature buck walks a line hitting those intersections to pick up ground scent. If he smells something interesting he detours toward the does, stays about 30 to 40 yards from them, then goes right back to his route. McKay teaches the same in hill and mountain big woods, and on long fields there's usually a buck cruising trail just back off the edge.

sections.heading: Perennial scrapes in the pre-rut
sections.text: Whitetail Evolution also hunts the downwind side of perennial scrapes, the big ones that show up in the same place every year. Mornings, they pick those just downwind of doe bedding, and evenings, those in the staging food or along the bedding-to-food trail. The whole herd uses scrapes to communicate, and a pre-rut buck checks them to learn which does are close to heat. Don't hunt over every scrape you find. They're the only source for this one.

sections.heading: The quiet side on a windy day
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis has one more rut tip for windy days. Deer blown off the ridges and open hardwoods pile in behind conifers, behind tall grass, and on sheltered slopes, and bucks cruise for does in that same pocket. He calls packing that many deer into the quiet side during the rut "like throwing gas on fire," so hunt it hard.

lessons.tryThis: On your map, mark every doe bedding area you know about. On a ridge system, also mark where several doe trails cross. Draw the line a buck would walk connecting those crossings and look for a tree along it.
lessons.headsUp: The sources disagree on how bucks check does. Whitetail Evolution and Next Step Outdoors say bucks cruise the downwind side of doe bedding. Dixon's drone tracking on ridge systems in the morning almost never saw bucks swing downwind of doe beds. They walked a line through the doe-trail crossings instead. In hill country, trust the crossings. The downwind cruising pattern comes from flatter farm and marsh country.

check.q: In Dixon's drone tracking, how close did a buck get when he detoured to check a doe group?
check.a: About 30 to 40 yards, and then he went back to his route.

check.q: On a windy rut day, where does Sturgis hunt?
check.a: The quiet side, behind conifers, tall grass, or sheltered slopes, where deer and cruising bucks pile in.

lessons.title: Reading rut sign
lessons.hook: In the rut, the woods change almost overnight. Sign appears where there wasn't any, bucks vanish off your cameras, and trails you counted on go quiet. Once you can read what that sign means, you'll know whether to sit tight, move, or wait.

sections.heading: Out-of-place sign means a hot doe
sections.text: The Hunting Public crew reads the woods on the way in. If you bump a couple of young bucks close together and see fresh scrapes with fresh urine in them and rubs that weren't there before, something's happening. It's likely a hot doe with a big buck locked down with her nearby, and the young satellite bucks circling them are leaving that sign. Hunt there, even if it's only 400 yards from the car. One of them learned this by blowing it about 15 times, walking in and flushing the doe and then a big 8-pointer.

sections.heading: Lockdown bucks use barriers
sections.text: During lockdown, when a buck stays with one doe, he may not walk through your funnel stand for a week and a half. The Hunting Public crew goes where bucks hold does instead. Look for spots where bucks pin does against a barrier every year, like the edge of a river in a bottom. The buck uses the barrier to keep other bucks off the doe's back side.

sections.heading: A short string of rubs marks his route
sections.text: Two or three rubs in a row mark a buck's travel route, so hunt right on it. In the rut, when scrapes dry up and bucks travel from one place to another, the Hunting Public crew looks for 2 or 3 rubs along the downwind side of a thicket, cedar in their example, even with little trail there, and sits it through the middle of the day. One buck may pass between about 8 AM and 4 PM, and they'd rather have one deer at 10 yards than see 15 at 200. Downwind Hunting, an unverified online list, adds that a buck rubs while walking forward, so the rubbed sides line up with his travel. Sit facing the smooth side so he walks toward you with the tree between you.

sections.heading: When a buck vanishes, wait
sections.text: Eddie McRae's three biggest bucks, in three different years, each vanished from their home cameras for about 7 days in the last week of October on his Georgia farms. Each was caught once or twice on other cameras trailing or breeding a doe, then went right back to his normal routine. McRae killed one the day after it came back. So when a core-area buck that's on camera every day suddenly disappears for about a week, don't panic or go looking for him. Wait, and hunt him hard as soon as he's back on his home camera. That late-October timing is McRae's local pattern, not a general rut date.

lessons.tryThis: On your next rut walk-in, slow down and look for sign that wasn't there last time, like new rubs, fresh scrapes, or young bucks close together. If you find it, sit nearby that day instead of walking past it to your planned stand.
lessons.headsUp: The rub-direction trick is the weakest idea here. It comes from a single unverified list whose wording about which side faces which way is muddled, and Whitetail Evolution says rub direction is only a rough hint. Trust the rub string as a route, and don't bet a sit on which way the scars face.

check.q: You walk in and bump two young bucks near fresh scrapes that weren't there yesterday. What might that mean?
check.a: A hot doe with a bigger buck locked down on her nearby. Hunt there.

check.q: Your best buck disappears from his home camera for about a week in the rut. What does McRae do?
check.a: He waits, because the buck is probably off with a doe, then hunts him hard as soon as he's back on camera.

lessons.title: Sit all day, or move?
lessons.hook: It's the middle of the rut, it's 11 in the morning, and your stand has been dead since daylight. Do you stay, or do you go find the action? Good hunters give opposite answers to that question, and the difference comes down to what you know about the buck you're after.

sections.heading: The case for sitting all day
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis sits all day in the rut from a stand between bedding and food with a pinch point, because deer have reasons to pass it all day, not just at dawn and dusk. Downwind Hunting, an unverified online list, tells you to take vacation from November 2 to 15 and sit dawn to dark with enough food and water to stay. It claims harvest data shows more Boone and Crockett bucks killed in that window than any other, often at midday. Those dates only fit a typical northern rut and come much later in parts of the South, so use your local timing.

sections.heading: The case for moving off a dead spot
sections.text: Jeff Danker of Realtree says rut action is local. One hunter has a hot doe near him and has the best rut ever, while another half a mile away sees nothing. So if your spot is dead, move toward the freshest sign, like big fresh rubs or a hot doe's area, which can stay good for about 5 days. In Iowa, after a couple of dead days in a stand he'd hung in summer, he pulled it at 9 AM, moved about 200 yards deeper into the timber, had a good evening, and called in a 12-point at 5 yards the next morning. The Hunting Public crew, mobile public-land hunters, move after an hour or two of nothing.

sections.heading: The case for sitting his center
sections.text: Lee Ellis of Seek One was always a step behind a 203-inch buck he called Zeus, which showed up at 7 or 8 camera spots, until he worked out the center point the buck passed through to get between them. He used the same lesson on a 170s typical, sitting one tree about 8 or 9 days straight until the buck came through on a doe. When a buck shows up on many cameras, stop chasing each photo, find that focal spot, and sit it day after day, as long as your access is clean. As Ellis puts it, you have to be ahead of them, not behind them.

sections.heading: Noise matters less, the wind still matters
sections.text: Danker hung that Iowa set loudly at 9 AM, trimming with a pole saw, and still had a great hunt that evening and killed a big buck the next morning. He believes the rut is the time of year you can be less careful about noise when moving or hanging a new set midday. He's clear that it isn't permission to be careless, and you still have to play the wind.

sections.heading: Bucks on a doe pay less attention to wind
sections.text: Jamie McKay has watched bucks hot on a doe's trail come right through his wind, and other hunters have seen the same. So in the peak rut, with a hot doe around, he'll hunt a good spot even on a marginal wind. Remember that the does with that buck still have noses, so this only applies to the buck.

lessons.tryThis: Before your rut hunt, decide which case you're in. If one buck keeps showing up on several cameras, find his center and plan to sit it. If you have no read on any buck, pick a pinch between bedding and food for an all-day sit and give yourself permission to move after a dead day.
lessons.headsUp: Two disagreements. Danker and the Hunting Public crew move off a dead spot, while Ellis sits one tree for 8 or 9 days. Moving fits when you have no read on a buck, and sitting fits when cameras show one buck circling a center you can reach cleanly. On wind, McKay will hunt a marginal wind in the peak rut, while Sturgis and Informed Outdoors say never force a stand on the wrong wind, and even Danker's rut advice includes keeping the wind right.

check.q: A buck shows up on seven of your cameras during the rut. What would Ellis do?
check.a: Stop chasing the photos, work out the center point he passes through, and sit it day after day if access is clean.

check.q: Danker says you can be less careful in the rut. Less careful about what, and what still matters?
check.a: Noise when moving or hanging a set midday. The wind still matters.

lessons.title: Calling in the rut
lessons.hook: The rut is when calling feels like it should work best, and sometimes it does. Other times a loud call sends a mature buck the other way. The hunters here agree on some basics and disagree sharply on the most aggressive call you can make.

sections.heading: Save rattling for the right time
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis saves rattling for the peak rut through the post-rut and second rut. His reasoning is simple. In the pre-rut and early rut, does are coming into heat and every buck can find one, so why pick a fight? Late in the rut and after it, does are harder to find and big bucks keep moving and searching, so a fight sounds worth checking out. Before that he does at most a little light tickling in mid-October, which rarely brings deer in. His Wisconsin peak is about November 2 to 7, and he points out November 15 there is already post-rut.

sections.heading: Rattle hard at a far-off cruiser
sections.text: The Hunting Public crew had a situation where a cruising buck was too far off to hear a grunt and the leaves were too crunchy to sneak closer. Normally they'd move toward the deer. Instead, high on a ridge in 2020, they rattled hard with lots of realistic noise, and the buck came straight in to about 5 yards. The hunter had left his bow behind and never got a shot, so have your bow in your hand before you start.

sections.heading: Add ground noise
sections.text: A real rutting buck isn't silent except for grunts. He's moving, snapping branches, rubbing, and scraping. So while you grunt or rattle, the Hunting Public crew scrapes the ground, stomps, breaks branches, and shakes saplings. From a treestand, tie your pull-up rope to a branch or to rattling antlers on the ground and move it around. They say it adds a surprising amount to a calling sequence.

sections.heading: The snort-wheeze as a last resort on a distant buck
sections.text: A snort-wheeze is the aggressive warning one buck gives another. Sturgis says mature bucks usually got old by being shy and avoiding fights, so they tend to leave when they hear it, and used randomly it spooks far more bucks than it attracts. He uses it only on a mature buck far away that won't come to anything else, like bucks you can see already fighting out in a field. In late October he snort-wheezed back at two bucks fighting 200 yards away and pulled in a different buck from about 100 yards off to the side, which came so slowly that it arrived after dark. Sturgis shot him the next morning. He backs this with a story from researcher John Ozoga's Michigan enclosure, where the aggressive top buck died young from fighting and a shy buck ranked around tenth ruled for years.

sections.heading: Or on a buck that's hung up
sections.text: Mark Kenyon of MeatEater uses the snort-wheeze differently. If a buck heard you and shows semi-positive signs but won't commit, like making a rub or scrape, puffing up, lingering, or paralleling you, he tries it as his last move. He does it by mouth as loud as he can with a cupped hand, or with a call that has a funnel piece. It's a challenge to come and fight, so the buck either comes in or leaves.

lessons.tryThis: Practice a rattling sequence at home with ground noise added. Rattle, then rake leaves, snap a stick, and shake a sapling or your pull rope. Time how long the whole thing takes, and keep your bow within reach the whole time you do it in the woods.
lessons.headsUp: There are two splits here. Both Sturgis and Kenyon call the snort-wheeze a last resort, but Sturgis uses it only on distant bucks and says not to call at all once a buck has looked your way, while Kenyon uses it on a buck hung up nearby. On rattling, the Hunting Public crew rattled loud on public land, while Kenyon and Sturgis say keep it subtle outside top-tier ground like Iowa or Kansas. Kenyon also thinks a soft tickle can pull bachelor bucks before the pre-rut, which Sturgis says rarely works.

check.q: Why does Sturgis save rattling for the peak rut and later?
check.a: Earlier, every buck can find a doe, so there's no reason to fight. Later, does are scarce and bucks are searching, so a fight is worth checking.

check.q: What's the difference between Sturgis's and Kenyon's snort-wheeze?
check.a: Sturgis uses it only on a distant buck that won't come to anything else. Kenyon uses it on a nearby buck that heard him but is hung up.

lessons.title: Decoys and bottled scent
lessons.hook: Walk down the hunting aisle in October and you'll see decoys, buck urine, doe-in-heat lure, and a dozen other bottles promising to pull a buck in. Some hunters use them, and some never do. Before you spend money, it's worth knowing who is recommending what, because several of these tips come from the people selling the product.

sections.heading: Decoys belong in open country
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis never uses decoys. Most of his bucks, 70 to 80%, come from morning stands back in the brush in Minnesota and Wisconsin with shot windows of about 40 yards. On a travel route, he says, the first mature doe or fawn that spots a decoy and doesn't like it blows or spooks back the way she came and takes every deer behind her with her. Carrying one in and setting it up also means extra noise, walking, and scent right where you need to sneak. The only place he thinks a decoy makes sense is big open country during rut cruising hours, like Kansas or Iowa river bottoms or a cut cornfield edge, where a buck can see it from a quarter mile away. Everywhere else, strap in, sit down, stay quiet, and don't move.

sections.heading: Buck urine as a challenge
sections.text: A representative from the scent company Tink's, talking about her own Trophy Buck product, recommends pairing dominant buck urine with a decoy, grunting, or rattling. The idea is to set off a territorial reaction, so a buck comes in to defend his area and gets into range. She didn't say what part of the season to use it. This is the only source for it, and it's a product pitch, so weigh it that way.

sections.heading: Estrus lure only in the rut, doe urine any time
sections.text: The same Tink's rep says to use doe-in-estrus lure only in the rut and never in the early season, like September. A doe in heat months early doesn't make sense to deer, so it reads as a warning instead of an attraction. If you use one lure all season, she recommends plain doe urine, from early bow season through the post-rut, because deer that smell it just think other does are around and stay calm. Both are her own products, and she gave no field data.

sections.heading: Your own tarsal glands
sections.text: Downwind Hunting, an unverified online list, suggests a free alternative. When you or a buddy kill a buck, cut the tarsal glands from the inside of the hind legs, seal them in a glass jar, and freeze them to use as scent next season. It's scent from a local deer that matches your area. That's the only source for it, so treat it as an idea to try.

lessons.tryThis: Before you buy any decoy or lure, write down where you'd use it. If the answer is a brushy travel route or a morning stand near bedding, skip the decoy and put the money toward a stand for a wind you don't have covered yet.
lessons.headsUp: Hunters and the scent company don't agree. Sturgis and Informed Outdoors skip lures entirely, and Sturgis says old bucks follow a scent trail in on your downwind side. The Tink's rep uses estrus lure in the rut and doe urine all season, and pairs buck urine with a decoy with no season or cover limits, while Sturgis says decoys only fit big open country in the rut. The one thing both sides agree on is that estrus lure out of season is a mistake.

check.q: You hunt a brushy travel route between bedding and food. Should you put out a decoy?
check.a: Sturgis says no. The first doe that spots it and spooks can take every deer behind her. Decoys fit big open country in the rut.
