check.q: Where does the advice about estrus lure and doe urine come from, and why does that matter?
check.a: A rep from the scent company describing her own products, with no field data, so it's a sales view rather than a tested rule.

units.goal: Build them, place them, and skip the bottled stuff.

lessons.title: Where to put a mock scrape
lessons.hook: A mock scrape is one you make yourself, a patch of scratched-out dirt under a hanging branch, meant to get bucks to stop and leave their scent. Plenty of hunters build them and never see a buck at one. Most of the time the problem isn't how they built it. It's where they put it.

sections.heading: Right on the trail
sections.text: Put the scrape right over a trail deer already walk, not off to the side. Jeff Sturgis, who designs hunting properties for clients, compares a deer to a dog on a walk. The dog will pull 6 to 8 feet off the sidewalk to sniff a hydrant, but not 10 yards. A water hole might pull deer 10 yards but not 100, and a scrape beside a water hole instead of on a trail into it goes unused. Right on the trail, a deer nearly has to move its head to avoid the licking branch, and over time a good scrape can pull several trails together into one. Rip 'n Stik Outdoors adds that a spot on the travel route gets every kind of deer, including cruising bucks. Good examples are an oak ridge deer cross to eat acorns on their way to the fields at night and back in the morning, or right next to a real scrape if you find one.

sections.heading: One scrape, right where you'll shoot
sections.text: Sturgis makes one mock scrape per stand, no more and no less, and puts it where he expects to take the shot. Good spots are a flat where several trails come together like a bow tie, or a funnel, bench, habitat change, or waterway edge the trail runs through. If trails pass 20 yards down the hill and 10 yards up, a scrape at your shot spot pulls them to one place. A mock scrape doesn't bring more bucks onto your land. It stops the deer already passing, in the spot you want, and a buck that comes in locks onto the scrape and stares at it instead of you. Don't ring a food plot with scrapes or scatter them around, because more scrapes dilute what he calls the power of one until none get used. With a gun over a big food source, it can sit off to the side where you'd shoot, even at 120 yards.

sections.heading: Flat ground, and the plot entrance
sections.text: Sturgis's crew learned this from their own hillside scrapes that never got used. On camera, deer working a scrape like to spin all the way around, and flat ground likely holds scent better, so pick flat ground on the trail with about 10 to 12 feet between trees. Deer won't walk uphill and back down to work one. At a small hunting plot, he puts the scrape at the entrance trail where several trails merge before the plot, in brushy cover where deer have nowhere else to go, and you can mow a trail into it. Once a buck hits that scrape he's usually committed to walking out into the plot in front of the stand, so even a scrape out of bow range sets up the shot.

sections.heading: Don't let him look up at you
sections.text: Eddie McRae learned this one the hard way. A buck working his mock scrape looked up the licking branch, saw him in the stand, and spooked. The buck and a doe ran 35 yards straight downwind and tried to wind him for more than five minutes. Then they walked back in and the buck worked the scrape again, which McRae credits to his scent routine. So hang the licking branch where a buck working it isn't looking straight up at you.

lessons.tryThis: Walk the trail in front of one of your stands and find the exact spot you'd most likely shoot a deer. Check that it's flat, sits right on the trail, and isn't directly below your seat. That's where your scrape goes.
lessons.headsUp: Sturgis says bucks lock onto the scrape and ignore you, and McRae's story shows that stops working when the licking branch lines up with your stand. Also keep in mind that almost every placement rule here comes from one person, Sturgis, across a few videos. He has a lot of properties behind him, but it's one experienced hunter's system rather than a consensus.

check.q: Your stand is near a water hole. Should the scrape go right beside the water?
check.a: No. Put it on a trail leading into the water hole. Deer won't go out of their way to check a scrape.

check.q: How many mock scrapes does Sturgis put at each stand, and where?
check.a: One, right where he expects to take the shot.

lessons.title: Building the licking branch
lessons.hook: Scratching out the dirt is the easy part of a mock scrape. What makes it work is the licking branch hanging above it, because that's where deer leave the scent other deer come to check. Get the branch wrong and deer walk right past it.

sections.heading: What the branch is for
sections.text: Scrapes are where bucks check who's in the area. The Downwind Hunting list, a compiled article rather than one hunter's experience, describes bucks licking and rubbing the branch with the glands by their eyes and pawing the dirt below. To build one, pick a spot with bare dirt and hang a rope, vine, or branch from an overhead branch or a cord so it hangs over the scrape. If nothing hangs over the spot, Jeff Sturgis winches a live sapling over and ties it off.

sections.heading: Pick natural material
sections.text: Sturgis says natural material gets hit far more often than rope, and the most consistent natural scrapes he sees on more than 1,000 properties hang from vines. A hanging vine is his favorite and can last up to 7 years. White or red oak, jack pine up north, hemlock, beech, ironwood, or musclewood work too, or whatever branch deer use where you hunt. Aim for about 3/4 to 1 inch thick. Much over an inch looks like a trunk and deer won't play with it, and under 3/4 inch breaks too easily. Skip sappy branches and brittle soft woods.

sections.heading: Make it long, and let it swing
sections.text: A short 2-foot stick dangling from a long rope looks unnatural and gets ignored. In one video Sturgis hangs a long vine or branch, 8 to 15 feet, from paracord strung about 12 feet up between two trees or thrown over a branch, even 20 feet up. In another he describes a branch reaching 5 to 6 feet, up to 8 to 10, to where it's tied, hung on about 4 to 5 inches of cord. Either way it swings free from a single pivot point instead of being tied stiff, and that flex keeps bucks from breaking it at the top. The cord only costs him 30 to 60 cents.

sections.heading: Hang it low
sections.text: Sturgis hangs the branch vertically and free-swinging, with its tip about belt high, rather than using a horizontal branch at chest height. At that height every deer uses it, from fawns and does to young and old bucks, and each one leaves scent, so the scrape keeps getting stronger. A horizontal branch mostly gets used by bucks and needs a tree to mount on. He says hanging the branch too high is one of the most common mistakes his crew sees on client properties.

sections.heading: Paracord, never cable
sections.text: Hang scrapes with paracord, camo if you can get it, and never with steel cable or anything else a deer can't break. Sturgis has seen a buck rip down a steel cable strung with a row of scrapes, get it wound around his head and neck, and die. Paracord has little scent, and deer don't seem to notice it. This one comes from Sturgis alone, but it's an easy rule to follow.

lessons.tryThis: Before you build your first scrape, find a vine or a hardwood branch about 3/4 to 1 inch thick and at least 5 feet long. Hang it on paracord so it swings free with the tip around belt high, then give it a push to make sure it pivots from the top.
lessons.headsUp: The sources don't agree on height. Downwind Hunting hangs the branch about 5 feet over the scrape, aimed at bucks. Sturgis goes lower so the whole herd uses it, about belly to belt high on a person (one he showed was almost chest high). He also lists aspen as usable in one video and says to avoid brittle soft woods like aspen and tag alder in the other. When in doubt, use a vine or one of the hardwoods he names in both.

check.q: Why not hang the licking branch with steel cable?
check.a: A buck can tangle himself in cable he can't break. Sturgis saw one die that way. Use paracord.

check.q: Why hang the branch low rather than high?
check.a: At belt height every deer uses it and leaves scent, so the scrape builds up. A high or horizontal branch mostly gets used by bucks.

lessons.title: Timing, transplants, and what a scrape tells you
lessons.hook: Once you know where to put a mock scrape and how to build it, the next questions are when to put it in and how to tell whether it's working. The answers surprise a lot of hunters, because a scrape that looks dead can be one of the busiest spots on the property.

sections.heading: Build early, then stay out
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis builds his mock scrapes well ahead of the season, whenever he hangs the stand. He did one on September 1, and another about 7 weeks before bow season. He puts them near where deer bed and travel, sets a solar-powered camera on the scrape, and then leaves it alone for about two months. He guesses deer hit it within 6 to 10 hours, and he doesn't worry about disturbing the area that far out, because deer are back in there all the time. Even if the work keeps the oldest buck away for a bit, there's plenty of time before opening day for things to settle, and the camera does your scouting without you walking in.

sections.heading: Don't wait for the perfect spot
sections.text: Sturgis says the number one failure with mock scrapes is not using them at all. You can put one in at almost any stand in 15 to 20 minutes. Needing store-bought scent or rope shouldn't stop you, and his crew has thrown rope over branches 18 feet up and even used ladder stand sections to hang one where they wanted it. In an open food plot with no tree where you want the shot, cut a small red cedar and stand it up about 22 to 25 yards in front of the blind, with a vine hanging from it.

sections.heading: Move a real scrape
sections.text: Mike Rex used an older trick a lot before trail cameras. He transplants a real scrape from an area he isn't hunting. Wearing rubber gloves, he digs the top couple of inches of dirt into a clean 5-gallon pail, bags the licking branch and snips it off, and zip-ties it to a branch at the right height over flat ground in his spot. Then he scratches out a scrape and mixes in the dirt. The moved scrape carries other deer's urine and gland scent, and he says deer take it over immediately. He did this from late September through October.

sections.heading: Don't judge a scrape by its looks
sections.text: Sturgis's crew ran a 60-day camera test in October and November on a food-plot edge by a cornfield. A mock scrape got 210 hits from bucks, does, and fawns. A mock rub right next to it, which looked shredded, got 22 hits, all from bucks, and the average natural rub gets hit about 1.5 times a year. So for camera intel, use a scrape rather than a rub. And don't write a scrape off because it looks untouched. Most of the time bucks just leave scent from their forehead and the glands by their eyes on the branch, and they only paw the ground bare during the rut.

lessons.tryThis: The next time you hang a stand in the off-season, take 15 or 20 minutes to build a scrape in front of it and put a camera on it. Then stay out, and let the camera tell you who's using it.
lessons.headsUp: Everything in this lesson comes from single hunters, Sturgis for most of it and Rex for the transplant. The 210 to 22 result is Sturgis's crew's own count at one food-plot edge, not a controlled study. It's a strong hint that scrapes pull in more deer than rubs, but not proof that the same numbers will hold on your ground.

check.q: Your mock scrape looks untouched, with leaves over the dirt. Is it dead?
check.a: Not necessarily. Outside the rut, bucks mostly work the branch and rarely paw the ground bare. Check the camera.

check.q: For camera intel, is a mock scrape or a mock rub better?
check.a: A scrape. In Sturgis's crew's test a scrape got 210 hits from all kinds of deer, while a rub right next to it got 22.

lessons.title: Skip the bottled stuff
lessons.hook: Walk down the hunting aisle and you'll see a wall of scrape starters, drippers, and lures. It's natural to think a mock scrape needs one of them. Most of the hunters in this course say it doesn't, and some think the bottle does more harm than good.

sections.heading: Bare dirt and your own urine
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis makes his mock scrapes without store-bought scent. He scrapes out a big dirt patch, pees in it, and puts it in shooting range of his stand. Deer start using his within a day or two and keep using them all season once they're in a repeat pattern, and he doesn't see how scent could make them work faster or stronger. His partner Dylan sometimes adds scent, and they haven't tested the two side by side.

sections.heading: Bottled scent covers the real thing
sections.text: Deer leave scent from the glands by their eyes on the licking branch as a calling card. You can't smell anything on a real licking branch, but a deer coming by can pick out all 20 deer that hit it that day. Sturgis says a strong bottled scent covers and dilutes all of that, so he never puts bottled scents, gels, or lures on a mock scrape. Deer also rarely urinate in scrapes outside the rut, and mostly they just hit the branch and move on. A scent-eliminating spray to cut your own trail on the way in is fine. As a teenager he burned a whole bottle of urine in one 2-hour sit and killed nothing.

sections.heading: One hobby test, two lessons
sections.text: Rip 'n Stik Outdoors hung five different scrape scents side by side on an oak ridge deer were using heavily and watched them with one camera for two weeks, late October into the rut. The only one that got scraped under was a dripper, which claims to drip in daytime only and last 2 to 3 weeks, while the rope, paste, and poured scents got nothing. So if you do use a scrape scent, one that stays fresh may beat a one-time pour. The ridge also came up short overall. The camera caught only a bear, a few young bucks, and one confirmed scrape visit, and his own conclusion was that that much scent in one spot spooked the deer. If you use scent at all, keep it to one scent at one scrape. He doesn't normally use scents, and leaf fall and his own visits weren't ruled out, so treat all of this as a hint.

sections.heading: Skip lures and drag rags
sections.text: Sturgis and Informed Outdoors skip lures, attractants, and drag rags altogether, including buck bombs, powders, vanilla smoke puffs, and deer urine. They might work, but a puff that lasts 20 seconds won't decide whether you see deer. Lures fool young bucks, but old bucks tend to follow your trail out of curiosity and come in on your downwind side, the way you walked in. Laying scent also means extra walking, more chances to bump deer, and more of your scent and noise around the stand, so get to the stand and climb straight up. If you need a cover scent because deer will be downwind of you, the stand location is the mistake.

sections.heading: Check the law on urine
sections.text: If you do use a deer urine lure, check your state's and county's rules first. A Tink's representative, speaking for a company that sells these products, says some states and even single counties regulate natural deer urine, and synthetic versions exist for those areas. She didn't say which states, so look up your own.

lessons.tryThis: Build your next mock scrape with nothing but bare dirt, your own urine, and a good licking branch. Put a camera on it and see how quickly deer find it before you think about buying a bottle of anything.
lessons.headsUp: Not everyone skips scent. The Tink's rep, a product source, recommends doe urine all season and estrus lure in the rut, and Eddie McRae uses a cover scent made from a local plant. Rip 'n Stik's dripper result also leans toward scent, but it came from one uncontrolled hobby test. Sturgis's no-bottle rule comes from one hunter, backed by what he's seen on a lot of properties rather than a side-by-side test.

check.q: Why does Sturgis keep bottled scent off his mock scrapes?
check.a: It covers and dilutes the real scent deer leave on the branch, which is what other deer come to check.

check.q: You want a cover scent because deer will be downwind of your stand. What does that tell you?
check.a: The stand is in the wrong place. Move it instead of trying to cover your scent.

units.goal: Strategy: patterns, timing, stand rotation, and access to land.

lessons.title: Pick one buck and keep a record
lessons.hook: You've got a dozen bucks on camera and a whole season ahead of you. The hunters here who kill old deer year after year usually don't hunt a dozen. They pick one, learn everything they can about him, and write it all down, so each season teaches them more than the last.

sections.heading: Focus on one deer
sections.text: Lee Ellis of Seek One and Mike Rex, who hunts the southeast Ohio hills, both use cameras and scouting to find one specific mature buck, then put their effort into figuring him out. They stay open to shooting another mature deer that shows up, but the target is what drives the extra work, like hours and miles in February looking for his sheds. It also makes you better at hunting any deer his age. Without a target, they say, you start finding reasons to leave early, while a recent photo of him gives you the confidence to sit longer. About 90 percent of Ellis's mounted bucks came after more than a year of history with that deer. Since 2004, Rex's family hasn't killed a buck they didn't already know about. In woods too thick to glass, Rex calls cameras his eyes in the woods, though he warns that photos fool you on size in both directions.

sections.heading: Write it down
sections.text: Three sources here agree on keeping a written record. After every sit, note the date, time, wind direction, temperature, and what you saw. Keep your deer history, meaning which buck, where, when, and in what conditions, in a notebook or a hunting-app journal. Each season, write down the big picture too, like whether it was a wet or dry year, whether the acorns were good or a bust, and where you did and didn't find deer. Patterns only show up on paper. The Downwind Hunting list gives the kind of thing you'd find, such as deer coming through the north funnel every time the wind was southwest and the temperature fell below 40. Make sure every camera has the right date and time, because a camera with the wrong settings left one friend of theirs with no usable information. One of the Southern Outdoorsmen hosts points out that a season like a bust acorn year is hard to remember clearly later, and after his, he knows he won't sit a little creek bottom hoping deer slip through again.

sections.heading: Every sit is an experiment
sections.text: Treat each setup as a guess from your scouting, test it by hunting, and adjust. When a buck spooks, work out where he was, what he was doing there, and what you did to spook him, whether that was the wind, your movement, or when you drew. Bowhunters United, who hunt public land, once had a young buck come under their saddle tree and smell the climbing sticks at the base. They say that even after a lifetime they fail more than they succeed, and the ones who keep learning keep improving. Next Step Outdoors adds the other half. Get in and out clean, leave little scent, and hunt places other people aren't walking through. Then what you see is deer being deer, not deer reacting to you. You only have to be right once a season.

lessons.tryThis: Pick one buck from your photos and start a page for him today. After every sit this season, add a line with the date, time, wind, temperature, and what you saw, even on the days you see nothing.
lessons.headsUp: Ellis's 90 percent figure and Rex's family record are their own results, not a study, and most people don't have Ellis's near-photographic memory for camera photos. That's exactly why the others lean on a written record.

check.q: Why focus on one target buck instead of hunting whatever shows up?
check.a: It drives extra scouting and care, and gives you the confidence to sit longer. You can still shoot another mature deer.

check.q: A buck blows out of your setup. What should you work out afterward?
check.a: Where he was, what he was doing there, and what you did to spook him, like wind, movement, or drawing.

lessons.title: When to make your move
lessons.hook: Your target buck has been on camera at 2 AM, then 4 AM, and then one evening in daylight. Every part of you wants to go sit there tonight. Most of the mentors here would tell you to slow down, though they don't all agree on how much.

sections.heading: Night photos aren't an invitation
sections.text: Whitetail Evolution, Eddie McRae, and Mike Rex all say to stay out of a target buck's core until he gives you a reason to go. Night-only pictures at 10 PM, 2 AM, or 4 AM mean he's using the property, not that he's huntable. Watch cell cameras until he shows in daylight so regularly it's a no-brainer, like stepping into the same plot two evenings in a row, or until a major weather event hits. Then go aggressively, with the right wind and a clean way in and out. Whitetail Evolution killed a buck on opening day from cell-camera daylight information. McRae, on small Georgia acreage, had a buck showing in daylight about once a week at random, skipped a hot opener, and the buck showed that day. Rex says traveling hunters used to pick the first week of November and hope, and now cell cameras let them time the trip.

sections.heading: Don't chase the fresh photo
sections.text: Lee Ellis warns that a buck you just got on camera, especially at a scrape in daylight, is already ahead of you. Hunt the scrape or spot he hasn't hit in 3 to 5 days, because he's due there. One Tennessee buck ran a scrape line along a sewer line about every 3 to 4 days. Ellis has watched good hunters get worse after adding cell cameras, because they chase instant photos and always end up a step behind. The exception is a buck that moves into an area and stays for 3 to 5 days or the rest of the season. Then a photo means he's settled, and you rebuild your plan around it.

sections.heading: The bait-site exception
sections.text: Mike Rex hunts Ohio, where baiting is legal. If he gets a daylight photo of a target buck at a bait site, he hunts him within 48 hours, and he sets up on the trails leading to the bait rather than right over it. After the first day or two, he says, the buck goes almost completely nocturnal at that bait. Check your state's law before you use this at all.

sections.heading: Velvet season
sections.text: The Southern Outdoorsmen hosts say that if you have a velvet-season tag and a target buck is patternable at daybreak and dusk, take him then rather than waiting for hard antlers. In Mississippi the velvet season is about mid-September, and by then his antlers are done growing, so he won't add inches later and there's no promise of another chance. A velvet mount does cost more than a normal shoulder mount. This comes from one hunter.

lessons.tryThis: Look back through your target buck's photos and sort them into night and daylight. If the daylight ones aren't regular yet, stay out of his core and keep watching.
lessons.headsUp: Ellis and Rex seem to disagree about fresh photos. Ellis says a fresh daylight photo means you're already behind, so hunt where he's due in 3 to 5 days. Rex says a daylight photo at a bait site means hunt within 48 hours, before he goes nocturnal there. Ellis is talking about roaming bucks on scrape lines and Rex about an established bait site, which likely explains it.

check.q: Your buck is on camera only at night. Is it time to hunt his core?
check.a: No. Night photos mean he's using the property. Wait for a regular daylight pattern or a major weather event.

check.q: He just hit a scrape in daylight this morning. Where does Lee Ellis say to sit?
check.a: At a scrape or spot he hasn't hit in 3 to 5 days, because he's due there.

lessons.title: Every sit costs something
lessons.hook: The first time you sit a new stand, everything is in your favor, because the deer have no idea you exist. Every sit after that, you've left a little more of yourself behind. This lesson is about spending your sits wisely and keeping your ground feeling safe.

sections.heading: The first sit is your best sit
sections.text: Mike Rex treats every sit as using up a stand. A friend of his who has killed a lot of big deer found that, statistically, the first time you hunt a stand is your best chance at a buck there, so save that sit for the right wind and timing. The Downwind Hunting list puts numbers on it. Don't sit the same stand more than twice in a row, then rest it at least 5 days, rotating among three or four stands. It cites Mississippi State research that mature bucks change travel within two to three days of noticing repeated human activity, but that claim wasn't checked. Rex adds that a deer doesn't do the same thing every day, so you can still get him on a later sit.

sections.heading: Big woods play by different rules
sections.text: Jamie McKay bowhunted one proven tree in low-density big woods in North Alabama for about three weeks straight in its prime and killed several bucks from it. With fewer deer, each sit doesn't blow them out the way it does in small, dense farm country. He stopped when the woods changed, like after logging. Podcast host Beau Martonik, who hunts the Pennsylvania big woods where deer roam and aren't on tight patterns, keeps hunting the same general area rather than bouncing between spots, and Lee Ellis agrees. If the deer aren't there, bouncing around just chases your tail. He still watches his access and wind so his scent doesn't build up.

sections.heading: Be the sanctuary
sections.text: Eddie McRae hunts Georgia farms surrounded by neighbors who hunt hard with food plots, feeders, and ATV rides every day. He does the opposite and keeps his own intrusion as close to zero as he can. Pressure all around pushes deer to the safe spot, and deer won't pick food over safety. A mature buck also shies away from things that don't belong, like a 150-pound pile of corn, and corn is only about 10 percent protein anyway. If he puts out feed at all, he scatters a little by hand so it looks natural, mainly to hold deer in front of cameras.

sections.heading: Does tell you if your spot is healthy
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis uses doe and fawn arrival time at a food source as a health check. On a normal day they should be out about 45 minutes to an hour before dark, or maybe 15 minutes before on a nasty-weather day. If they only show up right at dark, something is wrong. Either the cover next to the food is too open to cross in daylight, or you're pressuring it, or both. He's seen that window across Michigan, Wisconsin, and Minnesota, and his point is simple. If the does won't come in daylight, a mature buck won't either.

lessons.tryThis: Next time you sit a food source in the evening, write down when the first does step out. If it's right at dark, look hard at the cover next to the food and at how often you've been there.
lessons.headsUp: Rex and the Downwind Hunting list say each sit burns a stand and it needs rest. McKay sat one proven big-woods tree for about three weeks and kept killing bucks. The difference is likely deer density, with small farm country on one side and big woods on the other. The list's rotation numbers and its research claim are unverified.

check.q: When is your best chance at a buck from a new stand?
check.a: The first sit. Save it for the right wind and timing.

check.q: Does on your food plot only show up right at dark. What does Sturgis say that means?
check.a: The cover next to the food is too open, or you're pressuring it. A mature buck won't come in daylight either.

lessons.title: Mornings, evenings, and matching the stand
lessons.hook: Some stands are for mornings and some are for evenings, and sitting one at the wrong time can blow out the deer you're after. The mentors here agree on the basic rule, and then split on early-season mornings depending on where they hunt.

sections.heading: Match the stand to the clock
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis's rule is simple. Stands on or watching food are for evenings only, stands by bedding are for mornings only, and stands between the two work any time, including all day. Walking in on deer at food in the morning, or near bedding in the afternoon when you don't know where they are, blows them out. A Southern Outdoorsmen guest who hunts feed trees in South Carolina and Georgia adds that you often can't tell which kind of spot you have by looking, so you learn it by hunting. One hardwood draw between two pine thickets showed him 10 bucks one morning and about 2 deer that evening. He killed a buck there the next morning, a friend killed one 200 yards away the next week, he killed another the week after, and they quit hunting it in the evening.

sections.heading: The morning mission
sections.text: Derek Dixon, who studies bucks with thermal drones, found a mature buck's longest daylight travel comes in the morning. He's usually up at or before first light and walks long, fairly straight routes of up to a mile to a mile and a half, hitting rubs and scrapes and checking doe trails, then beds near where the does will feed that evening. Dixon tracked one buck scent-checking 35 to 40 does along a single morning route. So hunt mornings along those travel lines, not at his bed.

sections.heading: Why some hunters skip early mornings
sections.text: On private farm ground with small, well-defined cover, Whitetail Evolution and Sturgis limit morning hunts until about mid to late October. Many older bucks are back in bed well before first light, so walking toward bedding at 5:30 or 6 you bump him. Whitetail Evolution bumped his target buck about an hour before daylight on October 24, a cold-front morning. One bump can turn a predictable buck random and push him to the neighbor's. They take an early morning only with real evidence he moves after daylight, and then set up off to the side on a long transition. The research doesn't dispute the bumping, but it shows mornings carry the most daylight travel, so the problem is getting in, not whether deer move.

sections.heading: Where early mornings do work
sections.text: Southern hunters see it differently. Early-season Alabama afternoons run about 87 degrees while mornings sit in the 60s, so the Southern Outdoorsmen hosts and one of their guests get in during the dark near oaks that are dropping and wait for daylight, when acorns start falling. The South Carolina guest killed most of his big bucks in the morning on feed trees, some within 30 minutes to an hour of daylight. Sturgis himself allows early mornings in big woods and on public land. He slips in to the back side of a precise bedding cover through thick cover or water and waits for bucks coming back from distant food about two hours after daylight.

lessons.tryThis: Label every stand you hunt as morning, evening, or all day, based on whether it's near food, near bedding, or between. If a stand keeps producing at one time of day, stop sitting it at the other.
lessons.headsUp: Midwest private-ground hunters like Whitetail Evolution and Sturgis limit early-season mornings so they don't bump bedded bucks. The Southern guests say most of their big early bucks come in the morning at feed trees, and one calls "don't hunt early mornings" a Midwestern thing. The likely difference is deer feeding in the timber versus in fields, and big public woods versus small defined cover.

check.q: Your stand overlooks a food plot. Morning or evening?
check.a: Evening. Walking in on deer at food in the morning blows them out.

check.q: What does Dixon's drone work say about where to hunt a buck in the morning?
check.a: Along his long morning travel routes, not at his bed.

lessons.title: Getting ground to hunt
lessons.hook: Sooner or later, every hunter who's serious about one buck runs into the same problem. The buck lives on ground you can't hunt. Here's how a few of the mentors find new ground, win permission, and read the land around them.

sections.heading: Door knocking is a numbers game
sections.text: Lee Ellis has been knocking on doors for permission since he was 15, and he expects about 95 percent of the answers to be no. Some days five knocks get five yeses, and other days 25 knocks get none, so he plans whole days of it. One two-to-three-day trip was a bust until the last couple of hours, when he got a yes on ground with a reportedly giant buck. When a landowner says they've seen a monster, he shows them a camera photo of a buck he knows the size of and asks whether theirs was bigger or smaller. A monster can mean anything from a 110 to an elk.

sections.heading: Ask why on a no
sections.text: When Ellis gets a no, he politely asks why, while reading the person so he doesn't push too far. Then he addresses it. He explains he's after one specific old buck, not every deer, offers to take does if they want fewer deer, and offers to help with work around the place. One landowner said no because she thought he'd shoot fawns, then said yes once she heard he was after a single mature buck. Getting onto one buck's ground took 6 to 8 months of repeat visits, and he was the only one who got access to that deer. Keep coming back.

sections.heading: Read the neighbors from the air
sections.text: On public land in a state where baiting is legal, one of the Southern Outdoorsmen hosts looks at aerial imagery for feeder shadows on private fields right off the public. Then he walks the public side of that line looking for sign, because deer feeding on the neighbor's bait will leave sign nearby. He isn't saying to hunt the property line itself. Check your state's baiting rules.

sections.heading: Don't write off a die-off area
sections.text: Mike Rex says not to write off a region hit by a severe die-off from EHD, a disease outbreak in deer. Expect a few rough years, then some of the best big-buck hunting about 4 to 6 years later, often with cheaper leases and land right after the outbreak. Jefferson and Harrison counties in Ohio had a big outbreak in 2017 and were first and second of 88 counties in record-book entries six years later. Fewer deer means better nutrition and less stress, and it clears out scrub bucks. He warns that if EHD comes back every 2 or 3 years, the rebound won't happen.

lessons.tryThis: Pick one afternoon and knock on five doors near where your target buck lives. When you get a no, politely ask why, and write down the answer so you know what to offer next time.
lessons.headsUp: Each idea in this lesson comes from a single hunter's experience, and the EHD rebound comes from Ohio counties. Rex's own warning matters here, since the rebound depends on the disease not returning every few years.

check.q: A landowner says no. What does Lee Ellis do next?
check.a: Politely asks why, then addresses it, like explaining he's after one old buck and offering to take does or help out.

check.q: An area just had a bad EHD die-off. Should you give up on it?
check.a: Not necessarily. Rex saw the best big-buck hunting about 4 to 6 years later, unless the disease keeps coming back.

units.goal: Saddles, mobile kits, ground setups, and tuning.

lessons.title: Getting into saddle hunting
lessons.hook: Maybe you've sat the same preset stands and ladders for years and keep getting the same results. That's exactly why Next Step Outdoors, who has saddle hunted for nearly a decade, made the switch. This lesson covers what to buy first, what to add later, and how to set it up so you can shoot from it. Everything here comes from that one hunter.

sections.heading: Start with the must-haves
sections.text: A saddle is a climbing-style harness you hunt from instead of a stand. It lets you stay mobile, hunt almost any tree, and be quieter than with a big metal tree stand. You don't need every gadget to start. Next Step Outdoors says to begin with the saddle, a way up the tree like lightweight climbing sticks, a small platform to stand on, a backpack to carry it all, a metal bow hanger on a gear strap, and a bow rope, which can be plain paracord. Four sticks got him 20 to 25 feet up in one video and 15 to 20 feet in another, and he calls 20 to 25 feet plenty high for almost any setup in the country.

sections.heading: Add the extras in order
sections.text: Add the rest over time as you learn. His order starts with a dump pouch on your hip that always holds your lineman's belt and tether, so your ropes are always with you. Next comes an auto-retracting bow hoist, which keeps the line from blowing around and snagging on sticks and branches. Then come knee pads, which you put on at the truck, so on long sits you can rest with your knees against the tree and alternate that with standing. After that come aiders, which are extra foot loops on your sticks. They let four sticks climb higher without extra weight when you need to get above a branch for shooting lanes, visibility, or cover. Saddle suspenders are next, to keep the weight of sticks and platform from dragging the saddle down, and last come small modifications like stealth-stripping your sticks so no metal clanks.

sections.heading: Set the platform and the bow
sections.text: Set the platform about 10 to 18 inches above your top climbing stick, so you step onto the top stick and then up onto the platform. Any higher and you can't step up onto it safely. Hang a gear strap above your tether, so the tether can still move down, and put a sturdy metal bow hanger on it for your bow and quiver. Your pack can hang off that strap or off the lineman's carabiner. With the bow right beside you, it takes very little movement to get it when a deer comes. He trusts metal over plastic or 3D-printed hangers because a bow falling 20 feet can end your season.

sections.heading: Practice the weak side
sections.text: You can shoot 360 degrees from a saddle, but one side is harder. The weak-side shot takes more movement than turning on a tree stand, and that movement can get you seen. Practice it before the season. Either go up and over your bridge and turn your hips, or stand on the platform and turn around the way you would on a stand, which is easier with a bigger platform. Either way, keep swinging around on your tether to a minimum.

lessons.tryThis: Before you buy anything, make two lists, the must-haves and the add-ons in his order. Buy only the first list. Once it's set up, practice the weak-side shot until you know which way you'll turn for it.
lessons.headsUp: This platform height runs opposite to the hang-on stand advice. Jeff Sturgis runs his sticks 1 to 2 feet above a hang-on stand's platform so you step down onto it, and he calls stretching up to the platform unsafe. Next Step Outdoors steps up onto a small saddle platform. They're describing different systems, so use each rule with its own setup.

check.q: Where does the saddle platform go relative to your top climbing stick?
check.a: About 10 to 18 inches above it, so you can step onto the top stick and then onto the platform.

check.q: Why is a dump pouch first on the add-on list?
check.a: It always holds your lineman's belt and tether, so your ropes are always with you.

lessons.title: Light, quiet, and one climb
lessons.hook: You're setting up in the dark, maybe close to a bedded buck, and a stick clanks against the platform. Mobile hunting lives or dies on how light and quiet your kit is and how cleanly you get it up the tree. This lesson is about carrying less, packing it tight, and climbing once.

sections.heading: Keep the kit light
sections.text: The heavier your kit, the less willing you are to move when a tree isn't right, and bigger stands make more noise to carry and set up. Mark Kenyon of MeatEater keeps a mobile hang-on stand under 10 pounds by itself. He points out that many so-called mobile stands weigh 18 to 20 pounds, which is too much once you add sticks, and that even 8 versus 16 pounds is a big deal. The Hunting Public crew went further. They switched from a hang-on and sticks that weighed over 20 pounds to a tethered saddle and light sticks that come in under 10 pounds for the whole setup. Light gear also makes it easier to go deep on public land, where the bedding is.

sections.heading: Kill every clank
sections.text: The Hunting Public stealth-strips everything so no metal clanks, because they sometimes set up within 80 yards of a bedded buck, and a clank ruins it. They've had bucks stand up right in front of them after a quiet setup. How you pack matters too. Before they had a proper pack, their gear hung off their shoulders and flopped around. Now they slide the saddle platform into a pack with the sticks cinched tight on the back, or strap the sticks to a hang-on with its own tree straps and carry it on backpack straps with a waist belt. It's compact and quiet, and the belt takes weight off your shoulders.

sections.heading: Rig on the ground, climb once
sections.text: The Hunting Public and Bow Only Outdoors both rig everything on the ground so they climb once. Pull the straps off the stand so they hang free, use a light stand, and put your harness on before you reach the tree. Carry the top sticks on your harness, or pull the stand up on your safety line. Bow Only Outdoors hangs the top two sticks in 7-inch loops, one on each side, with the stand bracket strapped to the harness. Clip two haul ropes to the harness, one for the stand and one for the bow, and set them on opposite sides of the tree away from limbs so they don't tangle. Keep pruners in a pocket so you can clip limbs on the way up. The alternative is untangling straps and digging in your pack up in the tree, with more movement and noise, or climbing down for more gear. There's a lot hanging off you with this system, so watch for tangles.

sections.heading: Space the sticks and plan the platform
sections.text: The Hunting Public hangs each climbing stick about knee height above the last and pushes it down with their weight to seat it before stepping on it, since the teeth grip once weighted. Decide where the platform goes before you climb, and put the top stick just to the side of it, which for them is the left, so you step straight into the stand. That keeps you from swinging your legs around the tree "like a monkey" in awkward positions.

sections.heading: Change at the tree
sections.text: Jamie McKay adds one more step at the bottom of the tree. On a long walk in, wear one thin shirt and pack your layers. When you get there, change into dry clothes and dry socks, and seal the sweaty ones in a zip bag or garbage bag in your pack. He says it's worth the extra 10 minutes, because getting damp clothes off keeps you much warmer on stand.

lessons.tryThis: Weigh your stand and sticks on a bathroom scale and write the number down. Then pack everything the way you'd carry it, walk around the yard, and listen. Anything that clanks gets strapped down or stripped before your next hunt.

check.q: Why does kit weight matter beyond sore shoulders?
check.a: A heavy kit makes you less willing to move when a tree isn't right, and bigger stands make more noise.

check.q: Where do your two haul ropes go when you rig for one climb?
check.a: Clipped to your harness, one for the stand and one for the bow, on opposite sides of the tree away from limbs.

lessons.title: Tuning and practice for the bow
lessons.hook: Good groups on the backyard target feel like proof you're ready. Eddie McRae, who has killed hundreds of deer with a bow and says he's never missed one, lost one, or failed to get a pass-through, thinks there's more to it. Everything in this lesson is his, so read it as one very experienced hunter's system.

sections.heading: Paper tune until it's habit
sections.text: Shoot rows of arrows through paper from 6 to 8 feet until every one leaves a clean bullet hole. Paper gives you instant feedback. Left or right tears mean the bow is out of tune or you're torquing it, and high or low tears usually point to the setup, like the rest or nock height. Even torque or a string twist from your release shows up in the tear. Figure out whether it's the bow or you, fix it, and repeat until it's habit. McRae compares it to a golf swing, because repeatable form, not perfect form, is what you're after.

sections.heading: Practice long so hunting shots feel short
sections.text: McRae practices outdoors at 50 yards minimum, and often at 60 and 80, even though he'd never shoot a deer that far. Every flaw in your form shows at long range. Once 60 to 80 yards is routine, a 20 to 30 yard shot feels like a chip shot.

sections.heading: Run the same routine every time
sections.text: McRae talks himself through the same routine on every shot. He grips, draws, finds his primary anchor, then his secondary anchor with the tip of his nose on the string, comes down onto the target from above, settles the pin, and executes. If anything feels off at full draw, like his anchor, he doesn't shoot. He backs off and restarts the whole routine. He once let a buck stand 9 minutes at 12 yards while he was on the ground, and when his anchor felt wrong at full draw, he pulled off and reset before shooting. Staying calm keeps you out of panic mode, which is hard to get out of once you're in it, and the confidence comes from reps.

sections.heading: A front-heavy arrow, not a heavy one
sections.text: McRae builds a 425 to 475 grain arrow with the weight up front, rather than a 600 to 700 grain heavy arrow. His is 450 grains total, with a 75-grain outsert and a 125-grain fixed-blade broadhead, so 200 grains sit up front. He says only a long-draw shooter needs to go near 500. Front weight flies straight like a throwing dart and drives penetration, and his broke through a buck's shoulder blade and heart quartering-to at 35 yards. His case against very heavy arrows is that they drop so much between 20 and 30 yards that misjudging the range can cost you the shot, while an arrow at 280 to 290 feet per second makes that error insignificant. He uses a simple cut-on-contact fixed blade because it has no mechanism to fail.

lessons.tryThis: Shoot a row of arrows through paper at 6 to 8 feet and read the tears before you change anything. Next time at the range, back up to 50 yards and shoot a few, and notice which flaws in your form show up there that you never see up close.
lessons.headsUp: McRae says himself that his arrow opinion stirs controversy. He notes that the heavy-arrow research, by Dr. Ashby, was aimed at African game, and he has used essentially the same setup since the late 80s. It's one hunter's view, and he knows others disagree, so weigh it that way.

check.q: Your arrows tear left or right through paper. What might be wrong?
check.a: The bow may be out of tune, or you may be torquing it. Figure out which, fix it, and shoot again.

check.q: Your anchor feels off at full draw with a buck standing there. What do you do?
check.a: Let down and restart the whole routine. Don't shoot on a bad anchor.

lessons.title: Shooting from the tree
lessons.hook: A buck steps out 25 yards away and below you, a shot you've practiced plenty on flat ground. Then the arrow hits high, or off to the side. Bill Winke says it's very easy to make that mistake in the excitement and never notice. This lesson is about the problems that only show up once you're off the ground.

sections.heading: Bend at the hip, not the arm
sections.text: For a downward shot, Winke draws and then bends at the waist over the side of his hip, so his bow arm keeps the same 90-degree angle to his upper body that he uses on flat ground. If you only drop your bow arm, your eye moves relative to the peep sight. The peep pulls away from your face, you raise the bow to re-center the pin, and the arrow hits high.

sections.heading: Don't bend forward either
sections.text: Bending straight forward at the waist causes a different miss. It tips, or cants, a compound, and a canted compound sends the arrow to the side, so a right-handed shooter hits right. The arrow leaves angled up and to the side of your sight line, and gravity pulls it straight down, not back toward the line. Winke has made this mistake many times himself and practices it every season. Once you're settled in the stand, take practice draws toward your likely shot spots and check that you're bending over the side of your hip. This is a compound problem, where the rest sits 2 to 3 inches above your hand. Traditional shooters shooting off the shelf cant on purpose, and it matters much less because the arrow sits right at the pivot point on the hand.

sections.heading: Put a bubble on your sight
sections.text: Winke also puts a bubble level on his bow sight and makes a centered bubble part of every sight picture, on the range and on a deer. It's how you catch a canted bow before the shot, which is exactly the mistake that's so easy to miss in the moment.

sections.heading: Hang the stand for your shot
sections.text: Mark Kenyon of MeatEater hangs a stand so a right-handed shooter shoots off the left side, using the tree to hide behind. Most people face the stand toward where they expect deer, which leaves them exposed. From a well-hung stand the shooting movement is small and the tree breaks up your outline. He also says shooting well from a stand is quicker to learn than shooting well from a saddle.

sections.heading: Traditional shooters, keep it modest
sections.text: If you shoot instinctively with a traditional bow, your aim runs on memory of how targets look from the ground. Samko Trad Bow points out that from 18 to 20 feet up, a deer at 10 yards looks tiny and throws off your judgment, while at 10 feet up an 18-yard deer feels like a chip shot. His advice is to keep your hunting height modest, about 12 to 16 feet, and practice from the height you hunt.

lessons.tryThis: Next time you're settled in a stand, before any deer show up, draw toward each likely shot spot. Check your bubble, and check that you're bending over the side of your hip rather than forward.
lessons.headsUp: Each tip here comes from a single hunter, Winke for form and the bubble, Kenyon for hanging the stand, and Samko Trad Bow for height. Winke also names a second big reason people seem to hit high, a deer jumping the string, but he doesn't cover it in this material.

check.q: You're a right-handed compound shooter and you bend forward for a steep shot. Where does the arrow likely go?
check.a: Right. Bending forward cants the bow, and a canted compound sends the arrow to the side.

check.q: Which side should a right-handed shooter shoot off when hanging a stand, according to Kenyon?
check.a: The left side, so the tree hides you and the shooting movement stays small.

lessons.title: Hunting from the ground and blinds
lessons.hook: You don't need a tree to kill a deer. Sometimes there's no good tree, and sometimes you'd rather just sit down where the deer are. Hunting from the ground puts you at a deer's eye level, though, and that changes what gives you away.

sections.heading: Sit low and stay seated
sections.text: A guest on Southern Outdoorsmen who has hunted only from the ground for 18 years sits low in a turkey lounger or low seat with a back, and stays seated. Deer don't easily recognize the human outline until you stand up on two feet, so a low, seated hunter reads as a stump. He's had does walk within 5 yards in open woods without noticing him, as long as he didn't move, and a comfortable seat keeps him more observant. He thinks tree stands help more in low hills and flat ground, where it's easier to get busted, while in the mountains sitting above the deer does the same job.

sections.heading: Break up your outline
sections.text: Your outline and the motion of drawing are what give a ground hunter away, so sit behind something that breaks you up. The best choice is a big tree at least as wide as you. On a mountainside, set your seat on the uphill side of it, where erosion often builds a flat spot you can scrape clear of rocks, and lean your gun or bow against the tree within reach. With a gun, that tree is also a solid rest, so you can stand up behind it and slide the gun around its side for a 100 to 150 yard shot. With no big tree, stick a few cut branches around you, low enough to shoot over, stake a screw-in tree umbrella in front as a mini blind, sit in a fallen tree's crown, or tuck into brushy cover and prune just one lane.

sections.heading: Move slow, and don't glow
sections.text: Every movement is exaggerated at ground level. The same guest leaves the phone alone, and when he turns his head, he does it slow as molasses, never quick and jerky. He practices moving slowly at home so it comes naturally. Your gear can give you away too, even up a tree. Eddie McRae once had a feeding doe at 30 yards snap her head up the moment he swatted a mosquito, though he sat 20 feet up in deep shadow with heavy cover and full camo. Under a black light, only his gloves glowed. Now he checks every piece of gear under a black light in a dark room, keeps anything that glows out of the woods, and skips regular detergent, because common blue liquid detergents carry UV brighteners you can't wash back out. The hosts backed this with Dr. Karl Miller of the University of Georgia, who tested hunting apparel and found some comes with brighteners from the factory.

sections.heading: Blinds done right
sections.text: Jeff Sturgis bowhunts from a small elevated blind, about 5 feet up, tucked into a clump of gray dogwood on a food plot edge so its top sits level with the brush. A wall of brush in front keeps deer from walking up to it, and he enters from the back to get in unseen. Deer in the field don't notice a blind that blends into the shrubs. He puts a red cedar licking tree for a mock scrape about 32 to 33 yards out to set up 20 to 30 yard shots. His one firm rule for a box blind facing a field is to never turn on a light inside, even a dim or colored one, because it will clear every deer out of the plot or field in front of you.

sections.heading: A short gun for tight woods
sections.text: If you hunt thick woods where 40 yards is your longest shot, a short, handy gun is a fine choice. The Southern Outdoorsmen hosts suggest a rifled-slug 20 gauge, a .45-70, or anything with a 16 to 20 inch barrel. In thick cover, especially in the rut when you can't hear deer coming, a deer pops in at 25 to 30 yards and is gone before you can move, and a long 28-inch barrel is hard to carry and swing through cover. Have a system for getting on the gun fast.

lessons.tryThis: Take every glove, hat, and jacket you hunt in into a dark room with a black light, and leave home anything that glows. Then practice turning your head slowly at home until it feels normal.
lessons.headsUp: Each tip here has a single source. The ground advice is one guest's experience and the blind setup is Sturgis's alone, so treat them as proven methods from one hunter, not rules.

check.q: What gives a ground hunter away most?
check.a: Your outline and the motion of drawing, so sit behind something that breaks you up, like a tree at least as wide as you.

check.q: Is a dim red light okay inside a box blind that faces a field?
check.a: No. Sturgis says any light, even a dim or colored one, will clear every deer out of the field.

m-access-access-scent-plan-01.action: Plan your walk to and from the stand to be as scent-free and quiet as possible; it matters as much as, or more than, your setup in the stand. Don't use a stand whose route or wind keeps putting your scent into known bedding or bumping deer.
m-access-access-scent-plan-01.why: This matters most for permanent stands (like a ladder stand always in the same tree). If getting there always blows scent into bedding, you'll have nowhere near the success of a stand that keeps your scent away.

m-access-afternoon-entry-least-bumping-0.action: If you want the least chance of bumping deer on the way in, favor afternoon sits and get in early (around 1 PM) instead of walking in during the morning movement.
m-access-afternoon-entry-least-bumping-0.why: At 1 PM a good share of bucks are bedded or moving slowly; in the morning you're walking in while bucks are in their main movement bout.

m-access-angle-past-bedded-buck-01.action: When walking near a spot where a buck may be bedded, don't walk straight toward it; angle past it.
m-access-angle-past-bedded-buck-01.why: In his experience a buck usually stays put and watches you walk by, even circling around him, and only gets up and runs once you're coming directly at him.

m-access-approach-from-below-01.action: In hill country, come in from below and from the downhill back side, and use the ridge to hide your approach. Never walk up and over the ridge top to reach a stand on the far side (Sturgis). For morning stands, walk in through creek bottoms, ravines, and low drainages, not from the top (Downwind Hunting).
m-access-approach-from-below-01.why: Crossing the top exposes you to any deer up there and to the food beyond; staying below the crest hides your movement and noise (Sturgis). In the early morning cool air drains downhill, so scent from a walk below drifts down and away from the ridges and benches where deer bed, while walking in from the top pushes your scent through the bedding before you sit (Downwind Hunting).

m-access-bottom-arrive-just-before-light.action: Walk into a bottom stand so you're settled about 10 minutes before daylight, not an hour before.
m-access-bottom-arrive-just-before-light.why: Before daylight the thermals haven't started lifting, so your scent just pools and saturates the bottom. Arriving late cuts that soak time.

m-access-climb-from-the-back-side-01.action: Approach and climb from the side away from where you'll be watching and shooting, so you aren't walking in with your back to the deer area or crossing your own shooting lanes.
m-access-climb-from-the-back-side-01.why: It keeps your entry both safe and hidden.

m-access-cross-food-only-when-empty-01.action: Only walk across food when you can count on no deer being on it. Cross food deer have stopped using: in Sturgis's area, once alfalfa frosts out in the fall it draws few deer, so he can cross a cut alfalfa field to his stand expecting nothing out there. For a morning sit near a food plot, walk in before daylight by the hidden route, sit late watching water for cruising bucks, and leave late morning or early afternoon (around 11 AM to 1 PM), when you can exit across the food plot.
m-access-cross-food-only-when-empty-01.why: Your access is only safe where you can count on no deer being. Deer aren't expected in the food plot at 11 AM or 1 PM, so walking out through it spooks nothing, while the late sit itself covers bucks cruising to water.

m-access-dead-end-trail-01.action: Make your access trail dead-end at the stand inside a wall of brush, so deer have no reason to keep walking your path past the tree.
m-access-dead-end-trail-01.why: If a trail continues past your stand, deer will follow it and smell where you climbed and touched. A doe may come back; a mature buck that smells it may not come back for two or three weeks.

m-access-dont-push-best-spots-early-01.action: Hunt the early season, but resist pushing into your best spots: the thickest cover and the stands meant for the rut. Don't sit a rut stand in early October.
m-access-dont-push-best-spots-early-01.why: Summer velvet-buck photos and social-media outliers tempt you in too soon. Pushing deep educates the deer with hunting pressure and lowers your odds in the higher-percentage pre-rut and rut.

m-access-drop-off-01.action: Have a partner walk or drive you to the stand and then leave, and be ready to shoot the moment you're settled. Deer often stand up or come investigate right as the other person walks or drives away.
m-access-drop-off-01.why: A deer that heard or saw the commotion often relaxes or comes to check it out once it sees someone leave. His youngest son killed a buck before Rex's truck had even left the field; the hosts tell the same story from their own hunts.

m-access-ebike-01.action: Use an e-bike (or any quiet way) to get to your spot without breaking a sweat.
m-access-ebike-01.why: In his words it's scent-free and quiet, and he never breaks a sweat getting to a spot.

m-access-enter-where-others-dont-01.action: On public land, enter where other hunters don't. Skip the spots where everyone parks: look on the map for stretches of road between official parking or access points, then walk down the road or get dropped off and cut in between them; even 5 to 10 minutes off the road can be excellent if it's far from any parking area. Or pick the hard way in: cross water, a marsh, or beaver dams in knee boots, or a wetland other hunters can't, to reach a series of ridges; or take a long, easy, flat walk (around 45 minutes) to put distance behind you.
m-access-enter-where-others-dont-01.why: Most hunters walk in from the parking lot, so ground that's close to the road but a mile or two from the nearest parking area often gets almost no pressure. Even a 20-minute walk that requires crossing a couple of beaver dams and a marsh eliminates 90 to 95% of hunters; most people won't get wet or walk far.

m-access-exit-unseen-01.action: Plan your exit as carefully as your entry, and don't let deer see or hear you leave. Assume a mature buck is watching: leave quietly and out of sight, especially from high vantage spots above where he lives (Rex). Leaving an evening stand, look first to see if the coast is clear, then walk out along an edge behind screening or straight through the middle of an ag field; if you have to bump deer, bump them off a crop field, not your food plot (Sturgis). At a staging food source, wait after dark for the deer to browse and move on toward the destination field, then climb down and slip away quietly (Whitetail Evolution). Don't bail out of your stand 20 minutes before dark just because nothing is in sight; deer may be filtering toward you unseen, and being caught climbing down can end the spot (McRae).
m-access-exit-unseen-01.why: Deer spooked off a big ag field forget it; deer spooked off a small plot you hunt learn to avoid it (Sturgis). The destination field is where most deer are heading, so at dark you can have 15 to 20 deer in the field or under your stand and no way out without blowing out the property (Whitetail Evolution). McRae climbed down early on a hot, muggy evening to avoid getting pinned; a doe and small buck at 40 yards caught him, blew, and spooked everything in the cutover, a camera showed his target buck watching him come down, and that buck never came back to that spot. Several times, before Rex and his son reached the truck after climbing down off the high wall, their camera caught the target buck watching them leave.

m-access-hang-and-hunt-01.action: Consider hunting with a portable hang-on stand you carry in and out each time. You can go in blind to a general area or a tree you picked on the map, get up quietly, hunt, and leave without leaving stands or much scent behind.
m-access-hang-and-hunt-01.why: It keeps pressure and ground scent low in an area, and he's killed some of his biggest bucks this way.

m-access-hidden-route-01.action: Keep cover between you and the deer all the way in. Tunnel your access behind tall cover (a mowed trail through about 5-foot switchgrass, a hedgerow, willows) rather than across food, and enter with the wind in your face or blowing off to the side away from where deer are (Sturgis). If there's a creek with high banks, walk up the creek bed to get past areas where deer may already be feeding in the dark, then climb out at your tree (sGtmLizXCwo guest).
m-access-hidden-route-01.why: Hidden access means deer don't see or pattern you coming in. Sturgis's blind access comes in 60 to 70 yards short of a long plot through screened cover, so they can get in and out all day without spooking deer in the field or the woods beside it. The guest's creek has 10 to 12 foot banks that hide them; they killed two bucks at one tree they'd have spooked walking in any other way, and the bucks came back 30 minutes after daylight from the direction they'd walked past.

m-access-in-before-the-break-01.action: Be in your stand before the weather breaks, not walking in after it has.
m-access-in-before-the-break-01.why: Deer get up and move quickly once it breaks. If you're already there you're less likely to bump them on the way in and more likely to catch them moving from bedding to food.

m-access-leave-no-trail-01.action: On public land, leave the main trail everyone uses early, and hide that you were ever there: don't crush ferns or trample vegetation, step around sandy or muddy spots that hold a print, and never leave flagging, tacks, or glow sticks to mark your way.
m-access-leave-no-trail-01.why: Anything that shows your path lets another hunter follow it and walk right to the spot you worked hard to find, whether it's 20 minutes or over an hour in.

m-access-light-discipline-01.action: Walking in or out in the dark, keep light to the bare minimum. Use the lowest setting your light has (1 to 2 lumens, 'moonlight') pointed straight down at your feet, or cover the lens with your thumb so only a sliver reaches the ground; never swing a bright light or a bobbing headlamp around. Be strictest in the open near fields and food plots; in deep woods on a morning walk where you don't expect deer, you can get away with more light.
m-access-light-discipline-01.why: Deer see light from hundreds of yards, and fields are where deer are before daylight. Walking a fence row with a mini Maglite in the 1980s, he had deer blowing and running 700 to 800 yards away with the wind in his face; on a Wisconsin gun opener he watched a headlamp push deer off a hillside 500 to 600 yards away.

m-access-morning-entry-modes-01.action: Pick one of three ways into a morning stand. (1) EARLY, an hour before light, only if once you're up your scent blows into a spot deer never use. (2) JUST IN TIME, right at daylight, if your scent could reach deer before light. (3) POST-DAYBREAK, if you have to cross open fields: wait and watch until the deer leave the field, then walk in.
m-access-morning-entry-modes-01.why: Every minute on stand before light is a minute your scent can spook deer before the hunt starts. None of the three is worse; let current sign and your cameras pick the stand, then use its entry.

m-access-morning-known-spots-01.action: On a morning feed-tree hunt, go to an area you've already scouted or hunted before, not a brand-new spot. If you check trees in the dark on the way in, keep it to that known patch, then climb the one that's being hit.
m-access-morning-known-spots-01.why: You can't read a new area well in the dark, and blundering around bumps the deer already feeding. He found his big South Carolina buck's tree in the dark because he knew that little patch and it was one of the first places he checked.

m-access-mowed-quiet-trail-01.action: Where your access trail runs through tall grass or brush, mow it about 6 feet wide (in July or August) so nothing brushes your legs and boots, and bend it at an angle so no one can look straight down it to your stand. On public land, pick routes that do the same job: open hardwoods, a sandy creek edge.
m-access-mowed-quiet-trail-01.why: It's quiet, you touch nothing on the way in, and you don't leave scent on the weeds.

m-access-muffle-the-ratchet-01.action: Cover the ratchet strap with your gloved hand while you ratchet to muffle it, especially on cool, still mornings.
m-access-muffle-the-ratchet-01.why: Ratchet straps are loud and sound carries far on a cold morning. Still, he killed a buck on a frosty, almost windless morning after ratcheting in and hasn't seen it spook deer.

m-access-no-scrape-near-entry-01.action: Don't put a mock scrape on something deer already come to, like an apple tree, and never near your walk-in route. Give deer no extra reason to hang out where you'll be walking.
m-access-no-scrape-near-entry-01.why: They're already coming to the apples, so a scrape there adds nothing and pulls attention away from your stand scrape. His post-daybreak entry trail passes that apple tree, and he doesn't want to run into a deer there at 8 AM, half an hour after daylight, on the way in.

m-access-one-bump-not-ruined-01.action: Don't abandon a spot because you spooked a deer there once. Worry instead about spending a lot of time in an area you haven't been in all year.
m-access-one-bump-not-ruined-01.why: Coyotes bump deer a dozen times a day; if deer never returned to places they'd been spooked, they'd have nowhere to go. What they do notice and react to is a lot of sudden human presence.

m-access-one-trip-midday-setup-01.action: When you set up a new spot in thick cover, do it all in one trip in the middle of the day (he went in at 10 AM, outside prime movement): walk it about an hour, clear the spot, hang cameras, then get out and don't come back. Watch it on cell cameras.
m-access-one-trip-midday-setup-01.why: Repeated trips are what do the damage. He credits the idea to Bobby Worthington (via a Parker McDonald interview): get it done in a day and get out.

m-access-pack-gear-quiet-01.action: Pack your stand gear so it stays inside the outline of your shoulders and hips and can't clank or snag: sticks stacked vertically, platform flat on your back, nothing wider than your body or taller than your shoulders; wear your saddle and knee pads in from the truck (Next Step Outdoors). If you carry a hang-on stand, soundproof it and pack it so the stand and sticks can't clank together or bang on brush, cattails, or trees, and balance the load evenly on both shoulders with a waist strap rather than chasing the lightest gear (Relentless Sportsman).
m-access-pack-gear-quiet-01.why: Gear that sticks out catches on brush and makes noise; if your body fits through a gap, your gear will too, so you can ease in to the tree quietly (Next Step Outdoors). Cast aluminum or steel stands are noisier than a saddle, which packs away almost silent. Weight distribution matters more than the weight itself: a 10 to 20 pound stand is hardly noticed if it's balanced, and even light gear is miserable if the sticks all hang on one side (Relentless Sportsman).

m-access-park-far-avoid-trails-01.action: Park at least 400 yards from your stand and walk in on a route that never crosses a deer trail. On public land, use creek beds, drainage ditches, and old logging roads.
m-access-park-far-avoid-trails-01.why: The walk from truck to tree is the biggest scent bomb most hunters set off. Southeastern outfitters cut dedicated access trails that avoid every deer travel corridor.

m-access-partner-shot-protocol-01.action: When hunting with a partner 200 to 300 yards apart, agree beforehand that if one of you shoots, that hunter stays in the tree and doesn't go after the deer until the other has finished the morning sit.
m-access-partner-shot-protocol-01.why: He tells partners: 'if you shoot, don't get down, just hang out, let me get my morning hunt in.' Getting down and walking around would spoil the other hunter's sit.

m-access-pick-tree-and-route-now-01.action: When you find a spot you want to hunt, pick the exact tree (or ground spot) and the access route right then, while you're standing there, and mark both on your mapping app. Clear dead branches and brush from the base of the tree so you can climb it quietly in the dark.
m-access-pick-tree-and-route-now-01.why: Knowing every bed, rub, and scrape does no good if you don't know where you can ambush a deer and how to get in without spooking him or other deer that would bump him. He's been burned for years by saying 'I'll figure that out later' and not getting back until the season.

m-access-prioritize-mornings-pre-rut-01.action: In the pre-rut, make mornings the priority. Don't hunt an evening stand if getting in or out of it could spoil a high-quality morning stand.
m-access-prioritize-mornings-pre-rut-01.why: Pre-rut bucks are moving more in the morning; a blown morning spot costs you the best sits.

m-access-protect-the-food-01.action: Protect your food sources from pressure above everything else. Don't drive an ATV through the property, don't access sloppily, and don't put blinds right on top of food plots. Don't bowhunt or put a blind on the field where deer gather to feed until dark unless you can get in and out without being seen and leave your stand without spooking deer off it; hunt that field from a distance with a gun if at all. Whenever you hunt a late-season food source (or a midday spot), make sure you can get in and out without spooking deer off it.
m-access-protect-the-food-01.why: Pressure a bedding area and a mature buck will often just slide to the next bedding area; pressure a food source and all the bedding areas around it are lost, because deer start coming only after dark and eventually stop coming. Blowing deer off that field spoils every bedding area around it, about 250 yards in every direction (roughly 30 acres), and turns it into a night-only field where mature bucks come only after dark because they recognize the pressure. One bad hunt can ruin a food source for two or three weeks, if the deer come back at all. He says about 95% of food plots are over-pressured, and a 30 to 40 acre neighbor who stays out can out-hunt someone with 400 acres who doesn't.

m-access-quiet-climb-one-trip-01.action: Get up the tree in one trip, quietly. Hang the first stick from the ground, carry the rest on a hip carabiner and the platform on the back of your saddle, and tie your bow to a hoist rope before anything else, leaving it on the ground laid with the attached cam closest to the tree so it pulls straight up. Buckle or wrap every loose strap so nothing flaps in the wind.
m-access-quiet-climb-one-trip-01.why: Going up and down to fetch each stick makes more noise, takes much longer, and gets you sweaty before the hunt. Handling the bow only once and not going up and down cuts the noise, and being quiet is what lets a saddle hunter set up as close to bedded deer as possible.

m-access-rain-washes-your-trail-01.action: When rain is due right after your hunt, use it: you can be a little more invasive on the way out, like swapping a trail-camera card, because the rain will wash away your trail.
m-access-rain-washes-your-trail-01.why: Access scent is the most critical thing on a small parcel. Normally the web of scent you leave walking to and from stands lingers 3-4 hours; after a rain it doesn't.

m-access-reach-food-from-the-edge-01.action: Hunt food sources you can reach from the outside of the property (for example food about 100 yards off a road). Never walk through or past a food source, or into the middle of the property, to get to a stand; that area is where the deer live.
m-access-reach-food-from-the-edge-01.why: Deer aren't living by the road, they're living behind the food, so you get in and out without them knowing. Driving half a mile into an interior field to hunt it ruins over half the property (he estimates 300 of 500 acres); on 40 acres, hunting a 5-acre plot in the middle ruins the whole thing.

m-access-rest-before-season-01.action: Finish your intrusive work (habitat jobs, hanging stands, trimming lanes, scouting, cameras, water holes) well ahead of the season, then stay out and let the ground rest until you hunt it. Whitetail Evolution finishes about a month before the opener; Mike Rex gets it done early in summer and stays out the last 2 to 4 weeks before the season; once Sturgis's water hole and stand are in, he leaves that part of the property completely alone (he won't even mow trails nearby) until he hunts it. Watch it with cellular or solar trail cameras so you don't have to walk in to check them. Then don't undo the rest in the first two days by pushing into your best stands because you're excited (Whitetail Evolution).
m-access-rest-before-season-01.why: Giving the property time to settle gives the deer a false sense of security, which creates predictable movement once the season opens (Whitetail Evolution). Mature bucks seen in fields all summer go sporadic 2 to 4 weeks before the season, and it isn't just acorns: a predator that wasn't around all summer suddenly shows up, only in daylight, pruning and scouting and squirrel hunting; old bucks have been through it before, and deer know days later that you were there (Rex). Left undisturbed, deer use keeps building by the day; Sturgis had bucks sparring on his water-hole dirt pad within two weeks. You only see the few on social media who got a buck early, not the hundreds who pushed too far, bumped their target buck, and never saw him again.

m-access-rotate-stands-01.action: If you have more than one stand, rotate them: come in one way and leave another, and hunt different sides and heights of the property in the morning vs the afternoon.
m-access-rotate-stands-01.why: Spreading out keeps the hunting pressure on any one spot low.

m-access-rut-less-careful-01.action: In the rut you can be less careful about noise when moving or hanging a new set midday (trimming with a pole saw is fine). Keep playing the wind.
m-access-rut-less-careful-01.why: His Iowa move was hung loudly at 9 AM with a pole saw and he still had a great hunt that evening and killed a big buck the next morning. He believes the rut is the time of year you don't have to be as careful.

m-access-safest-place-around-01.action: If your neighbors shoot whatever walks by, don't fight them. Make your place the safest spot around: the best food, the best cover, and very little hunting pressure. Lay off your spots while the neighbors pressure theirs, and hunt when the time is right.
m-access-safest-place-around-01.why: Deer that feel safe on your ground and unsafe next door (pre-hung stands, no care for the wind, baiting) are more likely to stay with you in daylight. Even so, deer don't stay on 100 acres all day, so there's only so much you can do.

m-access-setup-time-01.action: Budget stand setup time into when you leave for the tree, and practice in the yard before the season. Hunting Public: about 5 to 10 minutes to hang a stand and sticks on an easy straight tree, 10 to 15 minutes on a tree with branches you have to work around, about 30 minutes with camera gear. Bow Only Outdoors: about 15 minutes from reaching the tree to fully set up, 30 to 45 minutes on an odd or limby tree, 45 to 60 minutes if you're also setting up cameras; tear-down takes about 5 minutes.
m-access-setup-time-01.why: Hanging a stand takes real time and it varies a lot by tree. A good straight trunk and a plan for where the stand goes before you start keeps setup fast, and practice makes it routine. Coming down is much quicker, which helps when you're leaving late at night.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-access-silent-entry-near-bed-01.action: When slipping in close to where you think a buck beds, treat every step as the hunt: don't snap sticks, keep cover between you and the bedding, keep looking ahead, and take your platform and sticks apart and set them up dead silent.
m-access-silent-entry-near-bed-01.why: Beau filled his Pennsylvania tag 1.5 hours into opening day on a spot he believed had bedding close by.
