He credits that hyper-focus on one deer, plus the incoming weather, for the confidence and care that made it work; he has killed on the opener this way twice.

m-access-talk-to-hunters-01.action: On public land, expect other hunters and be courteous. Talk to people at the parking lot and ask where they're heading so you can avoid them. If someone beat you to a spot, practice first come, first served, and go to your plan B, C, or D.
m-access-talk-to-hunters-01.why: Knowing where others are means you don't walk 3 miles in to find a camera or a hunter already set up. He once gave up a thicket to a hunter who'd waited three years to hunt it, went to plan D, and killed a buck on one of his best gun hunts.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-access-two-routes-01.action: Give a thick-cover set two routes: a clipped, silent hunting path that brings you in the back door of the blind unseen, and a separate route (an old logging road) used only for camera and battery maintenance.
m-access-two-routes-01.why: You can slip in absolutely quiet without being seen on the hunting path, and maintenance trips don't foul it.

m-access-wind-and-wet-cover-noise-01.action: Use loud weather to get close. Save your most sensitive spots (like the middle of a bedding area) for a wet, windy day and go in during the dark; you can walk faster and get right in close (Hunting Public). On a windy evening, slip past bedding up high while the wind is loud up top and drop down to a stand in a low, quiet bowl below it, where deer will come in the evening (Sturgis). On a calm day with crunchy leaves, slow down and walk like a squirrel or a deer, not a person (Hunting Public).
m-access-wind-and-wet-cover-noise-01.why: Wet leaves are quiet and everything in the woods is moving in the wind, so deer neither hear nor see you; the Hunting Public crew has walked up within a few yards of deer in the dark with a headlamp on them, while on a calm, crunchy day your steps carry for hundreds of yards and alert everything. The wind noise covers your approach past the bedding up high: Sturgis did this a couple of nights before the video, dropping about 200 feet into a bowl whose draw carried the wind away toward a neighbor's house 300 yards off.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-calling-big-bucks-loners-01.action: Don't count on calling or rattling in the biggest, oldest bucks; many are loners that don't respond. Learn each buck's personality from watching him and from camera history: an aggressive 'bully' buck may come to rattling, a calm dominant one won't.
m-calling-big-bucks-loners-01.why: Lee Ellis has never had a giant come running to a call; young bucks come in again and again to rattling. He thinks some bucks get old partly because they're wired to be less vulnerable. A dominant buck he watched just flared his antlers at a bully and the bully backed off, so he rarely needs to fight. His late-season giant stayed alone while 10 to 12 other bucks grouped up.

m-calling-bleat-low-risk-01.action: A doe bleat or fawn bleat (or a bleat can) is a low-risk call: deer rarely respond to it, but it almost never spooks them, even with does and fawns around. Use it on a cruising or searching buck in the peak rut and post-rut, when a buck looking for a doe may come to it. Leave the fawn bleat at home in the early season if you're after bucks.
m-calling-bleat-low-risk-01.why: A call that works sometimes and rarely spooks beats an aggressive call that spooks deer a high percentage of the time. Early, fawns bleat all the time, so a buck won't go out of his way to check it out, it may only draw a doe looking for a lost fawn, and repeating it makes it suspicious.

m-calling-blind-call-timing-01.action: If you're going to blind call, do it when conditions give deer a reason to get up: a weather change, clouds rolling in, rain stopping, or the light changing around 5 PM. Not at 10 AM on an all-day sit after two slow hours.
m-calling-blind-call-timing-01.why: The dead midday lull is when you most want to make something happen and when you're least likely to call one in; the risk usually isn't worth it. Let the conditions work for you.

m-calling-blind-grunt-interval-01.action: Don't grunt at every deer. Blind call with a single short contact grunt about every 30 to 40 minutes, and only when no deer are in sight.
m-calling-blind-grunt-interval-01.why: Constant calling from one spot sounds fake and teaches a mature buck where your stand is. One quiet grunt that goes silent sounds like a deer that already moved on. It says Iowa and Illinois outfitters have switched to this.

m-calling-buck-grunt-tone-01.action: Shape buck grunts with your hands: hold the call between thumb and forefinger and 'choke' it with your other fingers, and cup the other hand tight like it's holding water to make a deep chamber. Vary choke, chamber, and air pressure. Don't assume you need the deepest old-buck grunt to call in a big buck.
m-calling-buck-grunt-tone-01.why: An open call doesn't sound like a buck in the timber. Every buck has his own voice, and a deep guttural grunt often turns out to be a little forkhorn, so size isn't in the depth of the tone.

m-calling-buck-urine-challenge-01.action: Use dominant buck urine together with a decoy, grunting, or rattling when you want to pull a buck in by challenging him on his turf.
m-calling-buck-urine-challenge-01.why: It sets off a territorial reaction: a buck comes in to defend his area, which gets him close and into range.

m-calling-call-less-01.action: Call less. Give a buck just what he needs to hear, then stop. Never use every call at once or all the time, and if nothing comes after a call, don't keep calling every 15 minutes. Avoid the big mistakes: over-calling, too much blind calling, getting aggressive at the wrong time, and throwing more calls at a buck that has turned tail and left. If the does, fawns, and young bucks around you are on edge and looking back over their shoulders, assume any mature buck in the area is already gone.
m-calling-call-less-01.why: Used wrong, calls hurt you more than they help. No matter how good or expensive the call, the more you call the more a deer figures out you aren't a deer, and the shy old buck often circles downwind, smells you, and walks off without you ever knowing he was there. Mature bucks take very little stress and don't think like the herd. Any call that spooks deer is the lowest hole in your bucket.

m-calling-decoys-open-country-only-01.action: Skip decoys in normal deer travel areas, between bedding and food, and at brushy morning stands; blend in instead: strap in, sit down, stay quiet, and don't move. The only place a decoy makes sense is big open country during rut cruising hours, like Kansas or Iowa river bottoms or a cut cornfield edge, where a buck can see it from a quarter mile away and come over.
m-calling-decoys-open-country-only-01.why: On a travel route, the first mature doe or fawn that spots the decoy and doesn't like it blows or spooks back the way she came and takes every deer behind her; he's seen it happen to friends again and again. Carrying one into brush and setting it upwind in your shooting lane also means extra noise, walking, and scent where you most need to sneak in. Overcalling and decoys are the opposite of blending in.

m-calling-early-soft-grunt-01.action: In the early season, call very little. Carry one call, a simple buck grunt, and use only a soft grunt or two or three on a buck you can see (Sturgis: about 50 to 60 yards; a buck won't come 150 yards out of his way for it). Kenyon: when you see bucks hanging out nearby but not coming your way (bachelor groups breaking up), a soft contact grunt or a little sparring tickle can draw them over; it works best when you're tucked in timber where they can't see the source, not on an open field edge.
m-calling-early-soft-grunt-01.why: Early-season bucks are social, sparring and sorting out the pecking order, so a low contact grunt ('there's a couple more of us over here') sparks curiosity and is very low impact if you don't overdo it. In high-pressure states deer get educated to calling fast, the same way turkeys do, so heavy early calling does more harm than good.

m-calling-ground-noise-01.action: Add realism to your calls: while grunting or rattling, scrape the ground, stomp, break branches, crash in the leaves, and shake saplings like a buck rubbing. From a treestand, tie your pull-up rope to a branch or to rattling antlers on the ground and move it around.
m-calling-ground-noise-01.why: A real rutting buck isn't silent except for grunts; he's moving, snapping branches, rubbing, scraping. It's been amazing how much ground noise adds to a calling sequence.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-calling-grunt-circle-back-01.action: If you grunt at a traveling buck and he walks on without looking, stay ready for the next 15 to 30 minutes. He may circle back to check you out for about 5 minutes before returning to his route.
m-calling-grunt-circle-back-01.why: A buck on his morning route with his nose low often ignores the call at first. Derek Dixon says rattling often brings one straight in instead.

m-calling-grunt-passing-buck-01.action: Carry a grunt call every sit, all season, where you can grab it without moving much (Sturgis keeps it in a hand-warmer tube at his waist belt). Use it on a buck you can see that is passing out of bow range, going the wrong way, or that walked under you without giving a shot, once he's gone past: give him a couple of soft grunts to stop or turn him (his example, a mature buck at 60 yards). Once he looks your way, stop calling and wait; only grunt again if he starts walking slowly away. Don't grunt at deer you can't see.
m-calling-grunt-passing-buck-01.why: It's very low impact, so you have nothing to lose on a buck that's leaving, and a searching buck will often turn around to a grunt. A grunt only carries about 50 to 80 yards in quiet conditions. Deer live by their ears and can pinpoint a sound within a few feet, so after he's heard you, more calling only raises suspicion; he grunted in a 170-plus-inch rut buck that came partway, called again while it stood deciding, and it walked off.

m-calling-inflection-01.action: Use tone and inflection on doe and fawn calls on purpose (rising versus falling, soft versus loud). Match the emotion you want to send, and watch the deer's reaction.
m-calling-inflection-01.why: The same call inflected differently means different things, like the way you say something to a person changes how they take it. Tone creates emotion, and that's what the deer responds to.

m-calling-no-blind-calling-01.action: Call only at a buck whose location you know: one you can see, or bucks you can hear sparring and grunting nearby. Don't call blindly into empty woods. On pressured public ground or where mature bucks are scarce, don't go out and bang rattling antlers hoping something comes; carry a rattle bag but use it very sparingly.
m-calling-no-blind-calling-01.why: Kenyon: nine times out of ten or more, blind calling just makes noise and spooks deer; on public land in early November a grunt call or antlers can do a lot of damage, and calling success is low for most hunters even in Iowa during the rut. Sturgis: knowing where the buck is also lowers the chance he gets downwind of you.

m-calling-rattle-downwind-blocked-01.action: Rattle only from a stand whose downwind side is blocked by something deer won't cross in daylight: a cliff or bluff, a swamp, an open creek, a lake or pond, an open horse pasture, open hardwoods, a field edge, or houses and a road. Don't have thick brush downwind of you. Rattle only where few hunters are around (Texas brush country, big wilderness, or the middle of large public tracts), and don't blind call every 20 to 30 minutes hoping something hears it.
m-calling-rattle-downwind-blocked-01.why: Almost every buck, shy or not, circles downwind of a call or antlers before he comes in. If he can get downwind, he smells you and your spot is ruined before the hunt starts; thick brush downwind gives him cover to do it. In the Michigan U.P. Sturgis heard one come from upwind, loop all the way downwind, blow, and run without ever being seen. Where hunter numbers are high, even young bucks quickly learn rattling means a hunter, and it tends to bring younger bucks, not the older age class.

m-calling-rattle-hard-cruiser-01.action: If you spot a cruising buck too far to hear your grunts and the leaves are too crunchy to sneak closer, rattle hard with lots of realistic noise instead of trying to move on him. Have your bow in your hand and ready before you start.
m-calling-rattle-hard-cruiser-01.why: In 2020, high on a ridge, loud realistic rattling brought a cruising buck straight in to about 5 yards. With the bow left behind him he never got a shot. Normally he'd move toward the deer, but crunchy leaves would have spooked it.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-calling-rattle-peak-to-post-rut-01.action: Save rattling for the peak rut through the post-rut and second rut. Before that, at most a little light tickling in mid-October leading into the pre-rut, which rarely brings deer in.
m-calling-rattle-peak-to-post-rut-01.why: In the pre-rut and early rut, does are coming into heat and every buck can find one, so why pick a fight? Late in the rut and after it, does are harder to find and big bucks keep moving and searching, so a fight sounds worth checking out.

m-calling-rattle-subtle-01.action: Rattle with a light tickling sequence like two bucks sparring, not a loud aggressive clash, then hang up the antlers and pick up a grunt call. Save loud, crashing fake fights for top-tier ground with lots of mature bucks, like an Iowa or Kansas tag (Kenyon). Sturgis's trick: tie the antlers to your bow rope, lower them to the base of the tree away from the metal stand, and scuff them in the dirt, leaves, and brush so it sounds like two bucks sparring on the ground.
m-calling-rattle-subtle-01.why: Real sparring is back-and-forth tickling, not rams butting heads. A mature buck often got old by avoiding fights, so aggressive rattling tends to send him away. A big fight is believable only where it could actually happen; on average ground (Kenyon's example, a South Carolina hunter) a loud fight mostly spooks deer. The ground scuffing places the sound where real bucks would be.

m-calling-read-first-reaction-01.action: Watch the buck closely the moment your first call reaches him. If his head snaps up and he gets nervous and jittery, stop calling. If he looks calm and curious, or stops to rake, rub, or scrape, he's callable, so keep working him.
m-calling-read-first-reaction-01.why: In the first 5 seconds he'll usually tell you whether he's callable. Hunters panic and push a buck that already said no.

m-calling-snort-wheeze-distant-01.action: Use a snort-wheeze only as a last resort on a mature buck far away that won't come to anything else, such as bucks you can see already fighting, grunting, and snort-wheezing out in a field.
m-calling-snort-wheeze-distant-01.why: It's an aggressive warning from one buck to another ('I'm the biggest, baddest buck here'), and mature bucks usually got old by being shy and avoiding fights, so they tuck their tail and leave. Used randomly it spooks far more bucks than it attracts. Once, in late October, snort-wheezing back at two bucks fighting 200 yards away pulled in a different buck from about 100 yards off to the side, but he came so slowly, rubbing and scraping, that he arrived after dark; Sturgis shot him the next morning.

m-calling-snort-wheeze-hung-up-01.action: If a buck heard you and is showing semi-positive signs but won't commit (makes a rub or scrape, puffs up, lingers hung up, or parallels you), try a snort-wheeze as the last move. Do it by mouth as loud as you can with a cupped hand, or with a call that has a funnel piece.
m-calling-snort-wheeze-hung-up-01.why: The snort-wheeze is a challenge, 'come and fight'. It's the most aggressive move you have: he either comes in or leaves.

m-calling-start-soft-01.action: Start soft. Call at a deer's natural volume, which is much quieter than most hunters think (a fawn bleat is so quiet you can barely hear it at 5 yards; use the least air you can). For a buck out of range, open with the lowest-risk call, a light contact grunt, and look for any sign he heard it (a pause, a stop, an ear turned your way). Only if he clearly didn't hear it, go louder and more aggressive (like a buck roar); once he notices, stop and watch what he does. If a buck is already within calling range (Kenyon's example, about 70 yards), don't open with rattling antlers.
m-calling-start-soft-01.why: Over-calling with volume is the most common mistake: it's like shouting 'HEY' at a stranger while staring at them, and deer freak out instead of answering. If a deer looks at your call and then fades off, you were probably too loud. Sometimes the problem really is just volume, so escalating only as needed keeps you from scaring off a buck the soft call would have worked on. Smashing antlers with a buck that close is 'a way to get a deer out of town'.

m-calling-stop-once-he-responds-01.action: Don't call to a deer that's already coming your way. Once a buck responds (stops, snaps his head toward your call and looks your way, or turns and starts toward you), put the call away, don't call again, and slowly get ready for the shot. Save calls for deer that are going to skirt your setup out of range or are walking away.
m-calling-stop-once-he-responds-01.why: He already knows exactly where the sound came from. A called deer comes in looking right at your spot, which makes the shot harder, and extra calls only draw more attention there. Calling again while he's staring (especially a bad note, too hard or too soft) tells him something is wrong; if he hears an odd deer-ish sound and 20 seconds later smells a human, he learns a negative association that hurts future hunts there. A deer walking away has a harder time pinpointing where the call came from.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-calling-tarsal-jar-01.action: When you or a buddy kill a buck, cut the tarsal glands from the inside of the hind legs, seal them in a glass jar, and freeze them to use as scent next season instead of store-bought scent.
m-calling-tarsal-jar-01.why: It's scent from a local deer, matching your area, and it's free.

m-gear-bow-ready-first-01.action: At the top, hang the bow hanger first (his usual spot is his left side, or a limb right in front if there is one), pull the bow up, and nock an arrow before you finish settling in. Hang the pack on a hook out of the way of your draw, with the grunt call and rattling antlers within reach.
m-gear-bow-ready-first-01.why: A deer can come by while you're still setting up, so be ready to shoot as early as possible.

m-gear-bubble-level-01.action: Put a bubble level on your bow sight and make a centered bubble part of every sight picture, on the range and on a deer.
m-gear-bubble-level-01.why: It's how you catch a canted bow before the shot.

m-gear-cover-hands-face-01.action: Cover your skin: when bowhunting, wear gloves and a face mask or headnet (or face paint), even in the early season; put them on once you're settled. A natural beard helps too. With a rifle or muzzleloader you can skip the headnet but still wear gloves.
m-gear-cover-hands-face-01.why: Deer pick out light, bare skin easily; Sturgis wants his white hands covered. With a gun, deer are usually 100+ yards out and much less likely to spot your face, but your hands still move to raise the gun.

m-gear-dim-light-not-colored-01.action: Carry a small rechargeable flashlight with a very dim low mode (a 'moonbeam' setting) for getting in and out, and don't count on a red or green lens to hide it: treat any colored light as fully visible to deer.
m-gear-dim-light-not-colored-01.why: A very low light barely spooks anything. Colorblind or not, deer still see the light itself; putting a red lens over the sun doesn't stop it burning your eyes.

m-gear-draw-weight-you-can-hold-01.action: Don't overdo draw weight. Pick a weight you can hold at full draw for about two minutes; 50 to 55 lb is enough for a pass-through at 30 to 40 yards.
m-gear-draw-weight-you-can-hold-01.why: On the ground you may have to hold while a deer clears a tree. What matters is holding steady, not raw weight.

m-gear-dress-warm-cold-01.action: For extreme cold, layer up with windproof outer layers, heavy merino base layers, a face mask, a knit cap, a hand-warmer muff, and battery-heated socks and vest. Buy good warm clothes once; they last decades.
m-gear-dress-warm-cold-01.why: When it's cold there's no substitute for being warm. You enjoy the hunt and stay on stand instead of shivering the whole time.

m-gear-dry-clothes-at-tree-01.action: On a long walk in, wear one thin shirt and pack your layers. At the base of the tree, change into dry clothes and dry socks and seal the sweaty ones in a zip bag or garbage bag in your pack.
m-gear-dry-clothes-at-tree-01.why: It's worth the extra 10 minutes: getting damp or wet clothes off keeps you much warmer on stand.

m-gear-front-weighted-arrow-01.action: Build a 425-475 grain arrow with the weight up front (his is 450 grains total with a 75-grain outsert plus a 125-grain fixed-blade broadhead, 200 grains up front) rather than a 600-700 grain heavy arrow. Only a long-draw shooter needs to go near 500. Use a simple cut-on-contact fixed blade.
m-gear-front-weighted-arrow-01.why: Front weight flies straight like a throwing dart and drives penetration; his broke through a buck's shoulder blade and heart quartering-to at 35 yards. Very heavy arrows drop so much between 20 and 30 yards that a range misjudgment can miss, while a 280-290 fps arrow makes that error insignificant. Fixed blades have no mechanism to fail.

m-gear-go-light-01.action: Go in light. For a stand you can walk or bike to, skip the big backpack: a hand-warmer muff or small pouch (or a very small pack) holds the essentials: gloves and a face mask, grunt tube, phone, rangefinder, binoculars, a spare release, a small flashlight, spare batteries in your pockets, maybe a meal bar. Drink plenty of water at the truck instead of carrying it. Leave the calls and gadgets you don't need at home.
m-gear-go-light-01.why: Everything you carry is a chance for noise, something to drop out of the tree, one more thing to forget, and more setup time in the stand. Less gear also removes the temptation to use products at the wrong time and place. After about 41 years of hunting, he brings less every year.

m-gear-grunt-breath-control-01.action: To control a grunt call, close your upper lip over the top half of the mouthpiece, rest the bottom on your lower lip, and breathe into it from your diaphragm without puffing your cheeks. Raise volume with more air pressure and by opening the chamber; practice fawn, doe, and buck volumes before the season.
m-gear-grunt-breath-control-01.why: It takes very little air to make the reed vibrate. Controlling air flow with your breathing, not your mouth, is the first step to sounding real. The buck setting gets loud with less air than the doe; too much pressure while choking the call locks the reed up.

m-gear-hang-on-all-day-comfort-01.action: For all-day sits (Kenyon's example: an 11 to 12 hour rut sit at a funnel or pinch point), a lightweight hang-on stand with a seat is usually more comfortable than a saddle; bring the seat pad. Take the saddle for a half-day strike. On a long sit in either, keep changing position (knees to the tree, lean, stand, lean back) so the pressure doesn't sit in one place.
m-gear-hang-on-all-day-comfort-01.why: Sitting on a seat is natural, the platform is bigger, and you can hang your pack and eat. The Hunting Public also noticed they moved around less in a stand, since in a saddle your weight hangs and it's easy to shift around. Neither is truly comfortable for 12 hours.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-gear-hang-on-in-cold-01.action: In cold weather, or if you'll own only one setup for the whole season in a cold climate, use a hang-on stand rather than a saddle.
m-gear-hang-on-in-cold-01.why: Big bulky clothes and boots are hard to use in a saddle, on its small platform or ring of steps, 20 to 25 feet up in the wind. Sitting with your back to the tree is warmer and makes it much easier to stay still for a long time; a saddle's discomfort makes you shift and lean, and that extra movement can get you seen. (Try it: sit still 5 minutes, then stand still 5 minutes.)

m-gear-hang-weapon-on-hook-01.action: Screw a gear hook or bow hanger into the tree (North American Whitetail puts it slightly above your head) and hang your bow or gun, and your backpack, there while you wait instead of holding them on your lap.
m-gear-hang-weapon-on-hook-01.why: Everything stays within reach and off your lap until a deer shows up. Downwind Hunting adds that body heat warms a stock or riser held on your lap, and lifting a warm weapon to shoot releases scent toward the deer; hanging keeps it at air temperature.

m-gear-harness-under-jacket-01.action: Bowhunters can wear a light jacket or shirt over the harness vest so the vest doesn't catch the bowstring on the draw, but make sure the tether attachment point stays easy to reach.
m-gear-harness-under-jacket-01.why: It keeps the harness out of the string's path and lets you layer more clothes than fit under the vest.

m-gear-hydrate-before-01.action: For a hot 4 to 5 hour evening sit, drink up on water before you walk in rather than carrying it. For an all-day sit, bring a small bottle of water plus high-calorie food (meal bars, a sandwich, a gel pack if you need one).
m-gear-hydrate-before-01.why: He has sat 5 to 6 hours in 100 F heat in Kentucky without carrying water this way. Less to carry means less noise; on all-day sits you need calories to stay alert.

m-gear-know-and-practice-your-setup-01.action: Pick the setup you know and trust (saddle or stand) and get very good with it rather than switching because of TV, YouTube, or marketing. Practice with your actual mobile setup before the season: hang the saddle or stand at home (one MeatEater host tethers to a back-patio beam), shoot the odd angles you'll get in the tree, and rehearse the whole setup until you can do it quietly in the dark. Relentless Sportsman: having both is ideal; if you can own only one, he recommends a hang-on stand.
m-gear-know-and-practice-your-setup-01.why: Confidence in your system is the difference maker; it's your brain, not the gear, that does the work. Otherwise opening night or the first day of your rut vacation means clanking around in the dark, sweating, while the sun comes up and here comes the buck.

m-gear-know-your-height-01.action: Know exactly how high you are. Use a pull-up rope of known length (his is 21 feet from the carabiner to the loop) to read your height in the tree, and learn the max height your stick setup reaches (his is 17 feet) so you can judge from the ground whether a tree's cover is reachable.
m-gear-know-your-height-01.why: Then you pick trees and heights on purpose instead of guessing. He marks his reach on the trunk and counts up from it to estimate heights.

m-gear-licking-branch-material-01.action: For a mock scrape, use a natural licking branch about 3/4 to 1 inch thick: a hanging vine (his favorite; one can last up to 7 years), white or red oak, jack pine up north, hemlock, beech, ironwood, or muscle wood, or whatever branch deer use locally. Make it long, reaching 5 to 6 feet (up to 8 to 10) to where it's tied, and hang it with paracord wrapped around a branch so it swings free. If no branch hangs over the spot, tie paracord across between trees and hang the branch from it on about 4 to 5 inches of cord. Avoid sappy branches, brittle soft woods, and a short 2-foot stick dangling from a rope.
m-gear-licking-branch-material-01.why: Natural material gets hit far more often than rope, and the most consistent natural scrapes he sees on 1,000+ properties hang from vines. Much over an inch looks like a trunk and deer won't play with it; under 3/4 inch breaks too easily. A short stick on a long rope looks unnatural and gets ignored. The free-swinging pivot keeps bucks from breaking it at the top the way they can when it's tied stiff.

m-gear-light-quiet-mobile-kit-01.action: Keep a mobile kit light and quiet. Mark Kenyon keeps a mobile hang-on stand itself under 10 pounds (many 'mobile' stands are 18 to 20 pounds, too much once you add sticks). The Hunting Public switched from a 20+ pound hang-on and sticks to a tethered saddle and light sticks under 10 pounds for the full setup, and stealth-strip everything so no metal clanks.
m-gear-light-quiet-mobile-kit-01.why: The heavier the kit, the less willing you are to move when a tree isn't right, and bigger stands make more noise carrying and setting up; even 8 versus 16 pounds is a big deal. When you set up close to a bedded buck, sometimes within 80 yards, clanking metal ruins it; they've had bucks stand up right in front of them after a quiet setup. Light gear also makes it easier to go deep on public land where the bedding is.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-gear-no-big-pack-in-tree-01.action: Don't hang a big backpack in the tree with you.
m-gear-no-big-pack-in-tree-01.why: A big pack in the tree can look like another person up there.

m-gear-one-trip-climb-rig-01.action: Rig everything on the ground so you climb once. Pull the straps off the stand and let them hang free, use a light stand, and put your harness on before you reach the tree. Carry the top sticks in your harness loops (Bow Only Outdoors hangs the top two sticks in 7-inch loops, one on each side, with the stand bracket strapped to the harness), or pull the stand up on your safety line. Clip two haul ropes (one for the stand, one for the bow) to the harness and put the stand and bow on opposite sides of the tree, away from limbs, so the ropes don't tangle. Keep pruners in a pocket.
m-gear-one-trip-climb-rig-01.why: Straps wrapped around the post and gear lashed to the stand mean untangling everything up in the tree with more movement and noise, and climbing down for more gear is another trip. With everything in reach you don't dig in the pack, and you can clip limbs on the way up. Light stands are much easier to handle up there. There's a lot hanging off you, so watch for tangles.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-gear-pack-low-out-of-shot-01.action: Once you're at height and don't need the lineman's rope, cinch it around the tree and use it as a hanger to hold your backpack low, on either side, out of the way of your shot.
m-gear-pack-low-out-of-shot-01.why: It keeps the pack off your hips and out of your shooting window without carrying a separate hook.
people: Deer and Deer Hunting (saddle product demo)

m-gear-pack-quiet-01.action: Pack your setup so nothing flops or clanks: slide the saddle platform into a pack with the climbing sticks cinched tight on the back, or strap the sticks to a hang-on stand with its own tree straps and carry it on backpack straps with a waist belt.
m-gear-pack-quiet-01.why: Before they had a proper pack, gear hung off their shoulders and flopped around. Cinched tight, it's compact, quiet, and the waist belt takes weight off your shoulders.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-gear-paracord-not-cable-01.action: Hang mock scrapes with paracord (camo if you can get it), never steel cable or anything else a deer can't break.
m-gear-paracord-not-cable-01.why: He's seen a buck rip down a steel cable strung with a row of scrapes, get it wound around his head and neck, and die. Paracord has little scent and deer don't seem to notice it.

m-gear-quiet-clothes-no-clang-01.action: Wear quiet clothing that won't rustle when you draw, and check your safety harness and stand for anything that can clang against the stand (ladder, tripod, or lock-on).
m-gear-quiet-clothes-no-clang-01.why: In bowhunting you have to move to draw, and loud, rustly clothes or a clanging harness give you away.

m-gear-red-green-headlamp-01.action: Use a red or green filter on your headlamp instead of white light when walking in.
m-gear-red-green-headlamp-01.why: It says white light floods the rods in a deer's eye and can be seen very far off, while red or green light is far less visible to deer and keeps your own night vision.

m-gear-rubber-boots-01.action: Wear rubber knee boots instead of leather hunting boots.
m-gear-rubber-boots-01.why: It says rubber doesn't absorb odor from your truck, house, or gas station, hoses clean, and leaves almost no ground scent, and that Southeastern deer trackers have worn them for decades.

m-gear-saddle-add-ons-order-01.action: Add saddle extras in this order: a dump pouch on your hip that always holds your lineman's belt and tether; an auto-retracting bow hoist; knee pads (put them on at the truck); aiders (extra foot loops) on your sticks; saddle suspenders; then small modifications like stealth-stripping your sticks.
m-gear-saddle-add-ons-order-01.why: The pouch means your ropes are always with you. A retracting hoist keeps the line from blowing around and snagging on sticks and branches. Knee pads let you sit with your knees against the tree and rest your legs, alternating with standing, on long sits. Aiders let four sticks climb higher without extra weight, for getting above a branch for shooting lanes, visibility, or where the cover is. Suspenders keep the weight of sticks and platform from dragging the saddle down.

m-gear-saddle-all-day-comfort-01.action: If a saddle hurts your hips or backside, adjust the tether and bridge until it fits your body instead of giving up on it. Once dialed, all-day sits are doable.
m-gear-saddle-all-day-comfort-01.why: He does several all-day saddle sits every season and doesn't find it less comfortable than a stand. His father, older and in heavy cold-weather layers, hunts from one too.

m-gear-saddle-for-mobile-quiet-01.action: Choose a tree saddle with light sticks and a small (or no) platform when you hunt public land, move often, want to move in real time to where you're seeing deer, or need a quiet walk in and a quiet climb. It is lighter and more packable, faster to hang and to pull down (so you can climb down and go after a buck you spot from the tree), and one kit hunts almost any tree. Stick with hung stands or ladders if you want casual hunting from the same stand every time.
m-gear-saddle-for-mobile-quiet-01.why: You carry a harness either way, so a saddle only adds a small platform that fits in a pack with the sticks on the back. There's no big metal stand to catch branches or bang against the sticks, the tree, your saw, or your quiver. The Hunting Public spotted a buck from the tree, climbed down, and killed him on the ground.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-gear-saddle-platform-height-01.action: Set the saddle platform about 10 to 18 inches above your top climbing stick, so you can step onto the top stick and then onto the platform. Hang a gear strap above your tether (so the tether can still move down) with a sturdy metal bow hanger for your bow and quiver, and hang your pack off it or off the lineman's carabiner.
m-gear-saddle-platform-height-01.why: Too high and you can't step up onto it safely. Keeping the bow on a hanger right beside you means minimal movement when a deer comes.

m-gear-saddle-starter-kit-01.action: To start saddle hunting, buy only the must-haves: the saddle (a climbing-style harness), a way up the tree (lightweight climbing sticks; four sticks got him 20 to 25 feet up in one video, 15 to 20 feet in another), a small platform to stand on, a backpack to carry it all, a metal bow hanger on a gear strap, and a bow rope (plain paracord works). Add the rest of the system (knee pads and other extras) over time as you learn.
m-gear-saddle-starter-kit-01.why: A saddle lets you stay mobile, hunt almost any tree, and be quieter than with a big metal tree stand; he switched because rotating through the same preset stands and ladders kept giving him the same results. You don't need every gadget to start. He trusts a metal bow hanger over plastic or 3D-printed ones because a bow falling 20 feet can end your season.

m-gear-short-gun-tight-woods-01.action: In tight woods where 40 yards is your longest shot, a short, handy gun (a rifled-slug 20 gauge, a .45-70, or any 16 to 20 inch barrel) is a fine choice. Keep it ready: have a system for getting on the gun fast.
m-gear-short-gun-tight-woods-01.why: In thick cover, especially in the rut when you can't hear deer coming, a deer pops in at 25 to 30 yards and is gone before you can move. A long 28-inch barrel is hard to carry and swing through cover.

m-gear-spare-release-01.action: Keep a spare release clipped in your pouch.
m-gear-spare-release-01.why: If you drop yours out of the tree or it stops working, the sit isn't over.

m-gear-stick-spacing-platform-plan-01.action: Hang each climbing stick about knee height above the last one and push it down with your weight to seat it before stepping on it. Decide where the platform goes before you climb, and put the top stick just to the side (he uses the left) of the platform so you step straight into the stand.
m-gear-stick-spacing-platform-plan-01.why: Knee-height steps are comfortable and the teeth grip once weighted. Planning the platform spot keeps you from swinging your legs around the tree 'like a monkey' in awkward positions.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-gear-uv-brighteners-01.action: Check every piece of hunting gear under a black light in a dark room. Anything that glows (UV brighteners) stays out of the woods. Don't wash hunting clothes in regular detergent; common blue liquid detergents carry brighteners that you can't wash back out.
m-gear-uv-brighteners-01.why: A feeding doe at 30 yards snapped her head up at Eddie McRae the moment he swatted a mosquito, even though he sat 20 feet up, deep in shadow, with heavy front and back cover and full camo. Under a black light, only his gloves glowed, 'like a black light poster'.

m-recovery-float-ungutted-01.action: If you'll float a deer out down a creek, don't field dress it first.
m-recovery-float-ungutted-01.why: An ungutted deer floats like a cork and can even pull a gutted one through deeper water; the gutted one had to be dragged through the shallows.

m-recovery-gut-shot-alive-01.action: Don't assume a gut-shot deer is dead after the usual 6 to 8 hour wait. Expect it may still be alive, bedded in thick cover hundreds of yards away, and check nearby water; it may get up to drink.
m-recovery-gut-shot-alive-01.why: A crossbow gut-shot buck Derek found by drone about 10 hours after the shot was alive, bedded 600 yards away, and later walked 200 yards to a creek to drink. Coyotes found it (likely off its trail, not downwind), tested it with bluff charges, and it died in the creek overnight.

m-recovery-level-shot-bearing-01.action: After a level shot from the ground, watch exactly where the deer runs, set a compass bearing to the last spot you saw it (turn the rotating dial to that direction), and follow the bearing even if you find no blood at first. It can take up to 100 yards before blood starts.
m-recovery-level-shot-bearing-01.why: From a tree the exit hole is low, so blood comes out quickly. On a level shot the chest has to fill up to the exit hole before blood leaves, so the start of the trail is sparse; once it reaches the holes, blood is everywhere.

m-recovery-marginal-hit-wait-01.action: If the hit looks marginal (only one lung, a shoulder-blade hit with shallow penetration, a steep top-down shot that passed low through one lung, or any hit you are unsure of), back out and give the deer a long time before you track it. Going in after about 5 hours often bumps a live deer. When the trail runs out, search the first thick cover or bedding area about 200-300 yards from the shot.
m-recovery-marginal-hit-wait-01.why: A single-lung deer can live more than 20 hours (Dixon has seen it; one single-lung deer he shot was killed by a rifle hunter three weeks later, and Beau's shoulder-blade, one-lung buck is still alive years later). A marginally hit deer left alone usually goes 200-300 yards into the nearest thick bedding cover and dies there (Sturgis). A pushed deer runs a couple hundred yards more (Dixon) or half to three quarters of a mile in big open woods (Sturgis) and is often never found, even with dogs.

m-recovery-plan-the-extraction-01.action: Before you sit, know how you'll get a deer out. From a steep bottom (his example: 250 to 300 feet of climb in about 250 yards), plan a vehicle ride instead of a drag. On long walk-ins (his Pennsylvania hunts, 1.5 hours in) bring a frame pack and plan to bone the deer out and pack it.
m-recovery-plan-the-extraction-01.why: Dragging a deer up a steep climb is brutal; a far-back hunt needs the gear to carry the meat out on your back.

m-recovery-same-night-with-help-01.action: If you saw the deer go down or stagger nearly out of sight, go back that night with help rather than leaving it until morning. Back out first and get people (he left his bow and stand at the tree). When the blood runs out, spread the group to circle and check the gap or funnel you think it was heading for.
m-recovery-same-night-with-help-01.why: He'd heard of a deer left overnight that got chewed up by scavengers. With five people circling, they found his buck near the gap he'd guessed.

m-safety-cam-stand-tight-01.action: After strapping the stand on, fold the platform up to take the weight off the straps, cinch the straps tighter, then fold it back down before you step on. This works for any stand that uses cinch straps.
m-safety-cam-stand-tight-01.why: Camming it over like that locks the stand tight to the tree so it won't slip when you put your weight on it.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-safety-climber-step-in-low-01.action: Set the climber at the base where you can step into it right off the ground (the uphill side of the tree on a slope makes this easier), and keep the top and bottom sections connected to each other the whole time you climb.
m-safety-climber-step-in-low-01.why: Stepping in is the only moment you aren't tethered, so do it as close to the ground as possible. If the top and bottom aren't connected and the bottom slips off your feet, it falls all the way to the ground and leaves you hanging.

m-safety-compass-big-woods-01.action: In big woods, carry a compass (he wears one around his neck) and learn to read a topo map: match a point or ridge you see to the map, take a heading, and walk it. Don't rely only on your phone or GPS.
m-safety-compass-big-woods-01.why: Phones and GPS units die or lose battery, and in big timber with lots of elevation change you need a way out that doesn't depend on them.

m-safety-drone-laws-01.action: Don't use a drone to scout or hunt deer on public land. Check your state's laws first; many ban it for hunting, and some require a permit to fly any drone on public land.
m-safety-drone-laws-01.why: Derek Dixon says it is illegal in his home state and banned on most public land, and you're likely to get caught and be in real trouble.

m-safety-haul-gear-with-pull-rope-01.action: Don't climb with a heavy pack or your weapon. Tie a pull rope to the stand and raise them after you're strapped in: firearm unloaded, bow with the arrow stored in the quiver. Put the rope on the side of the stand away from the climbing sticks, clear of the ladder and limbs, and attach it up high where your hand can reach it. Tie the bow on with a simple knot (to the cam, with the string clear) instead of trusting the rope's clip, and once the bow is up, drop the rope away from your feet.
m-safety-haul-gear-with-pull-rope-01.why: Your hands and balance stay free for climbing, and the gear doesn't snag on the sticks or limbs on the way up. A rope clipped low makes you lean way out over the stand to grab it. Clips can fail; the Kentucky Afield host has had a bow come loose and fall to the ground. A loose rope can tangle your feet or your bow when you draw.

m-safety-inspect-straps-01.action: Before the season and before you climb, test the seat and check every strap and cable on the stand. If a cable shows rust, buy a replacement; many parts now carry an expiration date.
m-safety-inspect-straps-01.why: Straps and cables are what hold you up; worn or rusted parts fail.

m-safety-lifeline-01.action: Use a lifeline on every stand: a strong industrial rope tied at the base of the tree and at your hunting height. Clip into it on the ground, slide it up as you climb the ladder or sticks, then sit and hunt without ever switching straps, and stay clipped until you're back down. Put one on for your kids and hunting partners too.
m-safety-lifeline-01.why: You stay connected from the ground to the seat and back, with no strap changeover at all. Jeff Sturgis started using them when his boys began hunting and wishes he'd protected himself sooner; he still sees experienced bowhunters' properties with no lifelines.

m-safety-pick-healthy-tree-01.action: Pick a climbing tree that is alive and healthy (full leaves, no dead branches), with firmly attached bark, and sized so your straps go around it (not too big) but not so small it's unsafe. Don't climb shaggy-bark hickory, sycamore, or any tree whose bark peels off in sheets.
m-safety-pick-healthy-tree-01.why: A climber may only bite about 1/8 inch into the tree. If that bark slides off, you go with it.

m-safety-platform-push-01.action: In a saddle, attach the tether at about chin height; you can push off the edges of a saddle platform (the grooves grip your boot) to swing around the tree for a shot. On a hang-on stand, stand flat and don't push hard on the platform's edges.
m-safety-platform-push-01.why: A saddle platform is built for being pushed on from the side, which is how you shoot around the tree. A hang-on platform pushed too far on one side can kick out from under you.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-safety-practice-at-home-low-01.action: Whatever you buy, practice setting it up and climbing in it in your yard, low to the ground, before the season. Don't let your first real climb be a hunt.
m-safety-practice-at-home-low-01.why: You don't need to be 15 or 20 feet up to learn it, and you'll be much smoother and safer when it counts. The Hunting Public host's first time in a saddle was nerve-wracking and he didn't know what he was doing; hang-on stands were the same when he started as a teenager. Once your system is down, either one gets very efficient.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-safety-stand-offset-step-down-01.action: Hang the stand about 90 degrees around the trunk from the side your ladder or sticks go up (anywhere from about 70 to 120 degrees is fine), and run the top of the sticks 1 to 2 feet above the platform so you step DOWN onto it. Never put the stand on the opposite side of the tree and higher than the sticks.
m-safety-stand-offset-step-down-01.why: You can climb up and just step over without stretching. The opposite-and-higher setup makes you stretch a leg around the trunk and push up to reach the platform, which is a bad, unsafe setup.

m-safety-stay-connected-ground-to-ground.action: Always wear a safety harness in a tree, every sit, no exceptions, and stay connected to the tree from the moment you leave the ground, while you hunt, and all the way back down. Never free-climb. Put your lineman's belt or rope around the tree before the first step, clipped to the harness at the waist, and slide it up as you climb so it stays above your waist; lean your weight back into it so both hands are free while you hang sticks and the stand. Use a lineman's rope at least as long as your stick ropes so it fits any tree the sticks do, and carry a second rope to clip above a limb before unclipping the lower one (leapfrogging past limbs). The saddle demo stays on two points while climbing (lineman's rope plus tether). With a climbing stand, tether before you start up: strap around the trunk, a screw-lock carabiner with the gate screwed shut, strap loose enough to slide up with you; set your feet, press down to lock the platform, then lock the seat as you go.
m-safety-stay-connected-ground-to-ground.why: Every year hunters die, break legs, or are paralyzed falling from tree stands, and nearly all of those falls are preventable with a harness; harnesses are cheap and sold everywhere, so there's no excuse. Staying on the lineman's rope means that if a stick kicks out or you slip, you're covered, and there's never a moment when nothing holds you to the tree. A carabiner that pops open is the same as no tether. The old way, one arm hugging the tree while holding the stand up with your chin, is neither smart nor safe.
people: Deer and Deer Hunting (saddle product demo)
The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-safety-tether-before-unclipping-01.action: At the top, attach your tether to the tree (a second rope or strap at about head or eye height) BEFORE you step from the sticks onto the platform, and only then take off the lineman's belt, so you're double connected during the step. Never unclip the lineman's belt until the tether is firmly attached. Coming down, do it in reverse: clip into the lower rope before you unhook the top tether. Next Step Outdoors also sets the bottom stick at about knee height, keeps every stick and platform strap parallel to the ground so it locks in when weighted, and sets the platform while standing on the second-to-last step.
m-safety-tether-before-unclipping-01.why: The changeover between the two straps is the moment you'd otherwise have nothing holding you; switching before you move means there's never a moment you aren't clipped to the tree. The Hunting Public host almost forgot the second tether himself. A level strap bites the tree and handles side pressure.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-safety-tether-high-01.action: Once the stand is up and locked in firmly (top and bottom, before you stand or move), hunt on a tree tether tied around the trunk and cinched tight at about head height, or eye level or higher, clipped to your harness's back strap. Don't hunt on the lineman's rope at your waist.
m-safety-tether-high-01.why: If you fall with the tether high and tight, you only drop a couple feet and it catches you where you can climb straight back into the stand; with it low, you can end up hanging too far below the stand to get back in. A high tether also keeps the rope clear of your bow arm so you can draw and shoot any direction.

m-scent-baking-soda-boots-tote-01.action: Put baking soda anywhere odor builds up: in the footbeds of your boots and in the corner of the box or tote where you store your hunting clothes.
m-scent-baking-soda-boots-tote-01.why: Same reason people keep an open box in the fridge. It keeps killing odor between hunts.

m-scent-baking-soda-mouth-01.action: On a morning sit, swish baking-soda water in your mouth and spit it out to kill bad breath.
m-scent-baking-soda-mouth-01.why: Morning breath odor is a real no-no; the baking soda neutralizes it the same way it does on your clothes.

m-scent-baking-soda-on-body-01.action: Use baking soda as your field scent spray. Pat-down: after your hunting clothes are washed and dried, put them on, mist yourself well with plain water from a spray bottle, then pat yourself all over with a sock filled with baking soda (two boxes in a breathable merino or cotton sock, tied off, with a second sock over it) and rub it in until you look like a snowflake. Spray: dissolve 1 tablespoon of baking soda in a quart of water by bringing it to a boil, let it cool, and spray it on your body, hair, and clothes.
m-scent-baking-soda-on-body-01.why: Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) neutralizes odor and is the active ingredient in many scent-control soaps and field sprays, just at a lower dose; the homemade version is far stronger and cheaper. He says it beats store spray by a wide margin and makes deer think you're farther away than you are. More than about a tablespoon per quart clogs the sprayer.

m-scent-baking-soda-wash-01.action: Wash hunting clothes in plain baking soda (about half a cup per load) instead of regular laundry detergent.
m-scent-baking-soda-wash-01.why: Regular detergent has UV brighteners that make fabric glow under UV light, and deer can see UV. Baking soda leaves no scent, brighteners, or residue.

m-scent-bland-food-01.action: Pack bland, low-odor food for the stand (plain crackers, plain granola, water instead of coffee). No peanut butter, jerky, or citrus.
m-scent-bland-food-01.why: Strong-smelling food puts odor into the air around your stand for the rest of the sit.

m-scent-boot-soles-01.action: Before walking in, rub your boot soles with dirt from the property you're hunting, then give each sole two sprays of hydrogen peroxide.
m-scent-boot-soles-01.why: It says soles carry rubber, asphalt, and gas-station odors; local dirt masks them with a smell that belongs there, and peroxide breaks down what's left and evaporates clean.

m-scent-cant-fool-the-nose-01.action: Never count on scent products to let a deer stand downwind of you. If a deer seems to walk downwind without winding you, assume a thermal was actually carrying your scent another way, not that your scent control worked.
m-scent-cant-fool-the-nose-01.why: He says you really can't fool their nose; the times it looks like you did, the air was moving differently than you thought.

m-scent-clothes-kept-apart-01.action: Keep hunting clothes, including underwear, away from household and vehicle smells, and put them on only when you arrive. McRae hangs them outside (his front porch), gets dressed there, and washes them rarely, in baking soda only, otherwise just letting them air out. Diamond Archery keeps them sealed in a bag and doesn't wear them on the drive to and from the spot.
m-scent-clothes-kept-apart-01.why: Anything you carry or wear into the woods should have no foreign odor. Inside the house clothes pick up cooking and household smells; stop for gas and you can get gas on your hands or clothes.

m-scent-doe-urine-all-season-01.action: If you use one lure all season, make it plain doe urine (not estrus). It can be used from early bow season in late August or September through the pre-rut, rut, and post-rut.
m-scent-doe-urine-all-season-01.why: Deer that smell it just think other does are around. It calms them, keeps them in their routine, and keeps them from spooking and tipping off bucks.

m-scent-estrus-in-rut-only-01.action: Only use doe-in-estrus lure in its season, the rut. Do not put it out in the early season, for example in September.
m-scent-estrus-in-rut-only-01.why: A doe in heat months before the rut doesn't make sense to deer, so it reads as a warning instead of an attraction.

m-scent-field-spray-gear-01.action: When you get to the field, spray a scent-eliminating field spray over everything you carry, not just your clothes: backpack, safety harness, hat, and rubber boots.
m-scent-field-spray-gear-01.why: Gear picks up odor too, and it all goes up the tree with you.

m-scent-freeze-clothes-01.action: After each hunt, seal your outer layers in a plastic trash bag and put the bag in the freezer until the next sit.
m-scent-freeze-clothes-01.why: It says freezing kills the bacteria that cause human odor.

m-scent-licking-branch-waist-high-01.action: Hang the licking branch vertically, free-swinging, with its tip about waist (belt) high, not a horizontal branch at chest height.
m-scent-licking-branch-waist-high-01.why: At waist height every deer uses it (fawns, does, young and old bucks) and each leaves scent, so the scrape keeps getting more powerful. A horizontal branch is mostly used only by bucks and needs a tree to mount on. Hanging it too high is one of the most common mistakes they see on client properties.

m-scent-natural-cover-scent-01.action: If you use a cover scent, use a plant that already grows everywhere in your woods, not a strong novelty smell. McRae boils dog fennel into a spray and stores his next hunt's clothes in a bag packed with dog fennel; before that he boiled mulch with pine limbs.
m-scent-natural-cover-scent-01.why: A smell deer live with 24/7 (rotting mulch, pine, dog fennel) draws no attention. A strong foreign smell like a vanilla spray makes deer curious at best, like you'd look around if you smelled a skunk or smoke, and on one property used for 10+ years deer learned to bolt at it because they linked it to people or being shot at.

m-scent-no-commercial-scent-on-mock-scra.action: Don't put commercial scent (bottled scents, gels, or lures) on a mock scrape. Rough up the ground, at most use your own urine, and let the deer that use it build up their own scent on the branch. A scent-eliminating spray to cut your trail walking in is fine.
m-scent-no-commercial-scent-on-mock-scra.why: Deer leave preorbital-gland scent on the branch as a calling card; you can't smell anything on a real licking branch, yet a deer coming by can pick out all 20 that hit it that day. A strong bottled scent covers and dilutes all that real deer scent. Deer also rarely urinate in scrapes outside the rut; mostly they hit the branch and move on.

m-scent-no-scent-trail-01.action: Don't leave a scent trail going in and out. Wear rubber boots whenever you walk into deer areas (to and from your stand, scouting, checking trail cameras), and don't let your boots, pants, and legs brush the grass and vegetation on the way. Wash your boots and hunting clothes, store the clothes in sealed tubs, and use a scent-elimination spray, mainly so you don't leave scent on the grass and sticks you brush past.
m-scent-no-scent-trail-01.why: Two hunters sitting five stands on 40 acres over a weekend with dirty boots leave a 'spider web' of scent over the whole property; a mature buck hits it and leaves. Rubber boots hold your scent in so deer don't smell where you've walked; you want deer never to know you've been there.

m-scent-one-scent-per-scrape-01.action: Keep a mock scrape simple: one scent at one scrape. Don't pile several lures together in one spot.
m-scent-one-scent-per-scrape-01.why: He hung five different scrape scents side by side on an oak ridge deer were using heavily. Over two weeks the camera caught only a bear, a few young bucks, and one confirmed scrape visit, far fewer deer than he expected there. His own conclusion was that the huge amount of scent in one spot spooked them and blew up the top of that ridge.

m-scent-pants-in-boots-01.action: In the early season, wear clean knee-high boots and tuck your pant legs INTO the boots rather than over them. Also avoid rubbing your sweaty hair or skin on brush along the trail.
m-scent-pants-in-boots-01.why: Each step pumps warm, moist air out of the boot. Pants tucked in send it up; pants over the boot shoot that scent down onto the ground you're walking on.

m-scent-rope-up-01.action: After hauling up the stand, don't leave the rope dangling to the ground. Tie it up short, then pack it away.
m-scent-rope-up-01.why: A deer walking by the tree can smell a rope hanging low.

m-scent-ruck-to-sweat-less-01.action: Get in shape for the season by rucking: walk with a weighted backpack regularly (even a mile a day helps).
m-scent-ruck-to-sweat-less-01.why: It matches what hunting is, carrying a pack and stand in. When your body is used to it you sweat much less walking in, which many hunters wrongly think is just how they're built.

m-scent-scent-free-at-home-01.action: Start scent control at home: use unscented soap, shampoo, deodorant, and laundry detergent. Eddie McRae goes further and cuts scented products out of his life all year, for everyday clothes too, not just in season. Then still play the wind.
m-scent-scent-free-at-home-01.why: Skin soaks up fragrances; McRae could still smell a scented hand soap on his hands the next morning after a shower, and a deer's nose is far better. You can't be too careful with scent, and it starts with preparation at home before you ever get to the field.

m-scent-scrape-dripper-01.action: If you use a scrape scent, a dripper that keeps the scent fresh may beat a one-time pour or a scented rope.
m-scent-scrape-dripper-01.why: In his test, the only one of five scents that got scraped under after two weeks was the dripper (it claims to drip in daytime only and last 2 to 3 weeks). The rope, paste, and poured scents got nothing.

m-scent-skip-lures-01.action: Skip scent lures, attractants, and drag rags (buck bombs, powders, vanilla smoke puffs, deer urine). Don't walk extra loops to lay a scent trail, and don't walk past your stand to put out lure; get to the stand and climb straight up. Spend that money and time scouting a spot deer will travel through anyway.
m-scent-skip-lures-01.why: They might work, but a puff that lasts 20 seconds won't decide whether you see deer; relying on them is wishful thinking. Lures fool young bucks, but old bucks tend to follow your trail out of curiosity and come in on your downwind side (the way you walked in). Laying scent means more chances to bump deer and more of your own scent and noise around the stand. If you need a cover scent because deer will be downwind of you, the stand location is the mistake.

m-scent-trim-hair-01.action: Before the season, trim the hair on your forearms and the back of your neck, and cover as much skin as you can with scent-free fabric.
m-scent-trim-hair-01.why: It claims body hair traps scent and releases it slowly, and says Kansas and Iowa outfitters recommend it.

m-scent-urine-laws-01.action: Before you use any deer urine lure, check your state's (and county's) rules on natural versus synthetic urine. Where natural urine is banned, use a synthetic version.
m-scent-urine-laws-01.why: Some states and even individual counties regulate natural deer urine. Synthetic versions exist for those areas.

m-scouting-ask-why-on-a-no-01.action: When knocking on doors for permission and you get a no, politely ask why (while reading the person so you don't push too far). Then address it: explain you're after one specific old buck, not every deer, offer to take does if they want fewer deer, and offer to help with work around the place. Keep coming back; don't give up after one or two visits.
m-scouting-ask-why-on-a-no-01.why: The 'no' is often based on a misunderstanding, like a landowner who thought he was out to shoot fawns; once she heard he was targeting one mature buck she said yes. The upside-down buck spot took 6 to 8 months of repeat visits, and he was the only one who got access to that deer.

m-scouting-august-lap-01.action: Have your cameras on your fall spots by early August. Expect a buck you haven't seen all summer to pass through once in August, then vanish until he moves in during October or November.
m-scouting-august-lap-01.why: Summer ranges are small. In August bucks seem to make a one-time 'reconnaissance lap' of their fall range (checking the does, other bucks, whether the woods got logged) and don't hang around. That single photo tells you he's in the area.

m-scouting-bait-next-door-01.action: On public land in a state where baiting is legal, look at aerial imagery for feeder shadows on private fields right off the public, then walk the public side of that line looking for sign.
m-scouting-bait-next-door-01.why: Deer feeding on neighboring bait or corn will leave sign on the public nearby, which tells you where they are.

m-scouting-bed-at-edges-01.action: When looking for bedding (on the map or on the ground), look first for habitat edges and diversity, like a wood edge against an old clearcut, then for food and water close by, then for terrain features such as saddles and thermal hubs. On the ground, don't assume deer bed in the middle of a thick area: look for beds on the EDGE of cover, where the deer can see danger coming from a distance, has the wind at its back, and can escape straight back through the thick stuff. The best ones have permanent water and several food sources within 40 to 50 yards and are places people rarely go.
m-scouting-bed-at-edges-01.why: No food or water means few deer, and bucks don't always bed on the textbook point; mixed cover is the strongest clue (Dixon, from thermal-drone work). Understanding how and why deer pick beds is what turned the Hunting Public's big-buck kills around; their example is a willow patch only 10 by 15 yards at the bottom of a hole next to water, with two big beds on the end looking across the water to the far hillside.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-scouting-blown-buck-wait-01.action: If you blow out a mature buck, give it about two weeks, then go look for him in the thickest, nastiest cover nearby instead of assuming he left the property. Re-inventory him with a camera, a mock scrape, a mineral block, and a little scattered feed.
m-scouting-blown-buck-wait-01.why: After a buck watched him climb down and never came back to that spot, he set up 430 yards away in the thickest cover on the corner of the property and had the buck on camera that same night.

m-scouting-buck-bed-clues-01.action: Spend real time in a promising bedding spot (about 10 minutes in a 40 by 50 yard area) looking at individual beds, rubs, tracks, and sheds before deciding what it is. A bed with a rub right beside it may be a buck bed; lots of small tracks and several small beds on a high spot near food point to a doe family group.
m-scouting-buck-bed-clues-01.why: A quick glance misses what's there. Old hair under the leaves with small rubs nearby suggested a buck bedded there earlier in the season and left once pressure picked up or the grass got knocked down, which may make it a satellite bed rather than his main one.

m-scouting-buck-personality-01.action: Watch bachelor groups in late summer for the bully: the buck that walks up and gets bedded bucks up, or strikes at them. Expect him to be a loner through the season. Calmer bucks, even the biggest on the property, tend to keep buddies.
m-scouting-buck-personality-01.why: The aggressive ones Derek filmed last summer turned out to be the solitary, other-deer-hating bucks in season. Knowing which kind of buck you're after helps you guess how he'll act; there are few hard rules with mature bucks.

m-scouting-bump-while-scouting-01.action: On big ground (public, a big lease or club) or a short trip to new public land, don't be afraid to walk bedding areas and bump deer while scouting. Scout into the wind so they hear or see you and leave without smelling you. Note where they were bedded, where they ran, and the feeding sign coming out, then look for similar spots. A bumped mature buck usually runs a few hundred yards and is back in the area within hours, so if a good buck runs off, let him go and hunt near where he settled later. Just don't push the same bedding area over and over.
m-scouting-bump-while-scouting-01.why: It's his home range. Dixon's intentional drone bumps matched GPS-collar studies: the buck runs 200 to 300 yards, stays on edge 30 minutes to an hour, and is back within about 8 to 12 hours; once or twice doesn't seem to change anything, but walking the same bedding 7 to 10 times in 5 or 6 days will. Hunting Public: a deer bumped on October 1 probably won't be in that spot on October 30 anyway because his food and interests change; gather intel on the 1st to kill one on the 15th.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-scouting-bumped-buck-hunt-nearby-01.action: If you bump a buck (he saw or heard you, not smelled you), don't give up on him. Watch where he goes, calm down, think about the next available cover or bedding area he's headed to, and either try to intercept him there the same day or come back in the next few days and hunt the nearby bedding areas.
m-scouting-bumped-buck-hunt-nearby-01.why: A spooked buck usually runs to the next cover and calms down within an hour or two, and often doesn't go far; now you know where he lives. They've killed several this way: a rut buck called straight back in right after it spooked with a doe, a Georgia buck shot a couple of hours after bumping it hard, and a big-woods buck killed the next morning about 300 yards from where he was bumped after running 400 to 500 yards.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-scouting-camera-at-intersections-01.action: Put trail cameras where multiple trails intersect, rather than on a single trail or a bluff top.
m-scouting-camera-at-intersections-01.why: Moving one camera about 300 yards from a bluff-top trail to an intersection took it from one big buck to two (a big 10 and an 8) on the same camera.

m-scouting-camera-high-and-dim-01.action: Mount trail cameras up high and angled down, or otherwise concealed, out of the deer's line of sight (6 to 7 feet, Sturgis). Set them to low glow and the shortest flash range you need (15 to 20 feet at a mock scrape); if deer still stare at it, mount it higher or dim the IR bulbs. In a new area, start cameras on travel corridors, pinch points, and food sources or the trails leading to them, and leave a camera where it's working, adding a second one rather than moving it.
m-scouting-camera-high-and-dim-01.why: Deer and bucks stare at glowing red IR bulbs, and mature bucks learn to avoid the camera by 100 yards; a Kentucky outfitter's buck stared at a bright camera and backed off, and after dimming it the same buck worked the scrape without noticing. A quick white flash bothers them far less than bulbs that stay lit (Sturgis). Some deer bolt at a flash, others spook at an infrared camera's click, some just don't like cameras; Rex has better luck with cameras concealed or up high than at deer eye level.

m-scouting-camera-lottery-01.action: Don't hang your stand right where a buck showed up on camera. Use cameras for what's in the area, then hunt the doe groups, trails, and sign nearby.
m-scouting-camera-lottery-01.why: A camera photo tells you where he was yesterday, not where he is today; the hosts call it 'lottery hunting.' He had one 8-point on camera, hunted that spot twice without luck, then killed him back at his doe group.

m-scouting-camera-on-scrape-01.action: Run a trail camera on a scrape (mock or natural). Put it about 6 feet high, a bit above your own head, angled down, off to the side about 15 feet from the scrape, aimed so the scrape sits in the left or right third of the frame and also covers the trail; use a heavier licking vine. Read the timing: a buck hitting it close to daylight at either end of the day is bedding close by; every day means a bed nearby, about once a week means he's just scent-checking for does. Expect far fewer pictures than on a food source.
m-scouting-camera-on-scrape-01.why: Once a camera is up around 5 to 6 feet deer don't pay it much attention; at eye level they notice it a lot more. Many cameras trigger on the center of the frame, so a swinging branch in the middle (especially on a windy ridge) causes false triggers (Sturgis). A scrape camera tells you whether the buck you're after is in the area, what bucks are around, and whether the nearby bed is probably his (Next Step Outdoors). Bucks never seen before show up at night at a scrape and walk straight to it.

m-scouting-cams-point-to-food-01.action: Use trail cameras to learn which way and at what times deer move through an area. If lots of deer pass a camera but aren't feeding there, they're headed to a food source: back out along their direction of travel and scout to find it.
m-scouting-cams-point-to-food-01.why: Travel direction and timing on a camera point you to the food they're going to, which is where you can set up.

m-scouting-cards-in-storm-01.action: Use hard rain and wind to change trail-camera cards and batteries, or add a camera, even in spots you normally can't get into during the season (he walks right up the valley through the food plots). Skip real thunder and lightning.
m-scouting-cards-in-storm-01.why: In nasty weather deer are pinned down and can't see, hear, or smell well because so much is going on in the woods, so you slip in and out without them knowing.

m-scouting-check-cam-history-01.action: Compare your trail-camera photos from year to year to see if the bucks on your property follow the usual pattern (bedded most of the day, moving at night, heading back to bed right before sunup) or are outliers.
m-scouting-check-cam-history-01.why: He does this every year; his bucks mostly match the collared-buck studies, which tells him when not to push in.

m-scouting-cold-scrape-buck-gone-01.action: If a mock scrape that used to get hit hard goes quiet for a year or two, consider that the mature buck using it may be gone before blaming the setup.
m-scouting-cold-scrape-buck-gone-01.why: Mature bucks make far more rubs and scrapes than young ones. Scrapes that went cold on their land often did so right after they shot the buck that lived there.

m-scouting-day-vs-night-photos-01.action: Check your trail-camera photos: you want fewer (at worst, equal) nighttime pictures than daylight pictures. If most photos on your ground are at night, it's being hunted too hard or deer only use it as a night food source, and you should change how you hunt and access it.
m-scouting-day-vs-night-photos-01.why: Mature bucks do 90 to 95% of their movement after dark over about a 3 square mile range. An older buck learns which property isn't safe in daylight and stops coming at all. His example: a buck missing from your cameras for 2 years was shot by a neighbor half a mile away who'd had pictures of him all along.

m-scouting-deer-types-01.action: Before you pick tactics, decide what kind of deer you're hunting: straight wild (no tolerance for people), suburban (used to people, pets, cars), managed (fed with plots, feeders, and troughs, conditioned to people), or public. Restricted public land with one or two access roads acts like wild deer; busy public land with trails, camping, ranges, and year-round use acts more like suburban or managed deer.
m-scouting-deer-types-01.why: Behavior type alone changes how far deer travel, how much intrusion they tolerate, and what will blow them out. His example: a managed-property county-record buck came to a feeder within about 45 minutes of the farm hand refilling it, and was shot that way.

m-scouting-doe-arrival-test-01.action: Use doe and fawn arrival time at a food source as a health check for your spot. On a normal-weather day they should be out about 45 minutes to an hour before dark (maybe only 15 minutes before on a nasty-weather day). If they only show up right at dark, something is wrong: the cover next to the food is too open for them to cross in daylight, or you are pressuring it, or both. Fix that before expecting a mature buck there in daylight.
m-scouting-doe-arrival-test-01.why: He has seen that 45 to 60 minute window on public and private land across lower and upper Michigan, Wisconsin, and Minnesota. If the does won't come in daylight, a mature buck won't either.

m-scouting-door-knock-numbers-01.action: Treat door-knocking for permission as a numbers game: expect around 95% no's and plan whole days of it. When a landowner says they've seen a 'monster', show them a trail-cam photo of a buck you know the size of and ask if theirs was bigger or smaller.
m-scouting-door-knock-numbers-01.why: Some days five knocks get five yeses; others 25 get none. One two-to-three-day trip was a bust until the last couple of hours produced a yes on ground with a reportedly giant buck. 'Monster' can mean anything from a 110 to an elk, so a reference photo gives you a real gauge.

m-scouting-fawn-dates-01.action: Note the dates you see brand-new fawns (tiny tracks, spotted fawns still wobbly) and back-date them to learn when your local does are actually being bred, instead of trusting the published rut date.
m-scouting-fawn-dates-01.why: On his Georgia farms he's seen a newborn around April 1-9 (bred in September) and newborn twins in the last week of August into early September (bred in February or March). He also saw more chasing, fighting, and breeding in September to mid-October than around the published early-November peak.

m-scouting-feed-sign-after-rain-01.action: Use rain to age sign under a feed tree. Rain lays the mulched leaves back down, so if you check a tree an hour or two after a rain and the leaves are freshly torn up (undersides still wet), deer were just there.
m-scouting-feed-sign-after-rain-01.why: A tree that was torn up yesterday looks different after rain; it settles back like dug-up yard does after two days. Fresh sign after rain is a clear read on current use.

m-scouting-feed-sign-not-acorns-01.action: Hunt the oak that deer are actually feeding on, not the one with the most acorns. Read the sign under the tree: leaves mulched up and turned over with individual hoof prints (not turkey scratching), acorn caps and busted acorn pieces. Ground covered in whole, uneaten acorns is NOT a good sign. Squirrels cutting in a tree tell you it's dropping. Don't rely on droppings. Check feed sign every time you walk out, and when a whole group of preferred oaks (like white oaks) starts dropping hard and fresh feed sign shows up there, move to them right away. Don't write off chestnut (mountain) oaks; hunt the ones with real feed sign.
m-scouting-feed-sign-not-acorns-01.why: If the acorns are still lying there, deer aren't eating them. The sGtmLizXCwo guest's best trees were so mulched up he had to hunt for an acorn, and he has killed many deer at torn-up white oaks with hardly any droppings under them; a tree with buck sign that's being fed on is worth hunting even without a pile of does. Many chestnut-oak ridges are covered in acorns that just rot, so hunters sit them, see nothing, and decide deer don't eat them; often deer are only feeding on a couple of trees. Jacob (ehHCF9zlTyg) saw feed sign under one or two big chestnut oaks get heavier every trip; deer only shifted once all the white oaks were dropping, feed sign there got heavy within a couple of days, and bucks came in on his first or second sit.

m-scouting-find-bed-and-food-01.action: When scouting, your main job is to find where deer bed and where they feed. Everything else (rubs, scrapes, tracks, rut travel) gets read in relation to those two.
m-scouting-find-bed-and-food-01.why: Deer are most active at dawn and dusk. They spend daylight in or near security cover, get up around dusk to feed through the night, and return to bed in the morning. That bed-to-feed trip is where a bowhunter intercepts them, and even rut cruising routes are built around doe bedding.

m-scouting-find-deer-first-01.action: On new ground, find the deer (and make sure a big buck actually lives there) before you worry about the setup. In thick country you can't glass, put in the boot leather: walk the woods for fresh sign (fresh droppings, stirred-up leaves, fresh tracks, the odd fresh rub), and if you have to, spook deer on purpose to see where and how they were bedded and what they're eating. If a spot has no good deer, move on to the next place and keep going until you find one.
