m-scouting-find-deer-first-01.why: A great setup does nothing if no deer walks by it, and if you're not around a big deer you're not going to kill one (Lee Ellis; his crew's motto is 'leave no stone unturned, the search never stops', and staying mobile is a big part of why they succeed). On a short trip to unfamiliar habitat (Hunting Public example: thick Georgia woods where deer could bed anywhere), jumping deer shows you what their bedding thickets look like and what food they're on.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-scouting-glass-open-country-01.action: Pick your scouting method by the country. Where you can see a long way (South Dakota, open country), glass: watch deer and bucks directly from a distance to see where they are and where they cross. A trail camera can help connect the dots, but direct observation is the way to see it. Elsewhere, drive the roads and read soft-dirt road ditches for tracks; where you see a bunch of tracks, go in and see how the deer are bedding and moving there.
m-scouting-glass-open-country-01.why: It's the fastest way to know deer are in a spot before you spend time walking it (Hunting Public). Seeing where the young deer go and where the buck hangs back teaches you the travel pattern, and you can then spot the same kind of place anywhere (Kenyon).
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-scouting-hidden-old-sign-01.action: When scouting after the season or in spring and summer, don't write off an area for lack of scrapes and rubs. Look for the faint remains, and trust what you saw there in the fall.
m-scouting-hidden-old-sign-01.why: Once beech trees finally drop their leaves, they bury most scrapes (he estimated 95% in one hot area), and old rubs fade. Someone who didn't know the spot would walk right by it.

m-scouting-hunt-log-01.action: Keep a written record. After every sit, write down the date, time, wind direction, temperature, and what you saw; keep your deer history (which buck, where, when, conditions) in a notebook or a hunting-app journal; and each season write down the general conditions (wet or dry year, good or bust acorns), where you did and didn't find deer, and what worked. Make sure every trail camera has the correct date and time. When similar conditions come back, repeat what worked and don't repeat what failed.
m-scouting-hunt-log-01.why: After a season you see patterns specific to your ground, like 'every time the wind was southwest and it dropped below 40F, deer came through the north funnel', and those only show up in a written record (Downwind Hunting). Most people don't have a near-photographic memory for trail-cam photos like Lee Ellis; Beau needs a written plan to fall back on when the season gets busy, and a camera with the wrong date and time gave a friend no usable intel. Seasons like a bust mast year are hard to remember clearly later; after his bust year the ehHCF9zlTyg guest knows he won't sit in a little creek bottom hoping deer slip through again.

m-scouting-hunt-where-deer-are-now-01.action: Judge sign by how fresh it is, not how much there is, and don't count on last week's or last year's pattern. A rub bleeding sap from this morning beats a woods full of old droppings and rubs. If a historically hot spot has no fresh sign this year, don't sit it and wait: scout on the way out, find where the deer adapted to (for example wetland browse below the ridge, the last green soybeans on the shady side of a field, or thick browse up from the creek bottom), and move there. Keep cameras on known spots across years, because patterns can come back when conditions repeat.
m-scouting-hunt-where-deer-are-now-01.why: Deer go where they have to be for food, not where they were last year. After deer feed in one spot for two weeks sign is everywhere, but they may already be gone; in Missouri white oaks drop from late August or early September, and by late September, when everyone hunts that sign, the deer have moved on (Hunting Public). McKay's usual creek bottom had no sign one year; moving up into thick browse got him into bucks, and he'd rather give up a morning hunt to scout than sit on sign he found last week. A Virginia hunter who saw more bucks than ever in a heavy acorn year won't see that hold in a bust year; Andrew's camera spot had bucks one year, nothing the next (not even in the rut), then they were back doing exactly what they did two summers earlier (ehHCF9zlTyg).
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-scouting-late-winter-scouting-01.action: Do your invasive, in-woods scouting in late winter and early spring (February to April), before green-up. Backtrack from sign you noted during the season (like a line of scrapes along an access path) to find the killing setups: pick the tree for each wind and work out how you'll get in at 3 AM. Pick up sheds while you're at it. A couple of hours here and there, even while turkey hunting, makes a big difference. Then in the fall, make quick after-work checks every couple of weeks, and when the sign turns fresh and the forecast wind matches the tree you picked, hunt it that weekend.
m-scouting-late-winter-scouting-01.why: The woods are open and last season's sign is still readable; once everything is green, thick, thorny, and full of poison ivy it's very hard. Shed antlers show which bucks made it through the season so you can pick targets (Next Step Outdoors). You do the invasive work when it can't hurt your season, and during the season you can spot-check without much pressure (Hunting Public).
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-scouting-learn-every-hunt-01.action: Treat every setup as a hypothesis and every sit as a lesson: form a guess from your scouting, test it by hunting, and adjust. When a deer (especially a mature buck) spooks, work out where he was, what he was doing there, and what you did to spook him (wind, movement, when you drew). Control the variables you can by getting in and out clean, leaving little scent, and hunting places other people aren't walking through.
m-scouting-learn-every-hunt-01.why: Bowhunting is trial and error: you'll get winded, get caught moving, and draw at the wrong time; even after a lifetime they fail more than they succeed, and the ones who keep learning keep improving (Bowhunters United). Controlling your own intrusion means what you see is deer being deer, not deer reacting to you; you only have to be right once a season, and sometimes luck helps (Next Step Outdoors).

m-scouting-leave-cameras-01.action: Don't pull or move a camera just because a promising new spot shows nothing in summer or after 10 days. Leave cameras in the same spots through the season (Beau leaves some a full year). Only pull one if it covered basically the whole season, about 4 months, with nothing.
m-scouting-leave-cameras-01.why: Bucks shift ranges when the season starts, so a spot that's empty now may fill up; a summer buck often leaves you right as the season opens. A buck may use a spot for just two weeks in November to breed the does he knows are there, then move to the next group. Both have surely moved cameras a week before the buck showed. Long-running cameras also reveal the windows, like a late-season group of deer moving in, that lead you to find the food they're on.

m-scouting-limit-camera-checks-01.action: Don't make special trips to check trail cameras during the season. Check SD-card cameras no more than about once every 14 days, or use cellular cameras so you don't have to walk in. Change cards only when you're already going to hunt that stand, in bad weather, or when you drive in after dark to retrieve a deer.
m-scouting-limit-camera-checks-01.why: Each check leaves scent, packs the ground, and teaches mature bucks that the trail gets human traffic (Downwind Hunting, citing Auburn research that weekly or more frequent checks shifted how mature bucks used the area). Driving around pulling every card on the property, like clients who do it the Friday night they arrive, hurts not only that hunt but the next week or two; hunters fail with trail cameras through that intrusion (Sturgis).

m-scouting-map-then-verify-01.action: Scout by air first, then by foot. Use aerial photos and topo maps (a US Topo layer on the public land overlay) at home to find benches, saddles, and points; even in unbroken forest the shaded sides of hills show the ridges. Then walk the spots you picked before you trust them, checking them off one by one (a laminated map card, or a phone screenshot you color in as you cover each area).
m-scouting-map-then-verify-01.why: Wandering around on foot without a plan wastes days and leads you into other hunters' sign; with a list of spots you can verify one important place even with only an hour (Sturgis). Mapping apps teach a lot, but you only learn how deer actually use the land by going there: a bowl that looks steep on topo can have a small bench deer hammer, and of ten thermal hubs that look good on a map maybe two are worth hunting (Dixon).

m-scouting-mark-doe-groups-01.action: All year, mark every spot where you keep finding does (bedding areas you see does in time after time), even if you don't know it's the same deer.
m-scouting-mark-doe-groups-01.why: In the rut bucks play connect-the-dots between doe bedding areas, so those marks become your rut spots.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-scouting-marsh-bedding-01.action: In a marsh or swamp, look for bedding at structure: trees or woody shrubs out in the grass, or any high spot. That's where the ground is high and dry enough to bed. Confirm with beds holding hair, matted grass, droppings, and grass tips nipped off around the bed.
m-scouting-marsh-bedding-01.why: Deer won't bed in open grass; they want shade and cover at their back with a view of where danger would come from and plenty of escape routes. Trees and shrubs only grow out there on dry ground.

m-scouting-missing-buck-not-dead-01.action: If a regular buck disappears from your cameras, don't write him off as dead. In the rut, a buck missing for a few days has most likely shifted his daily area: he uses about 200 acres a day all season, the same 200 acres day after day outside the rut but a different 200 acres each day in the rut. Over longer stretches, he may have been pushed out by a bully buck and can show back up a year or two later as the neighborhood's age structure shifts.
m-scouting-missing-buck-not-dead-01.why: MSU GPS collars: daily home range was remarkably steady at about 200 acres every week from September to February; in the rut the daily areas are far apart, outside it they overlap 'like rose petals'. Rex: it's happened to them many times; bucks move to where they don't have to fight every day, and some aggressive 'scrub' bucks in his area lived past 10 years, displacing others.

m-scouting-mock-scrape-build-01.action: Make a mock scrape with a licking branch hanging from above: pick a spot with bare dirt and hang a rope, vine, or branch from an overhead branch or cord so it hangs over the scrape. Height: about 5 feet above the scrape (Downwind Hunting) or belly to waist high on a person, so does and fawns use it too (Sturgis; one scrape he showed was almost chest high). Sturgis's build: run paracord about 12 feet up between two trees (or throw a rope over a branch, even 20 feet up) and hang a long vine or branch (8 to 15 feet) so it swings freely from a single pivot point instead of being tied rigid. Use something bucks naturally work: vines last longest, then jack pine; white oak, hemlock, and beech are fine; aspen works but is brittle. With no branch, winch a live sapling over and tie it off. Put a camera on it or hunt it.
m-scouting-mock-scrape-build-01.why: Scrapes are where bucks check who's in the area; they lick and rub the rope or branch with their eye glands and paw the dirt below (Downwind Hunting). Hanging from high up with a long, heavy vine looks natural (a short stick swinging on a rope doesn't) and the flex keeps bucks from breaking it; Sturgis's have lasted up to 7 years, and the paracord costs 30 to 60 cents.

m-scouting-mock-scrape-early-01.action: Build mock scrapes well before the season, whenever you hang the stand (he did his on September 1; another was about 7 weeks ahead), near where deer bed and travel. Put a solar-powered camera on it and then leave it alone to soak; he won't go back to that spot to hunt for about two months. Expect deer to hit it within hours, and don't worry about disturbing the area that far out.
m-scouting-mock-scrape-early-01.why: Deer get used to it and adopt it while you stay out, and the camera does the scouting without you walking in. Deer are back there all the time; even if the work keeps the oldest buck away briefly, there's plenty of time before opening day for it to settle.

m-scouting-next-food-source-01.action: Don't count on the early-season food pattern lasting. Watch for it to fade (soybeans turning yellow, native plants hardening off and going to seed, acorns starting to drop) and scout ahead so you already know what the deer will be eating in about 3 weeks, then move your stands when they switch.
m-scouting-next-food-source-01.why: When acorns start falling, patterns change very quickly and the deer seem to vanish. Their needs also change this time of year: from the high-protein summer diet (antlers, milk) to carbs to build fat for the rut and winter. A buck can lose up to 30% of his body weight in the rut.

m-scouting-night-only-not-nocturnal-01.action: If a buck shows up only at night on your camera, don't write him off as nocturnal. Look for where he spends daylight, such as deep timber feeding on acorns.
m-scouting-night-only-not-nocturnal-01.why: Derek went back and filmed bucks that were nighttime-only on October cameras and found them moving around all day, just not where the cameras were.

m-scouting-no-camera-on-active-scrape-01.action: Don't walk in and hang a trail camera close to an active natural scrape. Watch it from a distance, or put cameras on the approach trails instead.
m-scouting-no-camera-on-active-scrape-01.why: He's learned that setting a camera near a scrape that's getting hit all the time will shut that scrape down faster than anything, likely from the human scent and intrusion. Scrapes are mostly hit at night anyway.

m-scouting-observation-sit-01.action: Spend warm, wrong-wind, or poor-weather early-season days (for example when your only free day has poor weather) on observation sits instead of burning a good stand or pushing into the core: sit an edge stand you can reach without pushing into the property (off a road, by the barn or cabin, on the property line) that looks into a destination food plot, and watch which trails deer use in and out. Still bring your bow.
m-scouting-observation-sit-01.why: You're still hunting, and sometimes the buck walks by, but mainly you learn which trails deer use in and out of the food and where your target buck comes from, without pressuring the property. If nothing happens, you've lost nothing. A stand like that can still catch random movement (his example: a ladder stand in a bur oak dropping acorns, 5 yards from his pole barn, on the way from bedding to the plot and the neighbor's hayfield).

m-scouting-old-buck-stays-in-core-01.action: Expect an old buck to live out of one core area and rarely show up elsewhere in daylight. Treat night-only photos (2 to 4 hours after dark) as a buck that doesn't live on your ground; hunt the buck whose core you're in.
m-scouting-old-buck-stays-in-core-01.why: The older a buck gets, the more of a loner he is and the more he sticks to the core that kept him alive. His buck 'Junior' showed up away from his 30 to 40 acre core less than 10% of the time (more often late October into early November, back in the core by mid-November), and a neighbor a short way off never got one picture of him in four seasons. Another buck, seen 11 times in six weeks almost all at night, lived on the next property, where that neighbor saw him in daylight nearly every day and shot him.

m-scouting-one-photo-means-more-01.action: Treat one trail-camera photo of a buck as a sign he's in that area far more often than the camera shows. Hunt it with patience, protect your access, and consider a couple of stand options there. Don't wait for a cell camera to show him before you go.
m-scouting-one-photo-means-more-01.why: Beau figures one daylight photo a week means he's there 3 or 4 times; Derek would guess 6 to 10 times a week counting night. Beau has sat through great rut days with bucks cruising and none walked in front of the camera 20 yards away. Letting cell cams decide whether you hunt costs you opportunities.

m-scouting-post-gun-scout-01.action: In a heavily hunted state, scout right after gun season closes. Places full of deer then are where the pressure pushed them; target those holes during next year's gun season, especially thick, nasty cover where you'll get close shots.
m-scouting-post-gun-scout-01.why: Those are the spots nobody went during gun season. Most gun hunters look for places to shoot far with a scope; he'd rather be in thick cover with open sights and shoot one at 13 steps.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-scouting-read-rubs-01.action: Read buck sign this way: a rub on a bigger tree usually means an older buck (not necessarily a big rack). An area torn up with lots of rubs and scrapes means overlapping bucks of similar age competing, which is encouraging. Don't put much stock in track size.
m-scouting-read-rubs-01.why: He rarely sees spikes and yearlings hit big trees, though big bucks will destroy small ones. Most sign in his area is laid down by 3- and 4-year-olds. He's killed big deer with small feet and seen small deer with big feet. Actual sightings beat all sign.

m-scouting-read-trails-01.action: Treat the heavily beaten trails as doe-family bed-to-feed routes that point you to the preferred food and the general travel direction. Expect buck trails to be less obvious.
m-scouting-read-trails-01.why: Doe groups walk the same line every day, so their trails get pounded. The obvious trail still tells you the food and direction even if not every deer beds in the same place.

m-scouting-repeat-the-pattern-01.action: Once you find deer, figure out what that spot is (the kind of thicket they bed in, which acorns just fell, what elevation it is), then look for the same thing in three or four other places. Line up several spots, not one.
m-scouting-repeat-the-pattern-01.why: In the Georgia mountains the deer were hammering red oak acorns on one bench band below the midway bench, in the drainages. Once they matched that, they kept walking into fresh sign. Multiple spots give you backups.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-scouting-rub-direction-01.action: On a trail between food and bedding, check which side of the trees the rubs are on. Rubs facing the food suggest he used it in the morning going back to bed; rubs facing the bedding suggest an afternoon trail heading to food. Treat it only as a hint.
m-scouting-rub-direction-01.why: It helps piece together which trail a buck uses at which time of day, but he says it's far from an exact science and he doesn't base a strategy on rubs.

m-scouting-scout-for-people-01.action: Scout for people as hard as you scout for deer. Avoid any spot with signs of hunters: trash, tree stands, old blinds, footprints, beaten-down trails, ribbons, tacks, even old axe notches in trees. In summer, scrape bare a 'sand trap' patch of soil 2 to 3 feet across on a trail and check it later for how many different boot prints come through. Look for the combination of a remote spot, a history of buck sign (rubs and scrapes in the same places year after year, even a decade or more), and no people. When you find lots of deer sign, check whether it's daytime sign or all-night sign.
m-scouting-scout-for-people-01.why: Bucks lay down sign in the same places over the years because the lay of the land funnels them there; remote plus old sign plus no people is usually a great spot (Sturgis). Finding the deer usually means you've found an area people aren't using; sign in places people don't go is usually worth hunting, but sign made only at night won't give you a daylight shot (Hunting Public).
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-scouting-scout-in-and-out-01.action: Scout every time you walk to and from a stand, especially in wind and rain: look for rubs, fresh scrapes, tracks, and beaten-down trails that are just starting to form. Lightly check field edges near your less-trusted stands.
m-scouting-scout-in-and-out-01.why: Deer patterns change through the fall (his 'annual whitetail shift'): trails used heavily by late October often weren't being used in mid-September. Bad weather lets you look without leaving a footprint.

m-scouting-scout-mast-yourself-01.action: In summer, scout the acorn crop in your own hunting area yourself with binoculars, looking up into the treetops, to learn which oaks will drop. Pick an isolated limb with only sky behind it, sit under the tree, and brace your binoculars on a trekking pole to study it. Don't rely on someone else's mast report, even from the next county.
m-scouting-scout-mast-yourself-01.why: The buds get easier to see as summer goes on, and by late summer you can see the acorns; it gives you a head start on which trees deer will feed on in the fall (Hunting Public). Mast varies county to county and mountain to mountain; one mountain can be loaded while one 15 miles away is nearly bare (ehHCF9zlTyg).
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-scouting-scrape-over-rub-01.action: For trail-camera intel, use a mock scrape rather than a mock rub, and don't judge a scrape by how it looks. A scrape can look untouched and still be hit every day; bucks only paw it bare during the rut.
m-scouting-scrape-over-rub-01.why: In their 60-day test (October and November, food-plot edge by a cornfield), a mock scrape got 210 hits from bucks, does, and fawns while a mock rub right next to it, which looked shredded, got 22 hits, all bucks. The average natural rub gets hit about 1.5 times a year.

m-scouting-snow-south-slope-beds-01.action: After a fresh winter snow, walk and look for beds. In his hills the one consistent pattern was beds on south-facing slopes, where it's warmer and snow melts first.
m-scouting-snow-south-slope-beds-01.why: Beyond that he found no rhyme or reason (ridge versus low ground), which is why he shifted to hunting food and the trails into it.

m-scouting-snow-trails-01.action: After a fresh snow of about 2 inches, walk the whole property and photograph every deer trail, noting which get heavy traffic and which are single tracks.
m-scouting-snow-trails-01.why: Fresh snow records every step from roughly the last 12 hours; it shows what deer actually did, not what you guess they do.

m-scouting-speed-scout-01.action: On a short trip, speed-scout with a buddy instead of committing to one far-back spot. Leapfrog down a road: drop one person off, he walks a line about half a mile in, spends about 30 minutes, and comes back out; the other drives half a mile up the road and does the same. Regroup, compare notes, and repeat 10 to 15 times a day. If either finds something good, go back in together and figure it out right then. Aim for 5 or 6 backup spots, not one. Before picking a remote spot, add up the real walking time (in the dark, around ridges and rivers) against how many days you have.
m-scouting-speed-scout-01.why: It covers far more ground than one long walk, and working out the spot on the spot means you don't have to go back in later for more intel; it's worth missing hunts to find deer. A spot 3 miles away on the map can be a 3-hour walk in the dark, and finding another hunter's camera when you get there burns one of your four days. In Michigan they hunted mostly within half a mile of the road this way and it worked great.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-scouting-start-at-food-01.action: On a new property, cyber-scout first. In ag country, start at the crop field (or orchard, or crops on neighboring private land) and scout from the food back toward the bedding. With no clear destination food, walk until you find a concentration of sign, then work forward and backward from it to find the food and bedding.
m-scouting-start-at-food-01.why: The food is the easiest piece to find and the trails lead from it to the beds. Where food is scattered (a couple of oak flats, natural browse) sign is less concentrated and travel direction less defined, so it's harder but not impossible.

m-scouting-subtle-sign-01.action: Scout for the everyday sign, not just rubs and scrapes: buds and tender tips bitten off (browse), faint tracks, droppings, and faint trails. Hunt where deer are feeding and browsing right now.
m-scouting-subtle-sign-01.why: If you only look for obvious buck sign you'll never learn to see the tracks, droppings, and faint trails. Several of his best bucks came from spots where you'd be lucky to find a rub or scrape, and he's sat over heavy rubs and scrapes and seen nothing.

m-scouting-target-one-buck-01.action: Use trail cameras and scouting to find one specific mature buck, then put your effort into figuring him out and hunting him, while staying open to shooting another mature deer that shows up. A recent photo of the deer you're after is what gives you the confidence to sit longer and hunt more.
m-scouting-target-one-buck-01.why: Focusing on one deer drives the extra scouting (hours and miles in February looking for his sheds) and the extra care on every hunt, and makes you better even for other deer of that age; without a target you do worse and start finding reasons to leave early. About 90% of Lee's mounted bucks came after more than a year of history with that deer. Since 2004 Rex's family hasn't killed a buck they didn't already know about; in woods too thick to glass, cameras were 'eyes in the woods all the time' and the biggest game changer of his career.

m-scouting-track-traps-01.action: Make track traps so the ground tells you what's using a trail: clear the leaves off the ground on both sides of a log across a trail and rake patches of the trail bare (McKay), or rake a line across a ridge point deer travel with a hard-tooth rake, clearing the leaves and breaking up the dirt, or blow the leaves off with a leaf blower (ehHCF9zlTyg). Check them on your next trip for what came through and how big the tracks are. In a dry year when the ground won't hold tracks, don't rely on track hunting: check soft-soil creek crossings, use what you already know about the area and its best habitat, and put out trail cameras, moving each one after about 10 days with nothing.
m-scouting-track-traps-01.why: Deer hit the ground harder stepping over a log, and bare dirt shows tracks you'd otherwise miss or scrape away looking for them (McKay). Dry, hard ground doesn't show tracks even right after a light rain; a bachelor group of bucks walked within 10 yards of one listener and left none. A photo tells you even more than a track (ehHCF9zlTyg).

m-scouting-traditional-sign-01.action: Expect lots of random rubs and scrapes, and don't build a hunt around new, random sign. Mark it on your map and check next year whether it shows up again; sign that repeats in the same spot year after year earns a stand. Pay attention to signpost scrapes and rubs at landmarks: terrain features, habitat edges, certain flats that get scraped every season, tall lone trees left standing in big clearcuts, sapling beech trees that hold their leaves late, and a lone cedar in the hardwoods.
m-scouting-traditional-sign-01.why: A mature buck may make half a dozen small, random scrapes on one morning route and rub trees 20-plus times in a day, in daylight (Dixon); pre-rut and rut bucks leave a lot of random sign, a pushed-off subordinate buck may tear up a spot out of frustration, and a fresh rub only proves a buck was there once (Whitetail Evolution). Dixon watched bucks reach a signpost scrape or habitat edge and then change direction as if they'd just figured out where they were; Beau finds scrapes and sheds under tall hemlocks left in big Pennsylvania cuts, like a lighthouse for a boat at night. Rex: something about the wind currents and those trees makes the same places right for deer year after year, and where cedars are scarce every passing buck rubs a lone one.

m-scouting-transplant-scrape-01.action: To create a scrape in front of your stand, transplant a real one from an area you aren't hunting: with rubber gloves, dig the top couple inches of dirt into a clean 5-gallon pail, bag the licking branch and snip it off, zip-tie it onto a branch at the right height over flat ground in your spot, scratch out a scrape, and mix in the dirt.
m-scouting-transplant-scrape-01.why: The moved scrape carries other deer's urine and gland scent, and deer take it over immediately. He did this late September through October.

m-scouting-velvet-bucks-leave-01.action: Don't count on summer (velvet) trail-cam bucks being there in the season. Use summer scouting to learn the ground, check old sign, and run cameras on creek crossings, trail intersections, and transition lines. Count on a buck once he's on camera in hard antler.
m-scouting-velvet-bucks-leave-01.why: Bucks often move three or four miles after shedding velvet. Once hard-horned, the buck you have on camera is the one you get to hunt.

m-scouting-velvet-shift-find-core-01.action: When bucks shed velvet, expect a patterned buck to suddenly disappear. Don't give up on him: scout for the core area he shifted to within his home range (current food, water, cover, and security), and put out several trail cameras running 24/7 to learn how he moves there.
m-scouting-velvet-shift-find-core-01.why: Rising testosterone at velvet shed makes bucks testy. Bachelor groups spread out or break up, bucks get pushed out and shift within their home range, and food sources are changing at the same time.

m-scouting-walk-more-for-feed-trees-01.action: If you think feed trees 'don't work here', scout more ground. You won't find a hot tree in every 5-acre patch of hardwoods; keep walking until you find the one being hit. Feed trees work anywhere acorn oaks grow, and in pine country with few hardwoods they should be even easier to narrow down.
m-scouting-walk-more-for-feed-trees-01.why: He used to believe feed-tree hunting didn't work in his area and realized he just wasn't walking enough. It's harder in a heavy mast year when deer have 100 trees to choose from instead of 10.

m-scouting-warm-days-scout-01.action: Scout more than you hunt, especially when starting out (two to three times as much time scouting as hunting). Use warm days, when movement is poor (for example the warm days before a front in the pre-rut), to scout, check cameras, or do an easy evening sit, and stay out of your best morning spots until the cold arrives. Hunt the best days, when cold weather comes through. Ask why each trail is where it is, not just where.
m-scouting-warm-days-scout-01.why: Warm days are low-value hunts, and walking into a good morning spot early can blow it out before the days that count (Sturgis). The YOqPX18EAx4 guest spent his first five years relearning the mountains mostly walking with a stand on his back, working out why the trails existed; warm days are wasted in the stand.

m-scouting-waterhole-lead-time-01.action: A water hole done right can be hunted about 3 weeks after you put it in. He installed on August 30 to hunt the September 19 opener, and his target buck was using it by day 11. Installing in late September or early October to hunt it in the rut has also worked for him.
m-scouting-waterhole-lead-time-01.why: Young bucks come right in within a day or two, does and fawns hesitate then get used to it right away, and older bucks are slower but come.

m-scouting-waterhole-never-dry-01.action: Size a water hole so it won't dry out mid-season and you won't have to keep walking in to fill it. A 100-gallon tank lasts only about a month in drought with moderate deer use. Smaller surface area loses less: an 8-foot-wide tank evaporates over 3 gallons a day, a 4 by 6 foot one about 1.5.
m-scouting-waterhole-never-dry-01.why: Every trip to fill it spooks deer. Once it dries up, deer stop coming within about 2 weeks and then take 2 to 3 weeks to come back after you refill it, because they've moved to a different pattern.

m-shot-3d-target-hold-at-draw-01.action: Practice on a 3D deer target from different distances and angles, and practice holding at full draw for 5, 10, or more seconds before you shoot.
m-shot-3d-target-hold-at-draw-01.why: A 3D target has no bright dot, so you learn where to aim on a real body. In the field a deer often steps or turns after you draw, and letting down is too much movement, so you have to hold until it gives you a clear shot again. Tired muscles make an accurate shot much harder unless you've practiced it. Even experienced hunters sometimes draw too early out of excitement.

m-shot-aim-behind-shoulder-01.action: With a bow, don't aim tight on the shoulder. Aim for the center of the area from just behind the shoulder back to the last rib.
m-shot-aim-behind-shoulder-01.why: There's plenty of vital area there, while the vitals by the shoulder sit low and taper down. Focusing on the shoulder has been a bad mistake for him.

m-shot-aim-low-forward-01.action: With a bow, aim lower and farther forward than 'behind the shoulder, halfway up': go straight up the front leg about one third of the way up the body (the top of the heart). Inside about 17 to 18 yards aim dead on there. Beyond 20 yards aim low heart, and on an alert deer (for example one that came to rattling) expect him to duck.
m-shot-aim-low-forward-01.why: Most deer react to the sound of the shot by dropping their body to load their legs; past 20 to 25 yards they can drop 6 to 10 inches or more, turning a center-mass hold into a miss or a high, non-lethal hit. The low hold goes through both lungs, the top of the heart, and major vessels, for a quick kill and a good blood trail, and still hits the heart if the deer doesn't drop.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-shot-beginner-any-legal-deer-01.action: As a new bowhunter, don't hold out for a big buck. Set your goal on any legal deer you'd be happy with and that gets you excited, a doe included (unless the landowner you hunt with has specific rules). Get pickier only after you've taken a few.
m-shot-beginner-any-legal-deer-01.why: Hunting shows and social media make beginners wait for giant bucks; setting expectations too high gets frustrating enough that people quit. Early success is what gets you hooked. One Bowhunters United host says being picky early was a mistake; he was trying to shoot a doe the year he got his first buck.

m-shot-blind-bale-judge-distance-01.action: Before the season, blind bale shoot (eyes closed, close range) to fix your form and target panic, and practice judging distance by eye instead of ranging every shot.
m-shot-blind-bale-judge-distance-01.why: Deer often come in and give you a small window with no time to use a rangefinder, or you won't have one. New bowhunters bring bad habits like target panic and leaning on the rangefinder.

m-shot-double-lung-only-01.action: Only release when you're sure you can put the arrow through both lungs. Let deer walk if they're past your max range (his is 20 yards with a traditional bow), walking straight away, or close and steep: the steeper the downward angle, the smaller your window to hit both lungs, so pass on a deer right under or nearly under the tree and wait for a better angle. Be extra careful on does and young bucks, which are wiry and react faster at the shot than mature bucks. No frontal shots, and don't aim for the heart, spine, neck, or femoral artery.
m-shot-double-lung-only-01.why: A steep arrow tends to catch one lung and miss the other. A one-lung deer will very likely die, but it can take two or three days and you probably won't find it; the one year he hunted from 24 feet, he one-lunged four of the six deer he shot. Nobody is good enough to hit the small targets on purpose, and live animals move unpredictably. He has let hundreds of deer walk, including some of the biggest he's seen, at 23 yards or straight under the tree.

m-shot-downhill-bend-at-hip-01.action: For a downward shot from a tree stand, draw, then bend at the waist over the side of your hip so your bow arm stays at the same 90-degree angle to your upper body that you use on flat ground. Don't just drop your bow arm, and don't bend straight forward at the waist, which tips (cants) the bow. Once you're settled in the stand, take practice draws toward your likely shot spots and check that you're bending over the side of your hip, not forward.
m-shot-downhill-bend-at-hip-01.why: Dropping only the arm changes where your eye sits relative to the peep: the peep pulls away from your face, you raise the bow to re-center the pin, and the arrow hits high. Bending forward cants a compound, and a canted compound sends the arrow to the side (a right-handed shooter hits right): the arrow leaves angled up and to the side of your sight line, and gravity pulls it straight down, not back toward the line. In the excitement of a deer at 25 yards it's very easy to cant without noticing; Winke has made the forward-bend mistake many times himself and practices it every season.

m-shot-draw-when-head-hidden-01.action: Keep the tree or cover between you and approaching deer, and draw only when the deer's head is down or behind a tree or log. Then hold at full draw until it steps out into the open, or swing out, draw, and shoot. In a saddle, keep the tree between you and the deer by rotating slowly as they pass.
m-shot-draw-when-head-hidden-01.why: The drawing motion is what gets you caught. Once you're drawn and holding still, you won't get busted, as long as your draw weight is one you can hold. Staying behind the tree keeps you nearly invisible for most of the encounter, even in a tree with no cover, and a saddle lets you shoot almost 360 degrees around the trunk.

m-shot-eyes-closed-01.action: If a deer close by is staring right at you, close your eyes and very slowly lean your head behind the tree until it looks away.
m-shot-eyes-closed-01.why: The old saying is that if they can see your eyes, they'll pick you out. He did this with a doe feeding in front of him, and the big buck following her still came in; it became his first big bow buck.

m-shot-hang-for-left-shot-01.action: Hang a stand so a right-handed shooter shoots off the left side, using the tree to hide behind. Most people face the stand toward where they expect deer, which leaves them exposed.
m-shot-hang-for-left-shot-01.why: The shooting movement from a well-hung stand is minimal, and the tree breaks up your outline. Shooting well from a stand is quicker to learn than from a saddle.

m-shot-keep-bow-shots-close-01.action: Keep bow shots close, and pick setups where a deer walks right by you rather than ones where you see many deer far off. The Hunting Public want deer inside 20 yards, ideally 15 or less, and won't take 25 yards or more on a big buck. Mike Rex keeps every archery shot, crossbow or vertical bow, to 30 yards or less, even across a wide-open field. Bowhunters United wait for a deer inside about 25 to 30 yards that gives a good, clean, ethical shot, and say don't force one; expect your first bow kill to take time, even seasons.
m-shot-keep-bow-shots-close-01.why: Even a 400+ fps crossbow bolt is about three times slower than the sound of the shot (about 1,200 fps), so a deer can react before the arrow arrives. At 30 yards even a perfect shot can miss or wound because you can't predict how far a deer will move, drop, or wheel; at 40 to 50 yards a lot of bad things can happen, and you can't reliably read a deer's mood. Inside 10 to 12 yards they don't have time to react, and even a bad hit at 15 to 16 yards has killed deer. Across The Hunting Public's archery kills the average shot was 16 yards, very few over 30. Getting a deer that close is the hard part of bowhunting.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-shot-kneel-and-seated-practice-01.action: If you bowhunt from the ground, practice shooting from a seat and from your knees behind a tree, not only standing.
m-shot-kneel-and-seated-practice-01.why: Kneeling puts more of you on the ground, so your body sways far less at full draw than when standing sideways to the target.

m-shot-long-range-practice-01.action: Practice outdoors at 50 yards minimum, often 60 and 80, even though you'd never shoot a deer that far.
m-shot-long-range-practice-01.why: Every flaw in form shows at long range, and once 60 to 80 is routine, 20 to 30 yard shots feel like a chip shot.

m-shot-movement-over-noise-01.action: When deer are in view, worry more about movement than small sounds. A deep, muffled cough often doesn't alert deer, especially a group, but shifting in your seat does.
m-shot-movement-over-noise-01.why: Groups of deer make a lot of noise themselves. From years filming other hunters, he's seen small movements pop heads up more than quiet sounds.

m-shot-paper-tune-01.action: Shoot rows of arrows through paper at 6 to 8 feet until every one is a clean bullet hole. Left or right tears mean the bow is out of tune or you're torquing; high or low tears usually mean the setup (rest or nock height). Figure out whether it's the bow or you, fix it, then repeat until it's habit.
m-shot-paper-tune-01.why: Paper gives instant feedback: torque or a string twist from your release shows up in the tear. Repeatable form, not perfect form, is what you're after (like a golf swing).

m-shot-pick-a-spot-01.action: When a big buck shows up, stop looking at the antlers and pick a spot on the chest. Get into shooting position slowly and quietly, and know ahead of time where your stand seat and gear can clank; step off or range your shooting spots (scrapes, trails) before the deer comes.
m-shot-pick-a-spot-01.why: No amount of target practice prepares you for the adrenaline. His friend, staring at the rack, shot a giant buck in the antlers. Rex rushed to stand for the biggest typical he ever saw, clipped his boot on the seat with a 'pink', shook for 30 seconds, and cleanly missed at 21 yards he'd already stepped off.

m-shot-practice-before-season-01.action: Practice as much as you can before the season; it's the single most important thing in bowhunting. Set a standard before you hunt: hit a paper plate (6 to 8 inches) every time at 15 to 20 yards, including from an elevated stand. If you can't, don't go, and don't take long shots; wait for the right close opportunity.
m-shot-practice-before-season-01.why: Confidence in your gear and your shot comes from practice. The Hunting Public host missed many deer as a kid on bad shots before he practiced all summer and made a perfect 20-yard shot on his first bow buck; it was his uncle's rule for the kids. Shooting a target is one skill; sitting in a stand and being a good hunter is more to learn.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-shot-range-marks-01.action: As soon as you sit down, before anything else, range three objects in your shooting lanes (a stump, a limb, a rock) and memorize the yardages.
m-shot-range-marks-01.why: When a deer shows up you already know the distance within a yard, without the movement of raising a rangefinder.

m-shot-rifle-rest-01.action: Any time you can get a rest for a rifle shot, take it. On the ground, stand up behind your tree and use its side as the rest rather than shooting offhand.
m-shot-rifle-rest-01.why: It steadies longer shots (100 to 150 yards) so you don't miss.

m-shot-run-the-script-01.action: Every sit, play the whole shot in your head before any deer shows: which way they'll come, where you'll draw (when the deer is behind a big tree at 30 to 40 yards), and where you'll stop it broadside (about 20 yards, with a grunt if needed). Believe it will happen, and be ready.
m-shot-run-the-script-01.why: With a bow you're guessing every time, and you only have to be right once. The mental rehearsal is what lets you execute when a buck finally 'reads the script'.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-shot-saddle-weak-side-01.action: Practice the weak-side shot before the season if you saddle hunt: either go up and over your bridge and turn your hips, or stand on the platform and turn around like on a stand (a bigger platform helps). Keep swinging around on your tether to a minimum.
m-shot-saddle-weak-side-01.why: You can shoot 360 degrees from a saddle, but the weak side is harder and takes more movement than turning on a tree stand, which can get you seen.

m-shot-shot-routine-01.action: Run the same shot routine every time, talking yourself through it: grip, draw, primary anchor, secondary anchor (tip of the nose on the string), come down onto the target from above, settle the pin, execute. If anything feels off at full draw, like your anchor, don't shoot; back off and restart the whole routine.
m-shot-shot-routine-01.why: He calmly let a buck stand 9 minutes at 12 yards while he was on the ground, and when his anchor felt wrong at full draw he pulled off and reset before shooting. Staying calm keeps you out of 'panic mode', which is hard to get out of once you're in it. Confidence comes from reps.

m-shot-trad-height-distortion-01.action: If you shoot instinctively (traditional bow), practice from the height you hunt and keep that height modest (about 12 to 16 feet).
m-shot-trad-height-distortion-01.why: Instinctive aiming runs on memory of how targets look from the ground. From 18 to 20 feet a deer at 10 yards looks tiny and throws off your judgment; at 10 feet up, an 18-yard deer feels like a chip shot.

m-stand_placement-backup-stands-for-cond.action: Before the season, build a list of setups for different conditions: spots for hot days, for a cold front, for a dead-calm day, and low-impact spots close to the road for a morning (Hunting Public). On hunt day pick the spot that fits the conditions you got. If you must hunt a bad-weather day, sit a stand you have less faith in: off to the side, where you can get in and out safely without worrying about spooking deer. Save your best, most intrusive stands (like a morning bedding-area stand) for the good days.
m-stand_placement-backup-stands-for-cond.why: Nine times out of ten you won't have the right conditions for the great, intrusive spot in the middle of a bedding area. Hunters with only a couple of days force it anyway, go in on bad conditions or timing, leave their scent, and blow the spot out (Hunting Public). A bad day on a low-risk stand still gets you in the woods, since there's always a random chance at a buck, and lets you scout without burning a great spot (Sturgis).
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-stand_placement-between-bedding-and-fo.action: If you only get one stand, put it between bedding and food (and water if there is any): close to both, in neither. Look for a pinch that squeezes the movement (a ditch, a thick-cover edge, a bench, a swamp edge) and a hidden way in and out that doesn't cross bedding or food. On public land the best spot isn't in the oak flat; it's between the oak flat and where you expect the buck to bed. Water holes back in the woods, in wooded funnels about 100 yards off a food plot (not in the plot), make good morning and all-day stands; deer use water on the way between bedding and food even with a creek nearby.
m-stand_placement-between-bedding-and-fo.why: That's the spot deer pass morning AND evening, so it's the rare stand you can hunt any time, all season, and get in and out clean. A mature buck won't walk into a small open plot at 10, 1, or 3 in the afternoon, but he will visit water back in cover midday. Deer are efficient: even bedded 50 yards off a creek, they won't go backwards to it if water is on the way to food.

m-stand_placement-branchy-tree-for-hang-.action: Pick a branchy tree (a pine or other conifer, or any tree with lots of limbs) only for a hang-on stand, not a saddle. Face the stand toward the trail or funnel and let the branches sit behind and beside you. For a saddle, pick a trunk with few branches.
m-stand_placement-branchy-tree-for-hang-.why: In a saddle, branches stop you moving around the tree, which is the whole point of a saddle; often the only shot left is straight behind you. In a stand the same branches break up your outline, help you climb, and hold gear. He can use a hang-on in more trees than a saddle, despite claims that a saddle works in any tree.

m-stand_placement-buck-route-across-doe-.action: Look for the bucks' cruising route that runs parallel to fields, ridges and drainages and cuts across the doe trails (does tend to walk straight up the draws; bucks travel across them). For morning stands, find the spots on a ridge system where lots of doe trails come together (the X's where five trails meet) and connect those X's along the terrain: a traveling mature buck walks a line hitting those intersections. On long fields there's usually a buck cruising trail just back off the edge.
m-stand_placement-buck-route-across-doe-.why: A buck on a cross-route checks every doe trail he crosses, picking up ground scent. If he smells something interesting he detours toward the doe group, stays about 30 to 40 yards from them while he checks, then goes right back to his route (Dixon).

m-stand_placement-cover-behind-you-01.action: Pick a stand tree with lots of cover BEHIND you and to the sides (limbs, cedars, other trees, the slope of the ridge); that matters more than cover in front. A smaller tree sitting in front of the cover is often better than a big tree buried in it.
m-stand_placement-cover-behind-you-01.why: Back cover breaks up your outline while leaving your shooting lanes open: a deer that looks up sees trunk and branches, not a human shape. Sturgis chose an 8 to 10 inch red cedar over 12 to 14 inch trees and big white oaks because it sat in front of the cover and needed far fewer limbs cut.

m-stand_placement-downwind-of-doe-groups.action: In the pre-rut and rut, don't cross doe bedding off your map; set up on the downwind side of where the does are, to intercept bucks scent-checking them. Pre-rut mornings: slip in while deer are still out on the food and set up just downwind of the trail along the inside edge of the thick doe bedding cover. Pre-rut evenings: back away from the big destination food and set up downwind of a smaller staging food source, or downwind of the trail from doe bedding to it. Rut: mark doe bedding, work out which way bucks would scent-check it on the likely rut winds (usually cruising downwind of it), and plan a stand to intercept that.
m-stand_placement-downwind-of-doe-groups.why: Pre-rut and rut bucks scout doe groups by cruising the downwind side of where the does spend their time: the bedding in the morning and midday, the staging food and the route to it in late afternoon. It lets them check for a hot doe while covering a lot of ground. Mornings you also catch deer going from food back to bed.

m-stand_placement-early-season-leaf-cove.action: In the early season, use the leaves to hide: you can tuck into a hardwood (or pines with saplings around them) and get away with much more than later. But watch constantly, because you often won't hear deer coming, and expect finicky, swirling wind.
m-stand_placement-early-season-leaf-cove.why: With leaves still on the trees you're hidden. But the leaves on the ground have been trampled and weathered for nine months and hold moisture, so deer walk in almost silently; a big buck reached 25 yards before he noticed. The swirling early-season wind is the hard part, in flat land, hills, and mountains alike.

m-stand_placement-evening-above-empty-bo.action: In the evening, sinking air pulls your scent downhill, so sit above a bottom, ravine, or ditch that deer won't be using: tuck up the side of the ravine in open hardwoods, out of the brush, watching ground you don't expect deer to come up through below you (Sturgis), or, where bucks hook a ridge in the last hour to check scrapes, sit on the ground at the top of a ditch where you feel the air coming off the ridge and pulling down into the ditch (Hunting Public). Know each hill spot's time window: some only work the first hour of the morning before the wind starts swirling, others only the last hour of the day.
m-stand_placement-evening-above-empty-bo.why: As it gets dark your scent filters down and saturates the bottom, which is fine only if deer won't be down there. Up in a tree the wind can swirl too much; on the ground at the ditch head your scent is pulled down the ditch away from the deer, trading visibility for not being smelled.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-stand_placement-evening-near-bedding-s.action: For an evening sit, set up close to where the buck gets out of bed, not on a food source a few hundred yards away. Hunt the staging spot on the edge of his bedding cover: the flat with rubs and scrapes where he first comes out of bed, 50 to 100 yards off the bedding, over a ridge or around a thick corner so you can sneak in (Sturgis), off to the side of it rather than in it (Sturgis), or tight to the edge of the thick cover on a trail or trail intersection coming out of it (McKay). Get close but never walk into the bedding itself in the afternoon.
m-stand_placement-evening-near-bedding-s.why: The MSU GPS-collar data show the evening movement peak comes about 1 hour after sunset, when you're already walking out; before that bucks mill near cover. A buck that only has to move 50 yards to reach you can do it in daylight; one bedded a couple hundred yards from a food plot often arrives after dark. McKay: big bucks ease out of the thick only 15 to 20 minutes before dark. Sturgis: he's only on his feet in daylight right as he gets up, the staging spot near the food is usually full of does and fawns, and deer already coming past you means no calls, decoys, or scent needed.

m-stand_placement-ground-break-up-outlin.action: On the ground, sit behind something that breaks you up. Best is a big tree at least as wide as you: on a mountainside set your seat behind (uphill of) it, where erosion often builds a flat spot (scrape the rocks out), and lean your gun or bow against it within reach. With no big tree, stick a few cut branches around you (low enough to shoot over), stake a screw-in tree umbrella in front as a mini blind, sit in the crown of a fallen tree or right behind its trunk so only your head shows, or tuck back into brushy cover and prune just one lane.
m-stand_placement-ground-break-up-outlin.why: Your outline and the motion of drawing are what give a ground hunter away; something must break you up or you'll get busted when you draw. With a gun, the big tree is also a solid rest: stand up behind it and slide the gun around its side for a 100 to 150 yard shot.

m-stand_placement-ground-move-slow-01.action: On the ground you're at a deer's eye level, so stay in the game: no phone, and when you turn your head to look, do it slow as molasses, never quick and jerky. Practice moving slowly at home so it's natural.
m-stand_placement-ground-move-slow-01.why: Every movement is exaggerated at ground level. He writes these reminders down over and over so they stick.

m-stand_placement-ground-seat-low-profil.action: You don't need a tree stand. Sit low on the ground in a turkey lounger or low seat with a back, and stay seated. Deer read a low, seated hunter as a stump.
m-stand_placement-ground-seat-low-profil.why: Deer don't recognize the human outline easily until you stand up on two feet. He's had does walk within 5 yards in open woods without noticing him, as long as he didn't move. A comfortable seat also keeps you more observant.

m-stand_placement-high-wind-drop-below-r.action: In hills with 300 to 400 feet of relief on a windy day, get 50 to 100 feet or more below the ridge top on the lee side. You'll hear the treetops roaring above while hardly a leaf stirs where you sit.
m-stand_placement-high-wind-drop-below-r.why: Once you're down about 100 feet the wind mostly passes overhead. Deer can still be up in that top layer, but the calm pocket below is where they shelter and move.

m-stand_placement-hunt-the-thick-01.action: Don't be afraid of thick stuff. Pine thickets, grown-up cutovers, and privet thickets full of browse hold deer. Climb where you can see down just one or two old skidder trails; you don't need to see 50 to 60 yards.
m-stand_placement-hunt-the-thick-01.why: Deer feel comfortable moving through thick browse. McKay used to hunt only hardwoods; now he'd rather hunt a pine thicket. Hunters who walked THROUGH thick cover to reach a creek bottom saw nothing, while he backed off and sat in it and saw deer all morning.

m-stand_placement-hunt-winds-he-already-.action: Hunt a buck on the same winds he's already shown up on in your trail-cam photos.
m-stand_placement-hunt-winds-he-already-.why: Then you aren't asking him to do something he isn't already doing.

m-stand_placement-inside-corners-and-tra.action: Hunt inside corners: on a field edge, where the tree line bends in toward the timber (not an outside corner where the woods poke out into the field), and along transition lines where one cover type meets another (hardwoods meeting a thicket or short pines), especially where a thicket cuts back into an inside corner. For afternoon stands, inside corners of fields and small hidden plots (a quarter to half acre) that sit on the natural movement between bedding and the main food are pass-throughs; a big tree at an inside corner is a great stand on its own.
m-stand_placement-inside-corners-and-tra.why: Deer walking the edge cut across the inside corner instead of going all the way around, which funnels them, and they avoid exposed outside corners in daylight (Downwind Hunting). Deer walk transition lines summer and winter and are 'always bad about cruising in and out of corners'; McKay's first sit at one had 13 to 15 does and two bucks chasing a doe (McKay). Deer pass freely through these spots in daylight on the way to the big food but don't sit in them till dark, so they stay huntable (Sturgis).

m-stand_placement-late-season-browse-01.action: For December and January, favor stands near young hardwood regrowth and browse.
m-stand_placement-late-season-browse-01.why: That's the food deer lean on once the season's crops and mast are gone.

m-stand_placement-mock-scrape-at-the-sho.action: Make one mock scrape per stand or blind, no more and no less, placed exactly where you expect to take the shot (Sturgis says this is his rule about 95% of the time): on the flat where several trails come together like a bow tie, or the funnel, bench, habitat change, or waterway edge the trail runs through, with a trail camera on it. If trails pass 20 yards down the hill and 10 yards up, put the scrape at your shot spot to pull them to one place. With a gun over a big food source it can go off to the side where you'd shoot, even at 120 yards. Don't ring a food plot with scrapes or scatter them around the property.
m-stand_placement-mock-scrape-at-the-sho.why: A mock scrape doesn't bring more bucks to your land; it stops the deer already passing in the spot you want. Bucks coming in lock onto the scrape and stare at it, so they're focused on it and not on you, and they stop in your lane. More scrapes just dilute the 'power of one' until none get used; a buck has only so much time and energy for scraping and there are plenty of natural scrapes. Scrape, stand, and camera in one spot also lets you monitor the area.

m-stand_placement-mock-scrape-flat-groun.action: Put the mock scrape on flat ground on the trail with room to turn all the way around (about 10 to 12 feet between trees), not on a hillside.
m-stand_placement-mock-scrape-flat-groun.why: On camera, deer working a scrape like to spin and rotate 360 degrees, and flat ground likely holds scent better. They don't walk uphill and back down to work it. Sturgis's crew learned this from their own hillside scrapes that didn't get used.

m-stand_placement-mock-scrape-just-insta.action: Don't let the perfect spot stop you; you can install a mock scrape at almost any stand in 15 to 20 minutes. In an open food plot with no tree where you want the shot, cut a small red cedar and 'transplant' it about 22 to 25 yards in front of the blind with a vine hanging from it.
m-stand_placement-mock-scrape-just-insta.why: Not using mock scrapes at all is the number-one fail. Needing store-bought scent or rope is just a hurdle; Sturgis's crew has thrown rope over branches 18 feet up and used ladder-stand sections to hang one where they wanted it.

m-stand_placement-mock-scrape-no-bought-.action: Make mock scrapes without store-bought scent: scrape a big dirt patch and pee in it. Put them in shooting range of your stands.
m-stand_placement-mock-scrape-no-bought-.why: Deer start using his within a day or two and keep using them all season once they're in a repeat pattern; he doesn't see how scent could make them work faster or stronger.

m-stand_placement-mock-scrape-on-active-.action: Put a mock scrape right over a trail deer are already walking, not off to the side (even next to a water hole): for example on an oak ridge deer cross to eat acorns on the way to the fields at night and back in the morning, or next to a real scrape if you find one. Hang the licking branch (paracord works) over bare scratched-out dirt, on a flat, open spot with no trees or brush piles crowding it, in front of your stand where you can shoot. Pick the stand, scrape, and camera spot at the same time; Rip 'n Stik sets the camera about 10 yards off.
m-stand_placement-mock-scrape-on-active-.why: Deer won't go out of their way to check a scrape: like a dog pulling 6 to 8 feet off the sidewalk to sniff a hydrant, not 10 yards. A water hole might pull them 10 yards but not 100, and a scrape beside a water hole instead of on a trail into it goes unused. On the trail, a deer nearly has to move its head to avoid the licking branch. Over time a good one can pull several trails together into one (Sturgis). A spot on the travel route gets every kind of deer, including cruising bucks (Rip 'n Stik). Sturgis's tried-and-true scrape set this way had all their major bucks at it the year before.

m-stand_placement-mock-scrape-plot-entra.action: At a small hunting plot, put the mock scrape at the defined entrance trail where several trails merge before the plot, in brushy cover where deer have nowhere else to go. You can mow a trail into it. Once a buck hits that scrape he's usually committed to walking out into the plot in front of the stand.
m-stand_placement-mock-scrape-plot-entra.why: Even if the scrape itself is out of bow range (a gun shot), it sets up the movement so the deer walks into your shot from another angle.

m-stand_placement-mock-scrape-sightline-.action: When you build a mock scrape near your stand, place the licking branch so a buck working it is not looking straight up at you.
m-stand_placement-mock-scrape-sightline-.why: A buck working McRae's mock scrape looked up the licking branch, saw him, and spooked. He and the doe ran 35 yards directly downwind and tried to wind him for 5+ minutes, then walked back in and the buck worked the scrape again, which McRae credits to his scent routine.

m-stand_placement-morning-back-in-cover-.action: Set morning stands back in the cover or brush, where you wait for deer returning from food, with tight shot windows (about 40 yards), and sneak in slowly in the dark; set afternoon stands toward food (small hunting plots, or the major food plots for gun and muzzleloader). A bow works even in gun season at those morning ranges.
m-stand_placement-morning-back-in-cover-.why: That matches the daily movement: deer leave cover for food in the evening and come back to it in the morning. 70 to 80% of Sturgis's crew's bucks come from those morning brush stands, across about 30 stand locations in Minnesota and Wisconsin.

m-stand_placement-morning-back-side-of-b.action: For a morning stand, come in from the side and set up on the back side of the mature buck's bedding (he figures the buck is bedding somewhere within about a 300-yard window), at a habitat change where nothing beds: a steep ravine or drop-off, open mature hardwoods, or an open field. Wait for bucks coming back from food to bed.
m-stand_placement-morning-back-side-of-b.why: Your scent blows into the ravine or off the hill where no deer are, and once thermals rise it lifts away. You're waiting where the buck ends his morning.

m-stand_placement-morning-sit-above-deer.action: In the morning in hills or mountains, sit so the rising air carries your scent uphill away from the deer: above the sign you're hunting (on a narrow bench or ridge flat, on the higher ground above it; on a wide flat, at the back edge where the slope starts to climb), or at a low point beside a hollow that runs uphill, so your scent goes up the hollow away from deer below.
m-stand_placement-morning-sit-above-deer.why: Rising morning thermals carry your scent up and away from deer coming in below, and a hollow gives that rising air a predictable path (Sturgis). Being above deer also lets you see them before they see you: 'like being in a tree stand without being in a tree stand' (Southern Outdoorsmen guest).

m-stand_placement-move-to-where-deer-are.action: Set up where deer actually move, not where you planned. Use observation sits first in a new area or on a bedding area you found (late summer or early season, before pressure; from a distance; in big woods or tall marsh grass where trails and cameras don't tell you much). When you see a buck use a spot you're not covering, move onto it: that same afternoon (Next Step Outdoors), the next morning on the exact route he cruised the evening before (McKay), or after deer pass a spot 2 or 3 times (Hunting Public). If a trail is about 100 yards away, pull the stand and move in; climb test trees until one clearly works (Ellis tried three), then hunt that tree repeatedly and move only if busted or clearly wrong. When you reach a planned tree, check whether blowdowns or root balls have shifted the trail, and move to cover where deer will now walk. Use a mobile setup (a saddle or a light hang-on with sticks) so you actually move when a spot looks wrong. If the wind is wrong for a tree, set up on the ground within shooting distance.
m-stand_placement-move-to-where-deer-are.why: Deer don't do what you expect; a mobile setup gets you a shot where they are. Bucks repeat routes: McKay's buck came the same exact way at 10 AM the morning after he watched it cruise by. Moving closer changes how the wind hits you, so test the new spot's wind at ground, 10 ft, and 20 ft and refine over 5 to 15 sits (Hunting Public). Ladders, permanent stands, and big box blinds tempt you to stay put because relocating is a pain (Kenyon). A couple of downed trees moved Hunting Public's trail 20 yards: the planned tree gave a 40-yard shot, the new one an 8-yard shot at a big buck. Bucks in pressured places often travel away from the obvious trees where hunters are (Next Step Outdoors).
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-stand_placement-no-light-in-blind-01.action: Don't turn on a light inside a box blind that faces a field, even a dim or colored one.
m-stand_placement-no-light-in-blind-01.why: Covered or colored, it will clear every deer out of the food plot or ag field in front of you.

m-stand_placement-no-skyline-01.action: Near a ridge top, set up far enough down the slope that you have mountain behind you, even if the best sign is on top. Same rule for tree stands.
m-stand_placement-no-skyline-01.why: Deer looking uphill will pick out a hunter silhouetted against the sky.

m-stand_placement-off-the-main-trail-01.action: For a mature buck, don't set up only on the most beaten-down trail. Cover where he moves within the same general funnel, off to the side of the main trail: the secondary trails near the big worn-in trails (Rex), or about 20 yards downwind of a worn trail, in the cover (Downwind Hunting). Place stands and cameras for his route, not the does' trail.
m-stand_placement-off-the-main-trail-01.why: Mature bucks walk through the same funnel (30, 150, even 300 yards wide) all the time but rarely on the exact trail; Dixon rarely saw one on the same trail within 3 yards day to day. He crosses and scent-checks the main trail but breaks his own route around it, maybe 50 yards out front of the camera or behind it (Dixon). Rex's camera history: the oldest deer rarely use the trails the masses use. Downwind Hunting: in daylight a mature buck parallels a worn trail 10 to 30 yards downwind to scent-check it; the trail carries does and young bucks.

m-stand_placement-on-the-way-food-not-de.action: In the afternoon, don't hunt the big destination food (bean or hay field, ag, big plot, bait) and don't sit right over any food. Hunt on the way to it: a small food spot in cover (a kill plot, a clover trail, an apple, crabapple or pear tree, a white oak dropping acorns), a pass-through plot at the corner where cover and trails funnel deer into range, a small hunting plot about 100 yards from the bedding, a water hole, a transition zone, the line where open cover meets thick cover, a ditch crossing, or the 'spokes' (the most logical paths leading into the food, a little way off it). Hunt off to the side of the food, not in the middle of the doe traffic and not back in the bedding. Early in the season, if cameras or glassing show a buck hitting the same food every afternoon, slip in and cut him off between cover and that food. In hot weather, pick shaded food or water near cover on the way.
m-stand_placement-on-the-way-food-not-de.why: Deer feel safe in cover and hit the small 'appetizer' food earlier, in daylight, then move on toward the main food by dark, so you get shots and can slip out. An older buck may not step into a big field until after dark. On the destination field deer may stand in front of you all night, an old doe will eventually pick you off and snort, and bumping them on the way out makes them stay in bed longer (Whitetail Evolution, Rex). Old bucks are antisocial and wait for the crowd to thin, which is why your food-source photos of them are at midnight (Rex). Keeping the big food undisturbed keeps the whole movement intact (Sturgis). In heat, deer hang back in shade and hit the open field only after dark (Sturgis).

m-stand_placement-open-crossing-low-dip-.action: Where a mature buck has to cross open ground (a field) between two blocks of thick cover, look for the lowest dip that is also the narrowest gap between the covers. Nine times out of ten that's where he crosses. Even 6 to 10 feet of terrain relief is enough for bucks to stay out of sight.
m-stand_placement-open-crossing-low-dip-.why: He's out of sight in the low spot and exposed for the shortest time, and the low spot may also let him smell what's around. Ground that looks flat always has folds; you learn this hunting open prairie country where deer are very visible.

m-stand_placement-perennial-scrapes-pre-.action: In the pre-rut, hunt the downwind side of perennial (primary, hub) scrapes, the ones in the same place every year. Mornings: perennial scrapes just downwind of doe bedding. Evenings: perennial scrapes in the staging food or along the bedding-to-food trail. Don't hunt over every scrape you find.
m-stand_placement-perennial-scrapes-pre-.why: Scrapes are how the whole herd (does and fawns too, not just bucks) communicates, like dogs marking the same post. A pre-rut buck checks them to learn which does are close to estrus and which bucks are around.

m-stand_placement-perfect-pinch-not-olde.action: Don't assume the 'perfect' pinch point is where you'll kill the oldest buck. Expect it to produce 3- to 5-year-olds, while the oldest bucks may stop 60 to 80 yards short and loop around it through a ravine or drainage. In the rut, a doe coming through can pull him through anyway, so stay put.
m-stand_placement-perfect-pinch-not-olde.why: The 8.5-year-old 'Teflon Don' refused Rex's pinch twice, once backing out after spotting him and once circling on a perfect crosswind, then walked right under him 20 minutes later trailing a doe on November 16. Derek Dixon's drone work found the same: some old bucks never use a 30-yard-wide ridge pinch.

m-stand_placement-pinch-two-stands-cross.action: At a strong pinch point, hang two stands (his were about 70 yards apart) so you have one for each opposite wind, set high (30 to 35 feet) in trees with lots of cover. Pick the stand that gives a crosswind to the buck's approach: a little right for him, a little right for you.
m-stand_placement-pinch-two-stands-cross.why: His best pinch was an inside field corner with a steep ravine just beyond, leaving a 70-yard strip of woods everything had to use; they killed a lot of good bucks there. A buck with the wind at his back stops short, tests the air, and scans; one did that and spotted Rex even 30 to 35 feet up.

m-stand_placement-ridge-crest-parallel-t.action: On long ridges in open hardwoods, look for the trail that runs parallel to the crest about 15 to 20 yards off the top, where it's a bit thicker just over the crest.
m-stand_placement-ridge-crest-parallel-t.why: Deer hug the thicker tops where the ridge breaks over.

m-stand_placement-rifle-pinch-close-01.action: Rifle season doesn't need long shots. In close cover, a pinch point stand still works; many of Sturgis's gun-season bucks came at about 25 yards.
m-stand_placement-rifle-pinch-close-01.why: Pinch points put deer close no matter the weapon.

m-stand_placement-right-tree-not-easy-tr.action: Pick the tree that's right for the deer, not the one that's easiest to climb. A saddle (or a light hang-on and sticks) works on crooked and branchy trees a climber can't.
m-stand_placement-right-tree-not-easy-tr.why: Climbers need a perfectly straight tree with no branches, which forces you into the wrong spot.

m-stand_placement-rub-line-marks-route-0.action: A short string of rubs (2 or 3, or several rubs along a route) marks a buck's travel route; hunt right on it. In the rut, when scrapes dry up and bucks travel A to B, look for 2 or 3 rubs along the downwind side of a thicket (his example: cedar), even with little trail there, and sit it through the middle of the day (Hunting Public). When several rubs all have their scarred side facing the same way, read that as his direction of travel and sit facing the smooth, unrubbed side so he walks toward you with the tree between you (Downwind Hunting).
m-stand_placement-rub-line-marks-route-0.why: One buck may pass that spot every day between about 8 AM and 4 PM in the rut; Hunting Public would rather have one deer at 10 yards than see 15 at 200. A buck rubs pushing into the tree while walking forward, so rubs line up with his travel, and coming in with the tree between you buys time before he steps into your lane (Downwind Hunting).
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-stand_placement-rut-dead-spot-move-01.action: During the rut, if your spot is dead, move toward the action instead of waiting for it to come to you: Danker moves even 150 to 200 yards deeper into the timber toward the freshest sign (big fresh rubs, a hot doe's area), speed-scouting to find it; the Hunting Public crew picks up and moves after an hour or two of nothing.
m-stand_placement-rut-dead-spot-move-01.why: Rut action is local: one hunter has a hot doe near him and has the best rut ever, while another half a mile away sees nothing and says there was no rut. A hot doe's area can stay good for about 5 days (Danker). A light mobile setup makes moving easy (Hunting Public).
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-stand_placement-rut-sit-the-focal-poin.action: In the rut, when a buck shows up on many of your cameras, stop chasing each photo. Work out the focal spot he passes through to get between those places (the center of his rut range) and sit there day after day, ignoring where else he shows up, as long as your access is clean enough not to damage it.
m-stand_placement-rut-sit-the-focal-poin.why: Lee was always a step behind 'Zeus' (203 inches) across 7 or 8 camera spots until he found the center point. He used the same lesson on a 170s typical, sitting one tree about 8 or 9 days straight until the buck came through on a doe. 'You got to be ahead of them, not behind them.'

m-stand_placement-saddle-trunk-between-0.action: In a saddle, set up with the trunk between you and where you expect deer, so they come straight toward the tree, then draw and shoot around it, ideally to your strong side. Expect trouble with deer that show up from the side or behind.
m-stand_placement-saddle-trunk-between-0.why: Hiding behind the trunk works very well when a deer comes head-on; unless the tree is tiny it can't see you, which lets you hunt trees with almost no cover (Next Step Outdoors). But turning around the tree for a deer behind or beside you usually gets you picked off, by mature bucks and even by does and fawns (Relentless Sportsman).

m-stand_placement-saddles-hill-country-0.action: In hill country, hunt saddles between two high points, especially in the rut.
m-stand_placement-saddles-hill-country-0.why: A saddle is the easiest way over. In a big-hardwood national forest in late season, Rex watched deer use saddles to cross from one area to another. Trails tend to run along the ridges, so a buck going up and over crosses more and more doe trails in the rut.

m-stand_placement-scent-over-no-deer-gro.action: Pick the stand so your downwind side is ground deer won't use: set up at the edge of a defined line of deer movement and blow your scent into a creek, off a point, over a hillside, into a wet swamp, or into brush or timber they don't use, or over water (a slough, pond, river), very thick vegetation, or a steep hill or sharp drop-off. Don't sit in the middle of where they feed (an oak flat raining acorns, the middle of a food plot). This matters most for all-day sits between bedding and food (water holes you can slip into from the side often work) and whenever you plan to call, especially blind calling. Avoid open ground or lots of intersecting trails behind you.
m-stand_placement-scent-over-no-deer-gro.why: Nothing you do with clothes, sprays or gadgets hides you from a deer that's downwind (Sturgis: set up this way and you could smell like a pig and still shoot a deer). With a barrier downwind no deer can get downwind of you all day. A called mature buck's first instinct is to circle downwind of the sound to size up the other deer and, in pressured areas, check it isn't a hunter; if that's easy, he'll smell you (Hunting Public: a grunt in a rut bedding thicket sent a buck circling downwind before they had a lane).
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-stand_placement-shade-toward-food-end-.action: In the early season, put your effort into afternoon hunts on the buck's bed-to-feed route, at a man-made or natural pinch point between bedding and food, and shade the stand toward the food end, away from the bedding. Don't push right up against a known bedding area on opening day.
m-stand_placement-shade-toward-food-end-.why: Early-season deer are local and predictable on a bed-to-feed pattern; bucks aren't cruising for does yet.
