They sit in thick, high stem-count bedding all day, and the closer you get to it the more likely you bump the buck out of his bed and change the pattern. Near the food side you let them come to you.

m-stand_placement-shot-on-strong-side-01.action: Before you hang the stand or saddle, pick where your most likely shot will be (where deer step into a field, or the first opening a deer hits coming down the trail) and face the setup so that spot is straight in front of you or on your strong side. For a right-handed shooter the strong side is roughly 7 to 11 o'clock, with deer passing to your left; a left-hander wants the trail on his right. In a saddle, hang the bow on the side it comes off easiest (left for a right-hander) and tuck the pack small on your lineman's belt with the quiver on the same carabiner so neither side is blocked. Plan to shoot your expected shots seated, turning without standing.
m-stand_placement-shot-on-strong-side-01.why: Your weapon is already pointed that way, so you just lift the bow off the hanger, draw, and shoot with little movement. A standing human silhouette in a tree is probably the scariest thing a deer can see, so shooting seated cuts your movement (Sturgis). Weak-side shots can be made but are harder.

m-stand_placement-sign-in-swirl-back-out.action: When you find a pile of fresh sign (acorns and droppings everywhere, a hot scrape, a heavy trail, a rub line) in a spot where the wind will swirl, like down in a hollow, don't set up on top of it. Back out to the edge: the transition or travel corridor leading into it, where the wind is more consistent and you can get in, hunt, and get out without alerting deer.
m-stand_placement-sign-in-swirl-back-out.why: Deer spend lots of time in those spots because the thermals and swirling wind give them 360-degree protection. Hunting in the swirl blows the area out quickly, and deer start using that food only at night.

m-stand_placement-small-clearcut-edges-0.action: Around smaller clearcuts (up to about 25 to 30 acres) surrounded by mature timber, hunt the edges. Deer walk around the outside of the cut instead of crossing it.
m-stand_placement-small-clearcut-edges-0.why: Even does that bed inside the edge of the cut back out to the wood edge and follow it when they move; with timber all around they're never forced through.

m-stand_placement-small-shooting-lanes-0.action: Keep shooting lanes small. Trim just enough to get an arrow through where you expect a deer to stop (North American Whitetail), or clear about three small shooting holes instead of wide lanes (Sturgis). Leave the low brush standing behind and around the stand so you walk in behind a wall of brush, and pile the cuttings there. Sturgis puts the mock scrape in the middle hole: see the buck in one hole, shoot him in the next.
m-stand_placement-small-shooting-lanes-0.why: The woods open up as the leaves fall from September to December, so a lane that's snug in early season is wide open later. Deer are very unlikely to walk through the brush wall to get to you, you're hidden coming in, and you don't have to 'cut down the world' to get a shot.

m-stand_placement-spooked-buck-hunt-next.action: After you spook a mature buck at a spot, stop hunting that exact spot but keep hunting next to it in the same core area. He'll avoid the place he was bumped for weeks, but he doesn't leave the core.
m-stand_placement-spooked-buck-hunt-next.why: Sturgis spooked 'Junior' off a water hole about October 25 that the buck had used weekly for years; he never came back to it in the six weeks before Sturgis killed him, but kept coming out of the same core. Sturgis shot him on a food source in that core where he hadn't been seen for over a month; it felt like hunting 'where he wasn't'.

m-stand_placement-staging-cover-off-fiel.action: For an evening sit near a field or food, don't sit on the open field edge or the field corner where you saw bucks in summer, and don't set up on the open-edge trail the does and young bucks use. Back into the cover 30 to 100 yards (Kenyon), 50 to 100 yards where thick cover turns to more open understory (Downwind Hunting), or about 40 yards in (McRae), to the thick soft edge running the same way where a mature buck stages before stepping out. McRae cut a room-sized opening 40 yards inside the thick cover and hunted it from a ground blind with two 12-15 yard lanes, piling the cut brush against the blind. Dixon's advice is the same area: hunt the small staging cover near where the does feed, because a mature buck's evening movement is condensed.
m-stand_placement-staging-cover-off-fiel.why: Mature bucks go the same general way as the other deer but stay in cover, stop just inside the thick where they feel safe, and stage there a long time (an hour or more, Downwind Hunting), often last to come out or after dark. McRae's buck milled in his opening 9 minutes before stepping into a lane. Dixon's thermal-drone tracking showed evening daylight movement is 'a toddler scribbling' around a staging area under about 200 acres, with about three favored evening spots; one buck even re-bedded 5 yards off a winter food plot corner with 45 to 50 minutes of light left. If you only hunt the edge where the other deer show, you'll almost never get a bow shot at the buck and will wrongly decide he's nocturnal.

m-stand_placement-stand-height-high-01.action: Hang tree stands at 20 to 22 feet instead of the usual 12 to 15.
m-stand_placement-stand-height-high-01.why: It cites Texas A&M research that scent disperses better from higher up before reaching a deer's nose, and higher cuts the chance of a deer picking out your outline. It says the steeper angle makes little accuracy difference at 15 to 30 yards.

m-stand_placement-stand-height-low-01.action: You don't need to be very high. Samko sits 14 to 18 feet on about 70% of hunts (15 to 16 is his sweet spot) and often only 10 to 12 feet; Bow Only Outdoors typically sits 14 to 18 feet and adds an extra rope aider (about 3 to 4 feet) to reach 20 to 22 feet only when a spot needs it. 'Climb to the cover': go only as high as the tree's cover needs.
m-stand_placement-stand-height-low-01.why: The higher you are, the steeper the shot angle and the farther out a deer has to be. From 20 feet a compound or crossbow shooter loses the 5 to 8 yard shots and can only shoot from about 12 yards out; Samko's average shot is about 9 yards, many at 4 to 5. Bow Only Outdoors' biggest buck ever was shot from about 8 feet, with many good encounters at 8, 10, and 12 feet.

m-stand_placement-stand-level-or-back-01.action: Set the hang-on stand level or tilted just slightly back toward the tree, never forward or to the side. Pick the bracket height on the tree for your shooting lanes and any limbs you can hold.
m-stand_placement-stand-level-or-back-01.why: A tree leaning back a hair is ideal; you sit comfortably against the trunk instead of leaning out.

m-stand_placement-stand-work-in-rain-win.action: Hang, move, and maintain stands and clear shooting lanes during moderate or hard rain with lots of wind (not in thunder and lightning). Still wear your safety harness. While you're there, scout the area for fresh sign, since you picked it for expected movement.
m-stand_placement-stand-work-in-rain-win.why: Setting a stand means walking around and touching things, and normally that presence lingers a long time. In rain and wind your scent doesn't linger and the commotion hides you, so it's a non-event unless you spook deer right at the spot.

m-stand_placement-stand-work-in-summer-0.action: Hang stands and cut shooting lanes in summer (July), not the week before season. Cut with a fine-tooth pruning saw rather than loppers.
m-stand_placement-stand-work-in-summer-0.why: Every cut, step, and bolt leaves scent, noise, and visual change that takes weeks to fade. Done three months ahead, the spot smells like the woods again by October. Lopper cuts are green and sappy and bleed scent for days; saw cuts dry faster.

m-stand_placement-stay-outside-edge-pull.action: Stay on the outside edge of the deer movement; don't push another 30 yards in past it. If you need deer closer, pull or squeeze the movement toward you instead: drop a tree (private land), make a mock scrape about 25 yards in front of you, put in a water hole (Sturgis), or pile the limbs you cut from your lanes into brush piles that force deer to walk around them into a narrower window in front of you (Downwind Hunting).
m-stand_placement-stay-outside-edge-pull.why: If you cross a deer trail and a buck or doe ends up behind you, your hunt is blown. Downwind Hunting says Wisconsin land managers narrow travel corridors by 15 to 20 yards with brush piles, turning an open woodlot into a defined shooting lane.

m-stand_placement-terrain-gaps-deer-must.action: In hill and mountain country, mark where deer physically can't travel (cliffs, bluffs, rock walls, impassable slopes) with mapping software, then verify on foot. Hunt the gaps that are left: 'invisible funnels' often 30 to 150 yards wide (Dixon), the gap or ledge where deer actually get up and down a bluff (McKay), or a cut in a long high wall where doe trails funnel through (Rex). In the rut, sitting at the top of a drainage in one of these is high-odds; be ready for an all-afternoon wait. On gun-hunt days, sit at the bottom of a bluff gap so deer pushed off the top by other hunters come to you.
m-stand_placement-terrain-gaps-deer-must.why: Deer can't cross the wall anywhere else, so every buck Dixon tracked walked through those passable gaps. Stacking funnels with saddles and mixed habitat raises your odds. Bucks use them the same way: on a warm November afternoon Rex watched a 140-class buck walk to the cut in a 3/4-mile high wall, bed there, fall asleep, and wait about 2 hours until a doe came up the bank. McKay's gap had a scrape right at the top.

m-stand_placement-trail-and-terrain-junc.action: Look for spots where several trails pinch into one place: a creek crossing, the head of a draw where trails cut across, a bench that dumps out at a point, where two benches meet or a bench meets a saddle between two ridges, a gap through a bluff wall, or a clear lane through a blowdown or dying pines. Walk a trail until you hit where others join it.
m-stand_placement-trail-and-terrain-junc.why: Deer come from several directions instead of along one trail, which 'peaks the odds up greatly' (McKay). Deer follow benches like sidewalks to avoid climbing straight up or down, so bench junctions are natural travel intersections (Downwind Hunting). In a tornado blowdown a doe on the run in the rut takes the one clear path, and a buck follows (McKay).

m-stand_placement-trim-lanes-from-stand-.action: Trim shooting lanes while sitting in the stand at hunting height, not from the ground.
m-stand_placement-trim-lanes-from-stand-.why: A lane that looks clear from the ground often has a branch blocking it at the 15 to 20 foot height your arrow or bullet actually travels.

m-stand_placement-tucked-elevated-blind-.action: To bowhunt from a blind, tuck a small elevated blind (about 5 feet up) into a shrub cluster so its top sits level with the brush, with a wall of brush in front so deer can't walk up to it, and enter from the back. Put a mock-scrape licking tree about 30 yards out (his is 32-33) to set up 20-30 yard shots.
m-stand_placement-tucked-elevated-blind-.why: Deer in the field don't notice a blind that blends into the shrubs, and a back entrance lets you get in unseen. It's also where he goes when weather is involved.

m-stand_placement-walk-the-tree-deer-eye.action: When you find a spot, don't just drop a pin. Walk the deer trail and look at your tree from the deer's eyes: can he see you, where can you draw (for example when he passes behind a small cedar), which branches will be in the way. Note the height of the best cover (e.g., a fork at 18 ft means 4 sticks), whether it suits a saddle or a stand, and which wind it's for. Then track your route out so you know your access.
m-stand_placement-walk-the-tree-deer-eye.why: He doesn't want to leave a spot with questions unanswered. The details decide whether a deer walks into a shot or picks you off.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-stand_placement-watch-bedded-buck-from.action: For a buck bedded in a low hole out of the wind, set up on an adjacent ridge looking down into the bedding and watch for him to stand up and browse around mid-morning, then move in for the shot.
m-stand_placement-watch-bedded-buck-from.why: That buck was in his bed well before daylight, so there was no catching him on the way in; spotting him when he stood up mid-morning is how they killed him.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-stand_placement-waterhole-looks-natura.action: Make a water hole look natural: bury the tank so no edge sticks out (at or below grade), rake the area smooth, seed it before a rain so a green carpet grows instead of a bare dirt pad, clear dead branches and brush out of view, and use a black tank, not white or light blue. Never set the tank on top of the ground.
m-stand_placement-waterhole-looks-natura.why: When his tanks were only half buried, does stomped, stared and ran, and a whole herd split and left. A bare dirt pad and bright colors look like something that doesn't belong in the woods and make deer wary for months.

m-stand_placement-weather-break-food-nea.action: When a storm is about to break, wait at an isolated food source close to the bedding area.
m-stand_placement-weather-break-food-nea.why: Hungry deer that sat out the storm come off their beds and head straight to nearby food once the weather breaks.

m-where_to_hunt-be-the-sanctuary-01.action: When the neighbors all hunt hard (food plots, feeders, protein troughs, riding the property on ATVs every day), do the opposite: treat your ground like a sanctuary, stay out, and keep human intrusion as close to zero as you can. If you put out food at all, scatter a little by hand so it looks natural, never a pile.
m-where_to_hunt-be-the-sanctuary-01.why: Pressure all around pushes deer to the safe spot. Deer won't pick food over safety, and a mature buck shies away from things he knows don't belong, like a 150-pound pile of corn. Corn is only about 10% protein and deer have plenty of better natural food.

m-where_to_hunt-bed-with-a-view-01.action: In wooded hills with lots of coyotes and bobcats, look for mature bucks bedded on fairly open wooded ridges with a small patch of cover to break them up (a treetop, a fallen tree, a snag), not deep in the thickest brush.
m-where_to_hunt-bed-with-a-view-01.why: Predators that hunt by nose spend their time in the thick stuff and work on deer all year. Deer still browse in thick cover, but now bed where they can see, hear, and smell danger coming. In the late 70s and early 80s the same deer bedded in thick 'grouse cover.'

m-where_to_hunt-bedding-layers-from-food.action: Expect deer to bed in layers moving back from the food: does and fawns closest, then young bucks, then the mature buck farthest back in the depth of the cover, apart from the others. Walk back from the food, past the doe bedding, to the next change in habitat or habitat quality to find him. Distances by source: does and fawns in the first 50-100 yards, young bucks the next 100-150, mature bucks about 250-300 yards on managed private land and about 600 yards to half a mile on public land (Sturgis, 9Vhoz1xfjAU); mature buck about 300 yards of cover back from the food, farther if the area is packed with does and fawns (Sturgis, jJZLFq_elHM); in the late season does and fawns within the first 100 yards and bucks 200-400 yards out (Sturgis, rdhghXOJGhE); does bedded within 50 yards of a big food plot ringed by plain mature timber (Dixon). A big plot with no mixed cover around it holds does but no resident mature buck, so hunt it from the pre-rut through the late season, when bucks cruise through checking the does (Dixon). On a cover-poor ag lease (say 200 acres with only 20 in cover) he'll be in that 20 acres, next to whatever consistent food there is (Sturgis).
m-where_to_hunt-bedding-layers-from-food.why: Mature bucks don't want to bed with does and fawns or younger bucks, so deer layer themselves through the cover; does and fawns tolerate disturbance near food (traffic, a farmer driving by) and want to be close to the afternoon food (Sturgis). Too many does and fawns, and the social stress from them, push mature bucks deeper or off the property. In the cold, deer want to be close to food and won't travel half a mile every day to reach it. Dixon's thermal-drone flights found the does living beside a big timber-ringed plot while the bucks only passed through. You should find fewer and fewer deer the deeper you go ('depth of cover').

m-where_to_hunt-bust-mast-browse-01.action: In a bust acorn year, stop hunting for the one dropping oak and find what deer switched to. Hunt green browse where sunlight reaches the forest floor: forest edges, logged cuts, thickets with vines and shrubs (honeysuckle, greenbrier, jasmine, ragweed), knee-high browse with the buds bitten off, and thick privet with droppings everywhere. Look for nipped-off browse and follow whatever fresh sign you find, and scout in season to find it. Also check beech trees for beechnuts and thin-shelled hickories deer can crack (ehHCF9zlTyg guest).
m-where_to_hunt-bust-mast-browse-01.why: In Alabama's bust year the ehHCF9zlTyg guest walked miles looking for a dropping oak, found a few with a little sign, and never saw a deer on them; deer didn't travel far for a lone oak, they switched to whatever food was easy, and national forest areas being logged had far more sign and deer. In bad mast years McKay found privet thickets with more droppings than a food plot, and deer feeding on bluffside plants, while the usual hardwood spots were empty. Browse sign is subtle and takes more woodsmanship than spotting acorns.

m-where_to_hunt-creek-bottom-sign-is-nig.action: Treat rubs and scrapes along creek bottoms as mostly nighttime sign. If the bottoms have no food, move up into thicker cover with more browse.
m-where_to_hunt-creek-bottom-sign-is-nig.why: Creek bottoms are easy to find buck sign in, but much of it gets made after dark.

m-where_to_hunt-daylight-moves-in-cover-.action: Expect mature bucks to move in daylight inside and along the edge of thick cover, not across open ground. If a buck only shows on your camera after dark, assume he's up in daylight somewhere else, not nocturnal, and move your setup toward his cover (or the edge of the thick stuff) instead of sitting the food longer (MSU study). Bucks cut corners staying just inside the thick cover, following its edge between bedding and food, and almost never cross open timber you can see through; where there's a lot of hunting pressure, hunt how they move through that cover, because that's where you'll catch them in daylight if you catch them at all (Kenyon).
m-where_to_hunt-daylight-moves-in-cover-.why: Bucks are never more than about 50% bedded at any moment, day or night, and outside the rut they're bedded only about 38% of daylight; at midday many take two or three short bedding bouts with slow, snacking movement between. A buck bedded far away, maybe a couple thousand yards off your property, can be moving all afternoon and still reach your food after dark (MSU). Staying near safety is how they got old; they move there when the wind favors them and their nose tells them whether you're there, and in the rut with a west wind they walk the downwind side of the thick cover scent-checking it (Kenyon).

m-where_to_hunt-early-morning-back-of-be.action: Early-season mornings can work in big woods and on public land: get to the back side of a precise bedding cover (heavy brush, mounds, a ditch, an island of cover with oaks dropping acorns), coming in through thick cover or water where you don't expect deer, and wait for bucks returning from distant food a couple of hours after daylight.
m-where_to_hunt-early-morning-back-of-be.why: In wooded country deer travel farther between bedding and food and are used to moving more in daylight, so they're still walking back to bed after sunrise. That lets you slip in ahead of them, and on public land you want to be there before another hunter gets the chance.

m-where_to_hunt-food-in-its-window-now-0.action: Hunt the food that is in its window right now, on your own local calendar. Any one food (clover, beans, corn, peas, brassicas, wheat, rye, oats) draws deer for about 6 to 8 weeks of the season at most; in Sturgis's area green beans in September, standing corn not eaten until around November, beans gone once harvested in October, clover fading by early December. Learn when each oak species drops in YOUR area and hunt the ones dropping now: swamp chestnut oaks drop around Halloween in some places but mid-September in South Georgia, and some hunters' white oaks don't drop until November (ehHCF9zlTyg guest). A buck holds only where some food lasts all season with no gaps.
m-where_to_hunt-food-in-its-window-now-0.why: When a food source has a hole in its season, deer go elsewhere (Sturgis). An oak-drop calendar from someone in another region will send you to the wrong trees at the wrong time, and terrain and habitat can shift it too (ehHCF9zlTyg guest). If deer hit a neighbor's field instead of yours, look at pressure, location, early-season food to set the pattern, and winter cover before blaming the seed variety (Sturgis).

m-where_to_hunt-go-deep-01.action: On public land, be willing to get far past other hunters. McKay often walks 2 to 3+ miles and uses a GPS tracker (e.g. onX) to see where he's already been and go look at the places he hasn't. Sturgis uses a back-door approach to reach the middle of a big block (several hundred acres or more) whose access points are about a mile away in most directions, gets in there in the morning, and waits for deer to come back to him.
m-where_to_hunt-go-deep-01.why: Most of McKay's public-land bucks came from deep spots; before GPS he had to backtrack his own path, and seeing gaps in your track shows you overlooked spots. Hunters coming in from all the access points push deer toward the middle, where few people go; that's how Sturgis shoots most of his public-land bucks.

m-where_to_hunt-grass-edge-in-wind-01.action: Where there's tall grass (switchgrass, big bluestem, CRP) on field edges or near bedding, expect deer, and does hiding fawns, to bed in it in wind. Hunt the downwind edge of that grass on a windy day.
m-where_to_hunt-grass-edge-in-wind-01.why: Tall grass keeps deer out of the wind and weather, breaks up the sun, and hides them from view across an open food plot, so they feel safe there.

m-where_to_hunt-gun-day-escape-routes-01.action: On crowded public-land gun days, set up on the escape route other hunters will push deer into: a point leading up off a creek system, a gap off a bluff, below where people walk in.
m-where_to_hunt-gun-day-escape-routes-01.why: If you know which way the crowd is coming from, you can bowhunt the push, and it's worked well for him.

m-where_to_hunt-hot-dry-juicy-food-01.action: In hot, dry weather, hunt the food with the most moisture. Look for soft mass (apples, crabapples, pears, plums, persimmons) just outside the bedding area or on the way to the evening food, and lush green food: brassicas, clover, late beans or peas, oats. On public land, find the green spots where sunlight reaches the ground, like a wet swamp edge with trefoil or clover.
m-where_to_hunt-hot-dry-juicy-food-01.why: Fruit carries far more moisture than acorns, and deer that have sat dry all day crave it. Lush green food is the opposite of the dry cover they bed in all day, so it pulls them.

m-where_to_hunt-hot-shady-beds-01.action: When the early season runs hot (his example: 15° above average), don't stay home. Look for deer bedded in the coolest shade: a north-facing ridge under cliffs or boulders, or down in the sand of a dry creek bed, rather than a sunny cedar ridge.
m-where_to_hunt-hot-shady-beds-01.why: Deer are still there, they just use the area differently. Those beds can feel 10° cooler than the ground around them. And on public land, hot days mean almost nobody else is out.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-where_to_hunt-hot-water-on-the-way-01.action: In hot weather or an extended dry spell, sit water that lies between the bedding and the afternoon or evening food. Deer bedded high and dry will hit it first thing when they get up. Keep hunting it for a while even after rain comes back.
m-where_to_hunt-hot-water-on-the-way-01.why: They've sat hot and thirsty all day. They won't drop 300 feet and walk 700 yards to a creek and back, but they'll drink on the way to food, and they'll keep doing it all season. The drier it gets the more deer hit water (his tanks dropped 6-7 inches out of 20-24 after 18 days without rain). A drought sets a pattern: the morning after the first real rain, deer still came to the water holes with puddles everywhere, because that's where they plan to drink on the way to food. On a warm opener he saw a 2-year-old 8-point, a doe and fawn, and another doe at one.

m-where_to_hunt-hunt-dropping-oaks-01.action: Hunt the oaks that are actually dropping acorns this year, and favor white oaks. Use binoculars in late summer and early season to see which trees are loaded, and don't sit under a big oak just because it dropped the last two years (Grant Woods, McKay). When white oaks are dropping, bowhunt them; they're McKay's go-to tree. In the South Carolina/Georgia white-oak window a hot white oak is close to a sure thing morning and evening (sGtmLizXCwo guest: red oaks start first in the early season, then deer switch to white oaks, which peak around late October for about two weeks). Keep track of red oak stands across seasons; in the years they make a crop, deer and bucks pile into them (McKay).
m-where_to_hunt-hunt-dropping-oaks-01.why: White oak acorns taste better, so they're the first choice, and if a tree has no acorns this year there probably won't be deer there this year (Woods). Red oaks don't make a crop every year: one year a stand of red oaks was so thick with acorns 'you could rake it up with a five gallon bucket' and three hunters killed good bucks there (McKay). The sGtmLizXCwo guest tells his guests there's a 90% chance of a shot at a deer (maybe does, not always a buck) on a hot white oak in that window.

m-where_to_hunt-hunt-the-route-not-the-b.action: Don't build your hunting around sitting an individual buck bed. Hunt his route into and out of bedding instead. Once he arrives he may stand at a rub or scrape for 10 to 15 minutes, then lies down and stays within about a 50-yard circle (Dixon). In the Deep South's big woods, bucks don't reliably reuse a bed at all (McKay).
m-where_to_hunt-hunt-the-route-not-the-b.why: Very few people can position themselves on a buck inside that small circle; the travel in and out is where he's huntable (Dixon). In the Deep South bucks have endless places to lie down and GPS studies show they use a different bed every day, sometimes twice a day; a well-used bed McKay watched on camera was used by an 8-point, a spike, and several does, and sitting a bed hoping the buck comes back never worked for him.

m-where_to_hunt-late-bachelor-corn-01.action: In the late season in farm country, look for bucks grouped back up in bachelor groups on cut cornfields, the best food left. Expect the oldest buck to be off on his own rather than with the group.
m-where_to_hunt-late-bachelor-corn-01.why: Lee saw 10 to 12 bucks together on cut corn, but the giant he later killed was never with them.

m-where_to_hunt-late-bed-out-of-wind-01.action: In late-season cold (end of November into December, daytime highs of 5 to 10°F) with strong south winds, look for deer bedded on north-facing slopes out of the wind. Expect them to feed on south-facing slopes, not bed there.
m-where_to_hunt-late-bed-out-of-wind-01.why: Getting out of the wind saves them more energy than sun does; wind matters more than cloudy versus sunny. Bedding on south slopes to catch the sun is mostly a myth; he finds lots of sheds on south slopes because deer feed there overnight where the browse is.

m-where_to_hunt-late-cover-next-to-food-.action: In cold late season, look for spots with both ingredients: high stem-count cover (briars, hardwood regeneration, brush, upland cover, blowdowns) where deer bed and browse in daylight, right next to a good afternoon food source (standing corn, a clearcut, green food plots or brassicas, late-standing beans). You can hunt a big clearcut on public land almost like a cornfield.
m-where_to_hunt-late-cover-next-to-food-.why: Deer need daytime browse and cover, and they won't be in the brush unless good food is close by. A great food source with no thick cover nearby only gets visited at midnight, after deer sneak across open ground they know is pressured.

m-where_to_hunt-late-oct-scrapes-01.action: Toward the end of October, move to scrapes on the edges of thick cover and doe bedding areas, with setups for different winds. If you find a hot scrape on the edge of a bedding area, you know you didn't spook anything, and the wind is right, hunt it right away. If scrapes are your strength, take your vacation at the end of October, when bucks are heavily scraping, rather than during the rut.
m-where_to_hunt-late-oct-scrapes-01.why: When bucks start running scrape lines closer to doe bedding, a scrape puts a buck on a spot within bow range, and he comes in preoccupied so you can draw. He may be lying 70 yards away.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-where_to_hunt-lee-in-high-wind-01.action: When it's windy, don't sit your favorite exposed ridge-top oak. Hunt the quiet side, out of the wind: low ground, the lee side of a ridge, a low bowl or draw, or the downwind side of conifers, a swamp, thick brush, or a big tall-grass (switchgrass/CRP) field.
m-where_to_hunt-lee-in-high-wind-01.why: Deer do move more when it's windy, but they move to get OUT of the wind, which crowds a disproportionate number of them onto the quiet side. With the wind roaring 200 feet above him, it was nearly still 60 yards below, and that's where the deer went. His record day (over 40 deer, southwest Wisconsin, about 2010) was deer walking from a windy hollow, over a saddle, down into the lee draw.

m-where_to_hunt-lockdown-barrier-01.action: During lockdown, go to where bucks hold does, not to the funnel stand. Look for spots where bucks pin does against a barrier every year (his example: the edge of a river in a bottom) and hunt there.
m-where_to_hunt-lockdown-barrier-01.why: The buck uses the barrier to block other bucks from the doe's back side. A locked-down buck may not walk through your funnel for a week and a half.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-where_to_hunt-not-always-high-01.action: Don't assume mature bucks bed high (the 'top third of the elevation' idea). Look for benches and the flat on a point just before it drops off steeply, placed beyond the doe layer.
m-where_to_hunt-not-always-high-01.why: If food sits right next to the high ground, bucks won't bed there; the layering from food decides it, not elevation. If you put food down in that low flat, you'd erase the mature-buck bedding there.

m-where_to_hunt-not-always-leeward-01.action: Don't count on bucks bedding on the leeward side of a ridge. Expect them on the side they approach from (for example the side facing the food they came from) and on whichever side has thick cover, like mountain laurel.
m-where_to_hunt-not-always-leeward-01.why: Derek often found bucks bedded on the windward side facing into it, even at 5°F with sleet. Beau finds deer on the covered windward side when the leeward side is open timber, especially in pressured places.

m-where_to_hunt-overlooked-spots-close-0.action: Don't automatically hike to the back. Check the small, overlooked cover and the 'too easy' spots other hunters walk past or write off: spots close to the parking lot or road (the Hunting Public crew hunted mostly within half a mile of the road in Michigan), a small CRP thicket beside a timber line that everyone walked past on their way two miles into a river bottom, or a tiny corner of someone's lot with some hardwoods by a river, backed up to the big cover a buck lives in (Lee Ellis's 'breadcrumb' spots). Use your GPS track to see which pockets you haven't been into yet. On a short trip, count the real hours before picking a remote spot: 3 miles as the crow flies can be 4.5 miles on foot around ridges and rivers and 3 hours in the dark if you're trying not to spook deer. Keep five or six options so you can move to plan B, C, D.
m-where_to_hunt-overlooked-spots-close-0.why: Everybody goes way to the back to get away from the masses, so that's where the masses are, and the deer know it; old bucks survive by doing uncharacteristic things, which is why novices dropped in 'bad' or easy spots kill so many giant bucks every year (Mike Rex). The Hunting Public crew's 'buck nest' thicket produced encounter after encounter with big deer because hunters walked right by it, and going far back often just turns up someone else's camera and stand, burning a whole day of a four-day hunt. Most hunters look at a map and hit the obvious big properties first; some of Ellis's biggest bucks, including the 'upside down buck', came from nook-and-cranny spots nobody else bothered with.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-where_to_hunt-post-ehd-rebound-01.action: When choosing an area or lease, don't write off a region hit by a severe EHD die-off. Expect a few rough years, then some of the best big-buck hunting about 4 to 6 years later, often with cheaper leases and land right after the outbreak.
m-where_to_hunt-post-ehd-rebound-01.why: Jefferson and Harrison counties, Ohio, had a big outbreak in 2017 and were number one and two of 88 counties in record-book entries six years later: fewer deer means better nutrition and less stress, and it clears out scrub bucks. After the recent (about 2025) southeast Ohio outbreak, leases opened up and land prices dipped.

m-where_to_hunt-public-full-day-layout-0.action: On public land, get remote, then plan the whole day as a layout: a morning sit behind the bedding, then move around to set up mobile near the food for the afternoon.
m-where_to_hunt-public-full-day-layout-0.why: The same layering applies anywhere; hunting pressure just pushes the layers farther out. Using both ends of the day gets the most from each trip.

m-where_to_hunt-public-habitat-edges-01.action: Narrow a huge public area (10,000 acres) down to a few hundred by crossing off the parts near access points and people trails and the obvious hardwoods people wander into from their cars, then circling where several edges come together: a hillside meeting a swamp, mature timber meeting a clearcut, natural waterways, uplands turning to hardwoods, islands in a marsh. In steep country, look at benches, saddles, and points.
m-where_to_hunt-public-habitat-edges-01.why: Public land is big unbroken blocks of one habitat, so deer movement concentrates where habitats meet. Marshes and steep terrain limit where deer can travel, which makes their routes predictable.

m-where_to_hunt-rare-mountain-water-01.action: In the mountains, look on the map for an area that has very few spring heads or water sources, then find the one water source in it. Hunt around that spot.
m-where_to_hunt-rare-mountain-water-01.why: Where water is scarce, deer, bears, and other animals all get sucked into the one source there, so it concentrates them.

m-where_to_hunt-read-other-hunters-01.action: On public land, mark signs of other hunters as you scout: trash, trail markers, reflective tacks, trimmed shooting lanes and branches, tree stands, trail cameras. If the first obvious cover off the fields nearest the access is full of stands, move farther from the access into less obvious spots. A stand you find isn't a dead end; the owner may rarely hunt it, so a weekday sit can still work.
m-where_to_hunt-read-other-hunters-01.why: The most obvious places get the stands and the pressure. He found one stand 20 yards away and another 100 yards away in the first chunk of cover off the ag, so he skipped spending time on that area.

m-where_to_hunt-rut-hunt-the-does-01.action: In the rut, plan your hunts around the doe groups. Don't give up on a ridge full of does just because no buck has come through yet; the timing wasn't right, and when the rut is on, bucks will come to them (McKay, pre-rut and rut). In peak rut, expect some mature bucks to bed just downwind of a group of bedded does, sometimes with two or three other bucks nearby, and scent-check them for the 4 to 6 hours they're bedded midday (Dixon).
m-where_to_hunt-rut-hunt-the-does-01.why: 'Find the does, find the bucks' took McKay a long time to learn: his biggest bucks often came from where the does hung out, not where he got the buck's picture. After a long morning scent-checking does, bedding downwind of a doe group lets a buck keep working while he rests (Dixon).

m-where_to_hunt-rut-quiet-side-01.action: In the rut on a windy day, hunt the quiet side hard. Deer blown off the ridges and open hardwoods pile in behind conifers, behind tall grass, and on lee slopes, and bucks are cruising for does in that same pocket.
m-where_to_hunt-rut-quiet-side-01.why: Packing a disproportionate number of deer into the quiet side during the rut is 'like throwing gas on fire.'

m-where_to_hunt-rut-water-01.action: In the pre-rut and rut (late October and November), hunt water holes, even when it's cold (Sturgis). The best spot combines a water source with a perennial scrape on the downwind side of doe bedding or along the bedding-to-food trail, and water matters even more in a drought (Whitetail Evolution).
m-where_to_hunt-rut-water-01.why: Bucks are cruising and checking does, covering more ground than usual, and they work up a thirst, so they hit water more than usual; a drought makes the whole herd use it more.

m-where_to_hunt-satellite-bucks-sign-01.action: In the rut, read the woods on the way in. If you bump a couple of young bucks close together and see fresh scrapes (with fresh urine in them) and rubs that weren't there before, something is happening: likely a hot doe with a big buck locked down with her nearby. Hunt there, even if it's only 400 yards from the car.
m-where_to_hunt-satellite-bucks-sign-01.why: Satellite bucks circle a doe that a bigger buck is tending, and they leave the out-of-place sign. He learned this by blowing it about 15 times, walking in and flushing the doe and then a big 8-pointer.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-where_to_hunt-season-focus-01.action: Early bow season, focus on food, water, and bedding. In the rut, hunt trails, food, and water, and expect a buck chasing a doe to show up almost anywhere.
m-where_to_hunt-season-focus-01.why: Deer follow different patterns early than later in the season.

m-where_to_hunt-shed-marks-core-01.action: If you find a specific buck's shed, treat that spot as his core area and hunt it next season.
m-where_to_hunt-shed-marks-core-01.why: It's the closest thing to being in his bedroom. He found a buck's shed and a big bed on a bluff top above a thicket, then killed the buck the next season within sight of where the shed and bed were.

m-where_to_hunt-short-trip-sprint-01.action: On a short public-land hunt (like a 5-day gun opener trip), hunt it like a sprint, not a marathon: find the freshest sign of the moment, get right in on top of it, hunt it hard, and leave. Don't worry much about spooking something. Rain and poor weather make getting in close even easier.
m-where_to_hunt-short-trip-sprint-01.why: You aren't managing that ground for the whole season, so current sign beats long-term caution.

m-where_to_hunt-small-daylight-core-01.action: Hunt a mature buck at his small daylight core, not across his whole range. Outside the rut he usually moves only 200 to 300 yards in daylight, from where he beds to where he feeds (Sturgis: about 300 yards for about 90% of the season). Even in the rut he may cover 5 miles at night but stay in the same 10 to 15 acres of cover by day. Find that bed-to-food pair and set up on it, even on a small parcel. To find the core in pressured country, look for the 10-20% of the property that is nearly impossible to walk through: young regrowth about 8-10 years old with a very high stem count that still has grasses, weeds, briars, blackberry, privet, and green brier, ideally with a creek, and set up right on or inside it (McRae).
m-where_to_hunt-small-daylight-core-01.why: His home range may be about three square miles, but that is mostly night movement; if he covered it in daylight, crossing every fence line and hunter, he'd be dead (Sturgis). With food, water, and cover within a few steps he barely needs to move: McRae's Georgia bucks lived in cores of about 10-11 acres, and one lived 430 yards from a spot McRae camera-watched for months and never once walked by it, while neighbors on four sides never got his picture. Sturgis hunted the same bucks year after year on a Wisconsin piece with only about 30 acres of cover. The older the buck, the more he sticks to cover; rut miles are deceiving, and GPS-style tracks show he didn't leave his core cover in daylight.

m-where_to_hunt-start-at-current-food-01.action: Start every search for a buck at the current food source, then work back from it. On public land that might be a clearcut, white oaks dropping in early September, red oaks in October-November, an old homesite with apple trees, a swamp edge where hardwoods turn to conifers, or even a cluster of bait sites.
m-where_to_hunt-start-at-current-food-01.why: Food sets where everything else beds. On public land the 'food of the moment' changes through the season.

m-where_to_hunt-stay-in-one-area-01.action: Where deer roam and aren't on tight patterns, keep hunting the same general area (not necessarily the same tree) rather than bouncing between spots, while watching your access and wind so your scent doesn't build up there.
m-where_to_hunt-stay-in-one-area-01.why: If the deer aren't there, bouncing around just chases your tail. Beau has done better honing in on one area; Lee agrees.

m-where_to_hunt-storm-break-remote-food-.action: Right after a storm breaks, sit a remote food source inside cover near bedding, like an acorn flat by a mature buck's bedding area, even late morning or midday. Don't wait for the evening field.
m-where_to_hunt-storm-break-remote-food-.why: Hungry deer that were pinned down want to eat right away but won't walk out into open fields at 2 in the afternoon. He shot at a mature buck that came out near its bedding at about 11 AM after he snuck in on a rainstorm.

m-where_to_hunt-thermal-hub-bed-01.action: Look for mature-buck beds in thermal hubs, where several ridges and drainages funnel into one bowl, often on a point about 50 yards above the hub. Even a small hub with only a couple of ridges counts, especially with a mouth leading out to food and water, saddles nearby, and mixed habitat.
m-where_to_hunt-thermal-hub-bed-01.why: On one hub Derek could find a mature buck (not always the same one) bedded on the same point nearly every time he flew, day or night, whatever the wind or weather. Beau found two good bucks bedded on micro points in a small, halfway-up-the-hill bowl he'd never have picked from the map.

m-where_to_hunt-unpressured-refuges-01.action: Look for the ground that doesn't get hunted, because that's where old bucks end up. Ask 'where CAN'T people hunt?' instead of 'where can I hunt?': no-hunting zones in the suburbs, a big block whose owner won't give permission, ground that's hard to get into, or anywhere else that can't be hunted; then get permission as close to that ground as you can (Lee Ellis). After gun season, hunt the unpressured pockets of good cover and food, on your land or hidden spots on public land, and avoid ground that's been overhunted: machines driven all over, the same stands hunted over and over (Sturgis).
m-where_to_hunt-unpressured-refuges-01.why: Every big deer Ellis has hunted, suburban or rural, had a refuge where it could hide and get old; nutrition and genetics matter, but age is one of the biggest factors, and a buck that doesn't reach a certain age never hits his potential. Pressure pushes deer away, and the more mistakes, the bigger the ripple: Sturgis's clients often see no deer after gun season, then find tracks, rubs, scrapes, and beds everywhere in February, the first time nobody's been on the property for more than two weeks. Unpressured pockets are where the best of the herd ends up.

m-where_to_hunt-velvet-public-edges-01.action: For an August velvet hunt on public land, hunt habitat edges, and if there are bean fields on private land next to the public, cut off the deer in the woods on the way to the beans. Pick spots where you can lay eyes on deer, so you can move on them and reposition.
m-where_to_hunt-velvet-public-edges-01.why: Velvet bucks leave little fresh sign (no fresh rubs, maybe old scrapes still being hit) and are in bachelor groups, so they're in pockets: a spot can look great and have no bachelor group anywhere near. Seeing deer is the fastest way to find them.

m-where_to_hunt-waterhole-on-the-route-0.action: Hunt (or put) a water hole on the travel route between bedding and food, in a secure spot in the woods where deer already cruise and where you can picture a big buck stopping in the middle of the day. Not in the bedding, not in the food plot, and not somewhere you'd have to pull deer from 100 yards away.
m-where_to_hunt-waterhole-on-the-route-0.why: In the right spot a mature buck may hit the water every other day in daylight, while he might reach the food in daylight only once a week or every other week. More deer using it adds more scent, trails, rubs and scrapes, which makes deer even more comfortable there: a social hot spot.

m-wind-bottom-evening-needs-steady-wind-.action: Only sit a bottom in the evening when a strong, steady wind is funneling up the valley away from where deer travel. If the forecast shows the wind calming, skip it.
m-wind-bottom-evening-needs-steady-wind-.why: When the wind calms in a bottom, your scent drains downhill and spills into the area you're watching.

m-wind-bottom-overtop-swirl-01.action: Avoid a bottom stand when the wind blows straight over the ridge top into the bottom. Wind crossing the ridge from the sides is fine: it pulls back uphill.
m-wind-bottom-overtop-swirl-01.why: Wind that tops the ridge head-on tumbles down and swirls around the low ground.

m-wind-check-real-air-milkweed-01.action: Use the forecast wind only as a starting reference; once you're at the spot, read the real air with milkweed fluff, not a powder puffer. Release a fiber about every 10 minutes during the sit. Watch where it drifts down a ridge or through a small valley, and figure out where an incoming deer will hit your scent so you can stop and shoot him before he gets there.
m-wind-check-real-air-milkweed-01.why: The forecast often says west when it's really east or northeast at your spot, and hills make it swirl. Powder disappears within a couple of feet and just falls; milkweed floats and follows small thermal drafts that powder, a flag, or a lighter won't show, even straight up and behind you.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-wind-creek-crossing-downstream-01.action: At a creek crossing, climb right next to the creek on the DOWNSTREAM side of the trail, so the air sliding along the water carries your scent away from the crossing.
m-wind-creek-crossing-downstream-01.why: In a bottom, thermals follow the water, so being downstream keeps the crossing clean. He's had it fail in a very light swirling breeze, but it works enough that he keeps hunting bottoms others avoid.

m-wind-dont-force-wrong-wind-01.action: Know which wind directions each stand is safe on, and only hunt it on those. In hills, work out where the wind will actually carry your scent (its 'outlet') for each direction and list the 1 or 2 that are safe. If a great stand needs, say, a west wind to get in undetected and you don't have it, stay out and wait for that wind.
m-wind-dont-force-wrong-wind-01.why: In hills the ground, not the forecast direction, decides where scent ends up; once you know the outlet you rarely get surprised (Sturgis). Forcing a stand on the wrong wind lets your scent give you away; the sign then dies down and hunters blame the 'October lull' when they actually ruined the spot themselves (Informed Outdoors).

m-wind-evening-thermal-drain-01.action: In hills, plan an evening sit for two winds: the forecast (true) wind for most of the afternoon, and a downhill drain for the last 45 to 60 minutes of light. On a plain low ridge with no points or draws, a wind running clean down the valley eventually settles to the bottom in the last 45 minutes. (In the morning on that same ridge your scent comes back uphill to you.)
m-wind-evening-thermal-drain-01.why: Air keeps lifting while the temperature climbs. It levels off early afternoon and doesn't start falling until the last 45 minutes to an hour, which is when scent sinks. That last stretch is prime time.

m-wind-height-doesnt-beat-wind-01.action: Don't climb higher expecting to beat the wind. Choose height for shot angle and cover, and play the wind the same way you would at 12 feet.
m-wind-height-doesnt-beat-wind-01.why: He says there's no scent benefit at 20 feet over 12 in most situations; until you get to 25 to 30 feet the wind is a problem any way you cut it. He notes one well-known hunter who sits 30 feet up claims he never watches the wind.

m-wind-hunt-high-avoid-valleys-01.action: In steep hill country, hunt as high as you can, up on the ridges, where the forecast wind is the wind you actually get. Avoid valley and bottom stands, where it swirls and there's no good wind direction.
m-wind-hunt-high-avoid-valleys-01.why: A west wind hitting a north-south ridge turns 'like a tornado' in the valleys. Prove it with a campfire: count how often you move because the smoke follows you. On a ridge, a west wind is a west wind.

m-wind-morning-curl-at-bench-01.action: A morning wind forecast to come from the ridge top behind you often curls back into your face at a bench below. The more it hits the ridge at an angle, the more it rises at an angle on the opposite side.
m-wind-morning-curl-at-bench-01.why: The forecast wind rides over; the lifting thermal pulls air back up the slope toward you.

m-wind-morning-thermals-rise-01.action: Plan morning setups around rising thermals. Cool air sinks into the valleys at first light, then flips about 180 degrees and rises once the sun warms the forest floor. After that, bottoms and low spots are safer to hunt in the morning than the evening, because most wind directions carry your scent back uphill, and you can even sit above a bench with deer about 30 yards 'downwind' below you: the lift ramps your scent up and over them. Have more than one stand option so you can hunt the one that works for the flip.
m-wind-morning-thermals-rise-01.why: Morning sun warms the air and it rises, so scent climbs out of the low ground like a ramp over deer at lower elevation (Sturgis). Old deer learn to travel with some wind advantage and know about the flip too (Rex).

m-wind-mountain-check-dont-scratch-01.action: In mountains, don't scratch a good spot just because the forecast wind looks wrong for it. Go check the actual air there; most of the time (he says nine times out of ten) it's fine where you're sitting.
m-wind-mountain-check-dont-scratch-01.why: Mountain wind twists with the ridges and often has nothing to do with the forecast direction; another guest described it changing four directions on the walk up and ending 180 degrees from the forecast. Ridge tops hold the steadiest air. On a limited-day gun hunt, the timing matters more.

m-wind-old-buck-uses-wind-01.action: Expect an older buck to use the wind to his advantage on his way into a food source. Set up to catch that approach without being in his nose.
m-wind-old-buck-uses-wind-01.why: The older the buck, the more he uses the wind to go to food. It's an advantage for him, but it makes his route predictable, which you can exploit.

m-wind-prevailing-vs-front-winds-01.action: Set most of your stands up for south, southeast, and southwest winds, and save your northwest-wind stands for fronts. Expect harsh northwest winds only in the first day or two of a cold snap; by the second or third day temperatures moderate and the wind usually swings back to southwest, south, or southeast. A hard south wind means it's warming up; winds turning east usually mean rain is coming.
m-wind-prevailing-vs-front-winds-01.why: In settled weather the wind sits south to southwest (about 35% of the season). A northwest or north wind means temperatures are dropping, which doesn't happen every day, and cold doesn't keep deepening for weeks: it drops, then moderates. So northwest isn't the predominant fall wind people assume, and a strong wind can come from any side.

m-wind-ridge-point-light-over-calm-01.action: On a ridge point, prefer a light, defined wind (3 or 4 mph) over dead calm. With a little wind you know which side of the ridge your scent will slide down as it gets toward dark; in calm air it can pull down either side.
m-wind-ridge-point-light-over-calm-01.why: With no wind, sinking evening thermals pull your scent around unpredictably. He finds calm evenings 'pretty tough.'

m-wind-rut-bucks-ignore-wind-01.action: In the peak rut, when a hot doe is around, expect bucks to pay less attention to the wind and come through anyway. Hunt the good spot even if the wind is marginal.
m-wind-rut-bucks-ignore-wind-01.why: Bucks hot on a doe's trail aren't as alert; he and others have watched bucks come right through their wind.

m-wind-shift-arrives-early-01.action: Check the hourly wind for the hours AFTER your sit too. If the wind is forecast to swing overnight (say to northwest ahead of a cold front), expect puffs from the new direction every 5 to 10 minutes during your evening sit, and pick a stand that's safe on both.
m-wind-shift-arrives-early-01.why: Wind shifts don't flip all at once; the new direction creeps in hours early. Much of what hunters call 'swirling' in flat country is a forecast shift arriving early.

m-wind-stands-for-every-wind-01.action: Have stand options for every wind so you can always walk to the one the day's wind allows. Sturgis plans stands for every wind direction, mornings and afternoons, about 4 or 5 per wind (25 to 30 on a 500-acre property) rather than only for the 'predominant' wind. The Downwind Hunting list puts it per spot: hang two stands on opposite sides of the same funnel or trail, one for a north wind and one for a south wind, and sit only the one the wind allows.
m-wind-stands-for-every-wind-01.why: The predominant wind blows only about 35% of the time and the other directions share the rest about equally (Sturgis). You always have a downwind option instead of sitting one stand regardless of wind; hunters who kill mature bucks walk to the stand the wind tells them to (listicle).

m-wind-terrain-over-wind-route-01.action: Don't assume a mature buck travels with his nose into the wind. Pick travel stands by terrain and sign; the land shapes his route far more than the wind does. Still play your own wind at the stand.
m-wind-terrain-over-wind-route-01.why: With thermal drones Derek Dixon watched bucks walk with the wind in their face, on their side, and at their tail along a single route, because they can't walk straight lines in the hills. Where he wants to be matters more than the wind direction.

m-wind-wind-before-products-01.action: Make wind direction your main defense against a deer's nose; scent-control sprays, detergents, suits, and gadgets are only a backup on top of a good wind. Never sit a stand on a marginal wind because you trust your products. Know where your scent will blow (including how thermals and humidity move it) and use that to decide where to hunt and how to walk in.
m-wind-wind-before-products-01.why: No product will fool an older doe or buck's nose; you might get away with it on very young deer (Informed Outdoors, who blew countless sits trusting the marketing). The most any product can do is make deer think you're farther away than you are, and a mature doe will still come in downwind and pick you off; the wind is the single biggest thing in nature you can use in your favor (WHTL).

m-wind-wind-in-your-face-01.action: Set up so the wind blows from where you expect deer into your face, knowing they'll still sometimes come from where they want.
m-wind-wind-in-your-face-01.why: Wind direction and scent control are imperative. He believes in cover scents and attractants too, each at its own time, but didn't say when.

m-wth-bait-48-hours-01.action: If you get a daylight photo of a target buck at a bait site, hunt him within 48 hours, and set up on the trails leading to the bait rather than right over it.
m-wth-bait-48-hours-01.why: After the first day or two he goes almost completely nocturnal at that bait, and once the site is established your odds there drop fast.

m-wth-be-there-when-rain-stops-01.action: When a storm or all-day rain is coming through, watch the radar and hourly forecast for when it clears and be in your stand for it. If a clear-up is obviously close, walk in during the rain in rain gear so you're sitting when it stops. Sturgis's favorite: rain all day that clears about an hour before dark (or rain all night that breaks by morning), especially if it was windy all day ahead of the front. In warm, showery weather hunt the dry windows between rains, especially after it's rained all day; a little wind is good. McKay: when rain is forecast, head for the woods as soon as it stops.
m-wth-be-there-when-rain-stops-01.why: Deer held down by a storm have burned energy and missed feedings, so when it breaks they 'put the feed bag on' and activity can go through the roof; walking in during the rain also washes your trail away (Sturgis). Rain drops take away deer's hearing, so they wait it out and get up when it stops (Sturgis). McKay waited out a rainy morning and deer were crossing the road as soon as it quit; another rainy morning a buck tucked under a bluff was shot moving right after.

m-wth-big-temp-drop-01.action: Hunt a day that is much colder than the day before, even without a pressure change. How much: 15 F or more colder on the 24-hour average (MSU data; the effect starts past about 10 F); a 15 to 20 degree drop even while pressure is still low between fronts, especially if the wind has laid down from 25-30 mph to 8-12 (Sturgis; it doesn't need to be calm); in the South, the forecast high dropping about 11-15 F from the day before, like 60 to 49 or 60 to 45 (McRae's 'major weather event'). Treat a change within about 10 F either way as no change.
m-wth-big-temp-drop-01.why: MSU: change in bedding time was flat at about 0% for day-to-day swings between -10 and +10 F; past about a 10-15 F drop, bucks were bedded less the following day. Sturgis: pressure-only models miss about half the great days. McRae: in the South a 12-degree swing in the highs shocks deer; it only has to get a core-area buck up half an hour earlier to put him in daylight in front of you, and he killed his buck on his third weather-event sit.

m-wth-big-woods-repeat-sits-01.action: In low-density big woods, a proven tree can be sat over and over. McKay bowhunted his 'killing tree' for about three weeks straight in its prime and killed several bucks from it. Stop once the woods change (for example logging) and the deer stop using it.
m-wth-big-woods-repeat-sits-01.why: In big woods with fewer deer, each sit doesn't blow deer out the way it does in small, dense farm country.

m-wth-cold-dawn-small-01.action: A cold dawn helps a little in the morning, but don't count on it the way you'd count on a cool evening. Morning movement is high almost regardless of temperature, so mornings are the steadier bet when the weather is off.
m-wth-cold-dawn-small-01.why: Across the whole season, bucks with a 20-32 F dawn moved about 360 yards per hour and were bedded about 25% of the time, versus about 240 yd/hr and 30% bedded in the warmest dawn band (70-85 F). But once the rut stage is accounted for, the morning pattern was inconsistent: cold mornings were best in the pre-rut and peak rut, warmer mornings actually had more movement in the early rut, and in the post-rut cold beat 55-70 F by a little under 50 yd/hr. Some gaps were only about 5 yd/hr, inside the collar error.

m-wth-cold-front-trifecta-01.action: Hunt the first sit after a cold front passes, and put your best stand on it. The signs on a 7-day forecast graph: the temperature line drops while the barometric pressure line climbs to meet it ('when temps and pressure meet, bucks will be on their feet'), and the wind speed falls. Clay Hayes adds heavy rain easing to light or none, and calls it the 'perfect storm' when all of it lines up around daybreak. The evening after a windy front, when highs have stepped down (low 70s, then low 60s, then 50-60) and the wind is dying but still blowing, is a sit to take; so is the cold, calm back side of a storm or snowstorm. Whitetail Evolution: the same holds in the early season and the pre-rut.
m-wth-cold-front-trifecta-01.why: Sturgis says most of his top 25 mature bucks were shot when falling temperature, rising pressure, and dropping wind lined up; one cold, calm evening after a heavy windy snow he saw close to 50 deer, including the six-year-old buck he was after. Whitetail Evolution says studies and hunters around the country agree deer, older bucks included, move more after a front, and since every trip in leaves a trace you should spend trips on these days. Hayes: extreme weather keeps deer hunkered in thick bedding and makes them miss or delay feeding bouts, so when it breaks they're hungry and move quickly.

m-wth-cold-mornings-prerut-01.action: Save your morning sits for the first cold, frosty mornings of late October and November, especially just after a cold front. In the last 10 days of October watch the forecast lows: when they fall to about 35 F forecast (high 20s to 32 in the valleys), or the first toe-numbing 27-31 F mornings arrive, don't miss those mornings.
m-wth-cold-mornings-prerut-01.why: A cool pre-rut makes mature bucks very active, more in the morning than the evening; a hot one shuts them down. Less than 20% (about 15%) of his sits all season are mornings, yet mornings account for about 60-70% of his oldest bucks over decades, mostly with a bow in late October and November.

m-wth-dont-chase-fresh-photo-01.action: Don't rush to the spot where a buck just showed up on camera, especially a scrape he just hit in daylight; you're already behind him. Hunt the scrape or spot he hasn't hit in 3 to 5 days, because he's due. Know his rhythm: one Tennessee buck ran a sewer-line scrape line about every 3 to 4 days.
m-wth-dont-chase-fresh-photo-01.why: Lee Ellis has seen good hunters get worse after adding cell cameras, because they chase instant photos and always end up a step behind. Before cell cams, hunters knew a buck was around and rode out an area instead.

m-wth-early-cold-front-south-01.action: In the early season in the South, don't expect good bucks in daylight in October except when an unusual early cold front comes through; then be in the woods. One guest's setup for that cold morning: the edge of a bedding thicket in thick cover with good habitat variety and oaks close by.
m-wth-early-cold-front-south-01.why: McKay doesn't feel he can see a good public-land buck until November, but killed one on October 6 when an unusual cold front got it moving (he'd told people 'somebody's going to kill a good deer this weekend'). The guest's best encounter with a really good buck came October 7 in Tennessee after a cold front, about 35 F that morning: 14 deer, then a big buck walked in at 8:30 AM to 25 yards after he walked through a red and white oak ridge to the thicket edge.

m-wth-east-wind-slow-01.action: Expect less deer movement than usual on an east wind ('wind out of the east, fish bite least' holds for deer too).

m-wth-evening-before-rain-01.action: In hot early-season weather, the evening before a rain can hunt well when it's already about 10 degrees cooler than yesterday, cloudy with some wind, and the rain won't start until after dark. Use it to sit stands you don't use often on the southeast or east wind that comes ahead of the rain.
m-wth-evening-before-rain-01.why: The cooler, cloudy front side gets deer moving, and rain after dark will cover your exit.

m-wth-evening-temp-band-01.action: For evening sits, the best temperature band is about 32-55 F. When the last two hours of daylight fall in that range, rate the evening higher.
m-wth-evening-temp-band-01.why: This was the MSU study's most consistent weather finding: in the last two hours of daylight, the 32-55 F band had the highest movement rate in essentially every two-week stage from pre-rut to post-rut. Strickland trusts it because it repeats.

m-wth-evening-thermal-switch-01.action: Be settled on your evening stand before the evening thermal switch. Within 5 to 15 minutes of the thermals switching, bedded deer, especially mature bucks, stand up. They may still browse, groom, and linger in the bedding area for 30 minutes or more before heading to staging.
m-wth-evening-thermal-switch-01.why: It was the most consistent pattern in Derek Dixon's whole season of drone data: for weeks the evening get-up times lined up, and when he checked the weather it matched the thermal switch nearly every time. A buck getting up doesn't mean he walks past you 10 minutes later.

m-wth-extreme-cold-midday-01.action: In extreme cold (far below the normal high for the date), hunt late morning through midday, roughly 10 to 2 or 9 to 3, on browse like greenbrier, hardwood regeneration, clearcuts, or blowdowns.
m-wth-extreme-cold-midday-01.why: Daybreak is the coldest time of day, so deer save energy then and move once it warms up (for example from -10 or -15 F in the morning to 10 F midday). You see this especially on public land flats.

m-wth-falling-baro-midday-01.action: On a new moon or a falling barometer, skip the predawn walk. Head in around 8 AM and sit through 10 AM to 2 PM.
m-wth-falling-baro-midday-01.why: It cites a University of Georgia GPS-collar study: 60% of mature bucks' big daytime moves (over 500 m) happened between 10 AM and 2 PM. A falling barometer ahead of a cold front adds to it (deer behind on calories), and the early crowd has already spooked the woods and left.

m-wth-feeding-cycle-01.action: Expect whitetails to feed in bouts roughly every 5 hours: they get up, feed fast, then go back to bed (or lie down in the field at night) to chew their cud. Moon phase and hunting pressure can delay or shift the cycle.
m-wth-feeding-cycle-01.why: Deer are ruminants. They gulp food with little chewing to limit time exposed to predators, then process it later in a safe spot. That takes time, so feeding comes in cycles, not constantly.

m-wth-forecast-horizon-01.action: Pick your hunt days from the daily forecast 8 to 10 days out, then within 72 hours use the hourly forecast to assign which stand you sit each morning and evening by its wind.
m-wth-forecast-horizon-01.why: Wind direction comes from big weather patterns and is the most accurate part of the forecast; it holds 7 to 10 days out within about half a day. Rain and snow amounts are much less reliable.

m-wth-front-day-after-morning-01.action: The morning after a warm-to-cold switch is slightly better than the day the front hits, mostly about an hour after sunrise. It's a modest edge, not a sure thing.
m-wth-front-day-after-morning-01.why: On transition days, the day after had about 25 yd/hr more movement than the change day around an hour after sunrise. His grad student's view: over a 3-hour sit, 25 yards per hour is about 75 more yards of movement (he calls it '75 total steps'), which can decide whether a buck steps out.

m-wth-front-day-before-morning-01.action: On the day before a cold front arrives, hunt the morning. That afternoon was the weakest of the three transition days.
m-wth-front-day-before-morning-01.why: The day before the change had the most morning movement of the before / during / after days, and the least afternoon movement. His guess: bucks spent more of their day's movement in the morning.

m-wth-fronts-weather-small-edge-01.action: Treat weather as a small tiebreaker, not a reason a day will be great or dead. Don't count on a cold front, a warm front, a rising or falling barometer, or a temperature change by itself to put deer on their feet, and don't skip a good day because the barometer looks wrong. Within the same two-week stage of the rut, days under a cold (polar) air mass had slightly more daylight buck movement than warm (tropical) or moderate days.
m-wth-fronts-weather-small-edge-01.why: MSU: it took a very large sample and heavy math to see the weather signal at all; if your odds on a sit are 10%, cold weather might make them 11%, not 90%. Whitetail Properties: collar studies of wind, temperature, rain, snow, and pressure haven't found the movement changes hunters expect from any single one; some combination may matter and just hasn't been identified.

m-wth-headwind-moves-earlier-01.action: Expect a mature buck to move earlier on days the wind blows into his face along his travel route, and later (often after dark) on days it's at his back. Hunt a buck's route on the days the wind lets him smell ahead.
m-wth-headwind-moves-earlier-01.why: Rex charted 100+ wireless-camera events of a target buck coming down an east-west cut against historical wind data (Weather Underground). With a south wind in his face he came down about 2.5 hours earlier than with a north wind at his back, when he couldn't smell what was below. All but two events were after dark.

m-wth-late-afternoon-food-01.action: In the late season, hunt the afternoon food source and stay out in the mornings (the second rut is the only exception). Put a premium on those afternoon sits.
m-wth-late-afternoon-food-01.why: The food source is the bottom of the funnel for daylight movement: deer from several bedding areas come to it before dark. In the mornings they aren't moving much in daylight, so a morning hunt only pressures and pushes them.

m-wth-late-bitter-cold-early-feed-01.action: In the late season in farm country, bitter cold pulls bucks out to feed early in the afternoon. In milder late-season weather, expect does early and bucks only in the last 45 minutes.
m-wth-late-bitter-cold-early-feed-01.why: Host anecdote from late-season Iowa: at -7 F, big bucks were feeding 2.5 hours before dark. The next year, at upper 30s to low 40s, he saw many more does but the buck movement was mostly the last 45 minutes of light.

m-wth-late-rut-giants-01.action: Don't quit after the first-of-November rush. For the very biggest bucks, keep hunting the tail end of the rut (the second half of November in Ohio) when most bowhunters have slowed down.
m-wth-late-rut-giants-01.why: From Buckeye Big Buck score sheets: most record-book bucks (the 130-150 inch, 3- and 4-year-olds doing most of the breeding) die around the end of October and first of November, but the Boone and Crockett-class 4- to 7-year-olds are mostly killed the first week of season or at the end of the rut. His theory: they make fewer rut-crazed mistakes and feel safer once hunter numbers drop by mid-November. During the pre-rut and peak rut, just being out there matters most.

m-wth-late-season-storm-food-01.action: In the late season, hunt the food during and right after a big storm or front that drops the temperature, like a hard snow or ice storm. 'Cold' is relative to where you are: 60 F can be cold in Florida, -20 F in northern North Dakota.
m-wth-late-season-storm-food-01.why: A big system makes deer miss feedings and stresses them, and the cold makes them burn energy; afterward they have to eat to stay alive, which puts them on food in daylight (Sturgis). Rex's target buck was almost entirely nocturnal all season, then on January 29, in a level-three snow emergency with ice over snow, his stomach won and he came to the food in daylight; Rex's 16-year-old son killed him.

m-wth-light-rain-go-01.action: Hunt a light drizzle, misty rain, or light wet snow; skip thunderstorms and moderate or steady rain. During the rut, a light rain is no reason to stay home at all.
m-wth-light-rain-go-01.why: Blanton: deer seem to like moving in a light drizzle; in a hard, steady rain they bed down. Sturgis: in a light drizzle all their senses work (damp air helps their nose, the trees aren't thrashing so they can see, it's quiet enough to hear), and when they have their senses they move; in thunder and lightning they take cover and rarely feed in moderate steady rain. In the rut a little light rain won't keep any buck in his bed, it often comes with cooler temperatures and a quiet woods, and he has many memories of mature bucks coming through in the rain. Whitetail Properties: rain is the one weather factor a researcher (Penn State) found raised deer movement, especially buck movement, and wet woods let you move in quieter.

m-wth-limit-early-mornings-01.action: In the early season (until about mid to late October), limit morning hunts and put most sits in the afternoons, especially on private farm ground with small, well-defined cover. Don't try to slip into a buck's bedding area in the morning. Take an early-season morning sit only with real evidence he moves there after daylight (trail-cam photos at a water hole after sunrise, or seeing him cut a corner after daylight feeding through open hardwoods back to bed), and then set up off to the side on a long transition with a safe wind and approach, not on the food and not in the bedding. Start hunting mornings more as the pre-rut arrives.
m-wth-limit-early-mornings-01.why: Many older bucks are back in bed well before first light, so walking toward bedding at 5:30 or 6 AM you bump him or walk the same way he is. Whitetail Evolution bumped his target buck on October 24 (a cold-front morning), about an hour before daylight, standing under his stand 3 minutes before he walked up. On a property where movement is tight and predictable, one bump turns it random and can push him to the neighbor's.

m-wth-midday-wind-shift-01.action: When the hourly forecast shows a big wind shift in the middle of the day, be set up before the shift near a bedding point, finger, or the saddle between bedding areas. Bedded mature bucks often get up right as the new wind arrives and move to a new bed.
m-wth-midday-wind-shift-01.why: Derek Dixon watched a bedded buck in the rain stand up at 12:31 when the wind finished swinging from south to west, a shift his weather app had forecast for 12:30, then circle to a new spot. Beau Martonik, in Ohio muzzleloader season in January, waited out a rainy morning, moved toward a bedding finger when he felt a forecast 1 PM shift arrive, and had a buck walk up to 15 yards within minutes, headed over a saddle to bed on another point.

m-wth-moon-phase-ignore-01.action: Don't plan your hunt days around the moon phase. The old saying that the day after a full moon is poor because deer fed all night isn't supported. Plan around the time of year and pay far more attention to the wind than to the moon.
m-wth-moon-phase-ignore-01.why: GPS-collar studies with millions of deer locations across the whitetail range show very little difference in movement between moon phases. Some researchers found slight shifts (a little earlier in the evening, a little longer feeding in the morning), but not enough to plan around.

m-wth-moon-rise-set-01.action: Watch when the moon rises and sets, not just its phase. The closer moonrise or moonset is to dawn or dusk, the better he's seen deer move. On a full moon, expect a bit more midday movement.
m-wth-moon-rise-set-01.why: He's had deer pile into a food plot an hour before dark under a rising full moon, and seen almost nothing on a new moon.

m-wth-morning-mission-01.action: Expect a mature buck's longest daylight travel in the morning: he's usually up at or before first light and walks long, fairly straight routes (up to a mile to a mile and a half), hitting rubs and scrapes and checking doe trails, then beds near where the does will feed that evening. Hunt mornings along those travel lines, not at his bed.
m-wth-morning-mission-01.why: Derek Dixon calls it 'missional' movement: bucks seem to wake up with a list of points to hit. He tracked one buck scent-check 35 to 40 does along one straight morning route without wasting steps. At night they make another long trek (800 to 1,000 acres, a mile to a mile and a half), and they keep moving until about 2.5 to 3 hours after sunset.

m-wth-morning-or-evening-spot-01.action: Some spots are morning spots and some are evening spots, and often you can't tell by looking; you learn it by hunting them. Once a spot clearly shows it's a morning spot, stop hunting it in the evening.
m-wth-morning-or-evening-spot-01.why: One spot (a hardwood draw, an SMZ, between two pine thickets) showed him 10 bucks one morning and about 2 deer that evening. He killed a buck there the next morning, a friend killed one 200 yards away the next week, and he killed another big one the week after, so they quit hunting it in the evening.

m-wth-pick-best-weather-days-01.action: Hunt your best stands only on the best weather days and stay out of them the rest of the time; one great weekday morning and evening beats a warm five-day weekend. Don't go into a good spot on a windy, hot day when tomorrow is forecast calm to moderate wind with a temperature drop of 10 F or more; wait, and move your time off to match. On warm early-season days or the wrong wind, don't burn your best stands: wait for a cold front after a warm stretch (a 15 to 20 degree drop, the rain moving out, the wind slowing) and that afternoon push a bit deeper to a staging food source as bucks get out of bed. Spend warm bluebird days (his example: 75 F on October 15 in Michigan) with family or trading work time with your boss, so you're free when a big cold front shows up in next week's forecast.
m-wth-pick-best-weather-days-01.why: Sturgis only hunts by the weather and tags out most years, because he isn't burning out his stands on bad days; he picks the best time of day and the best day together and stays out of core areas otherwise. Whitetail Evolution: match your highest-impact stand locations with your highest-probability days, so when you do push in, something is in your favor. The goodwill and time you bank on bluebird days pays off when the important days arrive.

m-wth-pressure-alone-no-01.action: Weight temperature first. Don't rate a day up or down on barometric pressure, humidity, or dew point by themselves. The one small exception: very dry air (humidity under about 20%) trims movement a little.
m-wth-pressure-alone-no-01.why: When the MSU team isolated each variable, temperature drove the relationship and the others mostly rode along with it. Very low humidity cut movement by up to about 30 yd/hr with everything else controlled, which Strickland says isn't enough to call a day good or bad.
