Pressure varies very little and he couldn't point to a pressure result. Their meteorologist colleagues' point: these variables move together as a front, so judge the front, not one number.

m-wth-rain-hole-wait-for-drips-01.action: Count it as a real break when the rain has stopped completely (no drips falling through the trees) and the wind has dropped a lot. It doesn't have to go calm: 50 to 30 or 30 to 10 mph is a big drop. For snow, the break is when a heavy, windy snow (2-3 inches an hour) turns to light snow and calm. Watch the forecast for a hole several hours long (4-5 hours or more, often visible 5-10 hours to a day ahead) and go once it has been dry for at least an hour. Midday, sit a food source tucked in the woods next to bedding: an acorn flat, a small plot, a cut or hardwood regeneration area, or a hidden apple tree.
m-wth-rain-hole-wait-for-drips-01.why: Dripping trees keep the woods noisy; an hour without rain lets the drips come off and the woods quiet down. It's the change from extreme to quieter that gets deer up, not a particular number. The longer it rained before the break, the better: deer pop out to fill up after a stressful storm. A dry hole also gives you time to track a deer before the rain returns.

m-wth-read-the-day-01.action: Before choosing where to go, read the day's conditions: Are the leaves wet? Did it just rain? Is it windy or calm? Hot or cold? Is a cold front coming through? Each one changes where deer bed, how they move, and how close you can get.
m-wth-read-the-day-01.why: Deer hunting is extremely situational. The same spot can be right or wrong depending on the day, so the conditions come first.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-wth-rising-barometer-01.action: A morning with the barometer rising hunts better than one with it falling.
m-wth-rising-barometer-01.why: He's always seen better movement on a rising barometer. Higher pressure also means lower humidity, which he thinks holds deer down, especially in the East and Midwest.

m-wth-rut-all-day-01.action: In the rut, sit all day. Pick a between-bedding-and-food stand with a pinch point, where deer have reasons to pass all day, not only at dawn and dusk (Sturgis). Take vacation for the stretch when the pre-rut turns into the peak rut and sit dawn to dark with enough food and water to stay (the listicle puts it at November 2 to 15 across most of the range).
m-wth-rut-all-day-01.why: Deer have reasons to pass a between stand all day (Sturgis). The listicle says NDA harvest data shows more Boone and Crockett bucks killed in that 14-day window than any other, and that mature bucks move in daylight and make mistakes then, often at midday.

m-wth-rut-go-regardless-01.action: Plan your biggest block of days around the local rut, not the weather, and once it's on, spend as much time in the woods as you can. Go even when it's warm, and go even if you only get 45 minutes after work (off at 5, in the stand by 5:15, dark at 6) as long as the wind is right. Treat weather as a small tiebreaker inside the rut calendar. Movement steps up from no rut to pre-rut to early rut to peak rut, then tapers off.
m-wth-rut-go-regardless-01.why: MSU GPS data: bucks cover about 1,500-2,000 yards a day outside the rut and 4,000+ in it, move about 225 yards per hour on average (400+ in the rut), and are bedded about 35-38% of daylight outside the rut versus about 21% in it; weather effects were a few to about 50 yards per hour. Danker: it's the time bucks cover the most ground, and any sit can produce a buck you've never seen. Blanton: a buck that just left a bred doe can be on his feet looking for the next one at any time.

m-wth-same-dates-every-year-01.action: Use past years' records to plan the calendar. The pre-rut and rut start on about the same dates on your property every year, and many mature bucks show back up in a spot almost to the same date each year (for example around October 1) and disappear again about the same time. Plan hunt days around those dates, then use the conditions to pick the best days inside the window.
m-wth-same-dates-every-year-01.why: The timing is set by shrinking daylight, not by moon phase or temperature, so it's consistent year to year; weather, moon, and hunting pressure only change how much of the movement happens in daylight (Whitetail Evolution). Lee Ellis sees mature bucks show back up nearly to the day whether it was a hot fall or a cold one.

m-wth-save-spot-for-rut-week-01.action: Once you find a good doe area for the rut, don't overhunt it early. Pop in to check it (are the acorns dropping, are does there), back out, and stay out until the week you know the rut hits there; then hunt it hard. Don't shoot does there before the rut.
m-wth-save-spot-for-rut-week-01.why: It's where your main rut action will be, and the does come in at the same time frame every year. Bowhunters need to narrow it down further, to the exact trail the does walk.

m-wth-scrapes-after-storm-01.action: In the pre-rut, hunt scrapes right after a storm. If it's raining, even lightly, and you can see when it will stop, be in your stand near a perennial scrape about 15 minutes before it ends (Whitetail Evolution). Rex hunts scrapes from when they appear (late September in southern Ohio) through the pre-rut, especially right after a storm blows the leaves down; once the rut kicks in, switch from scrapes to simply being out there.
m-wth-scrapes-after-storm-01.why: Right after even a small storm, bucks often get up from bed and go freshen their scrapes, maybe because the rain washed the scent away or just because they were hunkered down (Whitetail Evolution). Deer hit scrapes hard after a storm, when falling leaves cover them, and right before the rut peaks; scrape use trails off quickly once the rut starts (Rex).

m-wth-second-rut-01.action: Don't miss the second rut, about 30 days after your local peak rut. Hunt it around unpressured pockets of cover and food; it's the one late-season time Sturgis hunts mornings too. If you only have about 9 days, split them: 4 or 5 days around the peak rut (early November in his area, timed with a good cold front if there is one) and 4 or 5 days during the second rut.
m-wth-second-rut-01.why: Maybe 15 to 20% of the does are bred then, deer are concentrated around the unpressured cover and food, and hardly anyone else is in the woods; he calls it the most missed opportunity in deer hunting. Putting every day on the peak rut throws that window away.

m-wth-skip-extreme-weather-01.action: Don't bother sitting through the worst of extreme weather: heavy rain, heavy snow, thunder and lightning, hail, or very heavy wind. Watch it from somewhere dry and get ready to go the moment it breaks.
m-wth-skip-extreme-weather-01.why: At the extreme, most deer stay in their bedding areas conserving energy. They're stressed, the woods are noisy, and they don't want to move. Heavy rain also washes a blood trail away fast if you do shoot one.

m-wth-sleep-01.action: Get a good night's sleep and eat well before a hunt, even if it costs you some hunting time.
m-wth-sleep-01.why: Tired, your mind isn't fully in the game and you won't stay alert on the ground.

m-wth-small-parcel-wait-for-rut-01.action: On a small private parcel (around 100 acres), accept that there may be no shooter buck bedding on your place in October. Shoot your does early in bow season and save your buck hunting for the pre-rut and rut, when bucks come off the neighbors' ground looking for doe groups.
m-wth-small-parcel-wait-for-rut-01.why: A buck may just not be where he wants to be in daylight on your land. On public land you have room to roam and follow him; on a small piece you often can't. For a working hunter with limited days, the rut is the great equalizer.

m-wth-south-early-mornings-oaks-01.action: In the Southeast, don't write off early-season mornings. Get in during the dark near oaks that are dropping or a hot acorn feed tree (one guest likes the cool creek bottoms) and be ready as it gets light: acorns tend to start falling as the sun comes up, and deer that fed nearby in the dark come back through after daylight.
m-wth-south-early-mornings-oaks-01.why: Early-season Alabama afternoons run about 87 F and you often see nothing until right at dark, while mornings are usually in the 60s, sometimes the 50s, and don't warm up until lunch; that guest has had more buck encounters since he stopped listening to 'don't hunt early-season mornings'. The South Carolina guest killed most of his big bucks in the morning on feed trees: in one spot bucks came 30 minutes after daylight from the area he'd walked past, and his biggest (or second biggest) came about an hour after daylight.

m-wth-stable-weather-fades-01.action: Treat a stable weather pattern as a low-value hunting day and look for weather change instead. Two or three days after a cold front, once temperatures settle into a new normal (his example: 70s the week before, down into the 50s, then holding in the 60s), movement drops off again.
m-wth-stable-weather-fades-01.why: He's organized his life and career since the early 90s around hunting the good-weather days (post cold front) and not the stable or bad ones, and credits that for his success.

m-wth-stand-burns-with-use-01.action: Treat every sit as using up a stand. The first sit in a fresh stand is your best odds, so save it for the right wind and timing (Rex). Don't sit the same stand more than two times in a row, then rest it at least 5 days, rotating between three or four stands (Downwind Hunting listicle).
m-wth-stand-burns-with-use-01.why: A friend of Rex's who has killed a lot of big deer found that statistically the first time you hunt a stand is your best chance at a buck there. The listicle cites Mississippi State research that mature bucks change travel within two to three days of detecting repeated human activity at a spot.

m-wth-stand-by-time-of-day-01.action: Match the stand to the time of day. Stands on or watching food = evenings only. Stands by bedding = mornings only. Stands between the two = any time, including all day.
m-wth-stand-by-time-of-day-01.why: Walking in on deer at food in the morning (or bedding in the afternoon, when you don't know where they are) blows them out.

m-wth-stay-mid-morning-01.action: Don't climb down at 8. Stay on a morning stand into mid-morning: the fastest buck travel is about 2 hours after sunrise (MSU), bucks often pass at 8 to 9:30 AM rather than at first light (Dixon and Martonik), and in the rut stay until 11 instead of leaving at 9:30, take a lunch break, and be back in by 1:30 (Danker). Stay especially on a travel route between food and bedding.
m-wth-stay-mid-morning-01.why: MSU: around sunrise and the hour after, bucks are still foraging on slow, twisting paths; about 2 hours after sunrise movement turns long and linear as they head to their first bed, and the rate peaks. Dixon: bucks are usually up before light, so a buck passing mid-morning has bedded farther away than you think or got up, groomed, and milled around (even with other bucks, even in the rut) before heading out. Danker counts leaving at 9:30 in the rut among his own biggest mistakes.

m-wth-target-buck-outside-rut-01.action: If you're after one specific buck, hunt him before and after the rut, mostly on afternoon sits over his feeding pattern. Hunt hard the first week of archery season, when bucks are still on their summer feeding pattern and food is much easier to figure out than bedding.
m-wth-target-buck-outside-rut-01.why: In the MSU GPS data, outside the rut bucks behave very consistently day to day (tight spread between bucks) and reuse the same daily area, so a pattern holds; in the rut they wander. Rex, from every Buckeye Big Buck score sheet: the Boone and Crockett-class Ohio bucks are mostly killed the first week of the season or at the tail end of the rut.

m-wth-ten-degree-drop-01.action: When the temperature drops 10 or more degrees from the previous day, drop other plans and sit from sunrise through the middle of the day.
m-wth-ten-degree-drop-01.why: It says deer movement spikes sharply on a 10-degree-plus day-over-day drop. A cheap thermometer read at the same time each morning is enough to see the trend.

m-wth-vanished-buck-wait-01.action: If a core-area buck that's on camera every day suddenly vanishes for about a week, he's probably off with a doe. Don't panic or go looking for him; wait, and hunt him hard as soon as he's back on his home camera.
m-wth-vanished-buck-wait-01.why: All three of McRae's biggest bucks, in three different years, vanished for about 7 days in the last week of October, each caught once or twice on other cameras trailing or breeding a doe, then returned to their normal routine. He killed one the day after it came back.

m-wth-velvet-shoot-01.action: If you have a velvet-season tag and a target buck is patternable at daybreak and dusk, take him then rather than waiting for hard antlers. By a mid-September velvet season his antlers are done growing.
m-wth-velvet-shoot-01.why: He won't add inches after velvet season (and he'll actually score a bit higher in velvet, before it dries). There's no guarantee you'll get another chance later in the season.

m-wth-wait-for-daylight-pattern-01.action: Stay out of a target buck's core until he gives you a reason to go. Night-only camera pictures (10 PM, 2 AM, 4 AM) mean he's using the property, not that he's huntable; hang back and let him stay comfortable. Watch cell cameras until he shows in daylight so regularly it's a no-brainer (you watch him step into the same plot two evenings in a row, cell cameras show him using one spot in daylight, or you have years of history of him hitting a certain apple tree in early October) or a major weather event hits. Then go aggressively, with the right wind and a fairly clean way in and out. If you live far away, use cell cameras to time the trip for when deer activity picks up instead of taking a fixed week off.
m-wth-wait-for-daylight-pattern-01.why: Early patterns are predictable but can vanish fast; Whitetail Evolution killed a buck on opening day from cell-camera daylight info, and the key is a reason to be aggressive, not the calendar. McRae can't afford to spook a buck living in a tiny core and can't count on a random once-a-season daylight appearance; he says he couldn't have had his success without cell cameras. Rex: real-time camera information has been huge for absentee landowners and traveling hunters, who used to just pick the first week of November and hope.

m-wth-warm-take-morning-01.action: On a warm spell, if you only get one sit, take the morning and skip the evening.
m-wth-warm-take-morning-01.why: Evening movement tracked temperature much more consistently than morning movement did, so heat hurts evenings more. Mornings stayed relatively steady.

m-wth-warm-weather-hurts-01.action: Downgrade warm days; warmth is the condition that hurts a hunt most. On hot days bucks leave their beds at the last second; on cool days they move earlier and more all day, so if a cooler day is coming, hunt that one. Ways the sources measure 'warm': the forecast high well above normal for the date (Blanton: Illinois late October, normal high 71, forecast 83, and he'd consider moving the trip); an absolute temperature climbing toward 75-80 F in the Deep South, where the sweet spot is about 30-50 F (MSU); tomorrow 10 F or more warmer than today (MSU: downgrade it, or use it to scout or hang cameras). In the late-October pre-rut, a hot stretch means mature bucks barely move and a cool stretch means they're very active, mostly in the morning (Sturgis), so save your best stands for the cool days.
m-wth-warm-weather-hurts-01.why: Nothing keeps a mature buck in his bed until after dark more than warmer-than-normal temperatures, any month and any region (Blanton). Most bad-weather days are hot days, and on those bucks don't move whatever the moon or anything else says (Sturgis). In the MSU data movement rose above each buck's recent baseline as collar temperature went from about 30 up to 50 F and fell below it toward 80 F, and a 10 F+ warm jump day-over-day raised bedding time.

m-wth-white-oak-hunt-now-01.action: If in the early season you find fresh sign and fresh rubs at the tail end of the white oak acorn drop, hunt it now with an aggressive setup, even on an 80 F evening. Don't save it.
m-wth-white-oak-hunt-now-01.why: In big woods deer only stay on white oak acorns for a very short time. The buck may be bedded 60 yards away and get up to feed about 30 minutes before dark. You won't be hunting him there in two weeks anyway, so blowing him out costs little.
people: The Hunting Public crew (Aaron Warbritton et al.)

m-wth-wind-drop-01.action: Hunt the day the wind speed drops, judged against what it has been. Sturgis's examples: after a day or two of 40-50 mph, a fall to 20 is huge; so are 20 down to 8-10 and 50 down to 30. The MSU data put the line at a daily average about 7-8 mph lower than the day before. A rise in wind, or a small change, doesn't matter. If it's still 15-30 mph on the drop, hunt the lee sides.
m-wth-wind-drop-01.why: Deer that have been hunkered down in big wind get up when it eases, even if it's still breezy (Sturgis's 15-point came on October 26, 2007 right after a cold front as the wind dropped, on the quiet side below a windy ridge, chasing does). In the MSU GPS data, change in bedding showed nothing for wind until the average speed dropped about 7-8 mph; then bucks bedded less.

m-wth-wind-region-east-01.action: In the East and Southeast, sustained winds of 15-20 mph will really cut deer movement. On the windy Plains and out West it matters much less; deer there are used to it.
m-wth-wind-region-east-01.why: Deer react to wind that's unusual for where they live. In Montana he's watched deer feed in alfalfa in 50 mph straight-line winds.

m-wth-windy-days-still-go-01.action: Don't skip a hunt just because it's windy (20+ mph). The wind level itself barely changed buck movement. Decide on comfort and safety instead: a box blind or ground blind instead of a climbing stand swaying in the wind.
m-wth-windy-days-still-go-01.why: In the MSU GPS data movement was essentially flat across wind speeds, with a slight bump near no wind and a slight increase above 20 mph, at most a 10-12 yd/hr change. Their earlier Oklahoma study found an uptick only in rare extreme winds (20-30+ mph), too few events to trust.
